0-toolkit/01-notation-and-conventions.title: Notation and conventions
0-toolkit/01-notation-and-conventions.content:
Toolkit · reference page · every row links to the section that develops the notation; this page only collects.
The site writes everything the way Erickson’s Models of Computation (whole book PDF) does, except for the handful of changes listed in §11. Section and result numbers are the book’s: “§3.8” is section 3.8 of both the book and the chapter page. Results in Chapters 1–5 carry the chapter number (Lemma 3.6, Theorem 5.7); in Chapters 7 and 9 they do not, so “Lemma 5” and “Theorem 12” live in Chapter 7 and “Theorem 1” in Chapter 9.
1. Strings































































































notationmeaningwhere\Sigmaan alphabet: a finite set of symbols§1.1a, b, cvariables for symbols§1.1w, x, y, zvariables for strings§1.1\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, 0110explicit symbols and strings, set in monospace§1.1\varepsilonthe empty string, of length 0§1.1a\cdot xthe string with first symbol a and rest x — the small dot puts one symbol in front; usually written ax§1.1w\bullet zconcatenation of two strings — the big dot; usually written wz§1.2\Sigma^*all strings over \Sigma: an infinite set, but every string in it is finite§1.1\lvert w\rvertthe length of w§1.2\#(a,w)the number of a‘s in w: \#(\mathtt{0},\mathtt{0110}) = 2more functionsw^Rreversal: (\mathtt{001})^R = \mathtt{100}″w^nn copies of w: w^0 = \varepsilon, (\mathtt{01})^3 = \mathtt{010101}″w^cbinary complement, every bit flipped: (\mathtt{001})^c = \mathtt{110} — not the complement of a language″w_ithe ith symbol of w, counting from w_1§1.5w[i..j]the substring w_iw_{i+1}\cdots w_j; it is \varepsilon if j<i§1.5w[1..n], w_1w_2\cdots w_nw spelled out, with n = \lvert w\rvert — which may be 1, or even 0§1.5prefix; suffix; substring; subsequencew = px; w = xs; w = xyz (always contiguous); delete symbols anywhere. Proper means “not w itself”: HE is a proper prefix and a proper suffix of HEADACHE§1.5
2. Languages
















































































notationmeaningwhereL, A, B, Clanguages: sets of strings, L\subseteq\Sigma^*§2.1\varnothingthe empty language: no strings at all§2.1\{\varepsilon\}the language whose one string is \varepsilon — not empty§2.1\{w \mid \ldots\}set-builder: all strings w such that …§2.1\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}exponents count copies: n 0s followed by n 1s§2.1A\cup B, A\cap B, A\setminus Bunion, intersection, difference§2.2A\oplus Bsymmetric difference: the strings in exactly one of A and B§2.2\overline{L}complement, always relative to \Sigma^*: \overline{L} = \Sigma^*\setminus L§2.2A\bullet B, ABconcatenation: \{xy \mid x\in A \text{ and } y\in B\}§2.2L^*Kleene star: concatenations of zero or more strings of L; \varnothing^* = \{\varepsilon\}^* = \{\varepsilon\}§2.2L^+Kleene plus: L\bullet L^*, one or more; L^+ = L^* if and only if \varepsilon\in L§2.2A^nA^0 = \{\varepsilon\} and A^n = A\bullet A^{n-1} (the proof of Arden’s rule)§2.2L^R\{w^R \mid w\in L\} (Lemma 4.4)§4.9\textsf{half}(L)\{w \mid ww\in L\} (Lemma 4.5)§4.9


                  
                  Three different "empty" things 
                  
                

\varnothing has no strings, \{\varepsilon\} has one string, and \varepsilon is a string, not a language. In a regular expression, \varepsilon stands for \{\varepsilon\}. They behave differently: \varnothing\bullet L = \varnothing but \{\varepsilon\}\bullet L = L.


3. Regular expressions























































notationmeaningwhere\varnothingthe expression for the empty language§2.3w, any string (also \varepsilon)the expression for \{w\}§2.3S+Tunion — never “one or more”§2.3STconcatenation§2.3S^*Kleene star§2.3precedencethe star first, then concatenation, then +: \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^* is \mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}^*), not (\mathtt{10})^*, and \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}^* is \mathtt{0}+(\mathtt{1}^*)§2.3L(R)the language of R; w matches R if w\in L(R); R and R' are equivalent if L(R) = L(R')§2.3RR^*one or more copies of R — the course’s expressions have no other “plus”§2.4subexpression, sizea subtree of the expression tree; the number of its nodes, invisible concatenations included§2.5
Not part of the syntax: \cap, complement, counters such as \mathtt{0}^n, and the conveniences of programming “regexen” — alternation bars, ?, {2,3}, back-references (§2.4).
4. Finite automata





















































































notationmeaningwhere(\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta)a DFA M: input alphabet, states, start state, accepting states, transition function — in this order everywhere on this site§3.2\delta\colon Q\times\Sigma\to QDFA transitions — total: exactly one edge per state and symbol§3.2\delta^*(q,w)the state reached from q by reading w: \delta^*(q,\varepsilon) = q and \delta^*(q,ax) = \delta^*(\delta(q,a),x)§3.2L(M)\{w \mid \delta^*(s,w)\in A\}; a language is automatic if it is L(M) for some DFA M§3.2drawingsstates are circles; an arrow from nowhere marks the start state; double circles mark accepting states; an edge labeled \mathtt{0},\mathtt{1} stands for two edges§3.2dump statea non-accepting state that loops to itself on every symbol; a drawing may leave it out only if it says so§3.2(p,q)\in Q_1\times Q_2a state of a product DFA: M_1 is in p and M_2 is in q§3.6F, za fooling set; a distinguishing suffix — this F is not the “final states” of other textbooks§3.8x\equiv_L y, [w]no suffix distinguishes x and y; the equivalence class of w§3.9\delta\colon Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\to 2^QNFA transitions: a set of states, possibly empty§4.32^Qthe power set of Q: all 2^{\lvert Q\rvert} subsets§4.1\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)the states reachable from q by zero or more \varepsilon-transitions, q included§4.3NFA acceptance\delta^*(s,w)\cap A\ne\varnothing: some walk from s to an accepting state spells w§4.1a set S\subseteq Q as a statea state of the subset construction; its start state is \{s\}§4.5R(p\to q)the regular expression on the edge from p to q in an expression automaton; \varnothing if there is no edge§4.8
5. Context-free grammars











































































notationmeaningwhereG = (\Sigma, \Gamma, R, S)terminals, nonterminals, production rules, start symbol§5.1a, b, c; A, B, C, S; w, x, y, zterminals; nonterminals; strings over \Sigma\cup\Gamma§5.1A\to\omegaa rule; C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} is two rules§5.1xAz\rightsquigarrow x\omega zone derivation step, applying the rule A\to\omega§5.1x\rightsquigarrow^* zz derives from x in zero or more steps§5.1L(A), L(G)\{x\in\Sigma^* \mid A\rightsquigarrow^* x\}, and L(G) = L(S)§5.1parse tree, leftmost derivationthe tree of rule applications; the derivation that always expands the leftmost nonterminal — exactly one per tree§5.2ambiguoussome string has two parse trees — a property of the grammar; inherently ambiguous: every grammar for the language is ambiguous§5.2nullable, unit ruleA\rightsquigarrow^*\varepsilon; a rule A\to B§5.3, §5.9CNFthe start symbol on no right side; every rule A\to BC or A\to a, except possibly S\to\varepsilon. In the conversion, S' is the new start symbol and T_a\to a protects the terminal a§5.8, §5.9M_A, s_A, t_Athe module of a recursive automaton for A, its start state, its single accepting state§5.7(x, q, \sigma)a recursive automaton’s configuration: unread input, current state, stack of return states (top first)§5.7[q]the nonterminal for state q when a recursive automaton is turned into a grammar (Lemma 5.6)§5.7
6. Turing machines
















































































notationmeaningwhere\Gamma, \squarethe tape alphabet, which contains the blank \square§6.2\Sigma\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\square\}the input alphabet§6.2\textit{start}, \textit{accept}, \textit{reject}the three special states; other states are italic words that say what they do, such as \mathit{seek1}§6.2\delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta)in state p reading a: write b, move by \Delta, enter q; \Delta = -1 is left, \Delta = +1 is right§6.2(q, x, i)a configuration: state, tape contents (trailing blanks not written), head position i\ge0; cell 0 is the left end§6.2\Rightarrow, \Rightarrow^*one step; zero or more steps. Every run starts at (\textit{start}, w, 0)§6.2accepts; rejects; crashes; runs foreverreaches \textit{accept}; reaches \textit{reject}; moves left from cell 0; none of these, ever. Halts means accepts or rejects§6.2missing transitionsgo to \textit{reject} — say so on an exam§6.2— in a transition table’s write columnwrite back the symbol that was read§6.3\mathtt{x}, \mathtt{\#}this site’s marks: a matched symbol; the left end of the tape§6.3\textit{halt}, M(w), M(w)\uparrowthe single halting state of a machine that computes a function; its output; M diverges on w§6.5\Delta = 0a stay-put move — a variant, removed with states Q\times\{0,1\}§6.4\delta(p,a)\subseteq Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}a nondeterministic machine’s options in state p reading a§9.1\Omega = \{1,\dots,r\}, x\in\Omega^*advice symbols and an advice string, one choice per step; r is the largest number of options in any \delta(p,a)§9.5
7. Encodings and named languages
Named languages, functions and the machines in proofs are set in sans-serif. The font carries no meaning; the definition does.









































































































notationmeaningwhere\langle M\ranglethe encoding of the machine M, a string§6.8, §7.4\langle M, w\ranglethe encoding of M together with an input string w§6.8\langle M_1\rangle\langle M_2\rangletwo encodings, one after the other (Theorem 14)§7.10Uthe universal machine: accepts \langle M,w\rangle iff M accepts w, rejects it iff M rejects w§6.8M^R, M^A, M^HM with accept and reject swapped; with every rejection turned into an endless loop; with every rejection turned into acceptance (Lemma 1)§7.3\textsf{Accept}(M), \textsf{Reject}(M)the strings M accepts; the strings it rejects§7.1\textsf{Halt}(M), \textsf{Diverge}(M)\textsf{Accept}(M)\cup\textsf{Reject}(M); everything else, \Sigma^*\setminus\textsf{Halt}(M) — crashes included§7.1\textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Reject}, \textsf{Halt}, \textsf{Diverge}with no argument: languages of pairs, such as \textsf{Halt} = \{\langle M,w\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } w\}§7.9\textsf{SelfAccept}, \textsf{SelfReject}, \textsf{SelfHalt}, \textsf{SelfDiverge}\{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \langle M\rangle\}, and likewise with rejects, halts on, diverges on§7.5, §7.7\textsf{NeverAccept}, \textsf{NeverReject}, \textsf{NeverHalt}, \textsf{NeverDiverge}\{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) = \varnothing\}, and likewise§7.10\textsf{DivergeSame}\{\langle M_1\rangle\langle M_2\rangle \mid \textsf{Diverge}(M_1) = \textsf{Diverge}(M_2)\}§7.10\mathcal{L}, \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L})a property, that is, a set of languages; \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\in\mathcal{L}\}. Also \textsf{RejectIn}, \textsf{HaltIn}, \textsf{DivergeIn}, \textsf{DecideIn}§7.11\textsf{ThisIsSparta}, \textsf{RevAccept}where Rice’s theorem does not apply: a behavior (decidable); self-reference (undecidable, by a reduction)§7.11\textsf{NeverLeft}, \textsf{LeftThree}behaviors: never moves left (decidable); moves left three times in a row (undecidable)§7.13M_wignores its input and runs M on w, so \textsf{Accept}(M_w) is \Sigma^* or \varnothing§7.10M_{\textsf{Accept}}, M_{\textsf{Reject}}, M_{\textsf{Diverge}}accepts every input at once; rejects every input at once; moves right forever§7.11\textsf{SR}, \textsf{DecideL}, \textsf{Wrap}, \textsf{WTF}, …machines in proofs; every machine in a reduction gets its own name§7.5–§7.11\textsf{half}, \textsf{swap}, \textsf{rev}functions on strings and on expressionsChapters 1, 2, 4\textsf{True}, \textsf{False}truth values


                  
                   \textsf{Accept}(M) is not \textsf{Accept}
                  
                

\textsf{Accept}(M) is a set of strings — the inputs that one machine M accepts. \textsf{Accept} is a set of encodings \langle M, w\rangle — every machine paired with every input it accepts. The first can be any acceptable language; the second is one particular undecidable language.


8. Complexity classes


















































notationmeaningwhereO, \Omega, \Thetaupper, lower and tight asymptotic bounds\textsf{TIME}(f(n)), \textsf{NTIME}(f(n))the languages decided in O(f(n)) time by a deterministic, resp. nondeterministic, multi-tape Turing machine§9.3\textsf{SPACE}(f(n)), \textsf{NSPACE}(f(n))the same, counting tape cells instead of steps§9.3\textsf{P}, \textsf{NP}\bigcup_k\textsf{TIME}(n^k) and \bigcup_k\textsf{NTIME}(n^k)§9.3verifier, certificatethe deterministic machine and the advice string in the definition of \textsf{NP}§9.6\textsf{SAT}the satisfiable boolean formulas§9.6NP-hard, NP-completeevery language in \textsf{NP} reduces to it in polynomial time; NP-hard and in \textsf{NP}§9.6Q_{t,i,q}, T_{t,i,a}, \Phi_wthe Cook–Levin variables (“after t steps, state q with the head on cell i”; “cell i holds a”) and the formula built from them§9.6
9. Writing it by hand






































































printedby handwhy\varepsilona clear epsilon — never \in, never ea missing or extra \varepsilon is the typical one-mistake deduction\varnothing and \{\varepsilon\}a slashed circle for the empty language; braces around \varepsilon for the one-string languagethey are different languages (§2)\mathtt{0}, 0110plain symbols; keep a, b, c and w, x, y, z for variablesa reader must tell explicit strings from variables\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}+ on the line, and parentheses whenever in doubta raised ^+ reads as Kleene plus; redundant parentheses are never wrong\rightsquigarrowa wavy arrow, or anything visibly different from \to\to writes a rule, \rightsquigarrow a derivation stepa DFAan arrow into the start state, double circles, every edge labeled, and the sentence “missing transitions go to a dump state” if any are missingthese are the “complete description” points of the DFA rubricstate namesshort words for what the state remembers: \mathit{last1}, \mathit{even}, (\mathit{even},\mathit{last1})mnemonic names are 2 of the 10 points\squarea small squarean empty cell in a transition table looks like a missing transition\langle M\rangle, \langle M, w\rangleangle bracketsM is a machine; \langle M\rangle is a string\textsf{Halt}, \textsf{SelfReject}the capitalized name; define a new one in set-builder formthe definition is what a grader checks\mathcal{L}a script L, or any letter, explicitly defined as a set of languagesRice’s theorem is about a set of languages: say which\overline{L}a bar over the letter — or \Sigma^*\setminus L, which cannot be misread
General rules for the write-up itself — no “clearly”, every machine named, any result from lecture cited by name — are on how exams are graded.
10. Same thing, different names


































































































































this sitealso callednoteacceptablerecognizable, semi-decidable, semi-computable, listable, recursively enumerable (r.e.)the book says recognizable in Chapter 6 and acceptable from Chapter 7 ondecidablecomputable, recursive§7.1M accepts LM recognizes L§6.2M decides LM is a decider for L§6.2co-acceptable”its complement is acceptable”this site’s word, not the book’s (§7.3)automaticregularthe same class, by Kleene’s theorem; the book uses both words (§3.7)DFAdeterministic finite(-state) automaton, finite-state machineaccepting states A, start state sfinal states F, initial state q_0other textbooks, which also order the tuple differentlydump statetrash state (the course rubrics), dead state, sink\varepsilon\lambda or \Lambdasome other textbooks\varepsilon-transition\varepsilon-move; “epsilon-transition” in this site’s headings\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)\varepsilon-closure of qother textbookssubset constructionpowerset construction, determinization§4.5Thompson’s algorithmThompson’s construction§4.6state eliminationMcNaughton and Yamada’s algorithmthe book’s attribution (§4.8)Moore’s algorithmtable-filling algorithm§3.10x\equiv_L yMyhill–Nerode (or Nerode) equivalence§3.9Kleene starKleene closurenonterminalnon-terminal (the book’s usual spelling), variable§5.1production rulerule, production§5.1recursive automaton—most other textbooks use pushdown automata instead: a different machine for the same languages (§5.7)runs foreverdiverges, loops; M(w)\uparrowa crash also puts the input in \textsf{Diverge}(M)advice stringcertificatefor the verifier in the definition of \textsf{NP} (§9.6)\textsf{Halt}the halting problemconcept page
11. Where this site departs from the book
The changes are small, but each one shows up when you put a chapter page next to the book.

The left-end marker. The Turing machine for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\} marks the left end of the tape with \mathtt{\#}; the book’s machine writes a dollar sign. The site’s machine also checks the format of the input first (extra states \mathit{block1}, \mathit{block2}, \mathit{block3}, \mathit{rewind}, \mathit{mark0}), because the book’s machine, which starts matching at once, also accepts strings such as 001010 (see the trap in §6.3).
The shift machine’s states are \mathit{hold0} and \mathit{hold1}; the book calls them 0 and 1 (§6.5).
Chomsky normal form. The nonterminals that protect terminals are T_a\to a; the book calls them A_a. The final grammar of the running example keeps the book’s names E\to\mathtt{0} and F\to\mathtt{1} (§5.9).
Grammars as tuples. G = (\Sigma,\Gamma,R,S) is this site’s shorthand; the book lists the four parts without a tuple (§5.1).
The DFA tuple is always (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) here; the book’s order varies from section to section. On an exam, name each component (“start state s, accepting states A”) and the order stops mattering.
One word for acceptable. The site says acceptable throughout, where the book’s Chapter 6 says recognizable, and it adds the word co-acceptable (§7.3).
Plainer section titles. Numbers always match the book, but some titles are descriptive where the book’s are jokes or generic: §7.2 “Lo, I Have Become Death, Stealer of Pie” is “Decidable without knowing the algorithm”, and §3.3 “Another Example” is “Proving a DFA correct”.
Chapter 9. The site defines \textsf{P} and \textsf{NP} explicitly (the book leaves them implicit), states the rejection half of the advice view with an explicit length t, and numbers the Cook–Levin tableau’s cells 0,\dots,N+2, with the input starting at cell 1 between two empty sentinel cells — unlike a Turing machine’s tape in Chapter 6, which starts at cell 0 (§9.6).

Related: proof templates · the big picture · how exams are graded · strings · languages · Turing machines
Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapters 1–9, as summarized on the chapter pages of this site, which every row links. The book’s own wording — recognizable in Chapter 6 and acceptable in Chapter 7, its synonym lists, the order of the DFA tuple, the names A_a, the dollar sign, 0 and 1, the attribution of state elimination, and the section titles — was checked against the chapter PDFs. The examples are the chapter pages’ own, checked there.

0-toolkit/02-proof-templates.title: Proof templates
0-toolkit/02-proof-templates.content:
Toolkit · reference page · each template is copied from the section linked below it; the rubric lines paraphrase the course’s standard rubrics (how exams are graded).


                  
                  How to use a template on the exam 
                  
                


Recognize the problem type. The table at the end maps each type to its template, its rubric and a worked problem.
Write the boilerplate first, word for word, with several blank lines in every case.
Fill in the claim and the hypothesis — or the set F, the names of the machines, the states of M' — in full, with variable names that do not clash.
Only then think about the real work (the inductive step, the suffix z, the machine M'), and write it into the gaps.
Reread every line for its reason: a definition, the hypothesis, a lemma, arithmetic. Never “clearly”.

The frame alone earns points: on the induction rubric, an arbitrary string, an explicit strong hypothesis and cases that cover every string are 5 of the 10 points, before any algebra. Templates marked assembled here have no boilerplate on their chapter page; they are built from that section’s recipe and worked examples, in its words where possible.


Chapter 1 string induction · Chapter 2 expression or grammar write-up, structural induction · Chapter 3 DFA correctness, describing a DFA, product construction, fooling set, closure · Chapter 4 language transformation · Chapter 5 what a grammar generates · Chapter 6 Turing machine · Chapter 7 diagonalization, reduction, Rice, dovetailing, Lemma 5
1. Induction on strings
Use it for any claim about every string — the Midterm 1 problem on a newly defined recursive string function, and identities such as (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R.


                  
                  Template — induction on strings 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string. 
Assume, for every string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, that [the claim holds for x]. 
There are two cases to consider. 
Case w = \varepsilon. … Therefore [the claim holds for w]. 
Case w = ax for some symbol a and string x. The induction hypothesis implies that [the claim holds for x]. … Therefore [the claim holds for w]. 
In both cases, [the claim holds for w]. \blacksquare


Variants (§1.4): peel the last symbol, w = xa; split w = a or w = u\bullet v with u, v non-empty (two base cases); or follow a definition with more cases, such as w = abx (base cases \varepsilon and every single symbol). If the hypothesis is applied with other values of the other arguments, it must say “for all” of them.
Source §1.3 · rubric induction, out of 10: 1 arbitrary object · 2 explicit strong hypothesis · 2 exhaustive cases · 1 base cases · 2 correct use of the hypothesis · 2 other details (details) · worked sorting a string
2. Writing up a regular expression or a grammar
Use it for “give a regular expression for L” (half of the Midterm 1 DFA problem) and “give a context-free grammar for L” (half of the non-regularity problem). Assembled here from the worked examples of §2.3 and §5.4, which all have this shape.


                  
                  Template — writing up a regular expression or a grammar 
                  
                

Idea. [how a typical string of L decomposes: into blocks that a star can repeat; by nesting; at the first point where a count balances; or by cases] 
Answer: [the expression — or the rules, one line per nonterminal] 
In English: [what each piece of the expression stands for — or, for a grammar, a description of the language of every nonterminal that makes sense on its own] 
Test: [\varepsilon and the shortest strings of L] are generated; [short strings outside L] are not.


Source §2.3 (Examples 1 and 2), §5.4 (Examples 1 and 2) · rubric regular expressions and grammars: 2 syntax · 8 correctness on exams, with deductions twice the homework ones — 2 for one mistake (often \varepsilon), 4 for a few wrong strings, all 8 for infinitely many; \varnothing or \Sigma^* earns nothing; ambiguity costs nothing; homework also needs the English (details) · worked 01 exactly twice (b), fooling set and grammar (b)
3. Induction on regular expressions
Use it for any claim about every regular expression — and, through an expression that represents it, about every regular language (§2.7).


                  
                  Template — induction on regular expressions 
                  
                

Let R be an arbitrary regular expression. 
Assume that every proper subexpression of R [has the property]. 
There are five cases to consider. 
Case R = \varnothing. … Therefore R [has the property]. 
Case R is a single string w (possibly \varepsilon). … Therefore R [has the property]. 
Case R = S+T for some regular expressions S and T. The induction hypothesis implies that S and T [have the property]. … 
Case R = ST for some regular expressions S and T. The induction hypothesis implies that S and T [have the property]. … 
Case R = S^* for some regular expression S. The induction hypothesis implies that S [has the property]. … 
In all five cases, R [has the property]. \blacksquare


Notes. Inducting on the size of R gives the same five cases. In the case R = S^* the hypothesis covers S, not S^*. If a case gets stuck, strengthen the claim, as in Lemma 2.5.
Source §2.6 · rubric induction (details) · worked the proof of Lemma 2.4 in §2.6
4. Proving a DFA correct
Use it for “prove that your DFA accepts exactly L”. Midterm-1-style DFA problems need no proof, but the meanings of step 1 are exactly what mnemonic state names should convey.


                  
                  Template — proving L(M) = L for a DFA
                  
                


Give each state q a meaning P_q, and claim: ”\delta^*(s,w) = q if and only if w has property P_q.”
Induct on w. Either peel the first symbol (w = ax) — then state the claim for every possible start state, as in §3.3 — or peel the last symbol (w = xa) and use \delta^*(s,xa) = \delta(\delta^*(s,x),a), which needs the claim only from s.
Conclude: w\in L(M) \iff \delta^*(s,w)\in A \iff w has one of the accepting properties \iff w\in L.



Source §3.3 · rubric induction (details) · worked the odd-number-of-1s proof in §3.3; state meanings in 01 exactly twice (a)
5. Describing a DFA
Use it for “give a DFA for L; no proof required” — with a regular expression for the same language, one of the five Midterm 1 problems. Assembled here from §3.2, §3.5 and the DFA rubric.


                  
                  Template — describing a DFA 
                  
                

[A drawing: an arrow from nowhere into the start state, double circles on the accepting states, a label on every edge — or, in text, the start state, the accepting states and the complete transition table.] 
“All missing transitions go to a dump state.” [Only if some are missing.] 
States: [for each state, a mnemonic name and what it remembers about the input read so far — e.g. ”\mathit{last1}: no 11 yet, and the last symbol read was 1”].


Source §3.2 (a total transition function; the dump state), §3.5 (name each state after what it remembers) · rubric DFAs: 2 unambiguous, complete description · 6 correctness (on exams) · 2 mnemonic state names; an NFA where a DFA was asked earns half credit (details) · worked 01 exactly twice (a)
6. Writing up a product construction
Use it for a DFA for ”L_1 and L_2”, ”L_1 or L_2”, ”L_1 but not L_2” — any boolean combination of languages that have simple DFAs.


                  
                  Template — writing up a product construction 
                  
                

Let M_1 = (\Sigma, Q_1, s_1, A_1, \delta_1) be a DFA for L_1: [its states and what each means, start, accepting states, transitions — or a drawing]. 
Let M_2 = (\Sigma, Q_2, s_2, A_2, \delta_2) be a DFA for L_2: [likewise]. 
Define M := (\Sigma,\ Q_1\times Q_2,\ (s_1,s_2),\ A,\ \delta) with \delta((p,q),a) := (\delta_1(p,a),\delta_2(q,a)), 
and with A := [the accepting pairs from the table]. 
By Lemma 3.1, M accepts w iff [the boolean combination], so L(M) = [the target language].


Source §3.6 (the definition, the table of accepting sets, Lemma 3.1, how it is graded); the template is the one on product construction · rubric DFAs — for a product, the complete description defines each factor completely, then the product’s states, start state, transitions and accepting states (details) · worked a product, written formally
7. Fooling-set proof
Use it for “prove that L is not regular” — on Midterm 1, paired with a grammar for the same language.


                  
                  Template — fooling-set proof (as in Lemma 3.6) 
                  
                

Let F =  [an explicit infinite set, e.g. \mathtt{0}^*]. 
Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F. 
The definition of F implies x =  […] and y =  […] for some integers i\ne j. 
Let z =  [a suffix that may depend on i and j]. 
Then xz =  […] \in L, because […]. 
And yz =  […] \notin L, because […]. 
So z distinguishes x and y. We conclude that F is a fooling set for L. 
Because F is infinite, L cannot be regular. \blacksquare


Choosing F. A simple language with one star and no union — \mathtt{0}^*, \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}, (\mathtt{01})^* — or L itself; the standard cases are tabulated in §3.8. Keep i\ne j: "i<j" needs “without loss of generality” and a symmetric argument.
Source §3.8 · rubric fooling sets: 4 an explicit infinite set that really is a fooling set (a finite set earns nothing) · 2 explicit suffix z · 2 one of xz, yz in L · 2 the other not (details) · worked fooling set and grammar (a)
8. Non-regularity by closure
Use it for a short non-regularity proof when the problem does not prescribe a method, and for true/false justifications. Assembled here from “the closure alternative” in §3.8.


                  
                  Template — non-regularity by closure 
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that L is regular. 
The language R =  [e.g. \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*] is regular, because [it is described by a regular expression]. 
Regular languages are closed under [intersection, complement, …], so L' =  [e.g. L\cap R] is regular too. 
But L' =  [a language known to be non-regular, e.g. \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}], which is not regular by [Lemma 3.6, or a fooling set]. 
This contradiction shows that L is not regular. \blacksquare


Only in this direction: if L\cap R turns out to be regular, nothing follows about L.
Source §3.8, closure properties · rubric none of its own — a problem that asks for a fooling set wants a fooling set · worked the closure alternative in fooling set and grammar
9. Language transformation
Use it for “prove that f(L) is regular for every regular language L” — the two-part Midterm 1 problem.


                  
                  Template — regular language transformation 
                  
                

Let M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) be a DFA that accepts L. 
We construct an NFA M' = (\Sigma, Q', s', A', \delta') with \varepsilon-transitions that accepts [the new language]. 
In English: M' remembers [each component of its state, and what it means], guesses [what, and when], and accepts when […]. 
Formally: Q' =  […], s' =  […], A' =  […], 
\delta'(q', a) =  […] for every state q' and every symbol a, 
\delta'(q', \varepsilon) =  […] for every state q' (write \varnothing where there are none). 
Why: M' can be in state […] after reading x if and only if […]; so it accepts exactly [the new language].


Which kind of language? For “strings whose transform is in L”, \{w \mid f(w)\in L\}, usually a DFA that simulates M on f(w) while reading w. For “transforms of strings in L”, \{f(w) \mid w\in L\}, usually an NFA that simulates M on a guessed preimage, with \varepsilon-transitions guessing the symbols that f deleted.
Source §4.9 (Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5), where this template is copied from; a shorter version is on language transformations · rubric transformations: 2 formal, complete description of M' built from an arbitrary DFA M (say DFA or NFA; list the \varepsilon-transitions) · 2 English explanation of the states and accepting states · 6 correctness — 1 states, 1 start state, 1 accepting states, 3 transitions; test L = \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^*, \Sigma^* (details) · worked insert and delete a 1
10. Proving what a grammar generates
Use it for “prove that G generates exactly L” — and for convincing yourself that a grammar you designed is right.


                  
                  Template — proving L(G) = L
                  
                


State the language of every nonterminal. If nonterminals use each other, the claims must be proved together, in one induction (mutual induction, §5.3).
L\subseteq L(G). Let w\in L be arbitrary; assume every shorter string of L is generated (or induct on a parameter, like n in Lemma 5.1). Split w into pieces that match the right side of one rule, apply the hypothesis to the pieces, and assemble a derivation S\rightsquigarrow\omega\rightsquigarrow^* w.
L(G)\subseteq L. Let w\in L(G) be arbitrary and fix a derivation of w; assume every shorter generated string is in L. Write one case per rule the derivation can start with; in each case w splits into pieces derived from the symbols of the right side, the hypothesis applies to each piece, and the pieces together satisfy the definition of L.
If the grammar has \varepsilon-rules, fix a shortest derivation of w (§5.3, “Careful with those epsilons”), or induct on the length of the derivation instead of the string.



Source §5.3 (Lemmas 5.1–5.4; careful with those epsilons; mutual induction) · rubric two inductions, each graded like an induction (details) · worked a grammar proof
11. Describing a Turing machine
Chapter 6 gives a recipe rather than a boilerplate. A design answer should contain:

the algorithm in English, phase by phase — scan, mark, walk back;
a transition table or diagram that implements exactly that description, with mnemonic state names and a one-line meaning for every state;
the sentence “missing transitions reject”;
a trace on \varepsilon, on a short string in the language, and on a near-miss.

Source §6.3 (the design recipe and “Writing a Turing machine on an exam”) · rubric none of its own; the DFA rubric’s demands — a complete, unambiguous description and mnemonic names — are the guide · worked the copy language
12. Undecidability by diagonalization
Use it for self-referential languages — defined by what a machine does with its own encoding — when no known undecidable language is easier to reduce from.


                  
                  Template — undecidability by diagonalization 
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{Dec} decides L. 
Build a new machine \textsf{Wrap} from \textsf{Dec}: [swap \textsf{Dec}‘s accept and reject states / redirect its accepting transitions to a looping state / …]. 
Then for every Turing machine M: \textsf{Wrap} [accepts, or halts on] \langle M\rangle if and only if M [does not …] \langle M\rangle. 
In particular, take M = \textsf{Wrap}. 
If \textsf{Wrap} [accepts] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then by the line above \textsf{Wrap} does not [accept] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle — a contradiction. 
If \textsf{Wrap} does not [accept] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then by the line above \textsf{Wrap} [accepts] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle — a contradiction. 
So \textsf{Dec} does not exist, and L is undecidable. \blacksquare


Against an acceptor (to prove L not acceptable, as in Theorem 9): assume only that \textsf{Dec} accepts L, turn its rejections into endless loops (Lemma 1), and derive ”\textsf{Wrap} halts on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle if and only if it diverges on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle”.
Source §7.7 (the template, Theorems 7–9), §7.5 (Theorem 6, the model argument) · rubric diagonalization: 4 wrapper machine · 6 contradiction, 3 per case (details) · worked the proof of Theorem 6 in §7.5; a doubled input on diagonalization
13. Undecidability by reduction
Use it for “prove that L is undecidable” when L is not self-referential: reduce from \textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Halt}, or any language already known to be undecidable.


                  
                  Template — undecidability by reduction from \textsf{Accept}
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{DecideL} decides L. 
Consider the following machine \textsf{DecideAccept}. Given \langle M, w\rangle, it writes the encoding \langle M'\rangle of the machine 
\quad M'(x): [for example: ignore x; run M on w; then …] 
and then runs \textsf{DecideL} on \langle M'\rangle and returns its answer. 
\Rightarrow Suppose M accepts w. Then M' […], so \langle M'\rangle\in L. So \textsf{DecideL} accepts \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts \langle M, w\rangle. 
\Leftarrow Suppose M does not accept w — it rejects or diverges. Then M' […], so \langle M'\rangle\notin L. So \textsf{DecideL} rejects \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects \langle M, w\rangle. 
In both cases \textsf{DecideAccept} is correct, and it always halts. So \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept}, which is impossible. 
We conclude that \textsf{DecideL} does not exist: L is undecidable. \blacksquare


Opposite answers. If \langle M'\rangle\in L exactly when M does not accept w, let \textsf{DecideAccept} return the opposite of \textsf{DecideL}‘s answer, as in the proof of Theorem 13 (§7.10).
Source §7.9 · rubric reduction: 4 the reduction (the new decider and M', in the right direction) · 3 for each direction (details) · worked AtLeastTwo (a); Theorem 13 in §7.10
14. Undecidability by Rice’s theorem
Use it for \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ has some property}\} — a property of the language M accepts, not of M or of its behavior. Assembled here from the recipe “Using Rice’s theorem” in §7.11.


                  
                  Template — undecidability by Rice's theorem 
                  
                

Let \mathcal{L} :=  [an explicit set of languages], so that the language in question is \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) = \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\in\mathcal{L}\}. [Check: two machines with the same language are both in it or both out.] 
Let Y :=  [a concrete machine, e.g. M_{\textsf{Accept}}]. Then \textsf{Accept}(Y) =  […] \in\mathcal{L}, because […]. 
Let N :=  [a concrete machine, e.g. M_{\textsf{Reject}}]. Then \textsf{Accept}(N) =  […] \notin\mathcal{L}, because […]. 
By Rice’s theorem, \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is undecidable. \blacksquare


Variants. If membership depends on \textsf{Reject}(M), \textsf{Halt}(M) or \textsf{Diverge}(M), or on the language M decides, use \textsf{RejectIn}, \textsf{HaltIn}, \textsf{DivergeIn} or \textsf{DecideIn} throughout, and describe Y and N by that language. Not for behavior (\textsf{ThisIsSparta} is decidable), self-reference (\textsf{RevAccept} needs a reduction) or trivial properties — and Rice’s theorem never proves “not acceptable”.
Source §7.11 (the recipe, Corollary 15, the variants) · rubric Rice: 4 a machine whose language has the property · 4 a machine whose language does not · 2 details, including the right variant of the theorem (details) · worked AtLeastTwo (b); the witnesses of Corollary 15 in §7.11
15. Acceptable by dovetailing
Use it for “prove that L is acceptable” when membership of \langle M\rangle is witnessed by finitely many accepting runs of M — "\textsf{Accept}(M)\ne\varnothing", ”M accepts at least two strings”. Assembled here from §7.10 and §9.5.


                  
                  Template — acceptable by dovetailing 
                  
                

The following machine accepts L. Given \langle M\rangle [if the input encodes no machine, reject]: 
for t = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, run M for t steps on each of the first t strings of \Sigma^* [in shortlex order], and accept as soon as [the runs so far show membership, e.g. two different strings have been accepted]. 
If \langle M\rangle\in L: [the witnesses x_1,\dots,x_k] are each accepted within some s steps, so in round t =  [the largest of s and the positions of x_1,\dots,x_k] all of them run long enough, and the machine accepts. 
If \langle M\rangle\notin L: no round ever [shows membership], so the machine never accepts — it runs forever, which an acceptor may do. \blacksquare


Why not one string at a time? If M runs forever on the first string tried, the search never reaches the others. Simpler cases need no dovetailing: \textsf{SelfAccept} is accepted by running U on \langle M, \langle M\rangle\rangle (Theorem 10).
Source §7.10 (an acceptor for the complement of \textsf{NeverAccept}), §9.5 (dovetailing) · rubric none of its own · worked AtLeastTwo (d)
16. Not acceptable, by Lemma 5
Use it for “prove that L is not acceptable” when its complement is acceptable but undecidable — \textsf{NeverAccept}, \textsf{Diverge}, the complement of \textsf{SelfAccept}. Assembled here from Lemma 5 and its consequence in §7.3.


                  
                  Template — not acceptable, by Lemma 5 
                  
                

The complement \overline{L} = \Sigma^*\setminus L is acceptable: [a machine that accepts it — run U, or dovetail]. 
\overline{L} is undecidable: [by diagonalization, a reduction or Rice’s theorem — or because L is undecidable, and decidable languages are closed under complement]. 
If L were acceptable too, the acceptable language \overline{L} would have an acceptable complement, so it would be decidable by Lemma 5 — a contradiction. 
So L is not acceptable. \blacksquare


Strings that encode no machine form a decidable set; counting them in L or in \overline{L} changes nothing. Other routes: diagonalization against an acceptor (Theorem 9), or Lemma 17 for a property that is not monotone (§7.12).
Source §7.3 · rubric none of its own · worked AtLeastTwo (d); \textsf{NeverAccept} in §7.10

0-toolkit/03-the-big-picture.title: The big picture
0-toolkit/03-the-big-picture.content:
Toolkit · all nine chapters on one page · every row links to the section that proves it; this page only collects.


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

Every language in the course sits in one of five nested regions. Regular languages are the ones a single left-to-right pass with a fixed amount of memory can decide; regular expressions, DFAs and NFAs describe exactly them. Context-free languages add unbounded nesting: grammars, or NFAs that call each other like recursive subroutines. Decidable languages are the ones some algorithm decides — a Turing machine that halts on every input. Acceptable languages are the ones whose members an algorithm can confirm: a Turing machine accepts exactly them and may run forever on everything else. Every inclusion is strict, and each boundary has its own tool for proving that a language lies outside it.


1. Five nested classes

five nested rounded rectangles: regular inside context-free inside decidable inside acceptable inside all languages, each with example languagesall languagesnot acceptable: Theorem 9 · Lemma 5 · Lemma 17SelfDiverge, NeverAccept, Diverge, {⟨M⟩ : Accept(M) is finite}acceptable  Turing machinesundecidable: diagonalization · reduction · RiceHalt, Accept, SelfReject, SelfAccept, Post's correspondence problemdecidable  Turing machines that halt on every inputnot context-free: beyond this course{0n1n0n}, {0p : p prime}, {w#w}context-free  grammars, recursive automatanot regular: an infinite fooling set{0n1n}, palindromes, balanced parentheses, #(0, w) = #(1, w)regular  regular expressions, DFAs, NFAsevery finite language, (0+1)*00, binary multiples of 5Five nested classes. Each band holds languages that belong to its class but not to the class inside it; the first language of each band (in red) is the standard witness that the inclusion is strict. The note at the right of a band names the tools that prove a language lies outside the inner class. The models that define each class are next to its name.

2. Equivalent models
Each class has several descriptions that are interchangeable, because each converts into the others by an algorithm.

Other names: acceptable = recognizable = semi-decidable = recursively enumerable; decidable = computable = recursive. The Church–Turing thesis — a claim about the world, not a theorem — says that the last two rows capture every algorithm, so “decidable” means “some program in any language decides it”.
3. The language zoo
Each language is listed under the smallest class that contains it; the last column says why it is not in the class inside. † marks a standard fact that the book does not prove.

4. Closure at a glance
“Yes” means: for every L, L' in the class, the result is in the class. “No” means some languages of the class give a result outside it. Constructions, counterexamples and the facts the book leaves unproved: closure-properties.

The standard witnesses for the “no” entries: the context-free languages \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{0}^j \mid i\ge1, j\ge0\} and \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{0}^j \mid i\ge0, j\ge1\} intersect in \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge1\} (§5.6), and De Morgan turns that into a failure of complement; \textsf{Halt} is acceptable but its complement is not (Lemma 5); and erasing the \#s from the decidable language \{\langle M,w\rangle\#^t \mid M \text{ halts on } w \text{ within } t \text{ steps}\} leaves \textsf{Halt}.
5. How to prove that a language is, or is not, in a class






























classto prove L is in itto prove L is not in itregulara regular expression; a DFA or an NFA; or closure — build L from regular languages by finitely many closed operations (§3.7, transformations)an infinite fooling set (§3.8; by Myhill–Nerode one always exists); or closure backwards — if \overline{L} or L\cap R with R regular is known to be non-regular, so is Lcontext-freea grammar, with the language of every nonterminal described (§5.4); a recursive automaton (§5.7); closure under \cup, concatenation, ^*, reversal and \cap regularbeyond this course: know that \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\} is not context-free; then if L\cap R with R regular is that language, L is not context-free eitherdecidablean algorithm that halts on every input — a Turing machine, or pseudocode by the Church–Turing thesis; L and \overline{L} both acceptable (Lemma 5); closure (Lemma 2)diagonalization (§7.5); a reduction from a known undecidable language (§7.9); Rice’s theorem for a property of \textsf{Accept}(M) (§7.11); Corollary 3acceptablea machine that accepts exactly L and may run forever elsewhere: simulate with U, dovetail over inputs and step counts, or guess nondeterministically (Theorem 1 of Chapter 9); closure under \cup and \cap (Lemma 4)L undecidable but \overline{L} acceptable (Lemma 5); a diagonal argument (Theorem 9); L = \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) for a property \mathcal{L} that is not monotone (Lemma 17) — in general, not monotone, compact and finitely acceptable (RMMS, §7.12)
Write-ups for each of these proofs, with the boilerplate: proof templates.
6. Placing a new language


                  
                  Recipe — four questions, in order (rules of thumb, then a proof) 
                  
                


One pass with fixed memory? If a left-to-right loop with finitely many finite-valued variables decides L, give a DFA, NFA or regular expression. If every algorithm you can think of keeps an unbounded count or an unbounded prefix, that quantity suggests an infinite fooling set.
Is the unbounded memory a stack? Nested matching — \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n, parentheses, palindromes, counts that go up and come back down — suggests a grammar. Comparing a string with a copy of itself, or three blocks with each other (w\mathtt{\#}w, \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n), is out of reach of grammars, but a Turing machine decides it.
Is it a question about machines? If membership of \langle M\rangle depends only on \textsf{Accept}(M) and the property is non-trivial, Rice’s theorem makes it undecidable. If it asks about a bounded run (exactly 300 steps), or about a behavior that confines the machine to finitely many configurations (never moving left), simulate: it is decidable. Otherwise look for a reduction from \textsf{Accept} or \textsf{Halt}, usually with the machine M_w that ignores its input and runs M on w.
Can a “yes” be confirmed in finite time? If every member has a certificate that simulation, dovetailing or guessing eventually finds — a step at which M accepts, a PCP solution — L is acceptable. If only the “no” answers have certificates, \overline{L} is acceptable, and an undecidable L is then not acceptable (Lemma 5).



7. Where running time fits


                  
                  P and NP inside the picture 
                  
                

Chapter 9 measures time on multi-tape Turing machines: \textsf{P} is the class of languages decided in polynomial time, \textsf{NP} the class decided in polynomial time by nondeterministic machines. Then
\text{regular}\ \subsetneq\ \text{context-free}\ \subsetneq\ \textsf{P}\ \subseteq\ \textsf{NP}\ \subseteq\ \text{decidable}.
Dynamic programming decides every context-free language in polynomial time (§5.8), \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\} takes O(n^2) steps (§6.3), and Theorem 1 of Chapter 9 simulates a nondeterministic decider deterministically in exponential time. Whether \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP} is open; the Cook–Levin theorem reduces the question to the single language \textsf{SAT} (§9.6).


8. Traps


                  
                  The mistakes that cost points on true/false questions 
                  
                


A subset or a superset of a regular language need not be regular: \varnothing\subseteq\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}\subseteq\Sigma^*. No class is closed under taking subsets.
Infinite unions are not closed operations. Every language is the union of its one-string subsets, and each of those is regular. Closure covers finitely many operations.
Every finite language is regular, however it is described: \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\le374\} is regular. And every finite language is decidable, even when nobody knows which strings it contains (§7.2).
Closure arguments run one way. If L\cap R is not regular for a regular R, then L is not regular; if L\cap R or L\cup L' is regular, nothing follows: \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}\cup\overline{\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}} = \Sigma^*.
A grammar does not prove that L is not regular — every regular language has a grammar. Non-regularity needs a fooling set or closure.
Context-free ∩ context-free can fail; context-free ∩ regular cannot. So L\setminus R is context-free whenever L is context-free and R is regular.
Rice’s theorem applies only to properties of \textsf{Accept}(M) — or of \textsf{Reject}(M), \textsf{Halt}(M), \textsf{Diverge}(M) with the matching variant. Not to behavior: \textsf{ThisIsSparta} and ”M has 374 states” are decidable, and \textsf{LeftThree} is undecidable only by a reduction. Not to self-reference (\textsf{RevAccept}). Not to trivial properties. And it proves undecidability, never unacceptability.
Undecidable is not unacceptable: \textsf{Halt} is acceptable. Unacceptability needs Lemma 5, a diagonal argument or Lemma 17.
Swapping accept and reject complements a DFA and a deterministic decider — not an NFA, not a nondeterministic Turing machine, and not a machine that may run forever.
The class belongs to the language, not to its description. A Turing machine for (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00} does not make that language non-regular; “the smallest class” is what a question asks about. And counting arguments name no language: they show that languages outside a class exist, never that a given one is outside.

0-toolkit/04-review-regular-and-context-.content:
Scope: Chapters 1–5, the material of Midterm 1 (Mon Sep 28), which the final exam (Fri Dec 11, 8–11 am) covers again. Each section links to the chapter page that proves its claims; this page only collects. How the classes fit together: the big picture.


                  
                  How to use this page 
                  
                

Read one section, close the page, and rewrite its definitions and formulas from memory; then compare. Whatever you missed goes on your cheat sheet (§9) or into tomorrow’s practice. Then work the five problem types of §1 on paper, under time.


1. The exam and how to attack each problem
The Midterm 1 practice exams have five problems in 120 minutes, one of each type below. Any result from lecture, the lecture notes, labs or homework solutions may be cited without proof. Words like “clearly”, “trivial” and “obviously” draw scrutiny, and an ambiguous answer is read unfavorably. Full rubrics: how exams are graded.


                  
                  Type 1 — true or false, with a one-sentence justification (10 parts) 
                  
                


Test the claim on tiny cases before deciding: \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \Sigma^*, \mathtt{0}^*, \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}, strings of length 0, 1 and 2.
True needs a reason that covers every case: name the closure property, construction or theorem. False needs one concrete counterexample.
Practice: §7 below, the traps in §8, and the “On the exams” box at the end of each chapter page.





                  
                  Type 2 — regular language transformations (two parts) 
                  
                


Which direction? For \{w \mid f(w)\in L\}, read w and simulate M on f(w) — often a DFA. For \{f(w) \mid w\in L\}, read the output and guess a preimage while simulating M on it — an NFA, with \varepsilon-transitions for symbols that f deletes.
Start from an arbitrary DFA M = (\Sigma,Q,s,A,\delta) for L. Describe M' in English (what each component of a state remembers, what it guesses, when it accepts) and formally: Q', s', A', and \delta'(q,a), \delta'(q,\varepsilon) in every case.
Check the edge cases L = \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^*, \Sigma^*.
Graded: 2 for a formal, complete description (say DFA or NFA, with or without \varepsilon-transitions) + 2 for the English explanation + 6 for correctness (1 states, 1 start, 1 accepting states, 3 transitions).
Templates: language transformation, §4.9 · model answer: Two language transformations · practice: Chapter 4 practice.





                  
                  Type 3 — induction on a recursively defined string function 
                  
                


Write the boilerplate first: an arbitrary string; a hypothesis for every shorter string, quantified over every other argument the proof changes; one case per case of the definition.
Induct on the argument the function takes apart, and peel what the definition peels (two symbols for a function defined on w = abx).
Justify every equation: a definition, the hypothesis (and why the string is shorter), a lemma, or arithmetic. If a case gets stuck, prove a small lemma first or strengthen the claim.
Graded: 1 arbitrary object + 2 explicit strong hypothesis + 2 exhaustive cases + 1 base cases + 2 correct use of the hypothesis + 2 other details.
Templates: induction on strings, §1.3 · model answer: Induction on a recursive string function · practice: Chapter 1 practice.





                  
                  Type 4 — not regular (fooling set), plus a grammar for the same language 
                  
                


Fooling set: choose F from the unbounded quantity an algorithm would have to remember (usually \mathtt{0}^* or \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}). Write arbitrary distinct x, y\in F with parameters i\ne j, build z from x‘s parameter, and prove xz\in L and yz\notin L, each with a reason. Check the edge case i = 0.
Grammar: decompose a typical string — an outer matching pair, the first point where a count balances, or cases — give each piece a nonterminal, and describe its language in English. Test \varepsilon and short strings that must be rejected.
Graded: fooling set 4 for an explicit infinite set that really is a fooling set (a finite set earns 0) + 6 for the proof (2 explicit suffix, 2 one string in, 2 the other out). Grammar 2 syntax + 8 correctness: -2 for one mistake (often \varepsilon), -4 for a few wrong strings, all 8 for infinitely many; \varnothing or \Sigma^* earns nothing; ambiguity costs nothing.
Templates: fooling-set proof, writing up a grammar, designing a grammar · model answer: A fooling set and a grammar for one language · practice: Chapter 3 practice, Chapter 5 practice.





                  
                  Type 5 — a DFA and a regular expression for one language (mnemonic state names, no proof) 
                  
                


DFA: write the one-pass algorithm first; states = the values of its variables; name each state after what it remembers. Draw the start arrow and double circles, and if you omit the dump state, say that missing transitions go to it.
Regular expression: cut typical strings into blocks; explain each piece; test \varepsilon and short strings in both directions. Only +, concatenation, ^*, \varepsilon, \varnothing and parentheses.
Graded: DFA 2 for a complete, unambiguous description + 6 correctness + 2 mnemonic names (an NFA where a DFA was asked earns half). Expression 2 syntax + 8 correctness, with the deductions of type 4.
Templates: describing a DFA, writing up an expression, §3.5 · model answer: A regular expression and a DFA for one language · practice: Chapter 2 practice, Chapter 3 practice.

Powers: w^0 = \varepsilon, w^n = w\bullet w^{n-1}.
Numbered results. Lemma 1.1: w\bullet\varepsilon = w. Lemma 1.2: \lvert w\bullet x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert+\lvert x\rvert. Lemma 1.3: (w\bullet x)\bullet y = w\bullet(x\bullet y). Each is an induction on the left argument.
Standard facts, each a short induction: (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R (the order flips), (w^R)^R = w, \#(a,xy) = \#(a,x)+\#(a,y), \lvert w^R\rvert = \lvert w\rvert, w^mw^n = w^{m+n}, and cancellation (xz = yz implies x = y). Cite one on an exam only if it comes from lecture, the notes, labs or homework; otherwise prove it first.
Pieces of a string. A substring is contiguous; a prefix starts at the beginning, a suffix ends at the end; a subsequence deletes symbols anywhere; proper excludes w itself. A string of length n has n+1 prefixes and n+1 suffixes.
Other splits (§1.4): w = a or w = u\bullet v with u, v non-empty (two base cases), or peel the last symbol, w = xa. Any split works if the cases cover every string and the hypothesis is applied only to shorter strings.

5. Chapter 4 — Nondeterministic automata
Chapter 4 · concepts: nfa, subset-construction, thompsons-algorithm, state-elimination, kleenes-theorem, language-transformations


                  
                  NFA, epsilon-reach, epsilon-removal and the subset construction 
                  
                

NFA: \delta\colon Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\to 2^Q; M accepts w iff some walk from s to an accepting state spells w. The \varepsilon-reach of q is everything reachable from q by zero or more \varepsilon-transitions, and
\delta^*(q,\varepsilon) = \varepsilon\text{-reach}(q),\qquad \delta^*(q,ax) = \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)}\ \bigcup_{p\in\delta(r,a)}\delta^*(p,x).
Removing \varepsilon-transitions (same states and start): A' = \{q \mid \varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)\cap A\ne\varnothing\} and \delta'(q,a) = \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)}\delta(r,a).
Subset construction (NFA to DFA, §4.5):
\begin{gathered}
Q' = 2^Q,\qquad s' = \{s\},\qquad A' = \{S \mid \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S)\cap A\ne\varnothing\},\\
\delta'(S,a) = \bigcup_{p\in S}\ \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(p)}\delta(r,a).
\end{gathered}
By hand, build only the reachable subsets, breadth-first from \{s\}, in a table with columns S, \varepsilon-reach(S), accepting?, and \delta'(S,a) for each a; \varnothing gets a row if it appears.




                  
                  Thompson's gadgets (expression to NFA, §4.6)
                  
                

Every gadget has one start state s and one accepting state t\ne s (Lemma 4.2).

























expressiongadget\varnothing, \varepsilon, a symbol astates s, t with no transition, s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t, or s\xrightarrow{a}tSTin series: t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_T; start s_S, accept t_TS+Tnew s, t: s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_S, s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_T, t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t, t_T\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}tS^*new s, t: s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_S, t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t, the bypass s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t, and a back edge for another copy — t\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s as the book draws it (t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_S works as well)
Two states per leaf, per + and per ^*, none per concatenation: (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^* gets 2\times(4+1+2) = 14.




                  
                  State elimination (NFA to expression, §4.8)
                  
                

Add a new start s with s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon} (old start) and a new target t with (every accepting state) \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t; a missing edge is \varnothing. Remove the old states one at a time; removing q sets, for every pair of remaining states p, r — including p = r,
R'(p\to r) = R(p\to r) + R(p\to q)\,R(q\to q)^*\,R(q\to r).
At the end, R(s\to t) is the expression (Lemma 4.3). O(n^3) operations, but the expression can reach length \Theta(4^n).


Kleene’s theorem (Theorem 4.1) is the cycle expression \to NFA (Thompson) \to DFA (subsets) \to NFA (a DFA already is one) \to expression (elimination). Every arrow preserves the language, not the size: subsets can cost 2^{\lvert Q\rvert} states, elimination exponential length. The book’s runs: (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^* gives 14 NFA states, 5 DFA states, 2 after minimization; (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*(\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{11})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* gives 18 (26 if each \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1} is built literally), 9, and 4.


                  
                  The two transformation lemmas ( §4.9)
                  
                

Let M = (\Sigma,Q,s,A,\delta) be a DFA for L.
Lemma 4.4 — reversal L^R = \{w^R \mid w\in L\}. Reverse every edge, add a new start s^R with \varepsilon-edges to the old accepting states, and accept only at s:
Q^R = Q\cup\{s^R\},\quad A^R = \{s\},\quad \delta^R(s^R,\varepsilon) = A,\quad \delta^R(q,a) = \{p \mid \delta(p,a) = q\}.
(Or by expressions: reverse every string and swap the factors of every concatenation.)
Lemma 4.5 — half \textsf{half}(L) = \{w \mid ww\in L\}. Guess the halfway state h, then run a left copy of M from s and a right copy from h side by side:
\begin{gathered}
Q' = Q^3\cup\{s'\},\qquad \delta'(s',\varepsilon) = \{(s,h,h) \mid h\in Q\},\\
\delta'((p,h,q),a) = \{(\delta(p,a),h,\delta(q,a))\},\qquad A' = \{(h,h,q) \mid h\in Q,\ q\in A\}.
\end{gathered}

                  CNF conversion, steps 0–6 (§5.9) 
                  
                


Add a new start S'\to S if S is on a right side or derives \varepsilon.
Split long rules: A\to X\alpha with \lvert\alpha\rvert\ge2 becomes A\to XB, B\to\alpha.
Find the nullable nonterminals, repeating until nothing changes.
Remove \varepsilon-rules: add every variant with some nullable occurrences deleted, delete every A\to\varepsilon, then add S'\to\varepsilon if S' is nullable.
Merge the nonterminals on a cycle of unit rules A\to B, and delete every rule A\to A.
Remove unit rules in reverse topological order, copying the target’s rules after the target is processed.
Replace each terminal a in a right side of length 2 by a new T_a\to a.

8. The traps that cost the most points


                  
                  Across Chapters 1–5 
                  
                


The induction hypothesis is too weak — stated only for x, or not quantified over the other arguments the proof changes (§1.4). State it for every shorter string, for all values of the other arguments.
Applying the hypothesis to a string that is not shorter, or without saying why it is shorter.
The missing or extra \varepsilon in an expression or grammar: the typical one-mistake deduction. Test \varepsilon every time.
Precedence: \mathtt{10}^*\ne(\mathtt{10})^* and \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}^*\ne(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*. Regex shorthand (+ for “one or more”, ?, [01]) is not allowed.
An incomplete DFA: missing transitions without the sentence about the dump state, or an NFA where a DFA was asked (half credit).
A fooling-set “proof” with one example pair, a finite set, a suffix chosen for a specific i and j, or only one of the two memberships checked. “Without loss of generality i<j” needs a symmetric argument.
Closure in the wrong direction: a regular intersection or union says nothing about L; a subset of a regular language need not be regular.
The subset construction without \varepsilon-reach on every row, accepting only if all states accept, or dropping the reachable \varnothing.
Transformations built for an example language instead of an arbitrary DFA, with \delta' undefined in some case (in particular \delta'(q,\varepsilon)), and never tested on \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^*, \Sigma^*.
State elimination that forgets p = r (the self-loops change) or the old direct term R(p\to r).
A grammar whose nonterminals are described by their role (“the middle part”) instead of their language — and two derivations offered as proof of ambiguity when they build the same parse tree.
CNF step 3 or step 5 done carelessly: every subset of the nullable occurrences, and the unit rules removed in the right order.
