\varnothing versus \{\varepsilon\}, L^+ versus L^*, Arden’s rule, regular-expression precedence.
The DFA tuple, \delta^*, and the product table of accepting sets.
The fooling-set template and the standard fooling-set table of §4; the Myhill–Nerode statement.
NFA \delta^* with \varepsilon-reach; the \varepsilon-removal and subset-construction formulas.
Thompson’s gadgets (four small sketches), the elimination rule, and the costs around Kleene’s cycle.
The transformation template, the reversal and half constructions, and the edge cases \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^*, \Sigma^*.
The grammars of §6, the regular-to-grammar table, and context-free closure (yes: \cup, concatenation, ^*, reversal, \cap regular; no: \cap, complement).
The CNF definition and the conversion steps 0–6.
The rubric numbers of §1 — they tell you what to write down first.

10. A study plan for the final


                  
                  From now to Dec 11 
                  
                


Until Midterm 2 (Mon Nov 9): keep it warm. The algorithms half comes first. Once a week, do one exam-length problem from Chapters 1–5, rotating through the five types of §1 (hard practice problems).
The first two weeks after Midterm 2: rebuild, chapter by chapter. For each of Chapters 1–5, read the chapter page’s definition, template and trap boxes, rewrite its section of this page from memory, then do the chapter’s easy practice problems and one medium.
Write the cheat sheets while you rebuild, by hand, from §9 here and from the proof templates.
The week after: timed. Work a Midterm 1 practice exam in 120 minutes with only your cheat sheet, and grade it yourself with the rubrics of §1. Redo every lost point a day later, without looking.
The last days: breadth. The true/false table of §7, the traps of §8, and the big picture — then the same routine for Chapters 6–9.



Related: the big picture · review of Chapters 6–9 · how exams are graded · practice problems
Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapters 1–5, summarized in our own words, with the book’s numbering; every definition, formula and result here follows the chapter page it links to. Exam format and rubrics: CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) course website and Midterm 1 practice exams, paraphrased. The study plan, the cheat-sheet list and the true/false items are original. The construction formulas (product accepting sets, \varepsilon-removal, subset construction, both versions of Thompson’s star gadget, the elimination rule, reversal and half) are checked on hundreds of random machines and on every small expression, and so are the true/false witnesses (\{\mathtt{0}^{2^n}\}^* = \mathtt{0}^*, the fooling set for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}\}) and the fooling-set table, by tools/checks/toolkit_2.py.

0-toolkit/05-review-turing-machines-and-.title: Review: Turing machines and undecidability (Ch 6–9)
0-toolkit/05-review-turing-machines-and-.content:
Scope: Chapters 6–9, tested on the final exam only (Fri Dec 11, 8–11 am; two handwritten double-sided cheat sheets). Each section links to the chapter page that proves its claims; this page only collects. How the classes fit together: the big picture; Chapters 1–5: the other review.


                  
                  How to use this page 
                  
                

Read one section, close the page, and rewrite its definitions and statements from memory; then compare. The heart of this half is Chapter 7: be able to write a diagonal argument, a reduction and a proof by Rice’s theorem from a blank page, about ten minutes each, with every machine named.


1. How this material is graded
An undecidability proof is graded out of 10 with one of three rubrics; choose the tool first (§6 below), then write to its rubric. Full rubrics: how exams are graded.





























proofgradedtemplatemodel answerdiagonalization4 for the wrapper machine built from the hypothetical decider + 6 for the contradiction (3 per case)diagonalization, §7.7Theorem 6 (§7.5)reduction4 for the reduction (the new decider and M', in the right direction) + 3 for yes-instances + 3 for no-instancesreduction, §7.9AtLeastTwo by reductionRice’s theorem4 for a machine whose language has the property + 4 for one whose language does not + 2 for the details, including the right variantRice, §7.11AtLeastTwo by Rice
If a machine has to be designed, give a transition table or diagram plus an English description of every state, use mnemonic state names, and say that missing transitions reject (template; §6.3; worked problem). The Midterm 1 format also had a true/false problem; §7 collects true/false statements about this material for practice. Practice: Chapter 6 practice, Chapter 7 practice.
2. Chapter 6 — Turing machines
Chapter 6 · concepts: turing-machines, acceptable-and-decidable, universal-turing-machine, church-turing-thesis


                  
                  Turing machine 
                  
                

A tape alphabet \Gamma with a blank \square; an input alphabet \Sigma\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\square\}; a finite set of states Q with \textit{start}, \textit{accept}, \textit{reject}; and
\delta\colon (Q\setminus\{\textit{accept},\textit{reject}\})\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}.
A configuration is (q, x, i): state, tape contents, head position; the run on w starts at (\textit{start}, w, 0), and a move left from cell 0 crashes. On each input the machine accepts, rejects, crashes or runs forever. M accepts L if \textsf{Accept}(M) = L; M decides L if it also halts — rejecting — on every string outside L.































conventionwhat it meansmissing transitionsgo to \textit{reject} — say so on an examthe left endmark it before the machine ever walks left; otherwise it may crasha crashneither accept nor reject: Chapter 7 counts the input as divergingcomputing a functionone halting state; the output is the tape at that moment without trailing blanks; M(w)\uparrow if M never haltsnamesacceptable = recognizable = semi-decidable = recursively enumerable; decidable = computable = recursive
Variants and what simulating them costs (§6.4, §6.6, §6.7, §9.4). None of them changes which languages are accepted or decided; they change only the running time.













































varianthow a standard machine simulates itcost of t stepsstay-put movesstates Q\times\{0,1\}: move right, then step backat most 2tk tracksone track over \Gamma_1\times\cdots\times\Gamma_kttape infinite both waysfold it at cell 0 onto two tracksO(t)k heads, or k tapesextra tracks mark the heads; every step sweeps across them\Theta(t^2), unavoidable in generalk tapes on a two-tape machinea cleverer simulationO(t\log t)recursion; random-access memorya call stack on an extra tape; a list of [\textit{address}\bullet\textit{data}] pairspolynomialnondeterminism (r options per step)breadth-first search of the computation treeO(t^2r^{2t}) on one tape, O(t\,r^t) with two
The quadratic loss is real: marked palindromes \{w\mathtt{\#}w^R\} take O(n) steps with two heads but \Omega(n^2) with one.
The universal machine (§6.8). U accepts \langle M,w\rangle iff M accepts w, and rejects it iff M rejects w. Symbols and states are fixed-length bit strings (\langle\textit{start}\rangle = \mathtt{1}\cdots\mathtt{1}, \langle\textit{reject}\rangle = \mathtt{0}\cdots\mathtt{0}, and on this site \langle\textit{accept}\rangle = \mathtt{0}\cdots\mathtt{01}, a code the book leaves open); a transition \delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta) is the block [\langle p\rangle{\bullet}\langle a\rangle\,|\,\langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle b\rangle{\bullet}\langle\Delta\rangle], and transitions into \textit{reject} are left out; a configuration is a list of cells [\langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle a\rangle] in which only the head’s cell carries a state other than \textit{reject}. One step: find the head’s cell, look up its block (none: reject), rewrite the cell, pass the state to the neighbor.
The Church–Turing thesis — every algorithm can be carried out by a Turing machine — is a claim about the world, not a theorem. It is what lets proofs describe machines in pseudocode.
3. Chapter 7 — Undecidability
Chapter 7 · concepts: diagonalization, halting-problem, undecidability-reductions, rices-theorem
The four languages of a machine. \textsf{Accept}(M), \textsf{Reject}(M) and \textsf{Diverge}(M) split \Sigma^*; \textsf{Halt}(M) = \textsf{Accept}(M)\cup\textsf{Reject}(M). M decides \textsf{Accept}(M) exactly when \textsf{Diverge}(M) = \varnothing. ”M does not accept w” means M rejects or diverges.

































resultstatementLemma 1from any M build M^R (swap accept and reject), M^A (rejections become endless loops: \textsf{Reject}(M^A) = \varnothing) and M^H (rejections become acceptances: \textsf{Accept}(M^H) = \textsf{Halt}(M))Lemma 2decidable languages are closed under \cup, \cap, \setminus — and complement, by Lemma 1(a)Corollary 3if L' is decidable and L\cap L', L\cup L', L\setminus L' or L'\setminus L is undecidable, then L is undecidableLemma 4acceptable languages are closed under \cup (run both in parallel) and \capLemma 5an acceptable L is decidable iff \overline{L} is acceptable; so if L is acceptable but undecidable, \overline{L} is not acceptableCantor’s theoremno f\colon X\to 2^X is onto; so some language is not acceptable
The named languages (complements taken among valid encodings):



























































languagedecidable?acceptable?complement acceptable?\textsf{SelfReject} = \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ rejects } \langle M\rangle\}no — Theorem 6yes — Theorem 11no\textsf{SelfAccept}, \textsf{SelfHalt}no — Theorems 7, 8yes — Theorem 10, Lemma 4no\textsf{SelfDiverge} = \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ diverges on } \langle M\rangle\}nono — Theorem 9yes\textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Reject}, \textsf{Halt} (pairs \langle M,w\rangle)no — Theorem 12 for \textsf{Halt}yes — run U, U^R, U^Hno\textsf{Diverge}nonoyes\textsf{NeverAccept} = \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) = \varnothing\}no — Theorem 13noyes — dovetail M over all inputs\textsf{LeftThree} (three left moves in a row on w)no — Theorem 20yes — simulate and waitno\textsf{NeverLeft}, \textsf{ThisIsSparta}yes — Theorem 19; simulate 300 stepsyesyes
Also undecidable: \textsf{NeverReject}, \textsf{NeverHalt}, \textsf{NeverDiverge} (the same reduction with the other languages of M_w), \textsf{DivergeSame} (Theorem 14), and \{\langle M,w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w^k \text{ for every } k\ge0\} (Theorem 16).

Venn diagram of acceptable and co-acceptable languages; their intersection is the decidable languages; example languages in each regionall languagesacceptableco-acceptable(complement acceptable)decidable= both (Lemma 5)SelfRejectSelfAcceptSelfHaltAccept, HaltLeftThreeSelfDivergeDivergeNeverAcceptregular languages{0n1n0n}NeverLeftThisIsSpartaneither: {⟨M⟩ : Accept(M) is finite}, {⟨M⟩ : Accept(M) is regular}Acceptable, co-acceptable, decidable. A language is decidable exactly when both it and its complement are acceptable (Lemma 5). SelfReject, SelfAccept, SelfHalt, Accept, Halt and LeftThree sit in the left lune: acceptable but undecidable, so their complements (such as SelfDiverge and Diverge) are not acceptable. NeverAccept is co-acceptable but not acceptable. Some languages are neither, such as the two at the bottom (Corollary 18).


                  
                  The direction of a reduction 
                  
                

To prove L undecidable, reduce a known undecidable language to L: assume a decider \textsf{DecideL}, and build from it a decider for \textsf{Accept} (or \textsf{Halt}, …) that writes down the encoding of a new machine M' and asks \textsf{DecideL} about it. The new decider never runs M'. The workhorse is
M_w(x)\colon\ \text{erase } x;\ \text{write } w;\ \text{run } M \text{ on } w,\qquad \textsf{Accept}(M_w) = \begin{cases}\Sigma^* & \text{if } M \text{ accepts } w,\\ \varnothing & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
Deciding L with the help of a decider for \textsf{Halt} proves nothing: every decidable language reduces to \textsf{Halt}.




                  
                  Template — the three proofs in skeleton form 
                  
                

Diagonalization. Suppose \textsf{Dec} decides L. Build \textsf{Wrap} from \textsf{Dec} (swap its answers, or redirect them to a loop) so that for every M, \textsf{Wrap} accepts (or halts on) \langle M\rangle iff M does not … \langle M\rangle. Take M = \textsf{Wrap}; both cases contradict. 
Reduction. Suppose \textsf{DecideL} decides L. \textsf{DecideAccept}: given \langle M,w\rangle, write \langle M'\rangle, run \textsf{DecideL} on it, return its answer (or the opposite). If M accepts w, then … so \langle M'\rangle\in L; if M rejects or diverges, then … so \langle M'\rangle\notin L. So \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept} — impossible. 
Rice. L = \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) for \mathcal{L} = \{\ldots\}; membership depends only on \textsf{Accept}(M); \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L} for Y = \ldots; \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L} for N = \ldots; so L is undecidable by Rice’s theorem.




                  
                  Rice's theorem and its variants 
                  
                

If \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L} for some machine Y and \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L} for some machine N, then \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) = \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\in\mathcal{L}\} is undecidable. (The proof, when \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L}: a reduction from \textsf{Halt} with \textsf{WTF}(x) = “run M on w, then Y on x”; otherwise apply it to the complementary property.) The same holds with \textsf{Reject}, \textsf{Halt} or \textsf{Diverge} in place of \textsf{Accept}, and for \textsf{DecideIn}(\mathcal{L}) with deciders Y and N. Use the variant that matches the definition.
Witnesses: M_{\textsf{Accept}} accepts everything (\textsf{Accept} = \Sigma^*); M_{\textsf{Reject}} rejects everything (\textsf{Accept} = \varnothing, \textsf{Halt} = \Sigma^*); M_{\textsf{Diverge}} moves right forever (\textsf{Accept} = \textsf{Halt} = \varnothing). Corollary 15: “accepts \varepsilon”, “accepts \mathtt{UIUC}”, “accepts exactly three strings”, “accepts every palindrome”, ”\textsf{Accept}(M) is regular / not regular / undecidable”, "\textsf{Accept}(M) = \textsf{Accept}(N)" are all undecidable.


When Rice’s theorem does not apply (§7.11): a property of the machine’s behavior or text (\textsf{ThisIsSparta}, ”M has 374 states”: decidable); self-reference (\textsf{RevAccept} = \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \langle M\rangle^R\}: undecidable, but by a reduction); a trivial property (no Y or no N: decidable); and unacceptability, which Rice never proves.


                  
                  The Rice–McNaughton–Myhill–Shapiro theorem ( §7.12)
                  
                

For a set \mathcal{L} of acceptable languages, \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is acceptable iff \mathcal{L} is monotone (acceptable supersets of its members are members), compact (every member has a finite subset that is a member) and finitely acceptable (its finite members, listed out, form an acceptable language). Lemma 17: not monotone ⇒ not acceptable. Corollary 18: ”\textsf{Accept}(M) is finite / infinite / regular / not regular / decidable / undecidable”, ”M accepts some string of \textsf{SelfDiverge}” and "\textsf{Accept}(M) = \textsf{Accept}(N)" are not acceptable.
Sanity check: "\textsf{Accept}(M)\ne\varnothing" is monotone, compact (a single string suffices) and finitely acceptable — and indeed dovetailing accepts that language.


Behavior (§7.13). \textsf{NeverLeft} is decidable: a machine that only moves right and has read more than \lvert Q\rvert blanks has repeated a state on a blank and will run right forever. \textsf{LeftThree} is undecidable: a simulation can be padded so that it never makes three left moves in a row until it would accept. Rules of thumb, not theorems: a behavior is probably undecidable if a machine could simulate an arbitrary machine while avoiding it and show it only on acceptance; probably decidable if it confines the machine to finitely many configurations or forces an endless loop after finitely many steps.
4. Chapter 8 — Universal models
Chapter 8 — a sketch in the book; treat it as background. A model that can simulate every Turing machine inherits both its power and its undecidability: a decider for “does this run stop?” would decide \textsf{Halt}.













































modelthe trick that simulates a Turing machinewhat becomes undecidabletwo-stack machinethe tape cut at the head: one stack holds the left part, the other the head cell and the right parthalting (one stack and one pass over the input give only context-free languages)counter machinesthree counters: the halves of the tape as base-\lvert\Gamma\rvert numbers; two counters: (a,b,c) stored as 2^a3^b5^cwhether a two-counter machine started at (0,0) halts; universal only for suitably encoded inputsFRACTRANthe prime exponents of N are counters; a fraction f applies only if Nf is an integer — a built-in zero testwhether the program haltsPost’s correspondence problemdominoes whose solutions spell a halting computation, the bottom row one configuration aheadPCP: undecidable but acceptable, so its complement is not acceptablematrix mortalitystrings as integer matrices, built from a PCP instanceis some product zero? (already for two 15\times15 or six 3\times3 matrices)mirrors, Wang tilesa ray’s position or a row of tiles encodes a configurationdoes the ray reach a region? can the plane be tiled?combinator calculus\mathsf{I}x\to x, \mathsf{K}xy\to x, \mathsf{S}xyz\to xz(yz); equivalent to the λ-calculusdoes a term have a normal form?
5. Chapter 9 — Nondeterministic Turing machines
Chapter 9 · concepts: nondeterministic-turing-machines, cook-levin-theorem

































notionwhat to know colddefinition\delta\colon (Q\setminus\{\textit{accept},\textit{reject}\})\times\Gamma\to 2^{Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}}; the runs on w form a computation treeaccept / rejectaccepts w if some branch accepts (others may run forever); rejects w if every branch rejects — then the whole tree is finite; otherwise neitherTheorem 1a deterministic machine accepts and rejects exactly the same strings: breadth-first search of the tree, O(t^2r^{2t}) steps on one tape, O(t\,r^t) with two; depth-first search can get stuck in an infinite branchadvice and dovetailingnumber the options 1,\dots,r; N accepts w iff some advice string makes the deterministic M accept (w,x). Dovetailing tries all advice strings of length t for t steps, t = 1, 2, \ldots: O(t\,r^t) with three tapes, O(t^2r^t) with onecomplexity classes\textsf{TIME}, \textsf{NTIME}, \textsf{SPACE}, \textsf{NSPACE} on multi-tape machines; \textsf{P} = \bigcup_k\textsf{TIME}(n^k), \textsf{NP} = \bigcup_k\textsf{NTIME}(n^k); \textsf{P}\subseteq\textsf{NP}\subseteq exponential time; \textsf{NP} = languages with polynomial-time verifiersCook–Levinif \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{P} then \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP}. For L\in\textsf{NP} with a verifier running N = \max\{1, n^k\} steps, the formula \Phi_w has variables Q_{t,i,q} (state q, head on cell i, time t) and T_{t,i,a} (cell i holds a), five kinds of constraints (boundaries, initialization, advice, transitions, acceptance), size O(N^2) = O(n^{2k}), and is satisfiable iff w\in L
So \textsf{SAT} is NP-hard — every L\in\textsf{NP} reduces to it — and, being in \textsf{NP}, NP-complete. To prove another problem NP-hard, reduce \textsf{SAT} to it: the same direction rule as for undecidability (§9.6).
6. Which tool for which question

7. True or false: twelve to practice






































































statementanswerone-sentence justificationEvery decidable language is acceptable.truea decider accepts its language (§6.2).If M does not accept w, then M rejects w.falseM may run forever, or crash.If L and \overline{L} are both acceptable, then L is decidable.truerun both acceptors in parallel (Lemma 5).The complement of every acceptable language is acceptable.false\textsf{Halt} is acceptable, but by Lemma 5 its complement is not.\textsf{Halt} is undecidable, so it is not acceptable.falsethe universal machine accepts it.”M has 374 states” is undecidable by Rice’s theorem.falseit is decidable — a property of the machine’s text, not of its language.Rice’s theorem shows that \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\ne\varnothing\} is not acceptable.falseRice proves only undecidability; dovetailing accepts this language.Deciding L with a subroutine that decides \textsf{Halt} proves that L is undecidable.falsewrong direction: every decidable language reduces to \textsf{Halt}.A nondeterministic machine rejects w if some branch rejects w.falseevery branch must reject (§9.2).Every language accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine is acceptable.trueTheorem 1 of Chapter 9.Some language decided by a two-tape machine is decided by no one-tape machine.falseone tape simulates two with a quadratic slowdown; only time changes.A finite-state machine with two stacks is as powerful as a Turing machine.truethe tape is two stacks cut at the head (§8.2).
8. The traps that cost the most points


                  
                  Across Chapters 6–9 
                  
                


“Does not accept” is not “rejects”. Every second case of a reduction must handle rejection and divergence.
A decider halts on every input, including strings that encode nothing; the decider you build in a reduction must halt even when M' would not.
Wrong direction. The hypothetical decider for the new language is the subroutine; the language you end up deciding is the known undecidable one.
Running M' instead of writing it down. \textsf{DecideAccept} only computes \langle M'\rangle; say what M' does on every input x.
Unnamed machines. “It accepts” is ambiguous with four machines around: name \textsf{DecideL}, \textsf{DecideAccept}, M and M'.
Diagonalization on the wrong machine. The contradiction comes from running the wrapper on its own encoding; say why that run halts.
Rice misapplied: to behavior or to the machine’s text, without the property written as a set of languages, without concrete Y and N, with the wrong variant, or to conclude “not acceptable”.
The union of acceptable languages run in series. The first acceptor may run forever; simulate in parallel (Lemma 4).
Swapping accept and reject complements only a deterministic decider — not a machine that may diverge, not a nondeterministic machine.
Machine design without the conventions: say that missing transitions reject, mark the left end, and trace \varepsilon and near-misses.
Confusing time with power. Tapes, heads and nondeterminism change running times, never which languages are decidable or acceptable.



9. What to put on your cheat sheet
The final allows two double-sided, handwritten letter sheets for the whole course. For Chapters 6–9:

The Turing-machine tuple, \delta‘s type, configurations, the four outcomes, and accepts versus decides.
The variants table with its costs (2t, \Theta(t^2), O(t\log t), O(t^2r^{2t}), O(t\,r^t)).
Lemmas 1–5 in one line each, and Corollary 3.
The table of named languages: decidable, acceptable, complement acceptable.
The three proof skeletons with their rubrics (4+6, 4+3+3, 4+4+2), and M_w.
Rice’s statement, its variants, the witnesses M_{\textsf{Accept}}, M_{\textsf{Reject}}, M_{\textsf{Diverge}}, and the four cases where it does not apply.
RMMS: monotone, compact, finitely acceptable; Lemma 17.
The rules of thumb for behavior, with \textsf{NeverLeft} and \textsf{LeftThree}.
Nondeterministic acceptance versus rejection; Theorem 1 and dovetailing; the definitions of P and NP; the Cook–Levin statement and its variables.

10. A study plan for the final


                  
                  Chapters 6–9 between Midterm 2 (Nov 9) and the final (Dec 11) 
                  
                


Read first, once. Chapter 6 for the definitions and conventions; Chapter 7 slowly, section by section, rewriting each template from memory; Chapters 8 and 9 for the statements in §4 and §5 above.
Drill the three proofs. Work the worked problem without looking, then the Chapter 7 practice problems: one diagonal argument, two reductions and two Rice proofs a day for a week, each graded against its rubric.
Classify languages fast. Go down the table of §3 and the zoo of the big picture covering the answers: decidable? acceptable? complement acceptable? which tool?
Design one machine end to end (Chapter 6 practice): passes in English, table, meanings, traces.
Write the cheat sheets by hand from §9 here and §9 of the Chapters 1–5 review, then finish with the true/false tables of both reviews and the traps.

0-toolkit/06-how-exams-are-graded.content:
Toolkit · reference page · the course’s standard rubrics, paraphrased — the course website is authoritative.


                  
                  A paraphrase, not the rubrics themselves 
                  
                

Everything on this page paraphrases the CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) course website: its exam schedule, the Midterm 1 practice exams and the standard grading rubrics. The course website is authoritative. Where this page disagrees with it, or with the instructions printed on an exam, they win.


1. All rubrics at a glance
Each standard rubric is out of 10 points.

On every problem (§10): “clearly”, “trivial” and “obviously” draw scrutiny; ambiguity is read unfavorably; an NFA where a DFA was asked earns half credit; \varnothing or \Sigma^* as a regular expression or grammar earns nothing; and any result from lecture, the lecture notes, labs or homework solutions may be used without proof.
2. Exams and cheat sheets

A cheat sheet is a double-sided letter-size sheet, and it must be handwritten. The formats of Midterm 2 and of the final exam are not described here; check the course website.
3. The Midterm 1 format
Midterm 1’s practice exams have 5 problems in 120 minutes, one of each type below. Students may use any result from lecture, the lecture notes, labs or homework solutions without proof — cite it by name: “by Lemma 3.6”, “by the product construction”.















































problem typewhat to hand intemplaterubricworked problemtrue/false, 10 partseach answer with a one-sentence justification——sample items close every chapter page: Ch 1, 2, 3, 4, 5regular language transformations, two partsfor each, an automaton built from an arbitrary DFA for Ltransformation§8insert and delete a 1induction on a recursively defined string functiona complete induction proofstring induction§4sorting a stringnon-regularity plus a grammar for the same languagea fooling-set proof and a context-free grammarfooling set, write-up§7, §5fooling set and grammara DFA plus a regular expression for the same languageboth, with mnemonic state names; no proof neededdescribing a DFA, write-up§6, §501 exactly twice
4. Induction

































pointsfor1starting from an arbitrary object: “let w be an arbitrary string”2an explicit, strong induction hypothesis — weak induction is discouraged2exhaustive cases: together they cover every object1the base cases2correct use of the induction hypothesis2the other details
The wording (“an arbitrary object”) fits every induction in the course — over strings, regular expressions, numbers or derivations. A proof that a grammar generates a language is two of them.


                  
                  What loses points 
                  
                


A hypothesis that is never written down, or a weak one (“assume the claim for x; prove it for ax”). State it for every smaller object.
Applying the hypothesis to something that is not smaller than w — or not saying why it is smaller.
Cases that miss strings: a definition with a case w = abx needs base cases for \varepsilon and for every single symbol.
Inducting on the wrong argument: concatenation takes its left argument apart, so the right one never gets smaller.
A step justified by “clearly” instead of by a definition, the hypothesis or a lemma.



Templates: string induction, structural induction, what a grammar generates · worked: sorting a string, a grammar proof · traps in context: §1.4, induction on strings
5. Regular expressions and grammars

















pointsfor2syntax8correctness (on exams)
Exam deductions are twice the homework ones:






























mistakehomeworkexamone mistake — often a missing or extra \varepsilon−1−2a few wrong strings−2−4infinitely many wrong stringsno correctness creditno correctness credit: −8the answer \varnothing or \Sigma^*no creditno credit
Homework answers must also explain each piece in English, and for a grammar, every nonterminal needs a self-contained description of its language. Ambiguity is not penalized: an ambiguous grammar that generates the right language earns full credit.


                  
                  What loses points 
                  
                


\varepsilon, forgotten or let in by accident. Test it first.
Precedence: \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^* is not (\mathtt{10})^*, and a misplaced star usually changes infinitely many strings.
Syntax that regular expressions do not have: \cap, complement, \mathtt{0}^n, a “plus” that means “one or more”.
A union with a forgotten case, like a grammar for “not of the form \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n” that misses every string containing 10 (§5.4, Example 2).
A nonterminal described by its role (“the middle part”) instead of by its language.



Template: write-up · worked: 01 exactly twice (b), fooling set and grammar (b), state elimination by hand · traps in context: §2.3, §5.4
6. DFAs and NFAs





















pointsfor2an unambiguous, complete description: a start arrow and double circles; say so if you leave out a trash (dump) state; a description in text gives the whole transition function; an NFA states its \varepsilon-transitions; a product construction describes each factor and the accepting states6correctness (on exams)2mnemonic state names
An NFA where a DFA was asked earns half credit. The rubric has no line for minimality; a clear machine with a few extra states is better than a minimal one you cannot explain (§3.5).


                  
                  What loses points 
                  
                


Missing transitions and no sentence about a dump state: the machine is incomplete — or an NFA, which earns half credit.
States named q_0, q_1, \dots with no meaning attached.
“Run both machines in parallel” with no description of the factors, the pairs and the accepting pairs.
Factors of a product that are not complete DFAs over the same alphabet: the union and the difference then lose strings.



Templates: describing a DFA, product construction · worked: 01 exactly twice (a), a product, written formally, subset construction by hand · traps in context: §3.2, §3.6
7. Fooling sets

























pointsfor4an explicit infinite set that really is a fooling set — a finite set earns nothing2for arbitrary distinct x, y\in F: an explicit suffix z2showing that one of xz and yz is in L2showing that the other is not


                  
                  What loses points 
                  
                


One example pair instead of arbitrary distinct x and y, written with parameters i\ne j.
“Assume i<j” without “without loss of generality” — or when the argument is not symmetric, because z was built from x.
Only one half shown, or a half with no reason.
A set described by what it should do (“all the prefixes we need”) instead of explicitly.
A suffix that depends on a DFA you are trying to rule out.



Template: fooling set · worked: fooling set and grammar (a) · traps in context: §3.8, fooling sets
8. Language transformations





















pointsfor2a formal, complete description of the new machine M', built from an arbitrary DFA M — say whether M' is a DFA or an NFA, and give its \varepsilon-transitions2an English explanation of the states and of the accepting states6correctness: 1 for the states, 1 for the start state, 1 for the accepting states, 3 for the transitions
Before handing in, run the construction on the edge cases the rubric names: L = \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^* and \Sigma^*.


                  
                  What loses points 
                  
                


A construction for one particular DFA or language: the claim is about every regular L.
\delta' left undefined for some state and symbol, or for \varepsilon.
The two kinds mixed up: \{w \mid f(w)\in L\} simulates M on f(w); \{f(w) \mid w\in L\} guesses w.
Complementing an NFA by swapping its accepting states.



Template: transformation · worked: insert and delete a 1 · traps in context: §4.9, language transformations
9. Undecidability
Chapters 6–9 are tested on the final exam only. An undecidability proof is graded with the rubric of its method.
Diagonalization

















pointsfor4the wrapper machine, built from the hypothetical decider6the contradiction: 3 for each of the two cases
Reduction





















pointsfor4the reduction: the new decider and the machine M' it writes down3”if”: a yes-instance (M accepts w) makes the new decider accept3”only if”: a no-instance (M rejects or diverges) makes it reject
Rice’s theorem





















pointsfor4a machine whose language has the property4a machine whose language does not2the details, including the right variant of the theorem


                  
                  What loses points 
                  
                


The wrong direction. Deciding L with the help of a decider for \textsf{Halt} proves nothing; the hypothetical decider for L must be the subroutine.
Running M'. The new decider only writes \langle M'\rangle down; it must halt on every input.
“Does not accept” read as “rejects”. It also means “diverges”, and the “only if” case must cover both.
Unnamed machines. Name the hypothetical decider, the decider you build, M and M', and never write “it”.
Rice where it does not apply: a behavior (\textsf{ThisIsSparta}), self-reference (\textsf{RevAccept}), a trivial property — or the wrong variant, such as a property of \textsf{Halt}(M) treated as one of \textsf{Accept}(M).
Diagonalizing against the wrong machine. The contradiction comes from running the machine built from the decider on its own encoding.



Templates: diagonalization, reduction, Rice · worked: AtLeastTwo; Theorem 6 in §7.5 · traps in context: §7.9, §7.11
10. General rules

“Clearly”, “trivial” and “obviously” draw scrutiny. A grader reads the step they introduce more closely. Write the reason instead: a definition, the hypothesis, a lemma.
Ambiguity is read unfavorably. When an answer can be read two ways, expect the reading that earns less: define every symbol, name every machine, label every edge. (An ambiguous grammar is a different thing, and costs nothing.)
An NFA where a DFA was asked earns half credit.
\varnothing or \Sigma^* as a regular expression or grammar earns no credit.
Cite instead of reproving. Any result from lecture, the lecture notes, labs or homework solutions may be used without proof.
Cheat sheets are handwritten: one double-sided letter sheet for a midterm, two for the final.

Related: proof templates · notation and conventions · the big picture
Sources for this page
Exam dates and scope, the cheat-sheet rules, the Midterm 1 format (from its practice exams) and the standard rubrics come from the CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) course website and are paraphrased here; the website is authoritative. The “what loses points” lists collect the traps of the chapter and concept pages linked from each section.

The book is careful, and every item below is small. They are listed because each one can cost points if it is copied onto a cheat sheet or used to check an answer. Every item was confirmed against the chapter PDF (cover date December 28, 2018), and every concrete one is also checked by the site’s scripts. Only items that would change an answer are listed — no spelling.

Not errors, but easy to trip over

State elimination’s name. Some summaries call §4.8’s method “Han and Wood’s algorithm”; the current book credits the idea to McNaughton and Yamada (1960), with Lee (1960) and Kleene (1951) before them. Same algorithm — state-elimination.

0-toolkit/index.title: Toolkit
0-toolkit/index.content:
Reference pages, not chapters. Come here to look up a symbol, copy a proof template, see where a language sits among the classes, or review a whole half of the course the week before an exam.

Notation and conventions — every symbol the site uses, how the book writes it, how to write it by hand, the other names you will meet for the same idea, and where this site departs from the book.
Proof templates — every exam boilerplate in course order (string induction, structural induction, DFA correctness, products, fooling sets, transformations, grammar proofs, diagonalization, reductions, Rice), each with its rubric line and a worked problem.
The big picture — regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ decidable ⊂ acceptable ⊂ all languages, a zoo of famous languages in their smallest class, closure properties side by side, and how to prove that a language is or is not in each class.
Review: regular and context-free languages — Chapters 1–5, the Midterm 1 material: what to know cold, every construction with its formula, the problem types, traps, a cheat-sheet list and a study plan.
Review: Turing machines and undecidability — Chapters 6–9, on the final only, in the same format.
How exams are graded — dates, cheat-sheet rules, the Midterm 1 format, and a paraphrase of every standard rubric with what loses points.
Errata in the book — the slips found in the textbook while writing this site, each with its correction.

The exams allow handwritten cheat sheets only (one double-sided sheet for a midterm, two for the final), so these pages are meant to be read and rewritten, not printed: the review pages end with a list of what is worth putting on a sheet.

1-models-of-computation/01-strings.title: Chapter 1 — Strings
1-models-of-computation/01-strings.content:
Chapter 1 · book pp. 1–18 · chapter PDF · next: Chapter 2 · practice: 8 problems


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

A string is either empty or a symbol followed by a string. Because that definition is recursive, every function on strings — length, concatenation, reversal, counting — is defined by the same two cases, and every proof about strings is an induction whose cases mirror the definition: w = \varepsilon or w = ax, with a hypothesis that covers every shorter string. Lemmas 1.1–1.3 (w\bullet\varepsilon = w, lengths add, concatenation is associative) state facts you already believe; their proofs are practice for a pattern that returns in every later chapter, for automata, regular expressions, grammars and Turing machines. Midterm-1-style exams devote a whole problem to exactly this kind of proof about a newly defined string function.


1.1 Strings
An alphabet \Sigma is a finite set; its elements are called symbols — bits, letters, ASCII characters, anything. A string over \Sigma is then defined the way a linked list is defined in a program:


                  
                  Definition — string, \Sigma^*
                  
                

A string over \Sigma is either

the empty string, written \varepsilon, or
an ordered pair (a, x), written a\cdot x or just ax, where a\in\Sigma is a symbol and x is a string over \Sigma.

\Sigma^* is the set of all strings over \Sigma. For a non-empty alphabet it is an infinite set, but every string in it is finite: it is built by finitely many applications of the second rule.


So STRING is shorthand for (\mathtt{S},(\mathtt{T},(\mathtt{R},(\mathtt{I},(\mathtt{N},(\mathtt{G},\varepsilon)))))) — six pairs, with the empty string at the end:

the string STRING drawn as six linked pairs ending in epsilonSTRING = (S, (T, (R, (I, (N, (G, ε))))))SSTRINGTTRINGRRINGIINGNNGGGεεA string is a symbol paired with a (shorter) string. Each box is one pair (a, x): the symbol on the left, the rest of the string on the right. The grey label under each box is the string that starts there; the last pair points to the empty string ε. The length is the number of boxes.
Conventions (the book’s, used on every page of this site): a, b, c are symbols; w, x, y, z are strings; explicit symbols and strings are set in monospace, like \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, 0110, STRING. Formally the symbol a and the one-symbol string a\cdot\varepsilon are different objects, but everyone writes both as a. The difference matters only inside proofs, where a\bullet z = a\cdot(\varepsilon\bullet z) = a\cdot z uses both cases of the definition of concatenation below.
Concept page: strings.
1.2 Two recursive functions
Because strings are defined recursively, functions on strings are defined recursively too: one case for \varepsilon, and one case for ax that calls the function on the shorter string x.


                  
                  Definition — length and concatenation 
                  
                

\lvert w\rvert := \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ 1 + \lvert x\rvert & \text{if } w = ax\end{cases}
\qquad\qquad
w\bullet z := \begin{cases} z & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ a\cdot(x\bullet z) & \text{if } w = ax\end{cases}
The small dot in a\cdot x puts one symbol in front of a string: it builds a pair. The big dot in w\bullet z glues two strings together. Both dots are usually left out.


Unfolding the definition on an example:
\mathtt{NOW}\bullet\mathtt{HERE}
= \mathtt{N}\cdot(\mathtt{OW}\bullet\mathtt{HERE})
= \mathtt{N}\cdot\big(\mathtt{O}\cdot(\mathtt{W}\bullet\mathtt{HERE})\big)
= \mathtt{N}\cdot\Big(\mathtt{O}\cdot\big(\mathtt{W}\cdot(\varepsilon\bullet\mathtt{HERE})\big)\Big)
= \mathtt{NOWHERE}.

the pairs N, O, W are copied and the last copy points to the unchanged string HEREwNOWεw•zNOWHEREεone new pair per symbol of wz = HERE, reused unchangedConcatenation recurses on its left argument. Computing NOW • HERE peels N, O, W off the left argument one at a time and rebuilds a pair for each (red); when the left argument has shrunk to ε, the base case returns z = HERE as it is. The right argument is never taken apart, so induction on w is the natural way to prove things about w • z.
Three consequences to keep in mind:

Concatenation recurses on its left argument. The right argument rides along unchanged until the base case returns it. So a proof about w\bullet z inducts on w and keeps z fixed (Lemma 1.2 below).
\varepsilon is a left identity by definition (\varepsilon\bullet z = z is the first case) but a right identity only by proof (w\bullet\varepsilon = w is Lemma 1.1).
Concatenation is not commutative — \mathtt{NOW}\bullet\mathtt{HERE} = \mathtt{NOWHERE} but \mathtt{HERE}\bullet\mathtt{NOW} = \mathtt{HERENOW} — but it is associative (Lemma 1.3), which is what licenses writing wxyz with no dots and no parentheses.

Chapter 3 defines a DFA’s extended transition function \delta^* by exactly this recursion on the input string (§3.2).
1.3 Induction on strings
Every proof about strings in this course follows two design rules.

The cases mirror the recursive definition. A string is either \varepsilon or ax, so the proof has a case w = \varepsilon and a case w = ax. (If the function in the claim is defined by other cases, mirror its cases — see \textsf{swap} at the end of this page.)
The induction hypothesis is as strong as possible: assume the claim for every string shorter than w — “there is no counterexample shorter than w”. In the case w = ax we have \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert - 1 < \lvert w\rvert, so the hypothesis applies to x, and to any other shorter string the argument needs.

This strong hypothesis costs nothing compared with the weak one (“assume the claim for x, prove it for ax”), the graders prefer it, and it still works when a proof needs a string two symbols shorter, or half as long.


                  
                  Template — induction on strings 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string. 
Assume, for every string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, that [the claim holds for x]. 
There are two cases to consider. 
Case w = \varepsilon. … Therefore [the claim holds for w]. 
Case w = ax for some symbol a and string x. The induction hypothesis implies that [the claim holds for x]. … Therefore [the claim holds for w]. 
In both cases, [the claim holds for w]. \blacksquare


Write this boilerplate first, with room in each case; then write out the claim and the hypothesis in full, with variable names that do not clash; only then start on the algebra.


                  
                  Lemma 1.1 
                  
                

w\bullet\varepsilon = w for every string w.




                  
                  Lemma 1.2 
                  
                

\lvert w\bullet x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert + \lvert x\rvert for all strings w and x.




                  
                  Lemma 1.3 
                  
                

(w\bullet x)\bullet y = w\bullet(x\bullet y) for all strings w, x and y.




                  
                  Proof of Lemma 1.2 — the model to copy 
                  
                

Let w and x be arbitrary strings. Assume that \lvert y\bullet x\rvert = \lvert y\rvert + \lvert x\rvert for every string y with \lvert y\rvert < \lvert w\rvert. (We induct on w, the argument that {\bullet} recurses on, and keep x fixed; the shorter string is called y because x is taken.) There are two cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. By the definitions of {\bullet} and \lvert\cdot\rvert,
\lvert w\bullet x\rvert = \lvert\varepsilon\bullet x\rvert = \lvert x\rvert = 0 + \lvert x\rvert = \lvert\varepsilon\rvert + \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert + \lvert x\rvert.
Case w = ay for some symbol a and string y. Then \lvert y\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to y, and
\begin{aligned}
\lvert w\bullet x\rvert &= \lvert a\cdot(y\bullet x)\rvert && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}\\
&= 1 + \lvert y\bullet x\rvert && \text{by definition of } \lvert\cdot\rvert\\
&= 1 + \lvert y\rvert + \lvert x\rvert && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= \lvert w\rvert + \lvert x\rvert && \text{by definition of } \lvert\cdot\rvert.
\end{aligned}
In both cases, \lvert w\bullet x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert + \lvert x\rvert. \blacksquare


What to copy: an arbitrary w (and x); a hypothesis written out in full, for all shorter strings; cases that cover every string; one justification per equation; and an explicit reason why the hypothesis applies (\lvert y\rvert < \lvert w\rvert). No step says “clearly”.


                  
                  Proof of Lemma 1.1 (click to expand) 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string, and assume that x\bullet\varepsilon = x for every string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert.

w = \varepsilon: w\bullet\varepsilon = \varepsilon\bullet\varepsilon = \varepsilon = w, by the first case of the definition of {\bullet}.
w = ax: w\bullet\varepsilon = a\cdot(x\bullet\varepsilon) by the definition of {\bullet}, and x\bullet\varepsilon = x by the induction hypothesis because \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert; so w\bullet\varepsilon = a\cdot x = w.

In both cases w\bullet\varepsilon = w. \blacksquare




                  
                  Proof of Lemma 1.3 (click to expand) 
                  
                

Induct on w: both sides then unfold by the definition of {\bullet}. (Inducting on y gets stuck — nothing in the definition takes a right argument apart.) Let w, x, y be arbitrary strings, and assume (z\bullet x)\bullet y = z\bullet(x\bullet y) for every string z with \lvert z\rvert < \lvert w\rvert.
Case w = \varepsilon. (\varepsilon\bullet x)\bullet y = x\bullet y = \varepsilon\bullet(x\bullet y), using the definition of {\bullet} twice.
Case w = az. Then \lvert z\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, and
\begin{aligned}
(az\bullet x)\bullet y &= \big(a\cdot(z\bullet x)\big)\bullet y && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}\\
&= a\cdot\big((z\bullet x)\bullet y\big) && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}\\
&= a\cdot\big(z\bullet(x\bullet y)\big) && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= az\bullet(x\bullet y) && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}.
\end{aligned}
In both cases (w\bullet x)\bullet y = w\bullet(x\bullet y). \blacksquare


Concept page: induction-on-strings.
1.4 More than one path up the mountain
The two-case boilerplate is the default, not the law. Any induction works as long as its cases cover every string and every string the hypothesis is applied to is shorter than w. A useful alternative: a string w is non-empty if and only if either

w = a for a single symbol a, or
w = u\bullet v for two non-empty strings u and v — and then \lvert u\rvert, \lvert v\rvert < \lvert w\rvert by Lemma 1.2, so the hypothesis applies to both pieces.


the string STRING split as S and TRING, and as STR and INGstandard:w = a·xSTRINGax|x| = |w| − 1§1.4:w = u•vSTRINGuv1 ≤ |u|, |v| < |w|Two ways to take a non-empty string apart. The standard proof peels off the first symbol, so the induction hypothesis applies to x. The proof of §1.4 splits w anywhere into two non-empty pieces (here after STR); both are shorter than w, so the hypothesis applies to each. That split needs two base cases: w = ε and w = a single symbol.
That split gives a proof with three cases — w = \varepsilon, w = a, w = u\bullet v — and two base cases, because a single symbol cannot be cut into two non-empty pieces. Another common variant peels off the last symbol: every non-empty string is x\bullet a with \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert - 1, which is how a DFA proof can follow the machine as it reads its input (§3.3).


                  
                  Quantify the hypothesis over the other arguments 
                  
                

In the proof of Lemma 1.2 the second argument x never changed, so the hypothesis could keep it fixed. Proving associativity with w = u\bullet v is different: each step below applies the claim (z\bullet x')\bullet y' = z\bullet(x'\bullet y') to a shorter z, and three of the four steps use other second and third arguments.
\begin{aligned}
\big((u\bullet v)\bullet x\big)\bullet y &= \big(u\bullet(v\bullet x)\big)\bullet y && (z, x', y') = (u,\ v,\ x)\\
&= u\bullet\big((v\bullet x)\bullet y\big) && (z, x', y') = (u,\ v\bullet x,\ y)\\
&= u\bullet\big(v\bullet(x\bullet y)\big) && (z, x', y') = (v,\ x,\ y)\\
&= (u\bullet v)\bullet(x\bullet y) && (z, x', y') = (u,\ v,\ x\bullet y)
\end{aligned}
So the hypothesis must read: ”(z\bullet x')\bullet y' = z\bullet(x'\bullet y') for all strings x' and y' and every string z with \lvert z\rvert < \lvert w\rvert.” A hypothesis about the fixed x and y alone justifies only the third step.




                  
                  Lemma 1.3 again, by the three-case split (click to expand) 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string. Assume that (z\bullet x')\bullet y' = z\bullet(x'\bullet y') for all strings x', y' and every string z with \lvert z\rvert < \lvert w\rvert. Let x and y be arbitrary strings.

w = \varepsilon: (\varepsilon\bullet x)\bullet y = x\bullet y = \varepsilon\bullet(x\bullet y) by the definition of {\bullet}.
w = a: (a\bullet x)\bullet y = (a\cdot x)\bullet y = a\cdot(x\bullet y) = a\bullet(x\bullet y), using a\bullet z = a\cdot z (§1.1) and the definition of {\bullet}.
w = u\bullet v with u, v non-empty: \lvert u\rvert, \lvert v\rvert < \lvert w\rvert by Lemma 1.2, so each of the four steps in the trap above is a legal use of the hypothesis, and they show (w\bullet x)\bullet y = w\bullet(x\bullet y).

In all three cases (w\bullet x)\bullet y = w\bullet(x\bullet y). \blacksquare


1.5 Indices, substrings, and subsequences


                  
                  Definition — pieces of a string 
                  
                

Let w be a string of length n.

Index: w_i is the ith symbol of w. Recursively, if w = ax, then w_1 := a and w_i := x_{i-1} for i > 1; w_i is undefined if i < 1 or i > n. We often write w = w_1w_2\cdots w_n or w[1..n] — but n may be 1, or even 0.
Substring: y is a substring of w if w = xyz for some strings x and z. The substring from position i to position j is w[i..j] := \varepsilon if j < i, and w[i..j] := w_i\cdot w[i+1..j] otherwise.
Prefix, suffix: p is a prefix of w if w = px for some string x (equivalently, p = w[1..j] for some 0\le j\le n); s is a suffix of w if w = xs for some string x (equivalently, s = w[i..n] for some 1\le i\le n+1).
Subsequence: a string obtained from w by deleting zero or more symbols, anywhere. Recursively, z is a subsequence of w if and only if z = \varepsilon; or w = ax and z is a subsequence of x; or w = ax, z = ay, and y is a subsequence of x.
Proper: a proper substring, prefix, suffix or subsequence of w is one that is not w itself.



The recursive definition of subsequence is “delete” spelled out symbol by symbol: the first symbol of w is either deleted (second case) or kept as the first symbol of z (third case).

the strings HEADACHE and MEATBALL in indexed cells, with a prefix, suffix, substring and subsequence markedwHEADACHE12345678prefix HEw[3..5] = ADAsuffix HEwMEATBALL12345678METAL = symbols 1, 2, 4, 6, 7: a subsequence, not a substringSubstrings are contiguous; subsequences need not be. In HEADACHE, HE is both a proper prefix (w[1..2]) and a proper suffix (w[7..8]), and w[3..5] = ADA is a substring. Deleting A, B and one L from MEATBALL leaves METAL, so METAL is a subsequence of MEATBALL — but its symbols are not adjacent, and METAL is not a substring.
Every substring is a subsequence, but not conversely: METAL is a subsequence of MEATBALL but not a substring of it, and 00 is a subsequence of 0110 but not a substring. (“Contiguous substring” says the same thing twice: substrings are always contiguous.)
How many? A string of length n has exactly n+1 prefixes and n+1 suffixes (counting \varepsilon and w itself), at most n(n+1)/2 distinct non-empty substrings, and at most 2^n distinct subsequences (counting \varepsilon and w). The bounds are reached when all n symbols are different. At the other extreme, 0000 has just five distinct substrings — \varepsilon, 0, 00, 000, 0000 — and these are also its only subsequences.


                  
                  Substring or subsequence? 
                  
                

“Contains 00” means as a substring unless the problem says subsequence, and the two languages are different: 0110 contains 00 as a subsequence but not as a substring. Read the problem statement twice — a correct answer to the wrong question is a wrong answer.


More recursive functions
The chapter’s exercises define many more functions by the same recursion and ask for proofs of their properties. The standard ones:






























functionbase caserecursive case\#(a, w), the number of a‘s in w\#(a,\varepsilon) := 0\#(a, bx) := [a = b] + \#(a, x)reversal w^R\varepsilon^R := \varepsilon(ax)^R := x^R\bullet apowers w^n (recursion on n)w^0 := \varepsilonw^n := w\bullet w^{n-1} for n\ge1binary complement w^c\varepsilon^c := \varepsilon(\mathtt{0}x)^c := \mathtt{1}\cdot x^c and (\mathtt{1}x)^c := \mathtt{0}\cdot x^c
Here [a = b] is 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise. For example, \#(\mathtt{0},\mathtt{0110}) = 2, (\mathtt{001})^R = \mathtt{100}, (\mathtt{001})^c = \mathtt{110}, and (\mathtt{01})^3 = \mathtt{010101}. Each of the following facts is a short induction on the argument that the definitions recurse on:

\#(a, x\bullet y) = \#(a, x) + \#(a, y), and \lvert w\rvert = \sum_{a\in\Sigma}\#(a,w);
\lvert w^R\rvert = \lvert w\rvert, \#(a, w^R) = \#(a, w), (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R, and (w^R)^R = w;
w^m\bullet w^n = w^{m+n}, \lvert w^n\rvert = n\lvert w\rvert, \#(a, w^n) = n\cdot\#(a,w), and (w^R)^n = (w^n)^R;
(x\bullet y)^c = x^c\bullet y^c, (w^c)^c = w, \#(\mathtt{1}, w) = \#(\mathtt{0}, w^c), and (w^R)^c = (w^c)^R;
cancellation: x\bullet z = y\bullet z implies x = y, and x\bullet y = x\bullet z implies y = z.



                  
                  Model exam answer — (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R for all strings w and x
                  
                

Which variable? Both {\bullet} and {}^R take strings apart from the front, and the front of w\bullet x is the front of w: induct on w and keep x fixed. What gets cited? The definitions of {\bullet} and {}^R, Lemma 1.1 and Lemma 1.3.
Let w and x be arbitrary strings. Assume that (y\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet y^R for every string y with \lvert y\rvert < \lvert w\rvert. There are two cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. By the definition of {\bullet}, Lemma 1.1, and the definition of {}^R,
(\varepsilon\bullet x)^R = x^R = x^R\bullet\varepsilon = x^R\bullet\varepsilon^R.
Case w = ay for some symbol a and string y. Then \lvert y\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to y, and
\begin{aligned}
(ay\bullet x)^R &= \big(a\cdot(y\bullet x)\big)^R && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}\\
&= (y\bullet x)^R\bullet a && \text{by definition of } {}^R\\
&= (x^R\bullet y^R)\bullet a && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= x^R\bullet(y^R\bullet a) && \text{by Lemma 1.3}\\
&= x^R\bullet(ay)^R && \text{by definition of } {}^R.
\end{aligned}
In both cases, (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R. \blacksquare


Once proved, a fact like this can be cited. The inductive case of (w^R)^R = w, for instance, becomes one line: \big((ax)^R\big)^R = (x^R\bullet a)^R = a^R\bullet(x^R)^R = a\bullet x = ax, by the definition of {}^R, the fact above, then a^R = a together with the induction hypothesis for x, and finally a\bullet x = a\cdot x (§1.1).


                  
                  Test the identity before you prove it 
                  
                

The order flips: (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R, not w^R\bullet x^R — with w = \mathtt{0} and x = \mathtt{1}, (w\bullet x)^R is 10 while w^R\bullet x^R is 01. Trying a two- or three-symbol example takes ten seconds and exposes most false “facts”, on true/false questions too.


When the definition has more cases, so does the proof. The exercise function
\textsf{swap}(w) := \begin{cases} w & \text{if } \lvert w\rvert\le1\\ b\cdot a\cdot\textsf{swap}(x) & \text{if } w = abx\end{cases}
exchanges adjacent pairs of symbols: \textsf{swap}(\mathtt{0110}) = \mathtt{1001} and \textsf{swap}(\mathtt{011}) = \mathtt{101}. A proof that \lvert\textsf{swap}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert, or that \textsf{swap}(\textsf{swap}(w)) = w, has three cases — w = \varepsilon, w = a, w = abx — and applies the hypothesis to x, which is two symbols shorter than w. The “every shorter string” hypothesis covers that for free.


                  
                  How the induction problem is graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams devote a whole problem to proving properties of a newly defined recursive string function, like the ones in the table above. It is graded out of 10: 1 for starting from an arbitrary string; 2 for an explicitly stated, strong induction hypothesis (weak induction is discouraged); 2 for cases that cover every string; 1 for the base case(s); 2 for applying the hypothesis correctly — only to shorter strings, with the right values of the other arguments; 2 for the remaining details. Lemmas 1.1–1.3, and any result from lecture, the lecture notes, labs or homework solutions, may be cited without proof.


Summary

A string is \varepsilon or a pair a\cdot x; \Sigma^* is infinite, but every string in it is finite.
Functions on strings are defined by the cases \varepsilon and ax. Concatenation recurses on its left argument; it is associative but not commutative.
String induction: an arbitrary w, a hypothesis for every shorter string, cases that mirror the definition, and a justification on every line.
Lemmas 1.1–1.3: w\bullet\varepsilon = w, \lvert w\bullet x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert + \lvert x\rvert, and associativity. Induct on the argument the definitions recurse on.
Other splits (w = a or w = u\bullet v; or w = xa) are fine. If the hypothesis is applied with different values of the other arguments, it must say “for all” of them.
Substrings are contiguous, subsequences need not be; prefixes and suffixes are special substrings; “proper” excludes w itself.
Reversal turns concatenation around: (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R. Test any identity on a tiny example before proving it.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Midterm 1 (Sep 28) covered induction on strings. Midterm-1-style exams (five problems in two hours) include one induction proof about a recursively defined string function, graded with the rubric above, and true/false items that test the definitions, such as ”(wx)^R = w^Rx^R for all strings w and x” (false) or “every subsequence of w is a substring of w” (false). The same proof pattern returns in the regular-expression, DFA and grammar proofs of Chapters 2–5, and the final exam (Dec 11) covers everything. Rubric details: how exams are graded.




                  
                  Practice this chapter 
                  
                

8 practice problems — 3 easy, 3 medium, 2 hard — each with a folded hint and a worked solution. Start with 1.1 Unfold an accumulator; the practice hub has the whole bank by difficulty and by topic.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 1 (§§1.1–1.5 and the exercises), summarized in our own words. The STRING, NOWHERE, HEADACHE and MEATBALL/METAL examples, Lemmas 1.1–1.3 with their proofs, and the three-case proof of §1.4 follow the book; \#(a,w), reversal, powers, binary complement and \textsf{swap} come from its exercises. The figures, the model proof of (w\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet w^R, and the 0110 and 0000 examples are original. CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) induction rubric for the grading notes. Every definition, lemma, identity and example on this page is checked by brute force over all short strings by tools/checks/ch01.py.

1-models-of-computation/02-regular-langu.title: Chapter 2 — Regular Languages
1-models-of-computation/02-regular-langu.content:
Chapter 2 · book pp. 19–30 · chapter PDF · prev: Chapter 1 · next: Chapter 3 · practice: 8 problems


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

A language is any set of strings. The regular languages are the ones built from the empty language and single strings by finitely many unions, concatenations and Kleene stars, and regular expressions are the notation for them: \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00} describes the binary numerals (without leading 0s) of the multiples of 4. Because the definition is recursive, a proof about regular expressions is an induction with five cases — \varnothing, a string, S+T, ST, S^* — and a proof about regular languages picks an expression and inducts on it. A handful of identities, including Arden’s rule for equations L = AL\cup B, let you calculate with languages without any induction. And a counting argument shows that almost all languages are not regular.


2.1 Languages


                  
                  Definition — language 
                  
                

A (formal) language over an alphabet \Sigma is any set of strings over \Sigma: any subset L\subseteq\Sigma^*. It may be finite or infinite.


Examples over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}: the empty language \varnothing; \{\varepsilon\}; \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{10}\}; all of \Sigma^*; the palindromes; the binary numerals of prime numbers. A language is the same thing as a yes/no problem — given a string w, decide whether w\in L — and the rest of the course asks which machines can solve such problems.


                  
                  Three different "empty" things 
                  
                


\varnothing is the empty language: it contains no strings at all.
\{\varepsilon\} is a language with exactly one string, the empty string. It is not empty.
\varepsilon is a string of length 0, not a language.

They behave differently: \varnothing\bullet L = \varnothing but \{\varepsilon\}\bullet L = L (§2.2), and \varnothing^* = \{\varepsilon\}. In a regular expression, \varnothing denotes \varnothing and \varepsilon denotes \{\varepsilon\}; a missing or extra \varepsilon is the typical “one mistake” deduction on a graded regular expression.


Concept page: languages.
2.2 Building languages
Languages are sets, so A\cup B, A\cap B, A\setminus B and A\oplus B are languages, and so is the complement \overline{A} := \Sigma^*\setminus A. Two more operations use the fact that the elements are strings.


                  
                  Definition — concatenation, Kleene star, Kleene plus 
                  
                


Concatenation: A\bullet B := \{xy \mid x\in A \text{ and } y\in B\}, usually written AB.
Kleene star: L^* is the set of strings w such that either w = \varepsilon, or w = xy for some x\in L and y\in L^*. Equivalently, L^* is the smallest superset of L that contains \varepsilon and is closed under concatenation: all concatenations of zero or more strings from L.
Kleene plus: L^+ := L\bullet L^*, all concatenations of one or more strings from L.



For example, \{\mathtt{HOCUS},\mathtt{ABRACA}\}\bullet\{\mathtt{POCUS},\mathtt{DABRA}\} contains four strings: HOCUSPOCUS, ABRACAPOCUS, HOCUSDABRA and ABRACADABRA. A concatenation can have fewer than \lvert A\rvert\cdot\lvert B\rvert strings, because different pairs can glue to the same string: \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{00}\}\bullet\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{00}\} = \{\mathtt{00},\mathtt{000},\mathtt{0000}\}. The star \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{11}\}^* begins \varepsilon, \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{00}, \mathtt{11}, \mathtt{000}, \mathtt{011}, \mathtt{110},\dots The two exceptions are \varnothing^* = \{\varepsilon\}^* = \{\varepsilon\}; for every other language, L^* is infinite. And \Sigma^* really is the star of the language \Sigma of one-symbol strings, so the notation of Chapter 1 is consistent.


                  
                  Lemma 2.1 
                  
                

For all languages A, B and C:

(a) A\cup B = B\cup A;
(b) (A\cup B)\cup C = A\cup(B\cup C);
(c) \varnothing\bullet A = A\bullet\varnothing = \varnothing;
(d) \{\varepsilon\}\bullet A = A\bullet\{\varepsilon\} = A;
(e) (A\bullet B)\bullet C = A\bullet(B\bullet C);
(f) A\bullet(B\cup C) = (A\bullet B)\cup(A\bullet C);
(g) (A\cup B)\bullet C = (A\bullet C)\cup(B\bullet C).





                  
                  Lemma 2.2 
                  
                

For every language L:

(a) L^* = \{\varepsilon\}\cup L^+ = L^*\bullet L^* = (L\cup\{\varepsilon\})^* = (L\setminus\{\varepsilon\})^* = \{\varepsilon\}\cup L\cup(L^+\bullet L^+);
(b) L^+ = L\bullet L^* = L^*\bullet L = L^+\bullet L^* = L^*\bullet L^+ = L\cup(L^+\bullet L^+);
(c) L^+ = L^* if and only if \varepsilon\in L.



These identities are the algebra of regular expressions: for instance, (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* simplifies to (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* by Lemma 2.2(a).


                  
                  Identities that look true but are not 
                  
                


Concatenation is not commutative: \{\mathtt{0}\}\bullet\{\mathtt{1}\} = \{\mathtt{01}\}\ne\{\mathtt{10}\} = \{\mathtt{1}\}\bullet\{\mathtt{0}\}.
Concatenation does not distribute over \cap. With A = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0}\}, B = \{\mathtt{0}\}, C = \{\mathtt{00}\}: A(B\cap C) = A\bullet\varnothing = \varnothing, but AB\cap AC = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{00}\}\cap\{\mathtt{00},\mathtt{000}\} = \{\mathtt{00}\}. Only A(B\cap C)\subseteq AB\cap AC holds.
L^+ = L^* only when \varepsilon\in L: for L = \{\mathtt{0}\}, L^+ is \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^* and L^* is \mathtt{0}^*.





                  
                  Lemma 2.3 (Arden's rule) 
                  
                

Let A, B and L be languages with L = A\bullet L\cup B. Then A^*\bullet B\subseteq L. Moreover, if \varepsilon\notin A, then L = A\bullet L\cup B holds if and only if L = A^*\bullet B.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

A^*B\subseteq L. Write A^0 := \{\varepsilon\} and A^n := A\bullet A^{n-1}, so that A^* = \bigcup_{n\ge0}A^n and therefore A^*B = \bigcup_{n\ge0}A^nB. So it suffices to show A^nB\subseteq L for every n\ge0, by induction on n. For n = 0: B\subseteq AL\cup B = L. For n\ge1, assuming A^{n-1}B\subseteq L, we get A^nB = A(A^{n-1}B)\subseteq AL\subseteq L, because L = AL\cup B.
A^*B is a solution (for every A): A(A^*B)\cup B = (A^+\cup\{\varepsilon\})B = A^*B by Lemma 2.1(a, d, e, g) and Lemma 2.2(a, b).
If \varepsilon\notin A, there is no other solution. Suppose L = AL\cup B but L\not\subseteq A^*B, and let w be a shortest string in L\setminus A^*B. Since B\subseteq A^*B, w\notin B, so w\in AL: w = xy with x\in A and y\in L. Because \varepsilon\notin A, the string x is non-empty, so \lvert y\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, and y\in A^*B by the choice of w. Then w = xy\in A(A^*B)\subseteq A^*B, a contradiction. So L\subseteq A^*B, and with the first part, L = A^*B. \blacksquare




                  
                  Arden's rule on a single equation 
                  
                

As in regular expressions, a string here stands for the language that contains just that string. If L = \mathtt{0}L\cup\mathtt{1}, then A = \{\mathtt{0}\} does not contain \varepsilon, so the only solution is L = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}. Check: \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\cup\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{0}^+\mathtt{1}\cup\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}.
The condition \varepsilon\notin A matters. The equation L = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0}\}\bullet L\cup\mathtt{1} is solved by \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} but also by \Sigma^*; Arden’s rule only says that \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0}\}^*\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} is the smallest solution.


Solving a DFA. Language equations turn a DFA into a regular expression. For each state q, let L_q be the set of strings that lead from q to an accepting state. For the odd-number-of-1s machine of §3.3:

two-state DFA: start state s loops on 0, accepting state t loops on 0, a 1 moves between them; under each state its language equationLs = 0Ls ∪ 1LtLt = 0Lt ∪ 1Ls ∪ {ε}0011stOne equation per state. Lq is the set of strings that lead from state q to the accepting state. A non-empty string in Lq starts with 0 or 1 and continues from the state that symbol leads to; and since t is accepting, ε ∈ Lt. The DFA accepts Ls, the strings with an odd number of 1s.
Arden’s rule on the second equation (A = \mathtt{0}) gives L_t = \mathtt{0}^*(\mathtt{1}L_s\cup\{\varepsilon\}) = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}L_s\cup\mathtt{0}^*. Substituting into the first equation and distributing gives L_s = (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1})L_s\cup\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*, and Arden’s rule again (\varepsilon\notin\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}) gives
L_s = (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1})^*\,\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*,
an expression for the strings with an odd number of 1s. Chapter 4 does the same job graphically, by state elimination.
2.3 Regular languages and regular expressions


                  
                  Definition — regular language 
                  
                

A language L is regular if and only if it satisfies one of these conditions:

L is empty;
L contains exactly one string (which may be \varepsilon);
L is the union of two regular languages;
L is the concatenation of two regular languages; or
L is the Kleene star of a regular language.



So every finite language is regular (it is empty, or a union of finitely many one-string languages), and so is \Sigma^*. Regular expressions are the compact notation for this definition: omit the braces around one-string sets, write + for union, and write concatenation by juxtaposition.


                  
                  Definition — regular expression, L(R), matching, equivalence
                  
                

A regular expression is \varnothing, a string w (possibly \varepsilon), or S+T, ST or S^* for regular expressions S and T, with parentheses for grouping. Its language L(R) is defined by

L(\varnothing) := \varnothing and L(w) := \{w\};
L(S+T) := L(S)\cup L(T), L(ST) := L(S)\bullet L(T) and L(S^*) := L(S)^*.

A string w matches R if w\in L(R). Two regular expressions are equivalent if they have the same language. Precedence: ^* binds tightest, then concatenation, then +.




                  
                  Precedence 
                  
                


\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^* means \mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}^*), the language \{\mathtt{1},\mathtt{10},\mathtt{100},\dots\} — not (\mathtt{10})^* = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{10},\mathtt{1010},\dots\}.
\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}^* means \mathtt{0}+(\mathtt{1}^*), not (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*.
\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00} means \mathtt{0}+\big(\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}\big): the union is applied last.

When in doubt, add parentheses; redundant ones are never wrong.


The book’s examples, all over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}:





















































regular expressionits language: the binary strings …\mathtt{0}^*made of 0s only (including \varepsilon)\mathtt{0000}\mathtt{0}^*made of at least four 0s(\mathtt{00000})^*made of 0s, a multiple of 5 of them(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*— all of them(\varepsilon+\mathtt{1})(\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0})that alternate: no 00 and no 11(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{0000}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*that contain the substring 0000((\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{000})\mathtt{1})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{000})without 0000: at most three 0s before each 1 and at the end((\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}))^*of even length\mathtt{1}^*(\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}^*)^*with an even number of 0s: after the leading 1s, the 0s come in pairs\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}that are binary numerals of multiples of 4, without leading 0s\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0})^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*that are non-empty binary numerals of multiples of 3 (leading 0s allowed)
The last expression is hard to invent directly; Chapter 4 derives it by state elimination from a DFA that tracks the remainder mod 3, with a separate non-accepting start state (the three remainder states alone would also accept \varepsilon, which the expression does not match). Different expressions can describe the same language: (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*, (\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0})^*, (\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*)^* and (\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{01}+\mathtt{10}+\mathtt{11})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}+\varepsilon) are all equivalent — union is commutative; every single symbol is in \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*; and every string splits into pairs of symbols plus at most one leftover symbol. Without the last factor, (\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{01}+\mathtt{10}+\mathtt{11})^* describes only the even-length strings.
By Kleene’s theorem (§3.7), the regular languages are exactly the languages that DFAs accept. Regular expressions have no symbol for \cap or complement, but regular languages are closed under both anyway — the DFA view proves it (Corollary 3.4).
Designing a regular expression


                  
                  Recipe — from a description to a regular expression 
                  
                


List short examples, in and out of the language, including \varepsilon and every string of length 1 and 2.
Find blocks. Cut a typical string into pieces that a star can repeat — runs, or chunks that end at each 1 — and handle the beginning and the end separately.
Write the expression piece by piece, and explain each piece in English. Homework requires the explanation, and it is how you catch your own mistakes.
Test both directions: every string the expression generates is in the language (nothing extra), and every string in the language is generated (nothing missing). Check \varepsilon explicitly.
“And” is hard. Expressions have no \cap. Refine the blocks until both conditions can be read off them (Example 2), or build a product DFA and convert it (Chapter 4).




two strings split into blocks: 0 100 0 100 100 0, and 10 0 0 10 followed by a final 1w010001001000010001001000∈ (0+100)*w10001011000101∈ ((0+10)(0+10))*(ε+1)pair 1pair 2final 1Designing by blocks. Top: a string in which every 1 is followed by 00 splits uniquely into blocks 0 and 100, so the language is (0+100)*. Bottom: a string with no 11 splits into blocks 0 and 10, possibly followed by one final 1; each block holds exactly one 0, so an even number of 0s means an even number of blocks — they come in pairs.


                  
                  Example 1 — every 1 is immediately followed by 00
                  
                

Idea. Each 1 must be followed by 00, so each 1 starts a block 100; these blocks cannot overlap, because a block’s second and third symbols are 0s. Every other symbol is a 0 standing alone.
Answer: (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{100})^*.
In English: \mathtt{100} is a 1 together with the two 0s it requires; \mathtt{0} is a 0 that belongs to no 1; the star allows any sequence of these blocks, in any order. The empty sequence gives \varepsilon, which is in the language because it has no 1 that could violate the condition.
Test: \varepsilon, 0, 100, 1000 and 0100100 match; 1, 10, 11 and 1001 do not, and none of them is in the language.
A wrong answer: (\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{100})^* forces every non-empty string to end with the block 100, so it misses 0, 00, 1000 and infinitely many other strings of the language.




                  
                  Example 2 — an even number of 0s and no substring 11
                  
                

Idea. In a string without 11, every 1 except possibly the last symbol is immediately followed by a 0. So the string splits into blocks 0 and 10, possibly followed by one final 1: the strings without 11 are exactly (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{1}). Each block contains exactly one 0 and the final 1 contains none, so the number of 0s equals the number of blocks — and it is even exactly when the blocks come in pairs.
Answer: \big((\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})\big)^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{1}).
In English: (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}) is two consecutive blocks, each a single 0 possibly preceded by one 1, and so contains two 0s and no 11; the star repeats such pairs; (\varepsilon+\mathtt{1}) allows one final 1, which cannot create 11 because every block ends with 0.
Test: \varepsilon, 1, 00, 010 and 1001 match; 0, 11, 101 and 0110 do not, and none of them is in the language.
Two wrong answers: dropping (\varepsilon+\mathtt{1}) misses 1, 001, 00001, …; and (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{1}) ignores the parity, so it also matches 0, 000, 00000, …. Both are wrong on infinitely many strings.




                  
                  How a regular expression is graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams ask for a regular expression (together with a DFA, Chapter 3) for a described language, with no proof required.
