The standard rubric, out of 10 points: 2 for syntax and 8 for correctness, with exam deductions twice the homework ones — 2 for one mistake (typically a missing or extra \varepsilon), 4 for a few wrong strings, and all 8 if infinitely many strings are wrong, as in each of the wrong answers above. An answer of \varnothing or \Sigma^* earns no credit. Homework answers must also explain each piece in English, as the examples do.


Concept pages: regular-languages, regular-expressions.
2.4 Things that aren’t regular expressions
Programming languages and editors provide regexen: patterns with many conveniences. In most of them + means “one or more”, union is written |, ? means “optional”, {2,3} means “two or three times”, [01] is a character class, and \1 refers back to an earlier group. Most of these are abbreviations — 0+ is \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*, 0? is \varepsilon+\mathtt{0}, 0{2,3} is \mathtt{00}(\mathtt{0}+\varepsilon) — but back-references are not. The regex (.*)\1 matches exactly the strings of the form ww, and \{ww \mid w\in\Sigma^*\} is not regular: \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} is an infinite fooling set for it, because the suffix \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} completes \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} to a square but not \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1} for j\ne i (§3.8). So a regex is not necessarily a regular expression. Shell globs (*.md, file?.txt) go the other way: they are much weaker than regular expressions.


                  
                  Use only the real syntax 
                  
                

A regular expression in this course is built from \varnothing, strings (including \varepsilon), + for union, concatenation, ^* and parentheses — nothing else. Write RR^* for “one or more copies of R” (the regex 0+1 means \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}, but the regular expression \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1} means “0 or 1”). There is no \cap, no complement, and no counter: \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n is not a regular expression, and \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\} is not even regular (Lemma 3.6).


2.5 Regular expression trees


                  
                  Definition — expression tree, size, subexpression 
                  
                

A regular expression tree is a leaf labeled \varnothing; a leaf labeled with a string; a node labeled {+} or {\bullet} with two subtrees; or a node labeled ^* with one subtree. (The cases mirror the definition of regular languages exactly.) The size of an expression is the number of nodes in its tree. A subexpression of R is an expression whose tree is a subtree of some tree for R; a proper subexpression is any subexpression other than R itself.


“Some tree” because concatenation and union are associative: \mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00} can be grouped as \mathtt{1}\bullet\big((\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}\big) or as \big(\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\big)\bullet\mathtt{00}, and both trees are fine.

expression tree with root plus, children 0 and a concatenation of 1 with the concatenation of a star of 0 plus 1 and the leaf 00R = 0+1(0+1)*000101+*00••+subexpression (0+1)*00rootsize 10: five internal nodes (+, •, •, *, +) and five leaves (0, 1, 0, 1, 00)The expression tree of 0+1(0+1)*00. Star binds tightest and + loosest, so the root is the + and the string 00 is a single leaf. Every subtree is a subexpression; the red one is (0+1)*00. The substring 0+1(0+1)* is a well-formed expression too, but no subtree spells it, so it is not a subexpression.
The size counts operators, including the invisible concatenations, but not parentheses: \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00} has 11 characters but size 10, and the book’s tree for the multiples-of-3 expression \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0})^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^* has 29 nodes for 22 characters.
Subexpression vs. substring. Every subexpression is a substring of R, but a substring that happens to be a well-formed expression need not be a subexpression. In the book’s example, \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} is a subexpression, but \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} and \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0} are not. Any expression can be parsed into its tree in linear time, so algorithms (and proofs) may assume they are handed the tree.
2.6 Proofs about regular expressions
To prove something about every regular expression, induct on its structure: the tree, not the characters. There are five cases, one for each kind of root, and the induction hypothesis covers the subtrees.

five small trees: a leaf empty set, a leaf string w, a plus node over S and T, a concatenation node over S and T, a star node over S∅w(a string, maybe ε)+ST•ST*SR = ∅R = wR = S + TR = S • TR = S*base casesthe hypothesis applies to S and TThe five shapes of a regular expression. The root of an expression tree is a leaf (∅ or a string) or one of the operators +, • and *. In the last three cases S and T are proper subexpressions — strictly smaller trees — so a structural induction may assume the claim for them.


                  
                  Template — induction on regular expressions 
                  
                

Let R be an arbitrary regular expression. 
Assume that every proper subexpression of R [has the property]. 
There are five cases to consider. 
Case R = \varnothing. … Therefore R [has the property]. 
Case R is a single string w (possibly \varepsilon). … Therefore R [has the property]. 
Case R = S+T for some regular expressions S and T. The induction hypothesis implies that S and T [have the property]. … 
Case R = ST for some regular expressions S and T. The induction hypothesis implies that S and T [have the property]. … 
Case R = S^* for some regular expression S. The induction hypothesis implies that S [has the property]. … 
In all five cases, R [has the property]. \blacksquare


If structural induction feels unfamiliar, induct on the size instead: “assume every regular expression smaller than R has the property”. The cases are identical, because S and T are smaller than S+T, ST and S^*.


                  
                  Lemma 2.4 
                  
                

If a regular expression does not use the symbol \varnothing, then its language is not empty.




                  
                  Proof of Lemma 2.4 — the model to copy 
                  
                

Let R be an arbitrary regular expression that does not use \varnothing. Assume that every proper subexpression of R that does not use \varnothing represents a non-empty language. There are five cases.

R = \varnothing. This case is impossible, because R does not use \varnothing.
R is a single string w. Then w\in L(R) = \{w\}, so L(R) is non-empty.
R = S+T. S is a proper subexpression of R, and it does not use \varnothing because R does not. So the induction hypothesis gives a string x\in L(S), and x\in L(S)\cup L(T) = L(R).
R = ST. Neither S nor T uses \varnothing, so the induction hypothesis gives strings x\in L(S) and y\in L(T). Then xy\in L(S)\bullet L(T) = L(R).
R = S^*. \varepsilon\in L(S)^* = L(R) by the definition of Kleene star. (The induction hypothesis is not needed.)

In all five cases, L(R) is non-empty. \blacksquare


The converse is false: \varnothing^* and \mathtt{0}+\varnothing use \varnothing, yet L(\varnothing^*) = \{\varepsilon\} and L(\mathtt{0}+\varnothing) = \{\mathtt{0}\}.


                  
                  The star case: the hypothesis covers S, not S^*
                  
                

In the case R = S^*, the expression S^* is R, so the hypothesis says nothing about it. Unrolling L(S^*) = \{\varepsilon\}\cup L(S)\bullet L(S^*) and then “applying the hypothesis to S^*” is circular. When the star case needs real work, use what the hypothesis gives about S, plus a second induction on the number of pieces: every string in L(S)^* is x_1x_2\cdots x_k with each x_i\in L(S).


2.7 Proofs about regular languages
A language is just a set: it has no recursive structure to induct on, and “smaller” means nothing useful — a subset of a regular language need not even be regular (\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mid n\ge0\}\subseteq(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*). So to prove that every regular language has a property, let L be regular, choose a regular expression R with L(R) = L (one exists by definition), and prove the property by induction on R.


                  
                  Lemma 2.5 
                  
                

Every regular language other than \varnothing is the language of some regular expression that does not use the symbol \varnothing.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

A structural induction proves a claim about every regular expression, and the subexpressions of an expression with a non-empty language can have empty languages (the \varnothing in \mathtt{0}+\varnothing). So state the claim in a form that holds for all of them: for every regular expression R, either L(R) = \varnothing, or L(R) = L(R') for some regular expression R' that does not use \varnothing. Assume the claim for every proper subexpression of R.

R = \varnothing: L(R) = \varnothing.
R is a string: R' = R itself.
R = S+T: if L(S) and L(T) are both empty, so is L(R). If only L(T) is empty, then L(R) = L(S) = L(S') for the \varnothing-free S' given by the hypothesis; symmetrically if only L(S) is empty. If neither is empty, R' = S'+T'.
R = ST: if L(S) or L(T) is empty, then L(R) = \varnothing by Lemma 2.1(c). Otherwise R' = S'T'.
R = S^*: if L(S) = \varnothing, then L(R) = \varnothing^* = \{\varepsilon\}, so R' = \varepsilon. Otherwise R' = (S')^*.

For a non-empty regular language L = L(R), the first alternative is impossible, so R' is the expression the lemma asks for. For example, \varnothing^* becomes \varepsilon, (\mathtt{0}+\varnothing)\mathtt{1} becomes \mathtt{01}, and \mathtt{0}\varnothing+\mathtt{1}^* becomes \mathtt{1}^*. \blacksquare


Stating the claim so that it covers every object the hypothesis will be applied to — here every subexpression, even one with an empty language — is the same move as quantifying over all arguments in §1.4, or proving a claim for every state of a DFA in §3.3.


                  
                  Structural recursion builds new expressions — reversal 
                  
                

Define \textsf{rev}(R) by recursion on R: \textsf{rev}(\varnothing) := \varnothing, \textsf{rev}(w) := w^R, \textsf{rev}(S+T) := \textsf{rev}(S)+\textsf{rev}(T), \textsf{rev}(ST) := \textsf{rev}(T)\,\textsf{rev}(S) (order swapped), and \textsf{rev}(S^*) := \textsf{rev}(S)^*. A structural induction, using (xy)^R = y^Rx^R from Chapter 1, proves L(\textsf{rev}(R)) = \{w^R \mid w\in L(R)\}. So the reversal of every regular language is regular. For example, \textsf{rev}\big(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}\big) = \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{00}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1}.


This is one of two standard ways to prove that a transformed language is regular; the other modifies a DFA (§4.9, language-transformations).
2.8 Not every language is regular
A counting argument shows that regular languages are rare, without exhibiting a single non-regular one. Work over the one-symbol alphabet \{\mathtt{1}\}.

Countably many regular languages. A regular expression over \{\mathtt{1}\} is a string over the seven symbols \mathtt{1}, +, (, ), ^*, \varepsilon, \varnothing. Read these symbols as the digits 1 to 7 and the expression as a base-8 numeral: different expressions get different positive integers. So the regular expressions, and therefore the regular languages, can be listed in a sequence.
Uncountably many languages. Write each real number 0\le\alpha<1 in binary as \alpha = 0.b_1b_2b_3\ldots (never ending in infinitely many 1s), and let L_\alpha := \{\mathtt{1}^n \mid b_{n+1} = 1\}. Different reals have different expansions, so different \alpha give different languages — and there are uncountably many reals in [0,1).

So all but countably many languages over \{\mathtt{1}\} are not regular. The same argument works for context-free grammars (§5.6) and for Turing machines (Chapter 7). A specific non-regular language needs a specific proof: the fooling sets of §3.8. One curious example: the set of all regular expressions over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} is itself a non-regular language, because its parentheses must balance — the prefixes (^i and (^j are distinguished by the suffix \mathtt{0})^i.
Concept page: counting-arguments.
Summary

A language is any set of strings; \varnothing (no strings), \{\varepsilon\} (one string) and \varepsilon (a string) are three different things.
AB, L^* and L^+ build new languages. Lemmas 2.1–2.2 are their algebra; concatenation is not commutative and does not distribute over \cap.
Arden’s rule: if \varepsilon\notin A, then L = AL\cup B if and only if L = A^*B — enough to turn a small DFA into an expression.
Regular languages are built from \varnothing and single strings by {\cup}, {\bullet} and {}^*; regular expressions write them down, with precedence ^*, then concatenation, then +.
Design expressions by cutting strings into blocks; explain every piece in English; test \varepsilon and short strings in both directions.
An expression is really a tree; subexpressions are subtrees, not arbitrary well-formed substrings.
Structural induction has five cases (\varnothing, string, S+T, ST, S^*); the claim must hold for every subexpression, even one with an empty language (Lemma 2.5). Prove facts about regular languages through an expression that represents them.
There are countably many regular languages but uncountably many languages.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Midterm 1 (Sep 28) covered languages, regular languages and regular expressions. On Midterm-1-style exams, the DFA problem also asks for a regular expression for the same language, graded as described above; the regular-language-transformation problem is graded as a construction of an automaton from an arbitrary DFA (§4.9), the automaton-side version of the structural recursion in §2.7; and the true/false part (each answer with a one-sentence justification) tests this chapter’s algebra and definitions — "\varnothing^* = \varnothing" (false: it is \{\varepsilon\}), ”L^+ = L^* for every language L” (false for L = \{\mathtt{0}\}), ”(\mathtt{10})^* and \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^* are equivalent” (false). The final exam (Dec 11) covers everything. Rubric details: how exams are graded.




                  
                  Practice this chapter 
                  
                

8 practice problems — 3 easy, 3 medium, 2 hard — each with a folded hint and a worked solution. Start with 2.1 Empty things, products and stars; the practice hub has the whole bank by difficulty and by topic.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 2 (§§2.1–2.8), summarized in our own words. The HOCUSPOCUS and \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{11}\}^* examples, Lemmas 2.1–2.5 with the proofs of Lemmas 2.4 and 2.5, the table of examples, the equivalent forms of (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*, the size-29 expression tree, regexen and globs, and the counting argument follow the book. The proof of Arden’s rule and its examples, the figures, the two design examples with their wrong answers, the reversal example (which anticipates Lemma 4.4), and the counterexamples in the traps are original. CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) regular-expression rubric for the grading notes. Every regular expression on this page is checked for exact equivalence with an automaton built from its English description, and every identity and example by brute force, in tools/checks/ch02.py.

1-models-of-computation/03-finite-state-.title: Chapter 3 — Finite-State Machines
1-models-of-computation/03-finite-state-.content:
Chapter 3 · book pp. 31–54 · chapter PDF · prev: Chapter 2 · next: Chapter 4 · practice: 10 problems


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

A DFA is an algorithm that reads its input once, left to right, and remembers only a constant amount of information: its current state. DFAs accept exactly the regular languages (Kleene’s theorem, proved in Chapter 4). Running two DFAs in parallel — the product construction — shows that regular languages are closed under every boolean operation. To show a language is not regular, exhibit an infinite fooling set; the Myhill–Nerode theorem says this method always works, and Moore’s algorithm finds the smallest DFA.


3.1 Intuition: a DFA is a loop with constant memory
Is a bit string a binary multiple of 5? Scan it once, keeping only the value of the prefix read so far, mod 5. Reading bit a turns the value v into 2v + a, so the remainder q becomes (2q + a) \bmod 5:
rem ← 0
for each bit a of w, left to right:
    rem ← (2·rem + a) mod 5
return rem = 0

The variable \mathit{rem} has five possible values. Those five values are the states of a DFA, one loop iteration is the transition function \delta(q,a) = (2q+a)\bmod 5, and the return condition is the set of accepting states \{0\}.

DFA with states 0 to 4 for binary multiples of 5011001100101234Binary multiples of 5. State q is the value of the prefix read so far, mod 5; reading the bit a moves to (2q + a) mod 5. The start state 0 is the only accepting state.
On input 00101110110 (which is 374 in binary) the machine visits 0,0,0,1,2,0,1,3,1,3,2,4 and ends in state 4, so it rejects — indeed 374 = 5\cdot 74 + 4. The empty string ends in the start state 0 and is accepted, so the machine treats \varepsilon as a numeral for 0.
3.2 Formal definitions


                  
                  Definition — deterministic finite-state automaton (DFA) 
                  
                

A DFA is a tuple M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta):

\Sigma — the input alphabet (finite);
Q — a finite set of states;
s\in Q — the start state;
A\subseteq Q — the accepting states;
\delta\colon Q\times\Sigma\to Q — the transition function, defined for every state and every symbol.

The extended transition function \delta^*\colon Q\times\Sigma^*\to Q follows the recursive definition of strings:
\delta^*(q, w) := \begin{cases} q & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ \delta^*(\delta(q,a),\,x) & \text{if } w = ax.\end{cases}
M accepts w iff \delta^*(s,w)\in A, and the language of M is L(M) := \{w\in\Sigma^* \mid \delta^*(s,w)\in A\}. A language is automatic if it is L(M) for some DFA M.


As a graph, a DFA is a directed graph whose vertices are the states and in which every state has exactly one outgoing edge per symbol. Every string traces exactly one walk from s; the DFA accepts if the walk ends in A. Two identities, each a short string induction, get used constantly:
\delta^*(q, xy) = \delta^*\big(\delta^*(q,x),\,y\big), \qquad \delta^*(q, xa) = \delta\big(\delta^*(q,x),\,a\big).


                  
                  A DFA's transition function is total 
                  
                

Every state needs an outgoing edge for every symbol. Drawings usually omit the dump state (a non-accepting state that loops to itself on every symbol); that is fine on an exam only if you say so — “all missing transitions go to a dump state”. An automaton with missing edges and no such sentence is an incomplete DFA (or an NFA, which earns half credit where a DFA was asked for).


Concept page: dfa.
3.3 Proving a DFA correct

two-state DFA for strings with an odd number of 1s0011stAn odd number of 1s. s means “even so far”, t means “odd so far”. A 0 never changes the parity; a 1 always flips it.
The two-state DFA above should accept exactly the strings with an odd number of 1s. To prove that, give every state a meaning and prove all the meanings at once. Here the meaning of s is “even number of 1s so far” and of t is “odd so far”. The claim needs both start states, because peeling the first symbol of w moves the machine to a different state:


                  
                  Claim (stronger than needed) 
                  
                

For every string w: if \#(\mathtt{1},w) is even, then \delta^*(s,w) = s and \delta^*(t,w) = t; if \#(\mathtt{1},w) is odd, then \delta^*(s,w) = t and \delta^*(t,w) = s.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) — a model string induction 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string, and assume the claim for every string shorter than w. There are three cases.

w = \varepsilon. \#(\mathtt{1},\varepsilon) = 0 is even, and \delta^*(s,\varepsilon) = s, \delta^*(t,\varepsilon) = t by the definition of \delta^*.
w = \mathtt{0}x. Then \#(\mathtt{1},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},x), and \delta^*(s,w) = \delta^*(\delta(s,\mathtt{0}),x) = \delta^*(s,x), \delta^*(t,w) = \delta^*(t,x). The induction hypothesis for x (shorter than w) gives exactly the claim for w.
w = \mathtt{1}x. Then \#(\mathtt{1},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},x)+1 has the opposite parity, and \delta^*(s,w) = \delta^*(t,x), \delta^*(t,w) = \delta^*(s,x). If \#(\mathtt{1},x) is even, the hypothesis gives \delta^*(t,x)=t and \delta^*(s,x)=s, so \delta^*(s,w)=t and \delta^*(t,w)=s — correct, because \#(\mathtt{1},w) is odd. The odd case is symmetric.

In every case the claim holds for w. Since A = \{t\}, M accepts w iff \delta^*(s,w) = t iff \#(\mathtt{1},w) is odd. \blacksquare




                  
                  Template — proving L(M) = L for a DFA
                  
                


Give each state q a meaning P_q, and claim: ”\delta^*(s,w) = q if and only if w has property P_q.”
Induct on w. Either peel the first symbol (w = ax) — then state the claim for every possible start state, as above — or peel the last symbol (w = xa) and use \delta^*(s,xa) = \delta(\delta^*(s,x),a), which needs the claim only from s.
Conclude: w\in L(M) \iff \delta^*(s,w)\in A \iff w has one of the accepting properties \iff w\in L.



On exams that ask only for a DFA (“no proof required”), the state meanings still matter: they are what the mnemonic state names are supposed to convey.
3.4 Real-world examples
Anything with finitely many configurations that changes in response to discrete inputs is a finite-state machine: a railway clock (720 states, one input “tick”), a Rubik’s cube (about 5.2\times10^{20} states, one input symbol per quarter turn, start and accept in the solved state), a vending machine, a traffic light. The number of states may be astronomical; what matters is that it is finite and fixed in advance, independent of the input length.
3.5 Designing DFAs: DFAs are algorithms


                  
                  Recipe — design a DFA by writing the algorithm first 
                  
                


Write a single left-to-right loop over the input that uses a fixed number of variables, each with a fixed, finite set of possible values (known before the input arrives — no counters that grow with n).
States = all combinations of variable values. Start state = their initial values.
Transition function = one iteration of the loop body.
Accepting states = the combinations for which the final test returns true.
Drop states that are unreachable; merge states only when it makes the machine clearer.
Name each state after what it remembers (“last symbol was 1”, “seen 11”, “remainder 3”).



Example: strings containing 11. A first algorithm keeps a flag \mathit{found}\in\{\textsf{F},\textsf{T}\} and the last two symbols read (\varepsilon, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11): 2\times7 = 14 states, start (\textsf{F},\varepsilon), accepting every (\textsf{T},\cdot). It is correct but wasteful — only 10 of those states are reachable, and only the previous symbol matters (keeping just the last symbol leaves 5 reachable states). Thinking a little more gives the minimal machine:

three-state DFA for strings containing 1101010,1sabStrings containing 11, minimal DFA. s: no 11 yet and the last symbol (if any) is not 1; a: no 11 yet and the last symbol is 1; b: 11 has appeared (a sink: it never leaves).
Clarity beats minimality. A larger DFA whose states have obvious meanings is easier to get right, easier to explain, and earns the same credit; there is no prize for hand-minimizing.


                  
                  What can a DFA not remember?
                  
                

Anything that grows with the input: a count of 0s, the first half of the string, a stack of open parentheses. “Read once, constant memory” is the whole model — if your algorithm needs an unbounded counter, the language is probably not regular, and §3.8 shows how to prove it.


3.6 The product construction
Two DFAs over the same alphabet can run in parallel: the combined machine remembers one state of each.


                  
                  Definition — product construction 
                  
                

Given DFAs M_1 = (\Sigma, Q_1, s_1, A_1, \delta_1) and M_2 = (\Sigma, Q_2, s_2, A_2, \delta_2), define M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) with
Q := Q_1\times Q_2,\qquad s := (s_1, s_2),\qquad \delta\big((p,q),a\big) := \big(\delta_1(p,a),\,\delta_2(q,a)\big).
Only the accepting set depends on what you want:

























languageaccepting states AL_1\cap L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ and } q\in A_2\}L_1\cup L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ or } q\in A_2\}L_1\setminus L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ and } q\notin A_2\}L_1\oplus L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ xor } q\in A_2\}
The complement needs only one machine: keep M_1 and accept Q_1\setminus A_1.




                  
                  Lemma 3.1 
                  
                

\delta^*\big((p,q),w\big) = \big(\delta_1^*(p,w),\,\delta_2^*(q,w)\big) for every string w and all states p\in Q_1, q\in Q_2.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

Induction on w. If w = \varepsilon, both sides equal (p,q). If w = ax, then
\delta^*\big((p,q),ax\big) = \delta^*\big(\delta((p,q),a),\,x\big) = \delta^*\big((\delta_1(p,a),\delta_2(q,a)),\,x\big) = \big(\delta_1^*(\delta_1(p,a),x),\ \delta_2^*(\delta_2(q,a),x)\big),
by the definitions of \delta^* and \delta and then the induction hypothesis for x (which holds for every pair of states — that is why the lemma quantifies over all p, q). The last expression is \big(\delta_1^*(p,ax),\,\delta_2^*(q,ax)\big) by the definition of \delta^*. \blacksquare



four-state product DFA arranged in a 2 by 2 grid(parity of 0s, parity of 1s)11110000(E,E)(E,O)(O,E)(O,O)The product of two parity DFAs. The first component tracks the parity of 0s (E/O), the second the parity of 1s. A 0 moves vertically, a 1 horizontally. With accepting set {(E, O)} the product accepts “even number of 0s and odd number of 1s”; other accepting sets give ∪, \, ⊕ of the same two languages.
Cascading products handles any boolean combination of finitely many regular languages: “contains 11, has even length, and does not end in 0” is a product of three small machines.


                  
                  How a product construction is graded 
                  
                

The description must define each factor completely (its states, start, accepting states and transitions — or a drawing of it) and then the product’s states, start state, transition function and accepting set. “Run both machines in parallel” alone earns little. Name the product’s states by their components, as in (\textsf{E},\textsf{O}) above.


Concept page: product-construction.
3.7 Closure properties


                  
                  Theorem 3.2 
                  
                

If L and L' are automatic (over the same alphabet), then so are \overline{L} = \Sigma^*\setminus L, L\cup L', L\cap L', L\setminus L' and L\oplus L'.




                  
                  Theorem 3.3 (Kleene) 
                  
                

For every regular expression R there is a DFA M with L(M) = L(R), and for every DFA M there is a regular expression R with L(R) = L(M). (Proved in Chapter 4.)


So “automatic” is just another word for regular, and the two theorems combine:

Corollary 3.4. Regular languages are closed under complement, intersection, difference and symmetric difference. (Regular expressions have no symbol for \cap or complement — the DFA view proves it.)
Corollary 3.5. Automatic languages are closed under concatenation and Kleene star. (Easy for regular expressions, awkward for DFAs — until NFAs arrive.)



                  
                  Three ways to prove that a language is regular 
                  
                


Give a regular expression for it (Chapter 2).
Give a DFA — or an NFA (Chapter 4) — for it.
Build it from languages already known to be regular with closure properties: boolean operations, concatenation, star, reversal, and the transformations of §4.9.



The conversions between the three descriptions always exist but can be exponential (and sometimes must be). Full table: closure-properties.
3.8 Proving a language is not regular
A DFA has no memory except its state. If two strings x and y lead to the same state, then every continuation z leads xz and yz to the same final state:
\delta^*(s,x) = \delta^*(s,y)\ \Longrightarrow\ \delta^*(s,xz) = \delta^*(s,yz)\ \text{ for every } z\ \Longrightarrow\ \big(xz\in L \iff yz\in L\big).

schematic: strings x and y reach the same state q, then z leads to rsqrxyzsame stateWhy a distinguishing suffix forces two states. If x and y led to the same state q, then xz and yz would end in the same state r, so the DFA would accept both or neither. A suffix z with exactly one of xz, yz in L rules that out.


                  
                  Definition — distinguishing suffix, fooling set 
                  
                

A distinguishing suffix for x and y (with respect to L) is a string z such that exactly one of xz and yz is in L. A fooling set for L is a set F of strings such that every pair of distinct strings in F has a distinguishing suffix.




                  
                  Fooling sets give lower bounds 
                  
                

If F is a fooling set for L, then every DFA for L has at least \lvert F\rvert states, because no two strings of F can end in the same state. In particular: if L has an infinite fooling set, then L is not regular.


A finite example. F = \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{10}, \mathtt{11}, \mathtt{100}\} (the numbers 0–4) is a fooling set for the binary multiples of 5: for instance z = \mathtt{01} distinguishes 1 and 11, because 101 =5 is a multiple of 5 and 1101 =13 is not. So the 5-state DFA of §3.1 is as small as possible.


                  
                  Template — fooling-set proof (as in Lemma 3.6) 
                  
                

Let F =  [an explicit infinite set, e.g. \mathtt{0}^*]. 
Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F. 
The definition of F implies x =  […] and y =  […] for some integers i\ne j. 
Let z =  [a suffix that may depend on i and j]. 
Then xz =  […] \in L, because […]. 
And yz =  […] \notin L, because […]. 
So z distinguishes x and y. We conclude that F is a fooling set for L. 
Because F is infinite, L cannot be regular. \blacksquare




                  
                  Lemma 3.6 — \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\} is not regular
                  
                

Let F = \mathtt{0}^*. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F; then x = \mathtt{0}^i and y = \mathtt{0}^j for some integers i\ne j. Let z = \mathtt{1}^i. Then xz = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\in L. And yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i\notin L, because j\ne i. So F is a fooling set for L, and since F is infinite, L is not regular.


The same skeleton handles the standard examples; only F and z change. (For x\ne y written with i\ne j.)








































language Lfooling set Fdistinguishing suffix\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\} (Lemma 3.6)\mathtt{0}^*x = \mathtt{0}^i: z = \mathtt{1}^i\{ww^R \mid w\in\Sigma^*\} (Lemma 3.7)\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}x = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}: z = \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^i\{\mathtt{0}^{2^n} \mid n\ge0\} (Lemma 3.8)L itselfx = \mathtt{0}^{2^i}: z = \mathtt{0}^{2^i} (then 2^i+2^j is not a power of 2)\{w \mid \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w)\}\mathtt{0}^*x = \mathtt{0}^i: z = \mathtt{1}^i\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{2}^n \mid n\ge0\}\mathtt{0}^*x = \mathtt{0}^i: z = \mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{2}^i\{\mathtt{0}^p \mid p \text{ prime}\} (Lemma 3.9)\mathtt{0}^*a cleverer z — see the book
Choosing F. The fooling set usually comes from the unbounded quantity that any algorithm for L “obviously” has to remember — a count, a prefix, a position. Good candidates are a simple regular language with one star and no union (\mathtt{0}^*, \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}, (\mathtt{01})^*) or L itself. You choose F, so you may impose structure that L lacks: for “equally many 0s and 1s” we only ever use strings of the form \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j.
The closure alternative. If L were regular, then L\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* would be regular too (Corollary 3.4). For L = \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w)\} that intersection is \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}, which is not regular — so neither is L. This only works in that direction: a regular intersection proves nothing about L.


                  
                  Where fooling-set proofs lose points 
                  
                


One example pair is not a proof. The argument must work for arbitrary distinct x, y\in F, written with parameters i\ne j.
Check both halves: xz\in L and yz\notin L, each with a reason. “Clearly” is not a reason.
i < j needs a justification. Assume it only if you say “without loss of generality” and the argument really is symmetric — the suffix z = \mathtt{1}^i above is built from x, so swapping x and y changes it.
The set must be infinite and explicit. “Let F be the set of all prefixes we need” is not a set; a finite fooling set proves only a lower bound on the number of states.
z may depend on x and y, but not on anything else (in particular not on a DFA you are trying to rule out).





                  
                  How a fooling-set proof is graded 
                  
                

4 points for an explicit infinite set that really is a fooling set (a finite set earns nothing); 6 for the argument with arbitrary distinct x, y: 2 for an explicit suffix, 2 for showing one of xz, yz is in L, 2 for showing the other is not.


Concept page: fooling-sets.
3.9 The Myhill–Nerode theorem
Write x\equiv_L y when no suffix distinguishes x and y: xz\in L\iff yz\in L for every string z. This is an equivalence relation, and its classes are exactly “what an algorithm for L must remember”.


                  
                  The Myhill–Nerode theorem 
                  
                

For every language L, the following three numbers are equal (possibly all infinite):

the minimum number of states of a DFA that accepts L;
the maximum size of a fooling set for L;
the number of equivalence classes of \equiv_L.

In particular, L is regular if and only if every fooling set for L is finite. So a non-regularity proof by fooling set always exists — the only question is finding it.




                  
                  Proof sketch (click to expand) 
                  
                

(1) ≥ (2) is the fooling-set argument above. (2) = (3): a fooling set is exactly a set containing at most one string from each class. (1) ≤ (3): build a DFA whose states are the classes, Q = \{[w] \mid w\in\Sigma^*\}, with start [\varepsilon], accepting states \{[w] \mid w\in L\}, and \delta([w],a) = [wa]. This is well defined because x\equiv_L y implies xa\equiv_L ya, and \delta^*([\varepsilon],w) = [w] by induction, so the machine accepts exactly L. \blacksquare


Concept page: myhill-nerode-theorem.
3.10 Minimal automata: Moore’s algorithm
Two states p and q are distinguishable if some string z leads exactly one of them to an accepting state. Recursively: p and q are distinguishable if exactly one of them is accepting, or if \delta(p,a) and \delta(q,a) are distinguishable for some symbol a.


                  
                  Moore's algorithm (table filling) 
                  
                


Delete every state that is unreachable from s (graph search, O(n\sigma) time for n = \lvert Q\rvert, \sigma = \lvert\Sigma\rvert).
Mark every pair \{p, q\} with exactly one accepting state.
Repeat passes: mark \{p,q\} whenever \{\delta(p,a),\delta(q,a)\} is already marked for some symbol a. Stop after a pass that marks nothing (at most n passes, O(\sigma n^3) time in all).
Merge each group of mutually unmarked (equivalent) states. The result is the minimal DFA.

This is dynamic programming for “some string of length \le k distinguishes p and q”. Faster versions exist: O(\sigma n^2), and Hopcroft’s O(\sigma n\log n).


Example. Counting 1s mod 6 and accepting counts 0 and 3 decides “the number of 1s is a multiple of 3” with six states. Step 2 marks the 8 pairs between \{0,3\} and \{1,2,4,5\}. The first pass marks \{1,2\}, \{1,5\}, \{2,4\} and \{4,5\} (for example, reading 1 sends \{1,2\} to the marked pair \{2,3\}). The second pass marks nothing: \{0,3\}, \{1,4\} and \{2,5\} only ever lead to each other. Merging them leaves three states.

six-state ring DFA and the three-state DFA after merging equivalent states⟹6 states (count of 1s mod 6)3 states after merging111111111012345{0,3}{1,4}{2,5}Minimizing a wasteful DFA. Counting 1s mod 6 decides “the number of 1s is a multiple of 3”, but states i and i+3 can never be distinguished, so Moore's algorithm merges them. (Every state also loops on 0; those loops are omitted.)
Concept page: dfa-minimization.
Summary

A DFA (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) is a one-pass algorithm with a fixed, finite memory; \delta is total.
Prove a DFA correct by giving every state a meaning and proving all meanings together by induction.
Design by brute force: states = values of the loop’s variables; name them by what they remember.
Product construction: Q_1\times Q_2, run in parallel; the accepting set chooses \cap, \cup, \setminus, \oplus. Regular languages are closed under all boolean operations.
Not regular ⇔ an infinite fooling set exists (Myhill–Nerode). Write the proof with arbitrary x\ne y, an explicit z, and both membership checks.
Moore’s algorithm merges indistinguishable states; the minimal DFA is unique up to renaming.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams test this chapter three ways. DFA design (usually alongside a regular expression for the same language): mnemonic state names, a start arrow, double circles, and an explicit sentence about any omitted dump state; no proof needed unless asked. Non-regularity by fooling set, often paired with a context-free grammar for the same language (Chapter 5). True/false items such as “if L has a fooling set of size 5, every DFA for \overline{L} has at least 5 states” (true — the same suffixes distinguish the strings for \overline L). Rubric details: how exams are graded.




                  
                  Practice this chapter 
                  
                

10 practice problems — 4 easy, 3 medium, 3 hard — each with a folded hint and a worked solution. Start with 3.1 Closure and fooling-set verdicts; the practice hub has the whole bank by difficulty and by topic.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 3 (§§3.1–3.10), summarized in our own words; the multiples-of-5, odd-number-of-1s and contains-11 examples and the fooling sets of Lemmas 3.6–3.8 follow the book. The product and mod-6 minimization examples are original. CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) standard rubrics for the grading notes. Every automaton, run, fooling set and table-filling pass on this page is checked by tools/checks/ch03.py.

1-models-of-computation/04-nondeterminis.content:
Chapter 4 · book pp. 55–76 · chapter PDF · prev: Chapter 3 · next: Chapter 5 · practice: 10 problems


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

An NFA may have several transitions — or none — for the same state and symbol, and may move without reading anything (\varepsilon-transitions); it accepts a string if some sequence of choices ends in an accepting state. NFAs are no more powerful than DFAs: a DFA can track the set of states the NFA might be in (the subset construction), at a cost of up to 2^n states that is sometimes unavoidable. NFAs make Kleene’s theorem easy to prove: Thompson’s algorithm turns a regular expression into an NFA by gluing small gadgets with \varepsilon-transitions, and state elimination turns any NFA back into an expression. Above all, NFAs are the tool for proving that transformed languages are regular: start from a DFA for L and let an NFA guess whatever it cannot know. Reversal (Lemma 4.4) and \textsf{half}(L) (Lemma 4.5) are the models, and Midterm-1-style exams devote a whole problem to such constructions.


4.1 Nondeterministic state machines
A DFA has exactly one transition for each state and symbol. An NFA drops that rule: a state may have several transitions on the same symbol, or none at all. The book’s first example accepts the strings that contain 00 or 11:

four-state NFA: s loops on 0 and 1, s to a on 0, s to b on 1, a to c on 0, b to c on 1, c accepting with a loop0,10,10101sabcAn NFA for the strings that contain 00 or 11. On each symbol, s may stay put or guess that this symbol starts the pair: a 0 may move to a, a 1 to b. State a has no transition on 1 and b none on 0, so a wrong guess simply dies. State c means “pair found”; it accepts and never leaves.
On input 0110 the walk s\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}s\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}b\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}c\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}c ends in the accepting state c, so 0110 is accepted. It does not matter that other walks end elsewhere or get stuck — s\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}a is stuck at once, because a has no transition on 1. In general, if the input contains 00, some walk waits in s until the first 0 of the pair and then moves to a and c; if it contains neither 00 nor 11, a walk that moves to a or b gets stuck on the next symbol (if there is one), and no walk reaches c.


                  
                  Definition — NFA 
                  
                

A nondeterministic finite-state automaton is a tuple M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) exactly like a DFA, except that the transition function returns a set of states, possibly empty: \delta\colon Q\times\Sigma\to 2^Q, where 2^Q is the set of all subsets of Q. The extended transition function \delta^*\colon Q\times\Sigma^*\to 2^Q collects the ends of all walks labeled w:
\delta^*(q, w) := \begin{cases} \{q\} & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ \displaystyle\bigcup_{r\in\delta(q,a)}\delta^*(r, x) & \text{if } w = ax.\end{cases}
M accepts w iff \delta^*(s,w)\cap A\ne\varnothing — iff some walk from s labeled w ends in an accepting state. Its language L(M) is the set of strings it accepts.


Every DFA is an NFA: replace \delta(q,a) by the one-element set \{\delta(q,a)\}. So NFAs accept every regular language; §4.5 shows that they accept nothing else.
Running an NFA by hand. Keep the set C of states the machine could be in. Start with C = \{s\}; reading a replaces C by \delta(C,a) := \bigcup_{q\in C}\delta(q,a); accept iff the final set contains an accepting state. After reading w, C is exactly \delta^*(s,w).






















































iprefix of 10010Cprefix of 0101C0\varepsilon\{s\}\varepsilon\{s\}11\{s,b\}0\{s,a\}210\{s,a\}01\{s,b\}3100\{s,a,c\}010\{s,a\}41001\{s,b,c\}0101\{s,b\}510010\{s,a,c\}
On the second symbol of 10010 the walk in b dies, because \delta(b,\mathtt{0}) = \varnothing, while s starts a new one in a; the third symbol takes that walk to c, where it stays. So 10010 is accepted. On 0101 no walk ever reaches c, because a walk that moves to a or b dies on the next symbol; the final set \{s,b\} contains no accepting state, so 0101 is rejected.


                  
                  "Some walk", not "every walk" — and swapping does not complement 
                  
                


An NFA accepts w if at least one walk labeled w ends in A. It rejects w only if every walk fails, by ending outside A or by getting stuck; a string with no complete walk at all is rejected.
Exchanging the accepting and non-accepting states does not complement an NFA. With A = \{s,a,b\} the machine above accepts every string, because the walk that never leaves s always exists. To complement an NFA, convert it to a DFA first (§4.5), then swap.



Concept page: nfa.
4.2 Intuition
Nobody builds a nondeterministic machine; nondeterminism is a compact way to describe a search. Three equivalent pictures help:


                  
                  Three ways to think about nondeterminism 
                  
                


Clairvoyance. At every choice the machine magically picks a transition that leads to acceptance, if there is one. It still cannot accept a string that has no accepting walk.
Parallel threads. Every choice spawns a new thread; a thread with no transition dies; the machine accepts if some thread is in an accepting state when the input ends. The set C of §4.1 is the set of states of the living threads.
Proofs. A prover who knows the input supplies the choices, and the machine only verifies them: every step must be a legal transition, and the last state must be accepting. w\in L(M) iff a valid proof for w exists.



The third picture can be made formal. A proof for w = a_1a_2\cdots a_n is the sequence of states \omega = r_1r_2\cdots r_n that an accepting walk visits after s, and checking it is a job for a DFA over the alphabet \Sigma\times Q of pairs. This DFA starts in s, accepts in A, and from state q the pair (a,r) leads to r if r\in\delta(q,a) and to a dump state otherwise. Then M accepts w iff some \omega\in Q^{\lvert w\rvert} makes this DFA accept (a_1,r_1)(a_2,r_2)\cdots(a_n,r_n). For the machine of §4.1, the proof for 0110 is \omega = s\,b\,c\,c.
Guessing is the design tool of this chapter. The NFA of §4.1 guesses where the pair begins; the machines of §4.9 guess a state of another machine, or the symbols of a string they never see. Wrong guesses cost nothing, because only one thread has to succeed. The same three pictures return for Turing machines in §9.5.
4.3 Epsilon-transitions
An \varepsilon-transition p\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q lets the machine move from p to q without reading anything. Now \delta\colon Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\to 2^Q, and M accepts w iff there is a walk s = q_0\xrightarrow{a_1}q_1\xrightarrow{a_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{a_\ell}q_\ell with q_\ell\in A, every a_i\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}, and a_1a_2\cdots a_\ell = w: the \varepsilon‘s vanish from the label.


                  
                  Definition — \varepsilon-reach, and \delta^* with \varepsilon-transitions
                  
                

The \varepsilon-reach of a state q is the set of states reachable from q by zero or more \varepsilon-transitions: it contains q, and with every state r it contains every state of \delta(r,\varepsilon). For a set S of states, \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S) := \bigcup_{q\in S}\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q). The extended transition function takes the \varepsilon-reach before every symbol and at the end:
\delta^*(p, w) := \begin{cases} \varepsilon\text{-reach}(p) & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ \displaystyle\bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(p)}\ \bigcup_{q\in\delta(r,a)}\delta^*(q, x) & \text{if } w = ax,\end{cases}
and M accepts w iff \delta^*(s,w)\cap A\ne\varnothing.


By hand: start with C = \varepsilon\text{-reach}(\{s\}) instead of \{s\}, and after each symbol a replace C by \varepsilon\text{-reach}\big(\delta(C,a)\big).
Example. The NFA E has states p (start), q and r (accepting); it loops on 0 at p, on 1 at q and on 0 at r, and has the \varepsilon-transitions p\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}r. It reads some 0s, then some 1s, then some 0s: L(E) = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*, the strings whose 1s form a single block. Here \varepsilon\text{-reach}(p) = \{p,q,r\} needs two steps. On 0010 the sets are \{p,q,r\}, \{p,q,r\}, \{p,q,r\}, \{q,r\}, \{r\} — accepted; on 01010 the set becomes \varnothing at the second 1.
Removing \varepsilon-transitions. An \varepsilon-move can always be merged into the symbol transition that follows it, or into the acceptance test if no symbol follows — without new states.


                  
                  Definition — \varepsilon-removal
                  
                

Given an NFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) with \varepsilon-transitions, let M' = (\Sigma, Q, s, A', \delta'), with the same states and start state and
A' := \{q\in Q \mid \varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)\cap A\ne\varnothing\},\qquad \delta'(q,a) := \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)}\delta(r,a).
Then M' has no \varepsilon-transitions, and L(M') = L(M).


For E, before and after:













































state\delta(\cdot,\mathtt{0})\delta(\cdot,\mathtt{1})\delta(\cdot,\varepsilon)\varepsilon-reach\delta'(\cdot,\mathtt{0})\delta'(\cdot,\mathtt{1})in A'?→ p\{p\}\varnothing\{q\}\{p,q,r\}\{p,r\}\{q\}yesq\varnothing\{q\}\{r\}\{q,r\}\{r\}\{q\}yesr *\{r\}\varnothing\varnothing\{r\}\{r\}\varnothingyes
The new edges p\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}q, p\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}r and q\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}r absorb \varepsilon-moves, and p and q become accepting because they reach r by \varepsilon-moves alone. So \varepsilon-transitions are a pure convenience: allow or forbid them, whichever makes a construction easier.


                  
                  Why \varepsilon-removal is correct (click to expand)
                  
                

Write (\delta')^* for the extended transition function of M', which has no \varepsilon-moves. Claim: \varepsilon\text{-reach}\big((\delta')^*(q,w)\big) = \delta^*(q,w) for every state q and string w. Induct on w. For w = \varepsilon both sides are \varepsilon\text{-reach}(q). For w = ax,
\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon\text{-reach}\big((\delta')^*(q,ax)\big) &= \bigcup_{q'\in\delta'(q,a)}\varepsilon\text{-reach}\big((\delta')^*(q',x)\big)\\
&= \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)}\ \bigcup_{q'\in\delta(r,a)}\delta^*(q',x) \;=\; \delta^*(q,ax),
\end{aligned}
by the definition of (\delta')^*, then the induction hypothesis for x together with the definition of \delta', then the definition of \delta^*. Finally, (\delta')^*(s,w) contains a state of A' iff its \varepsilon-reach meets A, iff \delta^*(s,w) meets A. \blacksquare




                  
                  Where \varepsilon-moves bite
                  
                


\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q) always contains q itself, and it follows chains of \varepsilon-moves (p\to q\to r above), not just single edges.
\varepsilon-moves count before the first symbol and after the last one: whether M accepts \varepsilon depends on \varepsilon\text{-reach}(s), not on s alone.
After removing the \varepsilon-moves, every state whose \varepsilon-reach meets A must become accepting. Keeping A' = A = \{r\} above would reject \varepsilon, 1 and 01.



Concept page: nfa.
4.4 Kleene’s theorem


                  
                  Theorem 4.1 (Kleene) 
                  
                

For every regular expression R there is a DFA M with L(M) = L(R), and for every DFA M there is a regular expression R with L(R) = L(M). Consequently a language is regular if and only if some DFA accepts it — equivalently, some NFA, with or without \varepsilon-transitions.


This is Theorem 3.3 of §3.7. With NFAs as the intermediate model, every step of the proof is a short construction, and following the arrows turns any description into any other:

four boxes in a cycle: regular expression, NFA with epsilon-transitions, NFA, DFAregular expressionNFA with ε-transitionsNFADFAThompson's algorithm§4.6 · linear sizeremove ε-transitions§4.3 · same statessubset construction§4.5 · up to 2ⁿ statesstate elimination§4.8 · length up to Θ(4ⁿ)Free in the other direction: a DFA is an NFA, and an NFA is an NFA with ε-transitions.Kleene's theorem as a cycle of conversions. Following the arrows turns any of the four descriptions into any other, so all four describe exactly the regular languages. The grey notes give the size of the result for an input of size n. The subset construction also accepts ε-transitions directly, and state elimination works on any NFA, so the right-hand arrow is optional.
Each arrow is labeled with its section and the size of its result: the subset construction can need 2^n states, and state elimination can produce expressions of length \Theta(4^n). The \varepsilon-removal step is optional, because the subset construction and state elimination both handle \varepsilon-transitions directly.
So “regular”, “automatic” (Chapter 3) and “accepted by an NFA” are three names for one class, and each description is good at something different: expressions at union, concatenation and star; DFAs at complement, intersection (products) and lower bounds (fooling sets); NFAs at guessing — and at the transformations of §4.9.
Concept page: kleenes-theorem.
4.5 NFA to DFA: the subset construction
Running an NFA by hand was already deterministic: the set of current states is determined by the input read so far, and there are only finitely many sets. Make those sets the states of a DFA.


                  
                  Definition — subset construction 
                  
                

For an NFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta), possibly with \varepsilon-transitions, define the DFA M' = (\Sigma, Q', s', A', \delta') by
Q' := 2^Q,\qquad s' := \{s\},\qquad A' := \{S\subseteq Q \mid \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S)\cap A\ne\varnothing\},
\delta'(S, a) := \bigcup_{p\in S}\ \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(p)}\delta(r,a).
Without \varepsilon-transitions this is simply A' = \{S \mid S\cap A\ne\varnothing\} and \delta'(S,a) = \bigcup_{p\in S}\delta(p,a).


A DFA state is the set S itself; its \varepsilon-reach is computed when needed, for the acceptance test and for the transitions.


                  
                  Why it works (click to expand) 
                  
                

Claim: \varepsilon\text{-reach}\big((\delta')^*(S,w)\big) = \bigcup_{p\in S}\delta^*(p,w) for every set S and string w. Induct on w. For w = \varepsilon both sides are \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S). For w = ax, (\delta')^*(S,ax) = (\delta')^*\big(\delta'(S,a),x\big); the induction hypothesis turns the \varepsilon-reach of this set into \bigcup_{q\in\delta'(S,a)}\delta^*(q,x), which equals \bigcup_{p\in S}\delta^*(p,ax) by the definitions of \delta' and \delta^*. With S = \{s\}: M' accepts w iff \varepsilon\text{-reach}\big((\delta')^*(\{s\},w)\big) meets A, iff \delta^*(s,w) meets A, iff M accepts w. \blacksquare


Most of the 2^{\lvert Q\rvert} subsets can never occur, so build only the ones that can, breadth-first from \{s\}:


                  
                  Recipe — the incremental subset construction 
                  
                

Keep a table with one row per DFA state and the columns S, \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S), accepting?, and \delta'(S,a) for each symbol a.

Start with the single row \{s\}.
In each row, first compute \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S). The row is accepting iff that set contains an accepting state. For each symbol a, \delta'(S,a) collects \delta(r,a) for every r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(S).
Every set that appears in a transition column for the first time gets a row of its own — \varnothing included; it is the dump state.
Stop when every set in the transition columns has a row. The rows are the states of the DFA.

The classic slips: deciding acceptance from S instead of its \varepsilon-reach, reading a symbol before sliding along the \varepsilon-moves, dropping the row \varnothing, and listing all 2^{\lvert Q\rvert} subsets instead of the reachable ones.


For the NFA E of §4.3, with L(E) = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*:





















































S\varepsilon\text{-reach}(S)accepting?\delta'(S,\mathtt{0})\delta'(S,\mathtt{1})the strings that reach S→ \{p\}\{p,q,r\}yes\{p,r\}\{q\}only \varepsilon\{p,r\}\{p,q,r\}yes\{p,r\}\{q\}\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\{q\}\{q,r\}yes\{r\}\{q\}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\{r\}\{r\}yes\{r\}\varnothing\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\varnothing\varnothingno\varnothing\varnothingevery string not in L(E)
Five of the 2^3 = 8 subsets are reachable. The rows \{p\} and \{p,r\} have the same \varepsilon-reach and therefore identical transitions: they are equivalent, and merging them gives the minimal DFA, with 4 states. The construction is correct, but it does not promise a minimal result. The NFA of §4.1 behaves the same way: 5 of its 16 subsets are reachable — \{s\}, \{s,a\}, \{s,b\}, \{s,a,c\}, \{s,b,c\} — and the two accepting ones merge, leaving 4 states.
The price: exponentially many states
A DFA may need exponentially more states than an NFA for the same language — the subset construction is not just being careless.


                  
                  Exponential blow-up 
                  
                

For k\ge1 let L_k := (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^{k-1} be the set of binary strings whose kth symbol from the end is 1, where (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^{k-1} abbreviates k-1 copies of (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}). Some NFA with k+1 states accepts L_k, but every DFA for L_k has at least 2^k states.


The NFA has states 0, 1, \dots, k: state 0 (the start) loops on both symbols and also moves to 1 on a 1 — the guess “this 1 is the kth symbol from the end” — each state i with 1\le i<k moves to i+1 on either symbol, and only k accepts. A DFA cannot guess; it has to remember the last k symbols.


                  
                  Proof of the lower bound, by a fooling set (click to expand) 
                  
                

Let F := \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^k, the 2^k strings of length k. Let x\ne y be arbitrary strings in F, let i be a position with x_i\ne y_i, and let z := \mathtt{0}^{i-1}. The string xz has length k+i-1, so its kth symbol from the end is its ith symbol, x_i; likewise the kth symbol from the end of yz is y_i. Exactly one of x_i, y_i is 1, so exactly one of xz, yz is in L_k. Hence F is a fooling set of size 2^k, and every DFA for L_k has at least 2^k states (§3.8). \blacksquare


On this NFA the subset construction builds exactly 2^k states — every subset that contains state 0 — and the lower bound says that none of them is redundant. Most NFAs are much kinder: §4.6 turns a 14-state NFA into 5 DFA states, not 2^{14}.

4.6 Regular expression to NFA: Thompson’s algorithm


                  
                  Lemma 4.2 
                  
                

Every regular language is accepted by an NFA — in fact by an NFA with exactly one accepting state, which is different from its start state.


The proof is an algorithm due to Ken Thompson (1968): build the NFA bottom-up along the expression tree (§2.5), with a two-state gadget for each leaf and \varepsilon-transitions as glue. The single accepting state t\ne s is what makes the gluing easy, and it is exactly what the induction has to maintain.

Thompson's construction: base cases for the empty set, epsilon and a symbol; gadgets for union, star and concatenationR = ∅R = εaR = aSTR = S + T  (parallel)SR = S*STR = ST  (series)εεεεεεεεεεstststststThompson's algorithm, the book's gadgets. Top: the base cases, each with a start state s and a different accepting state t. Below: the NFAs for S and T (dashed boxes; only their start and accepting states are drawn, and these stop being start or accepting) glued with new ε-transitions — in parallel for S + T; around a loop for S*, where the lower edge skips S and the upper edge goes back for another copy; in series for ST, which adds no states.


                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

Let R be a regular expression for the language, and assume that every proper subexpression of R has an NFA with one accepting state, different from its start state. There are six cases.

R = \varnothing: two states s\ne t, no transitions. R = \varepsilon: s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t. R = a for a symbol a: s\xrightarrow{a}t. (A longer string is a concatenation of symbols.)
R = S+T: new states s and t, and the \varepsilon-transitions s\to s_S, s\to s_T, t_S\to t, t_T\to t.
R = ST: the \varepsilon-transition t_S\to s_T; the start state is s_S and the accepting state is t_T.
R = S^*: new states s and t, and the \varepsilon-transitions s\to s_S, t_S\to t, s\to t (zero copies of S) and t\to s (one more copy).

The old start and accepting states lose their roles, and new edges enter each old machine only at its start state and leave it only from its accepting state. So the walks from the new s to the new t spell exactly the strings of L(R). \blacksquare


Many textbooks close the loop of S^* from t_S back to s_S instead of from t back to s; that version is just as correct, and it changes only some of the \varepsilon-reaches in the table below. Either way the algorithm creates two states for each leaf, each + and each ^*, and none for a concatenation: the NFA has at most twice as many states as the expression has symbols and operators.
Example. The book’s (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^* — the strings with an even number of 1s — has 4 symbols, one + and two stars, so its NFA has 2(4+1+2) = 14 states:

                  Do not "optimize" the gadgets 
                  
                

Two tempting shortcuts, both from the book’s exercises, break the construction:

Identifying t_S with s_T for ST, instead of joining them with an \varepsilon-edge: for \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* the result accepts 10, because the loop of \mathtt{1}^* now returns to a state from which the loop of \mathtt{0}^* can be re-entered.
Building S^* without new states, by adding \varepsilon-edges s_S\to t_S and t_S\to s_S: for (\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1})^* the result accepts 0, by jumping from the middle of S straight to its accepting state.

Both break because the shortcut lets a walk leave a gadget in the middle, or come back into it. A larger correct NFA loses nothing.

4.8 NFA to regular expression: state elimination
The last arrow turns an automaton back into an expression. Label the edges with regular expressions, then remove the states one at a time, recording on the remaining edges every detour through the removed state. The book credits this formulation to McNaughton and Yamada (1960) — C. Y. Lee published a similar one the same year — as a modern version of Kleene’s own 1951 argument; you may also meet it as Han and Wood’s algorithm.


                  
                  Definition — expression automaton 
                  
                

An expression automaton has a start state s with no incoming edges, a target state t\ne s with no outgoing edges, and a regular expression R(p\to q) on every edge from a state p\ne t to a state q\ne s; a missing edge has label \varnothing. It accepts w iff w = x_1x_2\cdots x_\ell for some walk s = q_0\to q_1\to\cdots\to q_\ell = t with x_i\in L\big(R(q_{i-1}\to q_i)\big) for every i.


Every NFA becomes an expression automaton: add a new start state with an \varepsilon-edge to the old one, a new target with an \varepsilon-edge from each old accepting state, and merge parallel edges with +. (An old start state without incoming edges can serve as s itself.)


                  
                  Lemma 4.3 
                  
                

Every expression automaton accepts a regular language.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

Induction on the number of states. If Q = \{s,t\}, the automaton accepts L\big(R(s\to t)\big). Otherwise choose any state q\notin\{s,t\}, delete it, and for every remaining pair p\ne t, r\ne s — including p = r — set
R'(p\to r) := R(p\to r) + R(p\to q)\,R(q\to q)^*\,R(q\to r).
An accepting walk of the old automaton visits q in maximal runs. Each run is entered from some p\ne q and left to some r\ne q (neither s nor t is q), and the part of the input it reads matches R(p\to q)R(q\to q)^*R(q\to r); replacing every run by the new edge p\to r gives an accepting walk of the new automaton for the same string. Conversely, every new edge expands back into the old edge or a run through q. So the language does not change, the automaton has one state fewer, and the induction hypothesis applies. \blacksquare



state elimination: p to q labeled X, loop Y at q, q to r labeled Z, p to r labeled W, becomes p to r labeled W + XY*ZXZWY⟹W + XY*Zbefore: q is still thereafter eliminating qpqrprEliminating a state q. A walk from p to r either avoids q (label W) or enters q, loops there zero or more times, and leaves (XY*Z). The rule is applied to every pair p, r of remaining states, including p = r; a missing edge has label ∅, and a missing loop makes Y* = ∅* = ε.


                  
                  Recipe — state elimination by hand 
                  
                


Add the new s and t (unless the old ones already qualify), and merge parallel edges with +.
Eliminate the other states one at a time, in any order. For each eliminated q, list its predecessors and successors and update every pair p, r — including p = r, which changes a loop.
Simplify only with identities you can name: \varnothing terms vanish, \varepsilon R = R, \varnothing^* = \varepsilon.
The answer is R(s\to t). Test \varepsilon and a few short strings before you trust it.

                  Mind the empty string 
                  
                

The 3-state DFA that starts in its accepting state 0 reads \varepsilon as the number 0, like the mod-5 machine of §3.1, and accepts it. Eliminating its states (after adding a new start state) gives expressions with \varepsilon: the order 2, 0, 1 yields \mathtt{0}^*+\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{01}^*\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{10}^* — note \mathtt{0}^* where the book has \mathtt{00}^* — and the order 2, 1, 0 the compact (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{01}^*\mathtt{0})^*\mathtt{1})^*. Both describe \varepsilon plus the language above — and a missing or extra \varepsilon is the typical one-mistake deduction on a graded expression.


How big? With n states, state elimination performs O(n^3) operations on expressions, but each new label combines four old ones, so the expressions can grow by a factor of about 4 per eliminated state: length \Theta(4^n) in the worst case. The order matters in practice: on the 4-state DFA above, the six elimination orders give equivalent expressions with between 12 and 31 occurrences of symbols (the order used above gives 14).

4.9 Regular language transformations
The most exam-relevant use of NFAs is proving that a language built from L is regular whenever L is. There are two ways:

transform a regular expression for L by structural recursion, as for reversal in §2.7; or
transform a DFA for L into an NFA for the new language.

The asymmetry is deliberate: a DFA is the easiest input to reason about (exactly one state per prefix), and an NFA with \varepsilon-transitions is the most flexible output. Two kinds of transformed language come up, for a function f from strings to strings:

Strings whose transform is in L, \{w \mid f(w)\in L\}: the new machine reads w and simulates M on f(w) — often deterministically.
Transforms of strings in L, \{f(w) \mid w\in L\}: the new machine reads y, guesses a string w with f(w) = y, and simulates M on it. Nondeterministic choices guess symbols that f changed; \varepsilon-transitions guess symbols that f deleted.



                  
                  Template — regular language transformation 
                  
                

Let M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) be a DFA that accepts L. 
We construct an NFA M' = (\Sigma, Q', s', A', \delta') with \varepsilon-transitions that accepts [the new language]. 
In English: M' remembers [each component of its state, and what it means], guesses [what, and when], and accepts when […]. 
Formally: Q' =  […], s' =  […], A' =  […], 
\delta'(q', a) =  […] for every state q' and every symbol a, 
\delta'(q', \varepsilon) =  […] for every state q' (write \varnothing where there are none). 
Why: M' can be in state […] after reading x if and only if […]; so it accepts exactly [the new language].


Reversal


                  
                  Lemma 4.4 
                  
                

If L is regular, then so is L^R := \{w^R \mid w\in L\}.


Proof 1, by regular expressions. Reverse an expression recursively: \textsf{rev}(\varnothing) := \varnothing, \textsf{rev}(w) := w^R for a string w, \textsf{rev}(S+T) := \textsf{rev}(S)+\textsf{rev}(T), \textsf{rev}(ST) := \textsf{rev}(T)\,\textsf{rev}(S) — the order swaps — and \textsf{rev}(S^*) := \textsf{rev}(S)^*. A structural induction, using (xy)^R = y^Rx^R from Chapter 1, shows L(\textsf{rev}(R)) = L(R)^R; §2.7 works an example.
Proof 2, by automata. Run M backwards:


                  
                  Proof 2 of Lemma 4.4 — the reversed NFA 
                  
                

Let M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) be a DFA for L. Define the NFA M^R = (\Sigma,\ Q\cup\{s^R\},\ s^R,\ \{s\},\ \delta^R), where s^R is a new state and
\delta^R(s^R,\varepsilon) := A,\qquad \delta^R(q, a) := \{p\in Q \mid \delta(p,a) = q\}\quad\text{for } q\in Q,\ a\in\Sigma,
with no other transitions: s^R has no symbol transitions, and no other state has \varepsilon-transitions.
In English: M^R follows the edges of M backwards. With its first move it guesses the accepting state in which M‘s walk on w ends; reading w^R, it retraces that walk from the end; and it accepts iff it arrives at M‘s start state s.
Why: M^R has a walk from q to p labeled x^R iff \delta^*(p,x) = q (induction on x). So M^R accepts y iff y = w^R for some w that leads M from s into A — iff y\in L^R. \blacksquare


Reversing the edges of a DFA does not give a DFA: a state can have several incoming edges with the same symbol, or none. That is one reason the target of a transformation is an NFA.
Half of a language


                  
                  Lemma 4.5 
                  
                

If L is regular, then so is \textsf{half}(L) := \{w \mid ww\in L\}.


This is the first kind of transformation, with f(w) = ww, but simulating M on ww while reading w only once needs a trick. M processes the second copy of w starting from the state h := \delta^*(s,w) that it reaches in the middle — and h is known only at the end. So guess h at the start, run both halves side by side, and check the guess at the end.

On input ww, the DFA M passes through some state h at the midpoint. M′ reads w only once, so it guesses h with an ε-move and runs two copies of M side by side: one from s, playing the first copy of w, and one from h, playing the second. It accepts only if the first copy ends exactly at the guessed h and the second ends in an accepting state.


                  
                  Proof of Lemma 4.5 — the model to copy 
                  
                

Let M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) be a DFA that accepts L. We construct an NFA M' = (\Sigma, Q', s', A', \delta') with \varepsilon-transitions that accepts \textsf{half}(L).
In English: M' first guesses the middle state h. After that it remembers a triple (p, h, q): p is the state of a copy of M started at s, which plays the first copy of w; h is the guess, which never changes; and q is the state of a copy of M started at h, which plays the second copy. M' accepts iff the first copy has arrived exactly at h — the guess was right — and the second copy is in an accepting state.
Formally: s' is a new state, and
\begin{aligned}
Q' &:= \{s'\}\cup(Q\times Q\times Q),\\
\delta'(s',\varepsilon) &:= \{(s,h,h) \mid h\in Q\},\\
\delta'\big((p,h,q),a\big) &:= \big\{\big(\delta(p,a),\,h,\,\delta(q,a)\big)\big\}\quad\text{for all } p, h, q\in Q,\ a\in\Sigma,\\
A' &:= \{(h,h,q) \mid h\in Q,\ q\in A\},
\end{aligned}
with no other transitions.
Why: after reading w, M' can be in (p,h,q) iff p = \delta^*(s,w) and q = \delta^*(h,w). So M' accepts w iff \delta^*(s,w) = h and \delta^*(h,w)\in A for some h — iff \delta^*(s,ww) = \delta^*\big(\delta^*(s,w),w\big)\in A, iff ww\in L. \blacksquare


M' has \lvert Q\rvert^3+1 states, and its only nondeterministic move is the first one.
Two more examples


                  
                  Strings whose double is in L — a DFA suffices
                  
                

Let \textsf{double}(w) repeat every symbol of w: \textsf{double}(\varepsilon) := \varepsilon and \textsf{double}(ax) := aa\cdot\textsf{double}(x), so \textsf{double}(\mathtt{011}) = \mathtt{001111}. For a DFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) that accepts L, the DFA M' = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta') with
\delta'(q,a) := \delta\big(\delta(q,a),a\big)
accepts \{w \mid \textsf{double}(w)\in L\}. In English: M' feeds every input symbol to M twice, so its state after reading w is \delta^*\big(s,\textsf{double}(w)\big), and it accepts exactly when \textsf{double}(w)\in L. No guessing, no new states.
For the binary multiples of 3 (\delta(q,a) = (2q+a)\bmod 3, start and accepting state 0), \delta'(q,a) = (4q+3a)\bmod 3 = q: M' never moves, so it accepts every string. Indeed \textsf{double}(w), read in binary, is 3 times the number that w denotes in base 4.




                  
                  Transforms of strings in L — guess the preimage
                  
                

Let \textsf{ones}(w) := \mathtt{1}^{\lvert w\rvert} replace every symbol of a binary string by 1. For a DFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) that accepts L, the NFA M' = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta') with
\delta'(q,\mathtt{1}) := \{\delta(q,\mathtt{0}),\ \delta(q,\mathtt{1})\},\qquad \delta'(q,\mathtt{0}) := \varnothing,
and no \varepsilon-transitions accepts \textsf{ones}(L) := \{\textsf{ones}(w) \mid w\in L\}. In English: reading \mathtt{1}^n, M' guesses a string w of length n, one symbol per input 1, and runs M on it: M' can be in state q after reading \mathtt{1}^i iff some string of length i leads M from s to q. So it accepts \mathtt{1}^n iff some string of length n is in L. An input 0 kills every thread, because no \textsf{ones}(w) contains a 0.
Edge cases: \textsf{ones} maps \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^* and \Sigma^* to \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^* and \mathtt{1}^*; and (\mathtt{01})^* to (\mathtt{11})^*.




                  
                  Where transformation proofs go wrong 
                  
                


One example is not a proof. Start from an arbitrary DFA M for L; a machine for one particular language proves nothing about the others.
Mixing up the two kinds. \{w \mid \textsf{double}(w)\in L\} and \{\textsf{double}(w) \mid w\in L\} are different languages that need different machines: for L = \Sigma^* the first is \Sigma^* and the second is (\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{11})^*.
Not every transformation preserves regularity. \textsf{half}(L) is always regular, but \{ww \mid w\in L\} need not be: for L = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} it is \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1} \mid n\ge0\}, and \mathtt{0}^* is an infinite fooling set for it — the suffix \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} separates \mathtt{0}^i from \mathtt{0}^j.
Unstated cases. Define \delta' for every state and symbol, and say exactly which \varepsilon-transitions exist; “\varepsilon-moves where needed” describes no machine.





                  
                  How a transformation is graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams devote a whole problem, in two parts, to transformations. Each construction is graded out of 10: 2 for a formal, complete description of M' built from an arbitrary DFA M — say whether M' is a DFA or an NFA, and list its \varepsilon-transitions; 2 for an English explanation of what its states and its accepting states mean; 6 for correctness — 1 for the states, 1 for the start state, 1 for the accepting states and 3 for the transitions. Graders try the edge cases L = \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^* and \Sigma^*, so run your construction on them before handing it in.

Summary

An NFA’s transition function returns a set of states (possibly empty), and \varepsilon-transitions move without reading; the NFA accepts iff some walk labeled w ends in A. Run it by tracking the set of current states, closed under \varepsilon-moves.
Three pictures of nondeterminism: clairvoyant guessing, parallel threads, and verifying a proof supplied by a prover.
\varepsilon-removal keeps the states: A' is the set of states whose \varepsilon-reach meets A, and \delta'(q,a) = \delta(\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q),a).
Subset construction: DFA states are sets S, accepting iff \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S) meets A; build only the reachable sets, \varnothing included. Up to 2^n states — and “the kth symbol from the end is 1” really needs 2^k.
Thompson’s algorithm glues two-state gadgets with \varepsilon-edges (one accepting state \ne start, Lemma 4.2). State elimination applies R(p\to r) + R(p\to q)R(q\to q)^*R(q\to r) to every pair, p = r included (Lemma 4.3); expressions can reach length \Theta(4^n).
Kleene’s theorem (Theorem 4.1): regular expressions, DFAs and NFAs describe the same languages. Every conversion works; none promises a small result.
Transformations: from an arbitrary DFA for L, build an NFA — simulate M on f(w) for \{w \mid f(w)\in L\}, guess a preimage for \{f(w) \mid w\in L\}. Reversal (Lemma 4.4) and \textsf{half}(L) (Lemma 4.5) are the models.
