1-models-of-computation/05-context-free-.title: Chapter 5 — Context-Free Languages
1-models-of-computation/05-context-free-.content:
Chapter 5 · book pp. 77–96 · chapter PDF · prev: Chapter 4 · next: Chapter 6 · practice: 10 problems


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

A context-free grammar is a finite set of recursive rules such as C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}: each nonterminal names a language, and each rule is one way to build a string of that language from strings of others. Grammars generate every regular language and more — C generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mid n\ge0\}, which is not regular — and recursive automata, NFAs that call each other like subroutines, accept exactly the same languages. Every generated string has a parse tree; a grammar in which some string has two is ambiguous. Proving L(G) = L takes two inductions — everything in L is generated, everything generated is in L — with extra care for \varepsilon-rules and for nonterminals that refer to each other. Every grammar can be put in Chomsky normal form, and a counting argument shows that most languages are still not context-free.


5.1 Definitions
Regular languages are built from single strings by union, concatenation and Kleene star. Context-free languages replace the star by arbitrary recursion: a language may be defined in terms of itself, anywhere inside a rule.


                  
                  Definition — context-free grammar 
                  
                

A context-free grammar (CFG) G = (\Sigma, \Gamma, R, S) consists of

\Sigma — a finite set of terminals: the alphabet of the strings being generated;
\Gamma — a finite set of nonterminals (variables), disjoint from \Sigma;
R — a finite set of production rules A\to\omega, where A\in\Gamma and \omega\in(\Sigma\cup\Gamma)^*;
S\in\Gamma — the start symbol.

Rules with the same left side are combined with a bar: C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} is two rules. Conventions: a, b, c are terminals, upper-case letters are nonterminals, and w, x, y, z are strings over \Sigma\cup\Gamma.




                  
                  Definition — derivation, L(w), L(G), context-free language
                  
                


If A\to y is a rule, then xAz\rightsquigarrow xyz: one derivation step replaces one occurrence of a nonterminal by the right side of one of its rules. The surrounding x and z play no role — that is what context-free means.
x\rightsquigarrow^* z (”z derives from x”) if x = z, or x\rightsquigarrow y and y\rightsquigarrow^* z for some string y: a derivation is a sequence of zero or more steps.
L(w) := \{x\in\Sigma^* \mid w\rightsquigarrow^* x\} for any string w\in(\Sigma\cup\Gamma)^*, and the language of the grammar is L(G) := L(S).
A language is context-free if it is L(G) for some context-free grammar G.



Because steps ignore their surroundings, a derivation can be carried out inside any context: if x\rightsquigarrow^* y, then wxz\rightsquigarrow^* wyz. The book’s running example is
S\to A\mid B \qquad A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}C \qquad B\to B\mathtt{1}\mid C\mathtt{1} \qquad C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}
with terminals \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, nonterminals S, A, B, C and start symbol S. Every nonterminal generates its own language:






























nonterminalits languagewhyC\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}C\to\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} wraps a C-string in one more 0…1 pairA\{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m>n\}one or more extra 0s in front of a C-stringB\{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m<n\}a C-string followed by one or more extra 1sS\{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m\ne n\}L(A)\cup L(B)
For example, \mathtt{00011}\in L(S):
S\rightsquigarrow A\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}C\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}C\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{000}C\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00011}.


                  
                  A grammar is a recursive definition 
                  
                

Read each nonterminal as the name of a language and each rule as one way to build its strings. C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} says “a string of C is empty, or a string of C with a 0 in front and a 1 behind”: L(C) = \{\varepsilon\}\cup\mathtt{0}\,L(C)\,\mathtt{1}. A regular expression can recurse only through the star, which repeats pieces side by side; a grammar can put the recursive call between two symbols, and that nesting is exactly what lets C match every 0 with a 1.


Concept page: context-free-grammars.
5.2 Parse trees and ambiguity


                  
                  Definition — parse tree 
                  
                

A parse tree for a string w\in\Sigma^* (from the nonterminal A) is an ordered rooted tree in which

the root is labeled A — the start symbol S for a parse tree of L(G) — and every internal node is labeled with a nonterminal;
the children of a node labeled B spell, from left to right, the right side of some rule B\to\omega (a single leaf \varepsilon when the rule is B\to\varepsilon);
the leaves are labeled with terminals or \varepsilon, and read from left to right they spell w.




two parse trees: C over 0, C, 1 nested twice with C to epsilon in the middle; and S over A over 0 and the same C tree00εC1C1C000εC1C1CASparse tree of 0011 from Cparse tree of 00011 from SParse trees in the running example. Left: C → 0C1 twice, then C → ε; the leaves, read left to right, spell 0011 (ε is the empty string). Right: S → A, then A → 0C adds one extra 0, and the red subtree is exactly the tree on the left.
A parse tree records which rules were used where, but not in which order. A derivation fixes an order, so one tree usually corresponds to many derivations — but to exactly one leftmost derivation, the one that always expands the leftmost nonterminal. The derivation of 00011 in §5.1 is the leftmost derivation of the right-hand tree above.


                  
                  Definition — ambiguity 
                  
                

A string w is ambiguous (with respect to G) if it has more than one parse tree — equivalently, more than one leftmost derivation. A grammar is ambiguous if some string is ambiguous. A context-free language is inherently ambiguous if every grammar that generates it is ambiguous.


The grammar S\to\mathtt{1}\mid S{+}S generates the sums \mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1}{+}\cdots{+}\mathtt{1}, and it is ambiguous: 1+1+1 has two parse trees, with leftmost derivations
\begin{aligned}
&S\rightsquigarrow S{+}S\rightsquigarrow S{+}S{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}S{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1}{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1} && \text{(left tree)}\\
&S\rightsquigarrow S{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}S{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1}{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1} && \text{(right tree)}
\end{aligned}

two parse trees for 1+1+1 under S to 1 or S+S, one grouping the first two 1s, one the last two1S+1SS+1SS1S+1S+1SSS(1+1)+11+(1+1)One string, two parse trees. With S → 1 | S+S, the string 1+1+1 can be split as S+S after its first + or after its second; the red subtree shows which two 1s are added first. So the grammar is ambiguous.
A sum of k ones has one parse tree for each way to fully parenthesize it: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, \dots trees for k = 1, 2, 3, \dots (the Catalan numbers) — so 1+1+1+1 has five. The grammar S\to\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}{+}S generates the same language, (\mathtt{1}{+})^*\mathtt{1}, with exactly one parse tree per string: it groups every sum from the right, as \mathtt{1}{+}(\mathtt{1}{+}(\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1})). So ambiguity is a property of a grammar; this language is not inherently ambiguous. Inherently ambiguous languages do exist; the standard example is \{\mathtt{a}^i\mathtt{b}^j\mathtt{c}^k \mid i = j \text{ or } j = k\}. Its natural grammar S\to XC\mid AY, with L(X) = \{\mathtt{a}^i\mathtt{b}^i\}, L(Y) = \{\mathtt{b}^j\mathtt{c}^j\}, L(A) = \mathtt{a}^* and L(C) = \mathtt{c}^*, gives every \mathtt{a}^n\mathtt{b}^n\mathtt{c}^n two parse trees, and every other grammar for this language also has some ambiguous string (a proof beyond this course).


                  
                  Two derivations are not two parse trees 
                  
                

To show that a grammar is ambiguous, exhibit one string with two different parse trees (or two different leftmost derivations). Derivations that merely expand nonterminals in another order build the same tree: S\rightsquigarrow S{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1} and S\rightsquigarrow S{+}S\rightsquigarrow S{+}\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}{+}\mathtt{1} are two derivations of 1+1, which has only one parse tree.


Concept page: parse-trees-and-ambiguity.
5.3 From grammar to language
To prove that a grammar generates a language L, prove two inclusions, each by induction:

L\subseteq L(G): everything in L is generated — build a derivation;
L(G)\subseteq L: everything generated is in L — take a derivation apart.

For L(C) = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mid n\ge0\} these are Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2.


                  
                  Lemma 5.1 
                  
                

C\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n for every integer n\ge0.




                  
                  Proof of Lemma 5.1 — the model to copy 
                  
                

Let n be an arbitrary non-negative integer, and assume that C\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^k for every integer k with 0\le k<n. There are two cases.
Case n = 0. The rule C\to\varepsilon gives C\rightsquigarrow\varepsilon = \mathtt{0}^0\mathtt{1}^0.
Case n\ge1. Then 0\le n-1<n, so the induction hypothesis gives C\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^{n-1}\mathtt{1}^{n-1}, and
\begin{aligned}
C &\rightsquigarrow \mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} && \text{by the rule } C\to\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}\\
&\rightsquigarrow^* \mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{0}^{n-1}\mathtt{1}^{n-1}\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by the induction hypothesis, inside the context } \mathtt{0}\,\underline{\ \ }\,\mathtt{1}\\
&= \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n.
\end{aligned}
In both cases, C\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n. \blacksquare




                  
                  Lemma 5.2 
                  
                

Every string in L(C) is equal to \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n for some integer n\ge0.




                  
                  Proof of Lemma 5.2 — the model to copy 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string in L(C), and fix a derivation C\rightsquigarrow^* w. Assume that every string x\in L(C) with \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert is equal to \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^k for some k\ge0. The derivation starts with one of the two rules for C.
Case C\to\varepsilon. Then the derivation is C\rightsquigarrow\varepsilon, so w = \varepsilon = \mathtt{0}^0\mathtt{1}^0.
Case C\to\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}. Then the derivation is C\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow^* w. The 0 and the 1 are terminals, so every later step rewrites something derived from the middle C: w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} for some string x with C\rightsquigarrow^* x. So x\in L(C) and \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert-2<\lvert w\rvert, and the induction hypothesis gives x = \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^k for some k\ge0. Therefore w = \mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^k\bullet\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{0}^{k+1}\mathtt{1}^{k+1}.
In both cases, w = \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n for some n\ge0. \blacksquare


Together the two lemmas say L(C) = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mid n\ge0\}. Note the asymmetry: Lemma 5.1 inducts on the parameter n and builds a derivation; Lemma 5.2 inducts on the string and has one case per rule.


                  
                  Template — proving L(G) = L
                  
                


State the language of every nonterminal. If nonterminals use each other, the claims must be proved together, in one induction (mutual induction, below).
L\subseteq L(G). Let w\in L be arbitrary; assume every shorter string of L is generated (or induct on a parameter, like n above). Split w into pieces that match the right side of one rule, apply the hypothesis to the pieces, and assemble a derivation S\rightsquigarrow\omega\rightsquigarrow^* w.
L(G)\subseteq L. Let w\in L(G) be arbitrary and fix a derivation of w; assume every shorter generated string is in L. Write one case per rule the derivation can start with; in each case w splits into pieces derived from the symbols of the right side, the hypothesis applies to each piece, and the pieces together satisfy the definition of L.
If the grammar has \varepsilon-rules, fix a shortest derivation of w (next subsection), or induct on the length of the derivation instead of the string.



Careful with those epsilons
The grammar S\to\varepsilon\mid SS\mid\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0} generates exactly the strings with equally many 0s and 1s. In the case S\to SS, the naive proof writes w = xy with S\rightsquigarrow^* x and S\rightsquigarrow^* y — but nothing forces x and y to be shorter than w: one of them may be \varepsilon and the other w itself. Derivations can be arbitrarily long without making the string longer, as in S\rightsquigarrow SS\rightsquigarrow S\rightsquigarrow SS\rightsquigarrow S\rightsquigarrow\cdots\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{01}, and even \varepsilon has infinitely many parse trees. The fix is to pick the derivation carefully.


                  
                  Lemma 5.3 
                  
                

For the grammar S\to\varepsilon\mid SS\mid\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}, every string w\in L(S) satisfies \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w).




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) — induction with a shortest derivation 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string in L(S), and fix a derivation S\rightsquigarrow^* w with the fewest possible steps. Assume that \#(\mathtt{0},x) = \#(\mathtt{1},x) for every string x\in L(S) with \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert. There are four cases, by the first rule of the derivation.

S\to\varepsilon. Then w = \varepsilon, and \#(\mathtt{0},\varepsilon) = 0 = \#(\mathtt{1},\varepsilon).
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}. Then w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} with S\rightsquigarrow^* x and \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, so the hypothesis gives \#(\mathtt{0},x) = \#(\mathtt{1},x), and \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{0},x)+1 = \#(\mathtt{1},x)+1 = \#(\mathtt{1},w).
S\to\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}. Symmetric.
S\to SS. Every later step rewrites a symbol derived from the left S or one derived from the right S, so the remaining steps split into a derivation S\rightsquigarrow^* x and a derivation S\rightsquigarrow^* y with w = xy. If x were \varepsilon, the derivation S\rightsquigarrow^* y = w alone would be a derivation of w with fewer steps (it skips at least the first step), contradicting our choice. So x\ne\varepsilon, and likewise y\ne\varepsilon. Hence \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert and \lvert y\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, the hypothesis applies to both, and \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{0},x)+\#(\mathtt{0},y) = \#(\mathtt{1},x)+\#(\mathtt{1},y) = \#(\mathtt{1},w).

In every case, \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w). \blacksquare


The difficulty comes only from nullable nonterminals (A\rightsquigarrow^*\varepsilon) and cycles of unit rules (A\rightsquigarrow^* B\rightsquigarrow^* A): they are what let a derivation grow longer without the string growing. Inducting on the length of the derivation instead of the length of the string sidesteps the issue in every grammar. The other inclusion — every balanced string is generated — uses the decomposition in §5.4.
Mutual induction
When nonterminals refer to each other, no claim about one of them can be proved alone.


                  
                  Lemma 5.4 
                  
                

For the grammar S\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon, A\to\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}\mid\varepsilon: L(S) = (\mathtt{01})^* and L(A) = (\mathtt{10})^*.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) — both claims in one induction 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string, and assume both claims for every shorter string: for every x with \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, x\in L(S)\iff x\in(\mathtt{01})^* and x\in L(A)\iff x\in(\mathtt{10})^*. We use (\mathtt{01})^n = \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^{n-1}\mathtt{1} and (\mathtt{10})^n = \mathtt{1}(\mathtt{01})^{n-1}\mathtt{0} for n\ge1.

w\in L(S)\Rightarrow w\in(\mathtt{01})^*. A derivation of w from S starts with S\to\varepsilon (then w = \varepsilon) or with S\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1} (then w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} with x\in L(A); by the hypothesis about A, x = (\mathtt{10})^k, so w = \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^k\mathtt{1} = (\mathtt{01})^{k+1}).
w\in(\mathtt{01})^*\Rightarrow w\in L(S). If w = \varepsilon, use S\to\varepsilon. Otherwise w = (\mathtt{01})^n = \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^{n-1}\mathtt{1} with n\ge1; the hypothesis about A gives A\rightsquigarrow^*(\mathtt{10})^{n-1}, so S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow^* w.
The two claims about A are the same arguments with 0 and 1 exchanged, using the hypothesis about S.

So both claims hold for w. \blacksquare


5.4 More examples
The book’s grammars, each with the language of every nonterminal:





































languagegrammar (and what its other nonterminals generate)palindromes, w = w^RS\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilonnon-palindromes, w\ne w^RS\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}Z\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}Z\mathtt{0}, \ Z\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}Z\mid\mathtt{1}Z (Z: every string)\#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w)S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}\mid SS\mid\varepsilon, or S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}S\mid\varepsilon\#(\mathtt{0},w)\ge\#(\mathtt{1},w)S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}\mid SS\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\varepsilon\#(\mathtt{0},w)\ne\#(\mathtt{1},w)S\to O\mid I, \ O\to E\mathtt{0}O\mid E\mathtt{0}E, \ I\to E\mathtt{1}I\mid E\mathtt{1}E, \ E\to\mathtt{0}E\mathtt{1}E\mid\mathtt{1}E\mathtt{0}E\mid\varepsilon (O: more 0s than 1s; I: more 1s; E: equally many)balanced parenthesesS\to\mathtt{(}S\mathtt{)}\mid SS\mid\varepsilon (ambiguous), or S\to\mathtt{(}S\mathtt{)}S\mid\varepsilon (unambiguous)arithmetic expressions over \mathtt{X}, \mathtt{Y}E\to E{+}T\mid T, \ T\to T{\times}F\mid F, \ F\to\mathtt{(}E\mathtt{)}\mid\mathtt{X}\mid\mathtt{Y} (E: sums of one or more terms; T: products of one or more factors; F: a variable or a parenthesized expression)
Each grammar comes from decomposing a typical string of the language:

Non-palindromes. Compare w with w^R from the outside in; at the first (outermost) mismatch, w = x\,a\,z\,b\,x^R with a\ne b. The rules S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{1} build the matching outside x\cdots x^R, \mathtt{0}Z\mathtt{1} and \mathtt{1}Z\mathtt{0} place the mismatch, and Z fills in an arbitrary middle z.
Equally many 0s and 1s. A non-empty such string splits after its shortest non-empty prefix with equal counts. That prefix starts and ends with different symbols, and its middle and the rest of w are again balanced — for example \mathtt{00111001} = \mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{01}\cdot\mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{1001}. That is the rule S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}S, and it proves the missing inclusion of Lemma 5.3. (The rules do not force the shortest prefix, so this grammar is still ambiguous: 0101 splits as \mathtt{0}\cdot\varepsilon\cdot\mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{01} or \mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{10}\cdot\mathtt{1}\cdot\varepsilon.)
More 0s than 1s. Cut w after the first prefix with exactly one more 0 than 1s: w = x\mathtt{0}y with x balanced and \#(\mathtt{0},y)\ge\#(\mathtt{1},y). That is O\to E\mathtt{0}O\mid E\mathtt{0}E.
Expressions. Sums of terms, products of factors: the grammar is unambiguous, and its parse trees respect precedence and grouping — \mathtt{X+Y}\times\mathtt{X} parses as \mathtt{X}+(\mathtt{Y}\times\mathtt{X}), \mathtt{X}\times\mathtt{Y+X} as (\mathtt{X}\times\mathtt{Y})+\mathtt{X}, and \mathtt{X+Y+X} as (\mathtt{X+Y})+\mathtt{X}.

Designing a grammar


                  
                  Recipe — from a description to a grammar 
                  
                


List short strings in and out of the language, including \varepsilon.
Decompose a typical string: by an outer pair of matching symbols (nesting), at the first point where some count balances, or by cases — a union gets one nonterminal per case.
Give each piece a nonterminal and describe its language in English, in a sentence that makes sense on its own.
Write the rules and check each one against the descriptions: the strings a rule builds must be in the left side’s language (nothing extra), and every string of that language must be buildable by some rule (nothing missing).
Test: derive a few strings, and check \varepsilon and the short strings that should be rejected.





                  
                  Example 1 — \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j \mid i\le j\le 2i\}: every 0 is matched by one or two 1s
                  
                

Idea. Match the outer 0s with one 1 each and the inner 0s with two 1s each: \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j = \mathtt{0}^a\,(\mathtt{0}^b\mathtt{1}^{2b})\,\mathtt{1}^a with a = 2i-j and b = j-i, and both are non-negative exactly when i\le j\le 2i.
Answer: S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid T, \quad T\to\mathtt{0}T\mathtt{11}\mid\varepsilon.
In English: T generates \{\mathtt{0}^b\mathtt{1}^{2b}\mid b\ge0\}, the strings in which every 0 is matched by exactly two 1s. S generates the strings \mathtt{0}^a x\mathtt{1}^a with x\in L(T), that is, \mathtt{0}^{a+b}\mathtt{1}^{a+2b} for a, b\ge0 — exactly the language.
Test: \varepsilon, 01, 011, 0011, 00111, 001111 are generated; 0, 1, 001, 0111, 0101 are not, and none of them is in the language.
Variants. S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\mid\varepsilon is also correct, but ambiguous (00111 has two parse trees) — which costs nothing. S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\mid\mathtt{01}\mid\mathtt{011} misses only \varepsilon: one mistake. S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid S\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon generates all of \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mid j\ge i\}, including 0111, 01111, …: infinitely many wrong strings.




                  
                  Example 2 — binary strings that are not of the form \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n
                  
                

Idea. By cases: a string that is not \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n is either \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n with m\ne n — the running example — or not of the form \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* at all, which means it contains the substring 10 somewhere.
Answer: S\to A\mid B\mid N, with A, B, C as in §5.1, \quad N\to X\mathtt{10}X, \quad X\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}X\mid\mathtt{1}X.
In English: X generates every binary string; N the strings containing 10, which are exactly the strings not in \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*; C, A, B the strings \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n with m = n, m>n, m<n; and S the union of L(A), L(B), L(N) — every string except \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n.
Test: 0, 1, 10, 001, 0110 are generated; \varepsilon, 01, 0011 are not. Forgetting N is the classic error: S\to A\mid B alone misses 10, 110, 0110 and every other string containing 10.
So the complement of \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\} is context-free too — but complements do not always behave this well (§5.6).




                  
                  Describe every nonterminal — and mind the tree, not just the strings 
                  
                


On homework, every nonterminal needs a self-contained description of its language (”E generates the strings with equally many 0s and 1s”), not of its role (”E is the middle part”). Writing the descriptions is also how you find your own bugs.
A grammar can generate exactly the right strings and still be wrong for an application, because its parse trees have the wrong structure. The simple grammar S\to\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}\mid S{+}S\mid SS\mid S^*\mid\mathtt{(}S\mathtt{)} generates exactly the regular expressions over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} that do not use \varnothing or \varepsilon — yet it also parses \mathtt{0}^*{+}\mathtt{1}^* as if it were (\mathtt{0}^*{+}\mathtt{1})^*.




two parse trees for 0*+1*: one with plus at the root, one with star at the root over 0*+10S*S+1S*SS0S*S+1SS*Sintended: (0*)+(1*)also possible: (0*+1)*Right strings, wrong structure. The grammar S → 0 | 1 | S+S | SS | S* | (S) generates exactly the regular expressions over 0 and 1 that use neither ∅ nor ε, but gives 0*+1* two parse trees. In red: what the last * applies to — just the 1 on the left, the whole of 0*+1 on the right, which is the meaning (0*+1)*.
The fix builds precedence into the grammar, exactly like the expression grammar: a regular expression is a sum of terms, a term is a concatenation of factors, and a factor is a starred atom.
S\to S{+}T\mid T \qquad T\to TF\mid F \qquad F\to F^*\mid\mathtt{(}S\mathtt{)}\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}
generates the same strings, has one parse tree per string, and parses \mathtt{0}^*{+}\mathtt{1}^* as (\mathtt{0}^*){+}(\mathtt{1}^*). Here S generates all the expressions, T the expressions with no + outside parentheses, and F the single atoms — 0, 1 or a parenthesized expression — followed by zero or more stars.


                  
                  How a grammar is graded 
                  
                

Grammars are graded like regular expressions: out of 10 points, 2 for syntax and 8 for correctness, with exam deductions twice the homework ones — 2 for one mistake (typically a missing or extra \varepsilon), 4 for a few wrong strings, all 8 if infinitely many strings are wrong, as in the last variant of Example 1. A grammar for \varnothing or \Sigma^* earns nothing. Homework also requires the English description of every nonterminal’s language. Ambiguity is not penalized: an ambiguous grammar that generates the right language gets full credit.


Concept page: context-free-grammars.
5.5 Regular languages are context-free


                  
                  Every regular language is context-free 
                  
                

Induct on a regular expression R for the language (structural induction). Build grammars for the subexpressions first, with disjoint sets of nonterminals and start symbols S_1, S_2, and add a new start symbol S:





























expressionnew rules\varnothingS\to S (no derivation from S ever ends)a string wS\to wR_1+R_2S\to S_1\mid S_2R_1R_2S\to S_1S_2R_1^*S\to\varepsilon\mid S_1S


On the expression \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00} (the multiples of 4 from Chapter 2), with one nonterminal per node of the expression tree, named in preorder, the construction gives
\begin{aligned}
&S\to A\mid B && A\to\mathtt{0} && B\to CD && C\to\mathtt{1} && D\to EI\\
&E\to\varepsilon\mid FE && F\to G\mid H && G\to\mathtt{0} && H\to\mathtt{1} && I\to\mathtt{00},
\end{aligned}
a correct but wordy grammar; by hand, S\to\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}X\mathtt{00}, X\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}X\mid\mathtt{1}X says the same thing.
The inclusion is strict: \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mid n\ge0\} is context-free (it is L(C)) but not regular — \mathtt{0}^* is an infinite fooling set for it (Lemma 3.6, §3.8).
The same three constructions work for any two grammars with disjoint nonterminals, so context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and Kleene star. Reversing the right side of every rule reverses the language — the running example becomes a grammar for \{\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^m\mid m\ne n\} — so they are closed under reversal as well.
5.6 Not every language is context-free
The counting argument of §2.8 works for grammars too. Write a grammar as a string — terminals, nonterminals numbered in binary, arrows, bars and separators — and encode each character in binary: different grammars become different binary strings and hence, with a leading 1, different positive integers. So there are only countably many context-free languages over a fixed alphabet, but uncountably many languages: almost every language is not context-free.
A specific non-context-free language needs a specific proof, and those proofs are beyond this course. The canonical example is
\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\}.


                  
                  Why \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n is out of reach
                  
                

Grammars match symbols by nesting (C\to\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} pairs each 0 with a 1), and recursive automata (§5.7) do the same with a stack. Once the 1s have been matched against the first block of 0s, the count is used up — nothing is left to compare with the last block. (A Turing machine can go back and check; Chapter 6 opens with one for exactly this language.)




                  
                  Closure: intersection and complement fail 
                  
                

\{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{0}^j\mid i\ge1, j\ge0\} (S\to CR, C\to\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{01}, R\to\mathtt{0}R\mid\varepsilon) and \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{0}^j\mid i\ge0, j\ge1\} (S\to PD, P\to\mathtt{0}P\mid\varepsilon, D\to\mathtt{1}D\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{10}) are context-free. A string in both contains a 1, so it is \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b\mathtt{0}^c with b\ge1, a = b and b = c: the intersection is \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\mid n\ge1\}, which is not context-free (a grammar for it plus S'\to S\mid\varepsilon would generate the canonical example). So context-free languages are not closed under intersection — and therefore not under complement either, since they are closed under union and L_1\cap L_2 = \overline{\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}}.
The forced 1s matter: without them, both languages contain every string \mathtt{0}^k, and so does their intersection.


Concept pages: counting-arguments, closure-properties.
5.7 Recursive automata
Grammars have a machine model too. Think of each nonterminal as a subroutine: an NFA that may, in the middle of its run, call another NFA (or itself) and continue when the call returns.


                  
                  Definition — recursive automaton 
                  
                

A recursive automaton has an input alphabet \Sigma, a finite set N of module names with a main name S\in N, and for each A\in N a module M_A: an NFA whose edges are labeled with symbols of \Sigma, with \varepsilon, or with module names, with a start state s_A and a single accepting state t_A. Different modules have disjoint sets of states.
A configuration is a triple (x, q, \sigma): the unread input x, the current state q, and a stack \sigma of states to return to, written as a string with its top first. Writing q\xrightarrow{\ell}p for an edge from q to p labeled \ell, one move from (x, q, \sigma) is

read: if x = ax' and q\xrightarrow{a}p, go to (x', p, \sigma);
\varepsilon-move: if q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}p, go to (x, p, \sigma);
call: if q\xrightarrow{A}p for a module name A, push p and jump to A‘s start state: (x, s_A, p\,\sigma);
return: if q = t_A for some module A and \sigma = p\,\sigma', pop: (x, p, \sigma').

It accepts w if some sequence of moves leads from (w, s_S, \varepsilon) to (\varepsilon, t_S, \varepsilon).

Each module is an NFA whose edges may also carry a module name (blue): following such an edge calls that module, which must run from its start state to its accepting state before control returns to the edge's target. Module E accepts {0n1n}, one path per rule of E → 0E1 | ε; the main module S accepts extra 0s followed by a call of E, or a call of E followed by extra 1s.
An accepting run on 001 (stacks written top first):

The stack of return states is what lets the machine count, and why recursive automata are more powerful than NFAs. (Most other textbooks use pushdown automata, NFAs with an explicit stack; they accept the same languages.)


                  
                  Lemma 5.5 
                  
                

Every context-free language is accepted by a recursive automaton.


Construction. One module per nonterminal A. For each rule A\to X_1X_2\cdots X_k, add a path of k edges from s_A to t_A labeled X_1, \dots, X_k — an edge labeled with a terminal reads it, an edge labeled with a nonterminal calls that module — and for each rule A\to\varepsilon an \varepsilon-edge from s_A to t_A. Module E in the figure is exactly this construction for E\to\mathtt{0}E\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon. An accepting run then traces a parse tree: each call is a node, and its module’s path spells the node’s children.


                  
                  Lemma 5.6 
                  
                

Every recursive automaton accepts a context-free language.


Construction. One nonterminal [q] for every state q, generating the strings that take q‘s module from q to its accepting state, with every call along the way completed:

























moveruleread: q\xrightarrow{a}p[q]\to a\,[p]\varepsilon-move: q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}p[q]\to[p]call: q\xrightarrow{A}p[q]\to[s_A]\,[p] — run all of M_A, then continue from preturn: t_A, for every module A[t_A]\to\varepsilon
The start symbol is [s_S]. For the automaton in the figure:
\begin{aligned}
&[s_S]\to\mathtt{0}[a]\mid[s_E][b] && [a]\to\mathtt{0}[a]\mid[s_E][t_S] && [b]\to\mathtt{1}[b]\mid\mathtt{1}[t_S] && [t_S]\to\varepsilon\\
&[s_E]\to\mathtt{0}[c]\mid[t_E] && [c]\to[s_E][d] && [d]\to\mathtt{1}[t_E] && [t_E]\to\varepsilon
\end{aligned}
where [s_S] generates \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n\mid m\ne n\}, [a] generates \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n\mid m\ge n\}, [b] generates \mathtt{1}^+, [s_E] generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}, [c] generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^{n+1}\}, [d] generates \{\mathtt{1}\}, and [t_S], [t_E] generate \{\varepsilon\}. On an ordinary NFA (one module, no calls) the same rules turn the parity DFA of §3.3 into [s]\to\mathtt{0}[s]\mid\mathtt{1}[t], [t]\to\mathtt{0}[t]\mid\mathtt{1}[s]\mid\varepsilon.
Together, Lemmas 5.5 and 5.6 say: a language is context-free if and only if some recursive automaton accepts it.
Concept page: recursive-automata.
5.8 Chomsky normal form


                  
                  Definition — Chomsky normal form (CNF) 
                  
                

A grammar is in Chomsky normal form if the start symbol S appears on the right side of no rule, the rule S\to\varepsilon is allowed, and every other rule has one of two forms:
A\to BC \quad\text{(two nonterminals)}\qquad\text{or}\qquad A\to a \quad\text{(one terminal)}.


Parse trees in CNF are binary. In a parse tree of a string of length n\ge1, each of the n leaves hangs below its own node A\to a, and the nodes A\to BC form a full binary tree whose leaves are those n nodes — so there are n-1 of them, and 2n-1 nonterminal nodes in all. Each derivation step expands one nonterminal node, so every derivation of a string of length n\ge1 has exactly 2n-1 steps.

binary parse tree of 00011 with root S, children E over 0 and C, and so on0E0E0E1DC1FDCS5 leaves  ·  5 blue nodes A → a  ·  4 black nodes A → BC9 = 2·5 − 1 nonterminal nodes, so every derivation of 00011 takes 9 stepsA parse tree in Chomsky normal form. The tree of 00011 in the CNF grammar of §5.9. Each leaf hangs below its own node A → a (blue), and the nodes A → BC form a full binary tree with those n nodes as its leaves, so there are n − 1 of them: 2n − 1 nonterminal nodes in all.
So membership is decidable by brute force: try every derivation with 2n-1 steps. Much better is dynamic programming. For every substring w[i..j], shortest first, compute the set of nonterminals that derive it: A derives the single symbol w_i if A\to w_i is a rule, and A derives w[i..j] with i<j if some rule A\to BC and some split i\le k<j have B\rightsquigarrow^* w[i..k] and C\rightsquigarrow^* w[k+1..j]. Then w\in L(G) if and only if S derives w[1..n] (or w = \varepsilon and S\to\varepsilon is a rule). There are O(n^2) substrings with O(n) splits each, so this CYK algorithm (Cocke–Younger–Kasami) takes O(n^3) time for a fixed grammar — dynamic programming, as in the algorithms half of the course.
Concept page: chomsky-normal-form.
5.9 The CNF conversion algorithm


                  
                  Theorem 5.7 
                  
                

Every context-free grammar of total length L can be converted, in O(L^2) time, into an equivalent grammar in Chomsky normal form of total length O(L^2).




                  
                  The conversion, step by step 
                  
                


New start symbol. Add S'\to S, so that the start symbol appears on no right side. (Needed only if S appears on a right side or derives \varepsilon; otherwise S'\to S is dropped again after step 2, as in the example below. The book drops S' after step 2 whenever S' is not nullable, but if S is on a right side, as in S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid\mathtt{1}, that leaves the start symbol on a right side, which CNF forbids.)
Split long rules. Replace A\to X\alpha, where X is one symbol and \lvert\alpha\rvert\ge2, by A\to XB and B\to\alpha for a new nonterminal B; repeat until every right side has length at most 2.
Find the nullable nonterminals (A\rightsquigarrow^*\varepsilon): A is nullable if some rule A\to\omega has only nullable symbols on the right (in particular if A\to\varepsilon); repeat until nothing changes.
Remove \varepsilon-rules. For each rule, add every non-empty variant obtained by deleting some occurrences of nullable nonterminals; then delete every rule A\to\varepsilon, and add S'\to\varepsilon if S' is nullable (the only \varepsilon-rule of the result).
Merge equivalent nonterminals: those that derive each other by unit rules (A\rightsquigarrow^* B\rightsquigarrow^* A) — the strong components of the graph of unit rules A\to B — and delete every rule A\to A (merging creates them, and so does step 3, e.g. S\to S from S\to SS).
Remove unit rules. The unit-rule graph is now acyclic. Process the nonterminals so that B comes before A whenever A\to B (reverse topological order), replacing each A\to B by copies of all of B‘s rules. Copying can cost \Theta(nL) time for n nonterminals, and this step dominates the O(L^2) of Theorem 5.7.
Protect terminals. For each terminal a, add a new nonterminal T_a\to a and replace a by T_a in every right side of length 2.



On the running example (the grammar after each step):





































stepgrammar0S'\to S; \ S\to A\mid B; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}C; \ B\to B\mathtt{1}\mid C\mathtt{1}; \ C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}1C\to\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} becomes C\to\mathtt{0}D and D\to C\mathtt{1}: \ S'\to S; \ S\to A\mid B; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}C; \ B\to B\mathtt{1}\mid C\mathtt{1}; \ C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}D; \ D\to C\mathtt{1}2only C is nullable; S' is not, and S is on no right side, so S'\to S is dropped again: \ S\to A\mid B; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}C; \ B\to B\mathtt{1}\mid C\mathtt{1}; \ C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}D; \ D\to C\mathtt{1}3S\to A\mid B; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}C\mid\mathtt{0}; \ B\to B\mathtt{1}\mid C\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}; \ C\to\mathtt{0}D; \ D\to C\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}4no cycles of unit rules: nothing to merge5S\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}C\mid B\mathtt{1}\mid C\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}C\mid\mathtt{0}; \ B\to B\mathtt{1}\mid C\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}; \ C\to\mathtt{0}D; \ D\to C\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}6E\to\mathtt{0} and F\to\mathtt{1} (the T_{\mathtt{0}} and T_{\mathtt{1}} of step 6, named as in the book) protect the terminals; the result is below
Removing \varepsilon-rules changes what the nonterminals mean, but not the language of S: after step 3, C generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mid n\ge1\} and D generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^{n+1}\mid n\ge0\}. The final grammar, in Chomsky normal form, still generates \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n\mid m\ne n\}:
\begin{aligned}
S&\to EA\mid EC\mid BF\mid CF\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1} & A&\to EA\mid EC\mid\mathtt{0} & B&\to BF\mid CF\mid\mathtt{1}\\
C&\to ED & D&\to CF\mid\mathtt{1} & E&\to\mathtt{0}\qquad F\to\mathtt{1}
\end{aligned}


                  
                  Steps 3 and 5 are where conversions go wrong 
                  
                


Step 3 adds a variant for every subset of nullable occurrences: from A\to BC with both nullable, add A\to B and A\to C (never A\to\varepsilon).
Step 5 copies the rules of B as they are after B has been processed; in the wrong order, a unit rule can be copied into A and survive.



Summary

A grammar (\Sigma, \Gamma, R, S) is a recursive definition; L(G) is the set of terminal strings derivable from S.
Each parse tree corresponds to one leftmost derivation. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two parse trees; a language is inherently ambiguous if every grammar for it is.
L(G) = L takes two inductions: build derivations (L\subseteq L(G)) and take them apart, one case per rule (L(G)\subseteq L). With \varepsilon-rules use a shortest derivation; with mutually recursive nonterminals prove all claims together.
Design by decomposing a typical string — nesting, first balance point, or cases — and describe the language of every nonterminal in English.
Regular ⊊ context-free; context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation, star and reversal, but not under intersection or complement.
Counting: only countably many context-free languages. \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\} is the canonical language that is not context-free.
Recursive automata (NFAs that call each other) accept exactly the context-free languages.
Every grammar converts to Chomsky normal form (A\to BC, A\to a), where every parse tree of a length-n string has 2n-1 nonterminal nodes and membership takes O(n^3) time by dynamic programming.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Midterm 1 (Sep 28) covered context-free languages and grammars. On Midterm-1-style exams a grammar is usually asked together with a fooling-set proof that the same language is not regular (§3.8): the language is context-free but not regular, like \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\} or Example 1 above (for which F = \mathtt{0}^* works: name two of its strings \mathtt{0}^i and \mathtt{0}^j with i<j; then \mathtt{1}^i distinguishes them). The grammar is graded with the rubric in §5.4 — syntax, correctness, and on homework an English description of every nonterminal; ambiguity is not penalized. True/false items test the big picture: “every regular language is context-free” (true), “the intersection of two context-free languages is context-free” (false, §5.6), “if a grammar is ambiguous, its language is inherently ambiguous” (false — S\to\mathtt{1}\mid S{+}S). The final exam (Dec 11) covers everything. Rubric details: how exams are graded.




                  
                  Practice this chapter 
                  
                

10 practice problems — 4 easy, 3 medium, 3 hard — each with a folded hint and a worked solution. Start with 5.1 Closure and ambiguity, true or false; the practice hub has the whole bank by difficulty and by topic.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 5 (§§5.1–5.9), summarized in our own words. The running example and the languages of its nonterminals, Lemmas 5.1–5.6 and Theorem 5.7, the grammars of §5.4 (palindromes, non-palindromes, the \#(\mathtt{0},w) versus \#(\mathtt{1},w) family, parentheses, expressions), the 1+1+1+1 ambiguity example, the warning about the simple regular-expression grammar (here without its rules for \varnothing and \varepsilon), the construction of §5.5, the counting argument, recursive automata with the conversion of Lemma 5.6, the CNF conversion steps (with the corrected condition for dropping S', see step 0) and the final CNF grammar follow the book. Original: the figures, the trace, the design examples, the precedence grammar for regular expressions, the path construction for Lemma 5.5 (the book only sketches it), the closure discussion, the CYK paragraph, and the ambiguity examples beyond 1+1+1+1. CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) grammar rubric for the grading notes. Every grammar on this page is compared with a brute-force description of its language on all strings up to a length bound — 12 for the binary grammars (and their exact languages up to length 14), 15–16 for the sums and parenthesis grammars, 10 for the three-letter example, and 6 for the grammars over six symbols (their exact languages up to length 9–11) — and every derivation, parse tree, parse-tree count, automaton run and conversion step is checked by tools/checks/ch05.py.

1-models-of-computation/06-turing-machin.content:
Chapter 6 · book pp. 97–116 · chapter PDF · prev: Chapter 5 · next: Chapter 7 · practice: 6 problems


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

A Turing machine is a finite-state control attached to an unbounded tape that it can read, overwrite and walk along in both directions. On a given input it accepts, rejects, crashes off the left end of the tape, or runs forever, and the difference between accepting a language and deciding it (also halting on every input) organizes all of Chapter 7. Designing machines is tedious but mechanical — scan, mark, walk back — and every reasonable variation (stay-put moves, more tracks, heads or tapes, a tape infinite in both directions) accepts and decides exactly the same languages, at most quadratically slower. Turing machines can simulate a real computer and, through a universal machine, each other. That generality is the point: they are a terrible model for fast algorithms and the standard model for proving what cannot be computed.


In 1936, at the age of 23, Alan Turing defined these machines, described a single machine that can simulate all the others, and proved that no machine solves the halting problem — and therefore that Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem (decide whether a given statement of first-order logic is provable) has no algorithmic solution. Alonzo Church had reached the same conclusion a few months earlier with his λ-calculus; Turing then proved that the two models compute exactly the same functions.


                  
                  The Church–Turing thesis 
                  
                

Every function that can be computed “by finite means” — by any algorithm whatsoever — can be computed by a Turing machine.
This is a claim about the world, not a theorem: “algorithm” has no formal definition to prove it against, and Turing himself called his arguments for it appeals to intuition. The evidence is that every reasonable model proposed since 1936 — the λ-calculus, recursive functions, register machines, programming languages, and the strange systems of Chapter 8 — computes exactly the same functions.


Concept page: church-turing-thesis.
6.1 Why bother?
Turing machines are a poor model of speed. Small changes to the model change running times: reversing an n-bit string takes O(n) time on a machine with two tapes but provably \Omega(n^2) time with one. Nobody designs algorithms on them; algorithms are analyzed on random-access models instead.
They are an excellent model of impossibility. To prove that no algorithm solves a problem, we need a definition of “algorithm” that is

simple enough that one proof can reason about every possible machine at once — a handful of components and a single step rule; and
powerful enough to simulate every other reasonable model, including Turing machines themselves. Self-simulation is what makes the self-referential undecidability proofs of Chapter 7 possible.



                  
                  A DFA with a notebook 
                  
                

A DFA reads its input once, left to right, and its only memory is its current state. A Turing machine has the same kind of finite control, but its input sits on a tape that it may reread, overwrite and extend without limit, moving in either direction. Finite control plus unbounded rewritable memory is general computation.


6.2 Formal definitions


                  
                  Definition — Turing machine 
                  
                

A Turing machine M consists of

a tape alphabet \Gamma: a finite set with at least two symbols, one of which is the blank \square;
an input alphabet \Sigma\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\square\}, non-empty;
a finite set Q of states containing three distinct special states \textit{start}, \textit{accept} and \textit{reject};
a transition function \delta\colon (Q\setminus\{\textit{accept},\textit{reject}\})\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}.

\delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta) means: in state p, reading a, overwrite it with b, move the head one cell — to the left if \Delta = -1, to the right if \Delta = +1 — and enter state q. Nothing happens after \textit{accept} or \textit{reject}.


The tape has a left end, cell 0, and extends forever to the right; at every moment all but finitely many cells are blank.


                  
                  Definition — configuration, step, crash 
                  
                

A configuration is a triple (q, x, i): the current state q, the tape contents x\in\Gamma^* (followed by infinitely many blanks; trailing blanks may be written or left out, so (q,x,i) and (q,x\square,i) are the same configuration), and the head position i\ge0. If \delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta) then
(p,\ xay,\ i)\ \Rightarrow\ (q,\ xby,\ i+\Delta)\qquad\text{whenever } \lvert x\rvert = i,
that is, when the head is on cell i, which holds a. Every configuration has at most one successor, and \Rightarrow^* means zero or more steps. On input w\in\Sigma^* the machine starts in the initial configuration (\textit{start}, w, 0). If a step would move the head to position -1, there is no next configuration: the machine crashes.



tape with cells # 0 x 1 x 0 blank blank, the head in state reset on cell 3#0x1x0□□⋯01234567resetconfiguration(reset, #0x1x0, 3)A configuration. The machine of §6.3 on input 001100, one round in: state reset, tape #0x1x0 followed by infinitely many blanks, head on cell 3. Cells are numbered from 0; a move left from cell 0 crashes the machine.


                  
                  Definition — the four outcomes 
                  
                

On each input w, exactly one of these happens:

M accepts w: (\textit{start}, w, 0)\Rightarrow^*(\textit{accept}, x, i) for some x and i;
M rejects w: (\textit{start}, w, 0)\Rightarrow^*(\textit{reject}, x, i) for some x and i;
M crashes on w: the run reaches a configuration that tries to move left from cell 0;
M runs forever on w: none of the above, ever.

M halts on w if it accepts or rejects w; otherwise — if it crashes or runs forever — M diverges on w. (Chapter 7’s set \textsf{Diverge}(M) therefore contains the inputs on which M crashes.)




                  
                  "Rejects" and "does not accept" are different 
                  
                

A machine that does not accept w may reject it, crash, or run forever. Accepting and rejecting are definite answers that an observer eventually sees, but “does not accept” may never become visible: a machine that has run for a million steps may still accept at step 10^6+1. Chapter 7 is built on this distinction — \textsf{Reject}(M) and \Sigma^*\setminus\textsf{Accept}(M) are different sets in general (§7.1).




                  
                  Definition — accepting versus deciding a language 
                  
                

Let L\subseteq\Sigma^*, and let \textsf{Accept}(M) be the set of strings that M accepts.

M accepts (or recognizes) L if \textsf{Accept}(M) = L: M accepts every string in L and nothing else. On strings outside L it may reject, crash or run forever. L is acceptable if some Turing machine accepts it.
M decides L if M accepts every string in L and rejects every string in \Sigma^*\setminus L — equivalently, M accepts L and halts on every input. L is decidable if some Turing machine decides it.




























term used here and in the booksynonyms you will meetacceptablerecognizable (the book’s word in §6.2), semi-decidable, semi-computable, recursively enumerable (r.e.)decidablecomputable, recursiveM accepts LM recognizes LM decides LM is a decider for L
Every decidable language is acceptable, since a machine that decides L also accepts it. The converse fails: the halting problem is acceptable but undecidable (§7.9), and some languages are not even acceptable.


                  
                  Missing transitions 
                  
                

The definition makes \delta total on the non-halting states, but tables and diagrams usually leave many transitions out. The convention, in the book and on this site, is that every missing transition goes to \textit{reject}. Say so explicitly on an exam, exactly as you would mention the omitted dump state of a DFA.


Concept pages: turing-machines, acceptable-and-decidable.
6.3 A first example
The language L = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\} is not regular — \mathtt{0}^* is a fooling set, with suffix \mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{0}^i for \mathtt{0}^i, as in §3.8 — and it is the standard example of a language that is not even context-free (the proof is beyond this course). It is decidable. The machine below follows the book’s idea of marking one symbol of each block per round, with one addition: it checks the format of the input first.


                  
                  The algorithm in English 
                  
                

Phase 1: check the format. If the input is empty, accept. Otherwise its first symbol must be \mathtt{0}; overwrite it with \mathtt{\#}, which marks the left end of the tape and counts as the first matched 0. Scan right, checking that the input has the form \mathtt{0}^+\mathtt{1}^+\mathtt{0}^+, then walk back to the \mathtt{\#}.
Phase 2: match in rounds. Each round marks the first unmarked \mathtt{1} with \mathtt{x}, marks the first unmarked \mathtt{0} after the 1s with \mathtt{x}, walks back to the last \mathtt{\#}, and marks the next \mathtt{0} of the first block with \mathtt{\#}. Once the first block is used up, accept if and only if every remaining symbol is marked.
Whenever a step cannot find the symbol it needs, reject.


In the table, ”—” means “write back the symbol that was read”. Missing transitions reject.

                  Trace on 010
                  
                

The underlined symbol is the one under the head. The machine accepts after 14 steps.

On 0110, \mathit{verify} finds the unmarked 1 and rejects; on 0101, \mathit{block3} reads a 1 and rejects.


Each round walks across the input and back, so on an input of length n the machine halts within O(n^2) steps; on \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k it takes exactly 4k^2 + 9k + 1 steps (35 for 001100). It never crashes, because every walk to the left stops at a \mathtt{\#}, and cell 0 holds one from the first step on.


                  
                  The book's machine skips the format check 
                  
                

The machine printed in the book’s §6.3 (states start, seek1, seek0, reset, verify) starts matching immediately. Read with a move to the left after it marks a 0 — which is what the text and its traces do; the printed table says +1 there, a typo — it also accepts some strings outside L, such as 001010 (18 strings of length at most 12 in all), and because its start state has no transition on \square, it rejects \varepsilon, which is in L. Its matching idea is sound; it needs a format check like Phase 1. The general lesson: test a design on \varepsilon and on near-misses such as 001010, 0110 and 00, not only on members of the language.




                  
                  Recipe — designing a Turing machine 
                  
                


Write the algorithm in English as a few passes over the tape: scan for something, mark it, walk back.
Mark, don’t count. The state is finite; unbounded counts live on the tape as marked symbols.
Mark the left end before the machine ever walks left, so that it knows where to stop instead of crashing.
Each pass becomes one or two states, and “keep scanning” becomes a self-loop.
Write the transition table with a one-line meaning for every state, and say that missing transitions reject.
Trace the machine on \varepsilon, on a short member of the language, and on several near-misses.





                  
                  Writing a Turing machine on an exam 
                  
                

Turing machines were not on Midterm 1. If the final asks you to design one, give the transition table (or a state diagram) together with an English description of what each state does, use mnemonic state names, and say that missing transitions reject — the standards for DFAs, scaled up. Begin with the phase-by-phase description in English; the table should implement exactly that description.


6.4 Variations
The definition above is one choice among many. Books, courses and research papers vary it in harmless ways, and all of these variants accept and decide exactly the same languages:

halting: several accepting and rejecting states; halting whenever no transition applies; only accepting states (a crash then counts as rejection); halting by moving off the left end;
moves: stay-put moves (\Delta = 0); moves of several cells at once; steps that either write or move, but not both;
transition function: partial instead of total, with missing transitions rejecting (as in our tables);
left end: an end marker that cannot be overwritten, or a move left at cell 0 that leaves the head where it is instead of crashing.

Two machines are equivalent if they accept the same strings and reject the same strings (so they also diverge on the same strings, although one may crash where the other runs forever). To show that a variant adds no power, show that a standard machine can simulate it. The cost of the simulation matters for running time, never for decidability.


                  
                  Construction — removing stay-put moves 
                  
                

Let M have moves \Delta\in\{-1,0,+1\}. Build M' with states Q' = Q\times\{0,1\}, start state (\textit{start},0), accepting state (\textit{accept},0), rejecting state (\textit{reject},0), and
\delta'\big((p,0),a\big) := \begin{cases} \big((q,1),\,b,\,+1\big) & \text{if } \delta(p,a) = (q,b,0),\\ \big((q,0),\,b,\,\Delta\big) & \text{if } \delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta) \text{ with } \Delta\ne0, \end{cases}
\delta'\big((p,1),a\big) := \big((p,0),\,a,\,-1\big)\quad\text{for every state } p \text{ and symbol } a.
State (q,1) means “I moved right only because M wanted to stay put; step back”. On every input, M' accepts, rejects, crashes or runs forever exactly when M does, with the same final tape, and t steps of M take at most 2t steps of M'.



a stay-put transition from p to q replaced by two transitions through the state (q,1)in M: stay put⟹in M′: step right, then step back lefta/b,0a/b,+1c;−1pq(p,0)(q,1)(q,0)Removing a stay-put move. A transition δ(p, a) = (q, b, 0) of M becomes a move right into the new state (q, 1), which moves back left without changing the tape, whatever symbol c it reads. Transitions that move ±1 are copied between the states (p, 0) and (q, 0). Each stay-put step of M costs M′ one extra step.
For example, some definitions let the final transition into \textit{accept} stay put, and the machine of §6.3 could hand the cell from \mathit{mark0} to \mathit{verify} without moving. With those three stay-put moves, the construction produces a 24-state machine without them that behaves identically, one extra step per stay-put move.
6.5 Computing functions


                  
                  Definition — computing a function 
                  
                

Replace \textit{accept} and \textit{reject} by a single halting state \textit{halt}. If M halts on input w, its output M(w) is the tape contents at that moment, without the trailing blanks: M(w) = x if and only if (\textit{start}, w, 0)\Rightarrow^*(\textit{halt}, x, i) for some i, where x does not end with \square. If M never halts on w, then M diverges on w, written M(w)\uparrow, and M(w) is undefined. M computes a function f\colon\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^* if M(w) = f(w) for every w\in\Sigma^*.


Shifting. The book’s machine for w\mapsto\mathtt{0}w keeps in its state the symbol it still has to write. In each step it writes that symbol and remembers the one it overwrote. (The book names the states 0 and 1; here they are \mathit{hold0} and \mathit{hold1}, and \mathit{hold0} is the start state.)

On 101 it goes through \mathit{hold0}\colon\underline{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{01}, \mathit{hold1}\colon\mathtt{0}\underline{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{1}, \mathit{hold0}\colon\mathtt{01}\underline{\mathtt{1}}, \mathit{hold1}\colon\mathtt{010}\underline{\square} and halts with output 0101. In general it halts after \lvert w\rvert + 1 steps. Remembering the last k symbols in the state shifts by k cells.


                  
                  Binary increment = shift, then carry 
                  
                

Adding 1 to a binary number can carry into a new leading digit (111 + 1 = 1000), and a machine that walks left looking for room for the carry would crash at cell 0. Shifting first makes the room: the machine below shifts w one cell to the right with a 0 in front, exactly like the shift machine, and then adds 1 at the right end; the carry stops at that leading 0 at the latest.

If w is the binary representation of n (leading zeros allowed), the output is n+1 in binary with \lvert w\rvert + 1 digits: 1011 ↦ 01100, 111 ↦ 1000, and \varepsilon ↦ 1. Removing the leading 0 would take one more pass. The book’s binary adder (its §6.5.2) works in the same style: phases for scanning and adding, with the carry kept in the state.


6.6 Tracks, heads, and tapes
More hardware does not add power either. Each variant below is simulated by a standard machine; the last column gives the cost of simulating t steps.

two tapes with their heads, and the same information on one tape with four trackstape 1abba□⋯tape 210011□⋯⟹tape 1head 1tape 2head 2a1b▲0b0a1□1▲□□□□⋯one tape over a 4-track alphabetTwo tapes on one. Each cell of the single tape holds four things: the cell of tape 1, a mark if head 1 is there, the cell of tape 2, and a mark if head 2 is there. One step of the two-tape machine becomes a sweep across the used part of the tape to read the marked symbols, and a sweep back to write them and move the marks.


                  
                  The quadratic slowdown is unavoidable 
                  
                

After t steps the simulated heads can be up to t cells apart, so one sweep costs O(t) steps and t simulated steps cost O(t^2). No cleverer one-head simulation exists in general: the marked palindromes \{w\,\mathtt{\#}\,w^R \mid w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*\} can be decided in O(n) time with two heads — send one head to the far end, then walk the two heads toward each other, comparing — but need \Omega(n^2) time on a standard machine with one head.


Combining the simulations, any fixed number of tapes, heads and tracks, on tapes infinite in one or both directions, costs at most a quadratic slowdown. So decidability never depends on these details, and neither does running in polynomial time, which is what the classes P and NP of Chapter 9 measure.
6.7 Simulating a real computer
Two features of real programs remain, and Turing machines can simulate both.

Subroutines and recursion. Keep a call stack on an extra tape. To call a subroutine, push a record naming the state to return to and enter the subroutine’s states; to return, pop the top record and continue in the state it names. With the stack on its own tape, t steps of a machine with recursive calls take O(t) steps on a multi-tape machine, and so O(t^2) steps on a standard one.
Random-access memory. Keep the memory on a tape as a list of pairs [\textit{address}\bullet\textit{data}]. A read or write scans the list for the address, and appends a new pair if the address is not there yet. If every address and value has at most \ell bits, the kth access costs O(k\ell) steps on a multi-tape machine, so t accesses cost O(t^2\ell) — and O(t^3\ell^2) on a standard one-tape machine.

Every overhead is polynomial. So a Turing machine can run any program a real computer can run, at most polynomially slower, and “computable by a program in your favorite language” means the same thing as “computable by a Turing machine” — evidence for the Church–Turing thesis from the one model we actually build.
6.8 Universal Turing machines
A universal Turing machine U is an interpreter for Turing machines, written as a Turing machine. Its input is an encoding \langle M, w\rangle of a machine M together with an input w for M.


                  
                  The universal machine 
                  
                

U accepts \langle M,w\rangle if and only if M accepts w, and U rejects \langle M,w\rangle if and only if M rejects w: on every input, U gives the answer that M would give.


U has one fixed, finite alphabet, but the machines it simulates have arbitrarily large alphabets and state sets, so everything about M is written in binary, with a few punctuation symbols.


                  
                  The encodings 
                  
                


Symbols: each a\in\Gamma gets a distinct string \langle a\rangle of \lceil\lg\lvert\Gamma\rvert\rceil bits. A string is written symbol by symbol between brackets: \langle w\rangle = [\langle w_1\rangle{\bullet}\langle w_2\rangle{\bullet}\cdots{\bullet}\langle w_n\rangle].
States: each q\in Q gets a distinct string \langle q\rangle of \lceil\lg\lvert Q\rvert\rceil bits, with \langle\textit{start}\rangle = \mathtt{1}\cdots\mathtt{1} and \langle\textit{reject}\rangle = \mathtt{0}\cdots\mathtt{0}. The book fixes no code for \textit{accept}, but U has to recognize it, so fix one as well; this site uses \langle\textit{accept}\rangle = \mathtt{0}\cdots\mathtt{01}.
Moves: \langle -1\rangle = \mathtt{0} and \langle +1\rangle = \mathtt{1}.
Transitions: each \delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta) with q\ne\textit{reject} becomes a block [\langle p\rangle{\bullet}\langle a\rangle\,|\,\langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle b\rangle{\bullet}\langle\Delta\rangle]. Transitions into \textit{reject} are left out — they become missing transitions.
The machine: \langle M\rangle = [\langle\textit{reject}\rangle{\bullet}\langle\square\rangle]\,\langle\delta\rangle, where \langle\delta\rangle is the list of all blocks inside one more pair of brackets. The first block tells U how long the codes are.
Configurations: a list of cells [\langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle a\rangle], one per tape cell, inside one more pair of brackets. Here a is the cell’s symbol, and q = \textit{reject} in every cell except the one under the head, which carries the current state.





                  
                  Encoding the machine of §6.3 
                  
                

It has \lvert\Gamma\rvert = 5 symbols and \lvert Q\rvert = 12 states, so symbols take 3 bits and states take 4. Choose \langle\square\rangle = \mathtt{000}, \langle\mathtt{0}\rangle = \mathtt{001}, \langle\mathtt{1}\rangle = \mathtt{010}, \langle\mathtt{\#}\rangle = \mathtt{011}, \langle\mathtt{x}\rangle = \mathtt{100}, and \langle\textit{start}\rangle = \mathtt{1111}, \langle\textit{reject}\rangle = \mathtt{0000}, \langle\textit{accept}\rangle = \mathtt{0001}, \langle\mathit{seek1}\rangle = \mathtt{0110}, \langle\mathit{seek0}\rangle = \mathtt{0111}, \langle\mathit{reset}\rangle = \mathtt{1000}, with other distinct codes for the other states. Then

\delta(\mathit{seek1},\mathtt{1}) = (\mathit{seek0},\mathtt{x},+1) becomes the block [0110•010|0111•100•1];
\langle M\rangle is [0000•000] followed by a bracketed list of 25 such blocks, one for each transition in the table;
the input 010 is [001•010•001];
the configuration (\mathit{reset}, \mathtt{\#0x1x0}, 3) drawn in §6.2 is [[0000•011][0000•001][0000•100][1000•010][0000•100][0000•001]].

The book’s own example, for its seven-state machine with 3-bit codes, lists \langle\textit{start}\rangle = \mathtt{111} and uses it in the initial configuration, but writes \textit{start} as 001 inside its encoded transitions — a typo; by the rule above the code is 111 there too.




                  
                  How U simulates one step of M
                  
                

U keeps \langle\delta\rangle in one place and the encoded configuration in another (on separate tapes, or tracks of one tape).

Find the head: scan the configuration for the one cell whose state code is not \langle\textit{reject}\rangle.
Look up the transition: scan \langle\delta\rangle for the block whose left half matches that cell. If there is none, reject.
Apply it: copy the block’s \langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle b\rangle into the cell. If q = \textit{accept}, accept.
Move: reset this cell’s state code to \langle\textit{reject}\rangle and write \langle q\rangle into the neighboring cell in direction \Delta; at the right end, first append a fresh cell [\langle\textit{reject}\rangle{\bullet}\langle\square\rangle], so the encoded tape behaves as if it were infinite. Then repeat. (If the head would move left from the first cell, M crashes; then U must not answer either — it can simply loop forever.)

Initialization copies \langle w\rangle into this format, with \langle\textit{start}\rangle in the first cell.


So one fixed machine runs every program: a stored-program computer, described years before one was built. In Chapter 7, U does two jobs. It shows that \textsf{Accept} = \{\langle M,w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w\} is acceptable — U accepts it — and its ability to run a machine on any string, including the machine’s own encoding, powers the self-referential arguments that make \textsf{Accept} undecidable (§7.4). Chapter 8 replaces U by much smaller universal systems.
Concept page: universal-turing-machine.
Summary

A Turing machine is a finite control plus an unbounded tape: \delta\colon (Q\setminus\{\textit{accept},\textit{reject}\})\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}, configurations (q,x,i), start (\textit{start},w,0); a move left from cell 0 crashes.
On each input a machine accepts, rejects, crashes or runs forever. “Rejects” is not the same as “does not accept”.
M accepts L if \textsf{Accept}(M) = L; M decides L if it also halts on every input. Acceptable = recognizable = r.e.; decidable = computable = recursive; every decidable language is acceptable, not conversely.
Design machines in passes — scan, mark, walk back — with the left end marked; give a table plus an English meaning for every state; missing transitions reject. \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\} is decidable in O(n^2) time.
All reasonable variants are equivalent: stay-put moves (states Q\times\{0,1\}), several halting states, two-way infinite tapes, tracks, heads, tapes. One head costs a \Theta(t^2) slowdown, and that is unavoidable; two tapes cost only O(t\log t).
For functions: one halting state, the output is the final tape contents, and M(w)\uparrow when M diverges. The shift machine needs two states besides \textit{halt}, the increment machine three.
Recursion and random-access memory cost only a polynomial slowdown, so Turing machines compute everything real programs compute.
A universal machine U accepts \langle M,w\rangle iff M accepts w and rejects it iff M rejects w, by stepping through an encoded configuration.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Turing machines were not on Midterm 1. The final exam (Dec 11) covers everything, Chapters 6–9 included, and Turing machines appear there mostly through undecidability (Chapter 7) and through true/false items such as “every decidable language is acceptable” (true), “if M does not accept w, then M rejects w” (false: it may run forever or crash), “some language decided by a two-tape machine is decided by no one-tape machine” (false: the extra tape only saves time), or ”\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\} is decidable” (true). If you are asked to design a machine, give a transition table or diagram plus an English description of every state, and say that missing transitions reject. See also the review of Chapters 6–9 and how exams are graded.




                  
                  Practice this chapter 
                  
                

6 practice problems — 3 easy, 2 medium, 1 hard — each with a folded hint and a worked solution. Start with 6.1 Deciding, crashing and variants; the practice hub has the whole bank by difficulty and by topic.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 6 (§§6.1–6.8), summarized in our own words. The language \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\} with the idea of marking one symbol of each block per round, the shift machine, the list of variants, the stay-put construction, the simulation costs, the call-stack and memory-tape simulations, and the encodings and step of the universal machine follow the book. The machine with a format check, its trace, the increment machine, the encoded examples (with the code for \textit{accept}, which the book leaves open), the stay-put example and the figures are original; the remark about the book’s machine comes from simulating its transition table, and the one about its 001 for \textit{start} from comparing its table of codes with its encoded transitions. Every machine, trace, step count, construction and encoding on this page is checked by tools/checks/ch06.py — the main machine on all inputs of length at most 14, the stay-put construction on the machine above and on 300 random machines, and the encoding by running a string-level version of U against the machine itself.
