7.9 The halting problem via reduction
Now let the input carry the machine and the string separately:
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{Accept} &:= \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w\}, & \textsf{Halt} &:= \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } w\},\\
\textsf{Reject} &:= \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ rejects } w\}, & \textsf{Diverge} &:= \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ diverges on } w\}.
\end{aligned}
The universal machine shows that \textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Reject} and \textsf{Halt} are acceptable (run U, U^R, U^H).


                  
                  Theorem 12 
                  
                

\textsf{Halt} is undecidable.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

Suppose some machine \textsf{H} decides \textsf{Halt}. Build \textsf{SH}: on input w, reject if w is not the encoding of a machine; otherwise w = \langle M\rangle, so write \langle M, \langle M\rangle\rangle on the tape and run \textsf{H} on it, returning its answer. \textsf{SH} halts on every input, and it accepts \langle M\rangle exactly when M halts on \langle M\rangle. So \textsf{SH} decides \textsf{SelfHalt}, contradicting Theorem 8. \blacksquare


The same argument with \textsf{SelfAccept}, \textsf{SelfReject} or \textsf{SelfDiverge} shows that \textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Reject} and \textsf{Diverge} are undecidable; \textsf{Diverge} is not even acceptable, since its complement is (Lemma 5). The proof reduces \textsf{SelfHalt} to \textsf{Halt}: it solves \textsf{SelfHalt} with a solver for \textsf{Halt} as a subroutine. That is the general method.


                  
                  The direction of a reduction 
                  
                

To prove that L is undecidable, reduce a known undecidable language to L: assume that some machine decides L, and use it as a black-box subroutine in a machine that decides a language already known to be undecidable. Then the assumed machine cannot exist.
Reducing L to a known undecidable language — deciding L with the help of a decider for \textsf{Halt} — proves nothing: every decidable language reduces to \textsf{Halt} too.



box DecideAccept containing a box that writes down the encoding of M prime and a box DecideL; the encoding flows into DecideL, whose accept and reject are DecideAccept's answersDecideAccept⟨M, w⟩write down ⟨M′⟩M′(x):ignore xrun M on wthen … (depends on L)never run⟨M′⟩DecideL(hypothetical)acceptrejectA reduction from Accept to L. DecideAccept turns its input ⟨M, w⟩ into the encoding of a new machine M′ and returns whatever the hypothetical decider DecideL says about ⟨M′⟩. Writing down ⟨M′⟩ always terminates, because M′ is never run (dashed box). If ⟨M′⟩ ∈ L exactly when M accepts w, then DecideAccept decides Accept — impossible, so DecideL cannot exist.


                  
                  Template — undecidability by reduction from \textsf{Accept}
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{DecideL} decides L. 
Consider the following machine \textsf{DecideAccept}. Given \langle M, w\rangle, it writes the encoding \langle M'\rangle of the machine 
\quad M'(x): [for example: ignore x; run M on w; then …] 
and then runs \textsf{DecideL} on \langle M'\rangle and returns its answer. 
\Rightarrow Suppose M accepts w. Then M' […], so \langle M'\rangle\in L. So \textsf{DecideL} accepts \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts \langle M, w\rangle. 
\Leftarrow Suppose M does not accept w — it rejects or diverges. Then M' […], so \langle M'\rangle\notin L. So \textsf{DecideL} rejects \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects \langle M, w\rangle. 
In both cases \textsf{DecideAccept} is correct, and it always halts. So \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept}, which is impossible. 
We conclude that \textsf{DecideL} does not exist: L is undecidable. \blacksquare




                  
                  Reductions juggle four machines 
                  
                


Name every machine and never write “it” or “the machine”: the hypothetical decider (\textsf{DecideL}), the decider you build (\textsf{DecideAccept}), its input machine (M), and the machine whose encoding you write down (M').
\textsf{DecideAccept} never runs M'; it only writes \langle M'\rangle. M' may run forever — that is usually the point — but \textsf{DecideAccept} must always halt.
“Does not accept” means rejects or diverges, and the second direction must cover both. If M' runs M on w and M diverges, M' is stuck forever.
Wrong direction: building a decider for L out of a decider for \textsf{Accept} proves nothing.





                  
                  How a reduction proof is graded 
                  
                

Out of 10: 4 for the reduction itself — a correct description of the new decider and of M', in the right direction — 3 for showing that a yes-instance (M accepts w) leads to acceptance, and 3 for showing that a no-instance (M rejects or diverges) leads to rejection.


Concept pages: halting-problem, undecidability-reductions.
7.10 More undecidable languages
\textsf{NeverAccept} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) = \varnothing\}.


                  
                  Theorem 13 
                  
                

\textsf{NeverAccept} is undecidable.




                  
                  Proof of Theorem 13 — the model reduction 
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{NA} decides \textsf{NeverAccept}. Consider the following machine \textsf{DecideAccept}. Given \langle M, w\rangle, it writes the encoding \langle M_w\rangle of the machine
M_w(x)\colon \text{ erase } x;\ \text{write } w \text{ on the tape};\ \text{run } M \text{ (on } w).
Then \textsf{DecideAccept} runs \textsf{NA} on \langle M_w\rangle and returns the opposite answer (equivalently, it runs \textsf{NA}^R). \textsf{DecideAccept} always halts: writing \langle M_w\rangle is an algorithm, and \textsf{NA} halts on every input.

Suppose M accepts w. Then M_w accepts every input x, so \textsf{Accept}(M_w) = \Sigma^*\ne\varnothing, so \langle M_w\rangle\notin\textsf{NeverAccept}. So \textsf{NA} rejects \langle M_w\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts \langle M, w\rangle.
Suppose M does not accept w. Then on every input x, M_w either rejects (if M rejects w) or runs forever (if M diverges on w); either way \textsf{Accept}(M_w) = \varnothing, so \langle M_w\rangle\in\textsf{NeverAccept}. So \textsf{NA} accepts \langle M_w\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects \langle M, w\rangle.

In both cases \textsf{DecideAccept} answers correctly, so it decides \textsf{Accept} — which is impossible. Hence \textsf{NA} does not exist. \blacksquare


M_w is the workhorse of reductions: \textsf{Accept}(M_w) is \Sigma^* or \varnothing, depending on what M does with w. \textsf{NeverAccept} is not even acceptable, by Lemma 5: its complement (\textsf{Accept}(M)\ne\varnothing, plus garbage) is acceptable — in round t = 1, 2, \dots run M for t steps on each of the first t strings of \Sigma^*.
The same reduction with \textsf{Reject}(M_w), \textsf{Halt}(M_w) or \textsf{Diverge}(M_w) in place of \textsf{Accept}(M_w) shows that
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{NeverReject} &:= \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Reject}(M) = \varnothing\},\\
\textsf{NeverHalt} &:= \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Halt}(M) = \varnothing\},\\
\textsf{NeverDiverge} &:= \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Diverge}(M) = \varnothing\}
\end{aligned}
are undecidable too (reduce from \textsf{Reject}, from \textsf{Halt}, and from \textsf{Halt} again: \textsf{Diverge}(M_w) = \varnothing exactly when M halts on w). Each new undecidable language becomes a starting point for further reductions:


                  
                  Theorem 14 
                  
                

\textsf{DivergeSame} := \{\langle M_1\rangle\langle M_2\rangle \mid \textsf{Diverge}(M_1) = \textsf{Diverge}(M_2)\} is undecidable.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

Suppose \textsf{DS} decides \textsf{DivergeSame}. Fix a machine Y that accepts every input at once, so \textsf{Diverge}(Y) = \varnothing. The machine \textsf{ND} that, given \langle M\rangle, runs \textsf{DS} on \langle M\rangle\langle Y\rangle accepts exactly when \textsf{Diverge}(M) = \varnothing. So \textsf{ND} decides \textsf{NeverDiverge} — impossible. \blacksquare


7.11 Rice’s theorem
Most of these reductions follow one pattern, and Rice’s theorem does it once and for all. A property of languages is a set \mathcal{L} of languages; define
\textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\in\mathcal{L}\}.
For example, \textsf{NeverAccept} = \textsf{AcceptIn}(\{\varnothing\}).


                  
                  Rice's theorem 
                  
                

Let \mathcal{L} be a set of languages such that \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L} for some Turing machine Y, and \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L} for some Turing machine N. Then \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is undecidable.
Form closer to the proof: if \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L} and \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L} for some Turing machine Y, then \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is undecidable.




                  
                  Proof sketch (click to expand) 
                  
                

The form with \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L}. Suppose \textsf{AL} decides \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}). Build \textsf{DecideHalt}: given \langle M, w\rangle, write the encoding of
\textsf{WTF}(x)\colon \text{ run } M \text{ on } w \text{ and ignore the result};\ \text{then run } Y \text{ on } x \text{ and return its answer},
run \textsf{AL} on \langle\textsf{WTF}\rangle, and return its answer. If M halts on w, then \textsf{WTF} behaves exactly like Y, so \textsf{Accept}(\textsf{WTF}) = \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L}, and \textsf{AL} accepts. If M diverges on w, then \textsf{WTF} diverges on every input, so \textsf{Accept}(\textsf{WTF}) = \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L}, and \textsf{AL} rejects. So \textsf{DecideHalt} decides \textsf{Halt}, which is impossible.
The general form. If \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L}, use the first form with Y. If \varnothing\in\mathcal{L}, apply the first form to the complementary property \mathcal{L}' (all languages not in \mathcal{L}), which does not contain \varnothing and does contain \textsf{Accept}(N). Then \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}') is undecidable; it is the set of encodings minus \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}), so \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is undecidable by Corollary 3. \blacksquare




                  
                  Using Rice's theorem 
                  
                


Name the property. Write the language as \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) with an explicit set of languages \mathcal{L}, and check that membership of \langle M\rangle depends only on \textsf{Accept}(M): two machines with the same language must be both in or both out.
Give a machine Y with \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L}, concretely.
Give a machine N with \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L}, concretely.
Conclude: by Rice’s theorem, \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is undecidable.

Handy witnesses: M_{\textsf{Accept}} accepts every input at once (\textsf{Accept} = \Sigma^*); M_{\textsf{Reject}} rejects every input at once (\textsf{Accept} = \varnothing, \textsf{Reject} = \Sigma^*); M_{\textsf{Diverge}} moves right forever (\textsf{Accept} = \varnothing, \textsf{Diverge} = \Sigma^*).




                  
                  Corollary 15 
                  
                

Each of the following languages is undecidable:



























































\{\langle M\rangle \mid \ldots\}a machine with the propertya machine without it(a)M accepts \varepsilon (starting on an empty tape)M_{\textsf{Accept}}M_{\textsf{Reject}}(b)M accepts the string \mathtt{UIUC}M_{\textsf{Accept}}M_{\textsf{Reject}}(c)M accepts exactly three stringsa decider for \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{00},\mathtt{000}\}M_{\textsf{Reject}}(d)M accepts every palindromeM_{\textsf{Accept}}M_{\textsf{Reject}}(e)\textsf{Accept}(M) is regularM_{\textsf{Reject}} (\varnothing is regular)a decider for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}(f)\textsf{Accept}(M) is not regulara decider for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}M_{\textsf{Reject}}(g)\textsf{Accept}(M) is undecidablean acceptor for \textsf{SelfReject} (Theorem 11)M_{\textsf{Reject}}(h)\textsf{Accept}(M) = \textsf{Accept}(N), for a fixed machine NN itselfM_{\textsf{Reject}}, or M_{\textsf{Accept}} if \textsf{Accept}(N) = \varnothing


Extra parameters do not get in the way: fix them.


                  
                  Theorem 16 
                  
                

\{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w^k \text{ for every integer } k\ge0\} is undecidable.


For a fixed string w, the property \mathcal{L}_w := \{L \mid w^k\in L \text{ for every } k\ge0\} contains \textsf{Accept}(M_{\textsf{Accept}}) = \Sigma^* but not \textsf{Accept}(M_{\textsf{Reject}}) = \varnothing, which does not even contain w^0 = \varepsilon. So \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}_w) is undecidable; a decider for the language of pairs would decide it by appending the fixed w to its input.


                  
                  Rice's rejection, halting, divergence and decision theorems 
                  
                

The same proof works for the other languages of a machine. If \textsf{Reject}(Y)\in\mathcal{L} and \textsf{Reject}(N)\notin\mathcal{L} for some machines Y and N, then \textsf{RejectIn}(\mathcal{L}) := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Reject}(M)\in\mathcal{L}\} is undecidable. Likewise \textsf{HaltIn}(\mathcal{L}) (with \textsf{Halt}) and \textsf{DivergeIn}(\mathcal{L}) (with \textsf{Diverge}); and if some machine Y decides a language in \mathcal{L} and some machine N decides a language not in \mathcal{L}, then \textsf{DecideIn}(\mathcal{L}) := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ decides a language in } \mathcal{L}\} is undecidable.


Choose the variant that matches the definition, and describe the witnesses by that language: \textsf{NeverDiverge} = \textsf{DivergeIn}(\{\varnothing\}) with Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}} (\textsf{Diverge} = \varnothing) and N = M_{\textsf{Diverge}} (\textsf{Diverge} = \Sigma^*); \textsf{NeverHalt} = \textsf{HaltIn}(\{\varnothing\}) with Y = M_{\textsf{Diverge}} and N = M_{\textsf{Accept}}.


                  
                  When Rice's theorem does not apply 
                  
                


Behavior is not language. \textsf{ThisIsSparta} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \mathtt{SPARTA} \text{ after exactly 300 steps}\} is decidable — simulate 300 steps. Machines that accept every input after exactly 300 and after 301 steps have the same language, but only the first is in it, so it is not a property of \textsf{Accept}(M).
Self-reference. \textsf{RevAccept} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \langle M\rangle^R\} depends on M‘s own encoding, so Rice does not apply; it is undecidable by a reduction. Given \langle M, w\rangle, write \langle M'\rangle for “ignore the input; run M on w”: M' accepts \langle M'\rangle^R (and everything else) if M accepts w, and nothing otherwise.
Trivial properties. If every acceptable language has the property, or none does, there is no Y or no N, and the language is decidable: \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ is acceptable}\} is just the set of all encodings.
Rice proves undecidability only, not unacceptability — for that, see §7.12.





                  
                  How a proof by Rice's theorem is graded 
                  
                

Out of 10: 4 for a machine whose language has the property, 4 for a machine whose language does not, and 2 for the details — including stating the property as a set of languages and using the right variant of the theorem.


Concept page: rices-theorem.
7.12 The Rice–McNaughton–Myhill–Shapiro theorem
This section is optional in the book. Rice’s theorem says when \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is undecidable; this theorem says exactly when it is acceptable.


                  
                  Definition — monotone, compact, finitely acceptable 
                  
                

A set \mathcal{L} of acceptable languages is

monotone if every acceptable superset of a language in \mathcal{L} is also in \mathcal{L};
compact if every language in \mathcal{L} has a finite subset that is also in \mathcal{L};
finitely acceptable if the language \{\langle L\rangle \mid L\in\mathcal{L} \text{ and } L \text{ is finite}\} is acceptable, where \langle L\rangle lists the strings of L.





                  
                  The Rice–McNaughton–Myhill–Shapiro theorem 
                  
                

For every set \mathcal{L} of acceptable languages, \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is acceptable if and only if \mathcal{L} is monotone, compact and finitely acceptable.




                  
                  Lemma 17 
                  
                

If \mathcal{L} is not monotone, then \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is not acceptable.




                  
                  Proof sketch (click to expand) 
                  
                

Pick machines Y and N with \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L}, \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L} and \textsf{Accept}(Y)\subseteq\textsf{Accept}(N) (that is what “not monotone” provides). Given \langle M\rangle, write the encoding of the machine \textsf{WTF} that, on input x, runs Y on x, N on x and M on \langle M\rangle in parallel, and accepts if Y accepts x, or if N accepts x and M halts on \langle M\rangle. If M halts on \langle M\rangle, then \textsf{Accept}(\textsf{WTF}) = \textsf{Accept}(Y)\cup\textsf{Accept}(N) = \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L}; otherwise \textsf{Accept}(\textsf{WTF}) = \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L}. So \langle\textsf{WTF}\rangle\in\textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) exactly when \langle M\rangle\in\textsf{SelfDiverge}, and an acceptor for \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) would give an acceptor for \textsf{SelfDiverge}, contradicting Theorem 9. \blacksquare




                  
                  Corollary 18 
                  
                

Each of the following languages is not acceptable:


















































\{\langle M\rangle \mid \ldots\}the condition that fails(a)\textsf{Accept}(M) is finitemonotone: \varnothing is finite, \Sigma^*\supseteq\varnothing is not(b)\textsf{Accept}(M) is infinitecompact: no finite subset of \Sigma^* is infinite(c)\textsf{Accept}(M) is regularmonotone: \varnothing\subseteq\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}(d)\textsf{Accept}(M) is not regularmonotone: \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}\subseteq\Sigma^*(e)\textsf{Accept}(M) is decidablemonotone: \varnothing\subseteq\textsf{SelfReject}(f)\textsf{Accept}(M) is undecidablemonotone: \textsf{SelfReject}\subseteq\Sigma^*(g)M accepts at least one string in \textsf{SelfDiverge}finitely acceptable: w\in\textsf{SelfDiverge} iff the one-string language \{w\} has the property(h)\textsf{Accept}(M) = \textsf{Accept}(N), for a fixed machine Nmonotone if \textsf{Accept}(N)\ne\Sigma^*; compact if \textsf{Accept}(N) = \Sigma^*


7.13 Turing machine behavior: it’s complicated
Rice’s theorem covers properties of the language. Properties of a machine’s behavior have no such rule, and examples go both ways.
\textsf{NeverLeft} := \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ never moves left when run on input } w\}.


                  
                  Theorem 19 
                  
                

\textsf{NeverLeft} is decidable.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

Simulate M on w, one step at a time. Reject as soon as M moves left. Accept if M halts. Accept once M has read more than \lvert Q\rvert blanks, where Q is M‘s set of states.
The last rule is the heart of the proof. While M moves only right, it reads each cell exactly once; after the input it reads only blanks that it has never written on, so each of its moves there depends on its current state alone. Among more than \lvert Q\rvert blank reads, two happen in the same state q. Everything M did between those two moments — all right moves — therefore repeats forever: M never halts and never moves left, and accepting is correct. The simulation stops after at most \lvert w\rvert + \lvert Q\rvert steps, so this is a decider. \blacksquare



tape 0 1 1 followed by blanks, with the state at each cell: start, start, p, p, q, r, q, r; the two q's are highlighted011□□□□□⋯startstartppqrqrsame state, same symbol ⇒ the run repeats foreverinput wstates while reading each cell (the head moves right every step)Why NeverLeft is decidable. A machine that never moves left reads each cell once. Past the input it reads only blanks, so each move depends on its state alone. Here the state q repeats on a blank, and from then on the run cycles q, r, q, r, … to the right forever. Among |Q| + 1 blank reads some state must repeat, so a simulation can stop there.
\textsf{LeftThree} := \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ eventually moves left three times in a row when run on input } w\}.


                  
                  Theorem 20 
                  
                

\textsf{LeftThree} is undecidable.




                  
                  Proof sketch (click to expand) 
                  
                

Reduce from \textsf{Accept}. From \langle M\rangle, build M' that simulates M step by step with two changes. After each simulated step, M' moves right once and then left once, so it never makes three left moves in a row while simulating. And instead of entering the accept state, M' moves right three times and then left three times (changing nothing), and only then accepts; the right moves first keep it from falling off the left end. So M' moves left three times in a row on w exactly when M accepts w, and a decider for \textsf{LeftThree} would decide \textsf{Accept}. \blacksquare


\textsf{LeftThree} is acceptable (simulate and wait), so it sits with \textsf{Halt} in the left lune of the figure in §7.8; \textsf{NeverLeft} is decidable.


                  
                  Rules of thumb for behaviors (heuristics, not theorems) 
                  
                


Probably undecidable if a machine could simulate an arbitrary Turing machine while avoiding the behavior, and show it only when the simulation accepts: reentering the start state, revisiting the left end of the tape, writing a blank, moving left three times in a row.
Probably decidable if the behavior confines the machine to finitely many configurations, or forces it into an endless loop after finitely many steps: ever leaving the start state, reading the whole input, writing a non-blank symbol over a blank, never moving left.



Summary

\textsf{Accept}(M), \textsf{Reject}(M), \textsf{Diverge}(M) partition \Sigma^*; deciding means also \textsf{Diverge}(M) = \varnothing. “Does not accept” means rejects or diverges.
Decidable languages are closed under boolean operations, acceptable ones under \cup (in parallel) and \cap. Decidable = acceptable and co-acceptable (Lemma 5).
Diagonalization: run the machine built from a hypothetical decider on its own encoding. \textsf{SelfReject}, \textsf{SelfAccept}, \textsf{SelfHalt} are undecidable but acceptable; \textsf{SelfDiverge} is unacceptable; by Cantor, most languages are.
Reduction: decide a known undecidable language with a hypothetical decider for L — never the other way round. Writing \langle M'\rangle always halts; running M' need not.
\textsf{Halt}, \textsf{Accept}, \textsf{NeverAccept}, \textsf{DivergeSame}, … are undecidable; M_w (“ignore x, run M on w”) has language \Sigma^* or \varnothing.
Rice: a property of \textsf{Accept}(M) with a yes-machine and a no-machine is undecidable; use the variant that matches the definition. Not for behavior or self-reference. RMMS: non-monotone properties are not even acceptable.
Behaviors go either way: \textsf{NeverLeft} is decidable (\lvert Q\rvert blanks), \textsf{LeftThree} is not.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Chapters 6–9 are tested on the final exam (Dec 11) only. An undecidability proof is graded out of 10 with one of three rubrics: diagonalization (4 wrapper machine + 6 contradiction, 3 per case), reduction (4 reduction + 3 + 3 for the two directions), or Rice’s theorem (4 yes-machine + 4 no-machine + 2 details, including the right variant). Pick the tool first: a property of \textsf{Accept}(M) calls for Rice; self-reference or behavior calls for a reduction (usually with M_w) or a diagonal argument. True/false practice: “every acceptable language is decidable” (false: \textsf{SelfReject}); “the complement of an acceptable language is acceptable” (false: \textsf{SelfDiverge}); ”’M has 374 states’ is undecidable by Rice’s theorem” (false: decidable — a property of the machine, not its language). Rubric details: how exams are graded; review: Turing machines and undecidability.




                  
                  Practice this chapter 
                  
                

8 practice problems — 3 easy, 3 medium, 2 hard — each with a folded hint and a worked solution. Start with 7.1 Closure facts, true or false; the practice hub has the whole bank by difficulty and by topic.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 7 (§§7.1–7.13), summarized in our own words, with the book’s numbering (Lemma 1 through Theorem 20, no chapter prefix). The \Pi example, all named languages and their proofs, Rice’s theorem with the \textsf{WTF} machine and its variants, Theorem 16, the RMMS theorem with Lemma 17 and Corollaries 15 and 18, \textsf{NeverLeft}, \textsf{LeftThree} and the rules of thumb follow the book. The figures, the Lemma 4 example, the witness and failure columns of the corollary tables, the \textsf{RevAccept} reduction, the co-acceptability of \textsf{NeverAccept} and the bits of \pi are original. The definition of monotone asks only for acceptable supersets, as the RMMS theorem and Lemma 17 need (the book says every superset, but \mathcal{L} contains only acceptable languages). CS/ECE 374 A (Fall 2026) undecidability rubrics for the grading notes. The bits of \pi, Cantor’s theorem on small sets, the diagonal argument, the constructions of Lemma 1, the parallel simulations of Lemmas 4 and 5, the Rice witnesses, the \textsf{ThisIsSparta} machines, the \textsf{NeverLeft} decider (against long simulations of hundreds of random machines) and the \textsf{LeftThree} construction are checked by tools/checks/ch07.py.

1-models-of-computation/08-universal-mod.title: Chapter 8 — Universal Models
1-models-of-computation/08-universal-mod.content:
Chapter 8 · book pp. 137–144 · chapter PDF · prev: Chapter 7 · next: Chapter 9


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

A model of computation is universal if it can simulate every Turing machine. Anything that can simulate a Turing machine inherits both its power — it computes everything computable — and its undecidability: basic questions about the model, such as “does this run ever stop?”, become undecidable by a reduction from the halting problem. Astonishingly little suffices: two stacks, two counters, a list of fractions, a set of string dominoes, a few integer matrices, a system of mirrors, a set of square tiles, or three rewriting rules on strings of \mathsf{S}, \mathsf{K} and \mathsf{I}. Each section below names a model, the encoding trick that lets it simulate a Turing machine, and what becomes undecidable.


The book presents this chapter as a rough sketch rather than a finished chapter, so this page is shorter than the others and fills in a few standard facts where the sketch is silent.


                  
                  How universality spreads undecidability 
                  
                


Simulate. Give an algorithm that turns any machine M and input w into an object P_{M,w} of the new model (a program, an instance, a term) that “halts” if and only if M halts on w.
Reduce. A decider for “does P halt?” would then decide the halting problem (§7.9), which is impossible. So halting is undecidable for the new model.
Conversely, a Turing machine can usually simulate the new model, so the model computes exactly the computable functions — more evidence for the Church–Turing thesis.



8.1 Universal Turing machines
The first universal model is a single Turing machine: the universal machine U of §6.8 accepts \langle M,w\rangle if and only if M accepts w, and rejects it if and only if M rejects w. It stores M‘s tape as a list of equal-length cells [\langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle a\rangle] in which only the cell under the head carries a state other than \textit{reject}. To take one step of M it finds that cell, looks up the matching block of \langle\delta\rangle, rewrites the cell, and passes the state code to a neighboring cell. Every other model on this page is shown universal the same way: by simulating an arbitrary Turing machine, or a model already known to be universal.
Concept page: universal-turing-machine.
8.2 Two-stack machines
A two-stack machine is a finite-state control with two stacks, with the input initially on one of them: in each step it may pop the top symbol of each stack, push symbols, and change state, depending on its state and the popped symbols. A Turing machine’s tape is two stacks — cut it at the head.

the tape #0x1x0 cut at the head into a left stack x,0,# and a right stack 1,x,0#0x1x0□□⋯resetleft of the headhead cell and to its rightx0#left stacktop1x0right stacktop = head cellA tape is two stacks. Cut the tape at the head. The left stack holds the cells left of the head, nearest cell on top; the right stack holds the head cell and everything to its right, head cell on top (an empty right stack reads as a blank). A move right pops the right stack and pushes the written symbol onto the left stack. A move left pops the right stack, pushes the written symbol back onto it, and then moves the top of the left stack over to the right stack.
So one step of a Turing machine is a pop, a state change and a push — plus, for a move left, moving the top symbol of the left stack over to the right stack — and a move left with an empty left stack is a crash. Hence two-stack machines accept and decide exactly the same languages as Turing machines.


                  
                  One stack is not enough 
                  
                

A finite-state machine that reads its input once, left to right, with one stack is essentially a recursive automaton: it accepts only context-free languages, so it cannot even recognize \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\}. Going from one stack to two jumps from the context-free languages straight to everything computable.


8.3 Counter machines


                  
                  Definition — counter machine 
                  
                

A k-counter machine has a finite set of states and k counters, each holding a non-negative integer. In each step it looks at its state and at which counters are zero, then changes state and adds -1, 0 or +1 to each counter (never making one negative).



Three counters simulate a Turing machine. Read each half of the tape as a number in base \lvert\Gamma\rvert, with \square as the digit 0 and the cells nearest the head as the least significant digits: one counter holds the part left of the head (with an extra leading digit 1, so that the machine can tell when that part is empty), another the head cell and everything to its right. Reading the head symbol is “right counter mod \lvert\Gamma\rvert”. A move right multiplies the left counter by \lvert\Gamma\rvert and adds the written digit, and divides the right counter by \lvert\Gamma\rvert; a move left is symmetric. Multiplying and dividing by a constant (with the remainder remembered in the state) are loops of \pm1 steps that use the third counter as scratch space.
Two counters simulate three. Store three counters (a, b, c) as the single number 2^a3^b5^c. Adding 1 to b multiplies it by 3, subtracting 1 from c divides it by 5, and ”c = 0?” asks whether 5 fails to divide it — each again a \pm1 loop, with the second counter as scratch. So two counters are universal; in particular, it is undecidable whether a given two-counter machine, started with both counters at 0, ever halts.
But the input format matters. To compute a function f with three counters, turn (n,0,0) into (2^n,0,0), run the simulation to reach (2^{f(n)},0,0), and turn that into (f(n),0,0). With only two counters, even turning (n,0) into (2^n,0) is impossible — a hard theorem; the book cites Barzdin (1963), Yao (1971) and Schroeppel (1972). Two counters are universal only for suitably encoded inputs.

8.4 FRACTRAN


                  
                  Definition — FRACTRAN (Conway, 1987) 
                  
                

A FRACTRAN program is a finite list of positive fractions f_1, \dots, f_k. Its state is one positive integer N. In each step, find the first f_i for which N f_i is an integer and replace N by N f_i; if there is none, halt.


The exponents in the prime factorization of N are counters in disguise: multiplying by \tfrac32 subtracts 1 from the exponent of 2 and adds 1 to the exponent of 3, and it applies only when the exponent of 2 is positive — a built-in zero test. Extra primes can play the role of a counter machine’s states, so FRACTRAN is universal.


                  
                  Two tiny programs 
                  
                


[\tfrac32] turns 2^a3^b into 3^{a+b}, in a steps: it adds two counters.
[\tfrac{455}{33}, \tfrac{11}{13}, \tfrac{1}{11}, \tfrac{3}{7}, \tfrac{11}{2}, \tfrac{1}{3}] turns 2^a3^b into 5^{ab}: it multiplies, with the primes 7, 11 and 13 doing the bookkeeping.



For every computable function f there is a FRACTRAN program that turns 2^{n+1} into 3^{f(n)+1}. Again the encoding is unavoidable. Started at N = 1, a program either halts at once, with output 1 (if none of its fractions is an integer, none applies to 1), or runs forever (an integer fraction applies to every N, so some fraction always applies). So no FRACTRAN program turns every n directly into n+1.
8.5 Post’s correspondence problem


                  
                  Definition — Post's correspondence problem (PCP) 
                  
                

Given a finite list of dominoes (x_1/y_1), \dots, (x_n/y_n), each a pair of strings (top/bottom), is there a sequence of indices i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k with k\ge1, repetitions allowed, such that
x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\cdots x_{i_k} = y_{i_1}y_{i_2}\cdots y_{i_k}\,?




                  
                  An instance and its shortest solution 
                  
                

With a = (\mathtt{0}/\mathtt{100}), b = (\mathtt{01}/\mathtt{00}) and c = (\mathtt{110}/\mathtt{11}), the sequence c, b, c, a is a solution: the tops give \mathtt{110}\cdot\mathtt{01}\cdot\mathtt{110}\cdot\mathtt{0} and the bottoms \mathtt{11}\cdot\mathtt{00}\cdot\mathtt{11}\cdot\mathtt{100}, and both spell 110011100 (the book prints 110110100 here, a typo). No solution is shorter: every solution must start with c, because the top and bottom of a and of b already disagree, and no sequence of one, two or three dominoes works. Repeating a solution gives another one (cbcacbca), so a solvable instance has infinitely many solutions.



dominoes c b c a laid out so that top and bottom rows both read 1100111000100a0100b11011cthe three dominoes111100001111110000ccbbccaatopbottomc, b, c, a: both rows spell 110011100A solution of a correspondence instance. With the dominoes a = (0 / 100), b = (01 / 00) and c = (110 / 11), the sequence c, b, c, a spells 110011100 on both rows. The boxes show where each domino’s top and bottom strings land: the seams do not line up until the very end, which is what makes the problem hard.

PCP is undecidable. Dominoes can be designed so that every solution spells out a halting computation of a given machine, one configuration after another, with the bottom row always one configuration ahead of the top; the book notes that the simplest proof simulates a tag machine, another universal model.
PCP is acceptable: try all sequences in order of length, and accept when one works. Since PCP is acceptable but undecidable, its complement is not even acceptable (§7.3).
Shortest solutions can be enormous. The book lists the three-domino instance (\mathtt{0}/\mathtt{001}), (\mathtt{001}/\mathtt{1}), (\mathtt{1}/\mathtt{0}), whose shortest solution uses 75 dominoes, and others whose shortest solutions use hundreds. No computable function of the instance bounds the length of its shortest solution: with such a bound, searching up to it would decide PCP.

8.6 Matrix mortality


                  
                  Definition — matrix mortality 
                  
                

Given square integer matrices A_1, \dots, A_k, all of the same size, is some product A_{i_1}A_{i_2}\cdots A_{i_m} of them, with repetitions allowed, equal to the zero matrix?


Strings can be encoded as integer matrices so that concatenation becomes matrix multiplication, and a careful construction turns any PCP instance into a set of matrices that has a zero product if and only if the instance has a solution. So mortality is undecidable — even for two 15\times15 matrices, or for six 3\times3 matrices (Cassaigne, Halava, Harju and Nicolas, 2014). With a single matrix the question is easy: some power of an n\times n matrix is zero if and only if its nth power is. The order of the factors matters:
A = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad B = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix}:\qquad AB = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad BA = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\quad A^2 = A,\quad B^2 = B.
8.7 Dynamical systems
Continuous physical systems can be universal too. Reif, Tygar and Yoshida (1994) encode a Turing machine’s configuration as the coordinates of the point where a light ray crosses a unit square — one coordinate encodes the tape left of the head, the other the tape right of the head, just like the two stacks of §8.2 — and build a system of mirrors with quadratic surfaces (or of lenses) that carries the ray from one configuration’s point to the next one’s. So “does a ray starting here ever reach that region?” is undecidable: ray tracing, in general, is undecidable.
8.8 Wang tiles
A Wang tile is a unit square with a color on each edge. Given a finite set of tile types, with unlimited copies of each, can the plane be covered without rotating any tile, so that tiles that share an edge give it the same color?
A Turing machine’s run can be drawn as a tiling: row t spells out the configuration after t steps, and the colors on the horizontal edges carry each cell’s symbol (and, at the head, the state) up to the next row, so that the only way to complete a row is to compute the next configuration. If a special starting tile must sit in the corner and write the initial configuration, then a quarter of the plane can be tiled if and only if the machine never halts — so this version of the tiling problem is undecidable. Wang conjectured that every tile set that tiles the plane also tiles it periodically, which would make the unrestricted problem (no starting tile) decidable; Berger (1966) refuted the conjecture and proved the unrestricted problem undecidable, using tile sets that tile the plane only aperiodically.
8.9 Combinator calculus


                  
                  Definition — combinator terms and evaluation 
                  
                

A term is one of the combinators \mathsf{S}, \mathsf{K}, \mathsf{I} (or a variable x, y, \dots), or a pair (X, Y) of terms, meaning ”X applied to Y”. Application associates to the left, and the parentheses that this makes redundant are dropped: \mathsf{SKK(IS)} abbreviates (((\mathsf{S},\mathsf{K}),\mathsf{K}),(\mathsf{I},\mathsf{S})). Evaluation rewrites any subterm with one of the three rules
\mathsf{I}x\ \to\ x,\qquad \mathsf{K}xy\ \to\ x,\qquad \mathsf{S}xyz\ \to\ xz(yz).
A subterm that matches a left-hand side is a redex; a term with no redex is in normal form.


(Schönfinkel introduced combinators in the 1920s.) Several redexes may be available at once, so a reduction sequence depends on the order in which they are chosen.


                  
                  Reversing two arguments 
                  
                

\mathsf{R} := \mathsf{S(K(SI))K} swaps its two arguments. Rewriting the leftmost outermost redex at each step:
\mathsf{S(K(SI))K}xy \to \mathsf{K(SI)}x(\mathsf{K}x)y \to \mathsf{SI}(\mathsf{K}x)y \to \mathsf{I}y(\mathsf{K}xy) \to y(\mathsf{K}xy) \to yx.
Similarly \mathsf{SKK}x \to \mathsf{K}x(\mathsf{K}x) \to x, so \mathsf{SKK} does the job of \mathsf{I}: the two combinators \mathsf{S} and \mathsf{K} suffice.




                  
                  A term that runs forever 
                  
                

Let T := \mathsf{S(KI)(SII)}. Rewriting at each step the leftmost \mathsf{I}- or \mathsf{K}-redex if there is one, and otherwise the leftmost \mathsf{S}-redex:
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{SII}T &\to \mathsf{I}T(\mathsf{I}T) \to T(\mathsf{I}T) \to TT = \mathsf{S(KI)(SII)}T\\
&\to \mathsf{KI}T(\mathsf{SII}T) \to \mathsf{I}(\mathsf{SII}T) \to \mathsf{SII}T,
\end{aligned}
back where it started after six steps. Rewriting the leftmost outermost redex instead, the term never returns to itself but never stops either: it passes through \mathsf{SII}(\mathsf{I}T), \mathsf{SII}(\mathsf{I}(\mathsf{I}T)), … forever.


Combinator calculus is universal: it is equivalent to Church’s λ-calculus, and so to Turing machines. In particular, it is undecidable whether a given term has a normal form — whether evaluation can ever stop.
Summary

Universal means “can simulate every Turing machine”, and universality brings undecidability with it, by a reduction from the halting problem.
A tape is two stacks cut at the head, so two stacks are universal; one stack with a single pass over the input gives only the context-free languages.
Three counters simulate a tape (its halves as numbers); two counters simulate three via 2^a3^b5^c. But two counters cannot even compute n\mapsto2^n: universality needs suitably encoded inputs.
FRACTRAN is a counter machine in disguise: prime exponents are the counters. [\tfrac32] adds.
PCP is undecidable but acceptable. Example: c,b,c,a spells 110011100 on both rows, and no shorter sequence works.
Matrix mortality (even two 15\times15 or six 3\times3 matrices), ray tracing with mirrors and tiling the plane with Wang tiles are undecidable for the same reason.
Three rewriting rules, \mathsf{I}x\to x, \mathsf{K}xy\to x and \mathsf{S}xyz\to xz(yz), are universal; \mathsf{SII}(\mathsf{S(KI)(SII)}) can rewrite forever.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

The final exam (Dec 11) covers everything, Chapters 6–9 included. The book presents this chapter as a sketch, so treat it as background: it explains why undecidability shows up everywhere, and it supplies intuition for true/false items such as “a finite-state machine with two stacks is as powerful as a Turing machine” (true), “a finite-state machine that reads its input once with one stack can recognize \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\}” (false), or “Post’s correspondence problem is acceptable” (true). Undecidability proofs are graded as in Chapter 7; see how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 8 (§§8.1–8.9, explicitly a rough sketch), summarized in our own words. The two-stack and counter-machine simulations, the 2^a3^b5^c trick, the two-counter impossibility and its citations, the FRACTRAN definition and its 2^{n+1}\mapsto3^{f(n)+1} form with the remark about starting at 1, the PCP instance (whose string the book misprints), the long-solution instances, the mortality bounds, the ray-tracing reference and the combinators \mathsf{R} and \mathsf{SII}(\mathsf{S(KI)(SII)}) follow the book. The recipe, the halting remark for two-counter machines, the multiplication program, the single-matrix and order-of-factors remarks, the Wang-tile discussion (the book’s section is only a placeholder; Berger’s theorem), \mathsf{SKK} = \mathsf{I}, the stated reduction orders, the remark on computable bounds and the figures are standard facts or original. The two-stack and counter-number simulations (run against a real machine), the counter loops, both FRACTRAN programs, the PCP solution and the search showing that no shorter one exists, the 75-domino shortest solution (by a complete search), the matrix examples and every combinator reduction are checked by tools/checks/ch08.py; the longer PCP solutions and the matrix sizes are cited, not checked.

1-models-of-computation/09-nondeterminis.title: Chapter 9 — Nondeterministic Turing Machines
1-models-of-computation/09-nondeterminis.content:
Chapter 9 · book pp. 145–155 · chapter PDF · prev: Chapter 8


                  
                  In one breath 
                  
                

A nondeterministic Turing machine may have several transitions to choose from, and its possible runs form a computation tree. It accepts an input if some branch accepts, but rejects it only if every branch rejects — an asymmetry that deterministic machines do not have. Nondeterminism adds no computing power: a deterministic machine can search the tree breadth-first (depth-first search could follow an infinite branch forever), or try every sequence of choices — every advice string — in order of length. Both simulations take exponential time, and whether that blow-up is avoidable for polynomial-time machines is the P versus NP question. The Cook–Levin theorem reduces it to a single problem: if the satisfiability of boolean formulas can be decided in polynomial time, then P = NP.


9.1 Definitions
A nondeterministic Turing machine relates to a deterministic one (§6.2) the way an NFA relates to a DFA (§4.1): the transition function returns a set of options.


                  
                  Definition — nondeterministic Turing machine 
                  
                

A nondeterministic Turing machine N has the same components as a deterministic one — a tape alphabet \Gamma with a blank \square, an input alphabet \Sigma\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\square\}, and a finite set of states Q containing \textit{start}, \textit{accept} and \textit{reject} — but its transition function returns a set of triples:
\delta\colon \big(Q\setminus\{\textit{accept},\textit{reject}\}\big)\times\Gamma \to 2^{\,Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}}.
In state p reading a, the machine may perform any transition (q, b, \Delta)\in\delta(p,a): change to state q, write b, and move by \Delta. If \delta(p,a) = \varnothing, it moves to the reject state and halts.




                  
                  Definition — computation tree 
                  
                

The computation tree of N on input w has the initial configuration (\textit{start}, w, 0) as its root. The children of a configuration are the configurations reachable from it by one transition, and accepting and rejecting configurations are leaves. A branch is a path from the root: either finite, ending in a leaf, or infinite. A deterministic machine’s tree is a single branch.


A running example. The machine N below accepts the strings that contain 11 by guessing where the 11 starts. Every transition moves right and rewrites the symbol it reads; when there is a choice, choice 1 is listed first.













































optionschoice 1choice 2\delta(\textit{start}, \mathtt{0})(\textit{start}, \mathtt{0}, +1)—\delta(\textit{start}, \mathtt{1})(\textit{start}, \mathtt{1}, +1): keep scanning(\mathit{got1}, \mathtt{1}, +1): guess that 11 starts here\delta(\textit{start}, \square)(\textit{reject}, \square, +1): give up(\mathit{loop}, \square, +1): loop forever\delta(\mathit{got1}, \mathtt{0})(\textit{reject}, \mathtt{0}, +1)—\delta(\mathit{got1}, \mathtt{1})(\textit{accept}, \mathtt{1}, +1)—\delta(\mathit{got1}, \square)(\textit{reject}, \square, +1)—\delta(\mathit{loop}, a), every a(\mathit{loop}, a, +1)—
On each 1, N either keeps scanning or guesses that this 1 begins 11 and checks the next symbol. At the end of the input it may give up (reject) or — a deliberately bad option — loop forever. Let N' be the same machine without the looping option.

tree of configurations of N on input 011 with one accepting leaf at depth 3, two rejecting leaves at depth 4 and an infinite looping brancht = 0t = 1t = 2t = 3t = 4t = 5121212⋮ foreverstart011start011start011got1011accept011□start011□got1011□reject011□□loop011□□reject011□□loop011□□□The computation tree of N on input 011. Each node is a configuration: the state, and the tape with the head's cell in red. On a 1, N may keep scanning (choice 1) or guess that this 1 begins 11 (choice 2); at the blank after the input it may reject (1) or loop forever (2). One leaf accepts, so N accepts 011 — although two branches reject and one runs forever.
Concept page: nondeterministic-turing-machines.
9.2 Acceptance and rejection


                  
                  Definition — accepting, rejecting, deciding 
                  
                


N accepts w if some branch of its computation tree on w ends in an accepting configuration. Other branches may reject or run forever.
N rejects w if every branch ends in a rejecting configuration. Then every branch is finite, so the whole tree is finite (each configuration has finitely many children — König’s lemma): N halts within some number of steps, whatever it chooses.
Otherwise N neither accepts nor rejects w.

N accepts a language L if it accepts exactly the strings in L, and decides L if it accepts every string in L and rejects every string not in L.


In the example, N accepts 011 through the accepting leaf, although one of its branches never halts. On 010 no branch accepts and the looping branch never halts, so N neither accepts nor rejects 010: N accepts the strings containing 11 but does not decide that language. N' has no looping option; on 010 every branch of N' rejects, and N' decides the language.


                  
                  The asymmetry 
                  
                


Accepting needs one good branch; rejecting needs all branches to reject — so all of them must halt. As for deterministic machines, ”N does not accept w” is weaker than ”N rejects w”.
Swapping accept and reject does not complement a nondeterministic machine. With its accept and reject states swapped, N' accepts w whenever some branch of N' rejects w — and the branch that never guesses always does. So the swapped machine accepts every string, not the strings without 11. (For deterministic machines the swap works: Lemma 1(a) of Chapter 7.)



Theorem 1 below shows that for computability the asymmetry is harmless: nondeterministic machines accept exactly the acceptable languages and decide exactly the decidable ones, so the complement of a language decided by a nondeterministic machine is decidable — first remove the nondeterminism, then swap. With a time bound it is a real issue: whether the complement of every language in NP is in NP is a famous open question.
9.3 Time and space complexity


                  
                  Definition — complexity classes 
                  
                


\textsf{TIME}(f(n)): the languages decided by some deterministic multi-tape Turing machine in O(f(n)) time.
\textsf{NTIME}(f(n)): the languages decided by some nondeterministic multi-tape Turing machine in O(f(n)) time — on every input of length n, every branch halts within O(f(n)) steps.
\textsf{SPACE}(f(n)) and \textsf{NSPACE}(f(n)): the same with O(f(n)) tape cells instead of steps.
\textsf{P} := \bigcup_{k} \textsf{TIME}(n^k) and \textsf{NP} := \bigcup_{k}\textsf{NTIME}(n^k).



Why multi-tape machines? The number of tapes changes running times, but only a little: t steps of a k-tape machine can be simulated in O(t\log t) steps with two tapes and in O(t^2) steps with one tape, and the quadratic loss is sometimes unavoidable — marked palindromes take O(n) time with two heads but \Omega(n^2) with one (§6.6). Polynomial bounds survive these slowdowns, so \textsf{P} and \textsf{NP} are the same for every fixed number of tapes.
Some inclusions are free: a deterministic machine is a nondeterministic one with a single option each time, so \textsf{TIME}(f(n))\subseteq\textsf{NTIME}(f(n)), \textsf{SPACE}(f(n))\subseteq\textsf{NSPACE}(f(n)), and \textsf{P}\subseteq\textsf{NP}. Theorem 1, whose simulation works the same way for multi-tape machines, gives one in the other direction: \textsf{NTIME}(f(n))\subseteq\bigcup_c\textsf{TIME}(c^{f(n)}) for f(n)\ge n, so every problem in \textsf{NP} can be solved in exponential time. Whether \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP} is open.
9.4 Deterministic simulation via dovetailing


                  
                  Theorem 1 
                  
                

For every nondeterministic Turing machine N there is a deterministic Turing machine M that accepts exactly the strings N accepts and rejects exactly the strings N rejects. If every branch of N on input x halts within t steps, then M halts on x within O(t^2 r^{2t}) steps, where r is the largest number of options in any set \delta(p, a).




                  
                  The breadth-first simulation behind Theorem 1 
                  
                

M keeps a queue of encoded configurations on its tape, separated by markers; initially it holds only (\textit{start}, x, 0). Then M repeats:

If the queue is empty, reject.
Remove the first configuration c. If c is accepting, accept. If c is rejecting, discard it.
Otherwise append the (at most r) configurations reachable from c in one transition to the end of the queue.



Correctness. The queue processes the tree level by level, and each level is finite, so every configuration at depth d is reached after finitely many rounds. If N accepts x, an accepting configuration is eventually removed, and M accepts. If N rejects x, the tree is finite and has no accepting leaf, so the queue runs empty and M rejects. In the remaining case — no accepting leaf, but an infinite branch — M runs forever, which is right, because N neither accepts nor rejects.

the computation tree drawn with small circles numbered 1 to 7 in breadth-first order; the depth-first path is drawn in red and continues down the infinite branch121212depth-first search goes down here forever12347accept56rejectlooprejectloopt = 0t = 1t = 2t = 3t = 4t = 5numbers: breadth-first orderred: depth-first, choice 1 firstBreadth-first, not depth-first. The same tree as above. Depth-first search (red) tries choice 1 first: it finds a rejecting leaf, backs up, and then follows the looping branch forever, never reaching the accepting leaf. Breadth-first search visits the tree level by level and dequeues the accepting configuration seventh.
Why not depth-first? Backtracking — try choice 1, and only if that subtree fails, choice 2 — is the natural recursive search, but it explores the subtree of choice 1 completely before anything else. If that subtree contains an infinite branch, the search never returns, even when another choice accepts within three steps, as in the figure. Breadth-first search cannot get stuck, because it never goes deeper than level d+1 before finishing level d.
Running time. There are at most r^t configurations at depth t, so the tree has O(r^t) nodes (for r\ge2); each configuration fits in O(t) cells (assuming t\ge\lvert x\rvert), so the queue holds O(t\,r^t) symbols. With one head, copying a configuration of length O(t) to the far end of the queue takes O(t) trips of length O(t\,r^t): O(t^2r^t) steps per configuration, O(t^2r^{2t}) in all. With two tapes or two heads, one at each end of the queue, the copying costs O(t) per configuration and the whole simulation O(t\,r^t).
Compare the subset construction (§4.5): an NFA’s configuration is just a state, so a DFA can track the set of current states. A Turing machine’s configuration includes the whole tape, so the deterministic simulation tracks a list of whole configurations, which can grow exponentially with the running time.
9.5 Nondeterminism as advice
The choices can be supplied in advance. Number the options of every set \delta_N(p, a) as 1, 2, \dots in some fixed order, and let \Omega := \{1, \dots, r\}. A deterministic machine M reads its input w and also an advice string x\in\Omega^* on a separate read-only tape: at each step it reads the next advice symbol \omega and performs option \omega of \delta_N(q, a) (the last option, if there are fewer than \omega). So \delta_N(q,a) = \{\delta_M(q, a, \omega) \mid \omega\in\Omega\}, so each advice string of length t follows one branch of N‘s computation tree for up to t steps, and every branch is followed by some advice string.


                  
                  The advice view of nondeterminism 
                  
                


N accepts w if and only if M accepts (w, x) for some advice string x.
N rejects w if and only if there is a length t such that M rejects (w, x) within t steps for every advice string x of length t.



Example. For N on 011 (with \Omega = \{1, 2\}), the advice strings of length 3 that make M accept are exactly 121, 122, 221 and 222: the second step is the only real choice on the way to the accepting leaf (choice 2, “this 1 begins 11”), and the other two steps have a single option, so their advice symbols are ignored.
Trying the advice strings in order of length, and running each for as many steps as its length, is dovetailing:
Dovetail(w):
    for t ← 1, 2, 3, …
        done ← True
        for every advice string x of length t
            if M accepts (w, x) within t steps: accept
            if M has not halted on (w, x) after t steps: done ← False
        if done: reject

Correctness — a second proof of Theorem 1. If N accepts w through an accepting leaf at depth \ell, then in every round t < \ell the first t choices of that branch give a run that has not halted, so \textsf{Dovetail} does not reject; in round \ell the branch’s own advice makes M accept. If N rejects w, its tree has some finite depth D, and in round D every run halts and none accepts, so \textsf{Dovetail} rejects. Otherwise it runs forever.
Running time. If every branch halts within t steps, \textsf{Dovetail} stops by round t, after simulating \sum_{s\le t} s\,r^s\le 2t\,r^t steps of M (for r\ge2): O(t\,r^t) time with three tapes (input, advice, work) and O(t^2r^t) with one tape, where each simulated step shuttles between the work area and the advice. That beats the queue simulation’s O(t^2r^{2t}): recomputing configurations from scratch is cheaper than storing them and scanning past them.
9.6 The Cook–Levin theorem
The advice view describes \textsf{NP} without nondeterministic machines; the advice is a certificate that w\in L — a satisfying assignment, a tour, a coloring — that a deterministic verifier can check quickly.


                  
                  Definition — NP, in the form the proof uses 
                  
                

L\in\textsf{NP} if there are an integer k and a deterministic Turing machine M, the verifier, such that for every string w:

if w\in L, then M accepts (w, x) for some advice string x;
if w\notin L, then M rejects (w, x) for every advice string x;
M always halts within \max\{1, \lvert w\rvert^k\} steps.



\textsf{SAT} is the language of satisfiable boolean formulas: formulas built from variables with \wedge, \vee and \neg for which some assignment of \textsf{True}/\textsf{False} to the variables makes the formula true.


                  
                  The Cook–Levin theorem 
                  
                

If \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{P}, then \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP}.


The plan. Fix L\in\textsf{NP} with verifier M and exponent k. Given w of length n, let N := \max\{1, n^k\} and build a formula \Phi_w that is satisfiable if and only if some advice string makes M accept (w, x) — that is, if and only if w\in L. A fast algorithm for \textsf{SAT} run on \Phi_w then decides L.
The variables describe a run of M on w followed by an unknown advice string, for every time 0\le t\le N, state q and symbol a:

Q_{t,i,q} — “after t steps, M is in state q with its head on cell i”;
T_{t,i,a} — “after t steps, cell i holds the symbol a”.

The head starts on cell 1 and moves at most N times, so cells 1, \dots, N+1 suffice, plus an empty sentinel cell on each side, cells 0 and N+2. At time 0, cells 1, \dots, n hold w, cell n+1 holds a blank, and cells n+2, \dots, N+1 hold the advice.

grid of time steps by tape cells: row 0 holds a sentinel, the input 0 1, a blank, unknown advice cells and a sentinel; a highlighted window shows three cells of one row determining one cell of the nextt = 00start1□???⋯?t = 1⋯t = 2⋯t = 3⋯⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮t = N⋯input wblankadvice x (unknown)sentinelsentinelQt,i,q: after t steps the head is on cell i in state qTt,i,a: after t steps cell i holds the symbol aeach cell of row tis determined by thethree cells above itin row t − 1The Cook–Levin tableau. Row t is the configuration after t steps of the verifier M; the head starts on cell 1 in state start. Row 0 is fixed except for the advice cells, which the satisfying assignment chooses. Each entry of row t is determined by the three entries above it, so every transition constraint has constant size; with O(N) rows and columns, the formula has size O(N2).
The constraints come in five kinds:

Boundaries. The sentinel cells never hold the head or a symbol: all Q_{t,0,q}, Q_{t,N+2,q}, T_{t,0,a} and T_{t,N+2,a} are false.
Initialization. At time 0 the head is on cell 1 in state \textit{start} (and no other Q_{0,i,q} is true), cells 1,\dots,n hold the symbols of w, and cell n+1 holds a blank.
Advice. Each cell n+2, \dots, N+1 holds exactly one symbol at time 0 — which one is left to the satisfying assignment: this is where the formula guesses the advice.
Transitions. For 1\le t\le N and 1\le i\le N+1, each variable Q_{t,i,q} and T_{t,i,b} is equivalent to a formula of constant size in the time-(t-1) variables of cells i-1, i, i+1, following \delta.
Acceptance. Q_{t,i,\textit{accept}} is true for some t and i.



                  
                  The transition constraints in full (click to expand) 
                  
                

Q_{t,i,q} \iff \bigvee_{\delta(p,a) = (q,\,\cdot\,,+1)}\big(Q_{t-1,i-1,p}\wedge T_{t-1,i-1,a}\big)\ \vee \bigvee_{\delta(p,a) = (q,\,\cdot\,,-1)}\big(Q_{t-1,i+1,p}\wedge T_{t-1,i+1,a}\big)
T_{t,i,b} \iff \bigvee_{\delta(p,a) = (\cdot\,,b,\,\cdot)}\big(Q_{t-1,i,p}\wedge T_{t-1,i,a}\big)\ \vee\ \Big(T_{t-1,i,b}\wedge\bigwedge_{q\in Q}\neg Q_{t-1,i,q}\Big)
The head is on cell i in state q exactly when it just arrived from a neighboring cell by a transition into q. Cell i holds b exactly when the head just wrote b there, or b was there before and the head was elsewhere. Once the advice cells are fixed, these equivalences force the value of every later variable, so a satisfying assignment is the run of M on w with that advice — and the acceptance constraint holds exactly when that run accepts.


Size. M is fixed, so \lvert Q\rvert, \lvert\Gamma\rvert and \delta are constants. There are (N+1)(N+3)(\lvert Q\rvert+\lvert\Gamma\rvert) = O(N^2) variables and O(N^2) constraints of constant size, plus one acceptance constraint with O(N^2) literals. So \Phi_w has size O(N^2) = O(n^{2k}), and an algorithm can write it down in O(n^{2k}) time.
Conclusion. If some algorithm decides \textsf{SAT} in O(m^c) time for formulas of size m, then building \Phi_w and testing it decides w\in L in O(n^{2k}) + O(n^{2kc}) time, so L\in\textsf{P}. Since L was an arbitrary language in \textsf{NP}, \textsf{NP}\subseteq\textsf{P}; and \textsf{P}\subseteq\textsf{NP} always, so \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP}. \blacksquare


                  
                  What the proof really shows 
                  
                

The construction is a polynomial-time reduction from every language in \textsf{NP} to \textsf{SAT}: w\in L if and only if \Phi_w\in\textsf{SAT}. So \textsf{SAT} is NP-hard — at least as hard as every problem in NP. And \textsf{SAT} is itself in \textsf{NP} (a satisfying assignment is a certificate that a verifier checks in polynomial time), so it is NP-complete. The algorithms half of the course starts from here: to prove that another problem X is NP-hard, reduce \textsf{SAT} (or another known NP-hard problem) to X in polynomial time — the same direction rule as for undecidability (§7.9). See Algorithms.




                  
                  Reading "NP" correctly 
                  
                


NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, not “not polynomial”: every problem in \textsf{P} is in \textsf{NP}.
The definition is asymmetric, like acceptance in §9.2: yes-instances have short certificates; nothing promises short certificates for no-instances.
Cook–Levin is a statement about SAT; the reduction goes from an arbitrary L\in\textsf{NP} to \textsf{SAT}, never the other way.



Concept page: cook-levin-theorem.
Summary

A nondeterministic TM has \delta(p,a)\subseteq Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}; its runs form a computation tree rooted at (\textit{start}, w, 0).
Accept: some branch accepts (others may diverge). Reject: every branch rejects, so the tree is finite. Swapping accept and reject does not complement a nondeterministic machine.
\textsf{TIME}, \textsf{NTIME}, \textsf{SPACE}, \textsf{NSPACE} use multi-tape machines; the tape count costs at most a quadratic factor, so \textsf{P} and \textsf{NP} do not depend on it. \textsf{P}\subseteq\textsf{NP}\subseteq exponential time.
Theorem 1: a deterministic machine accepts and rejects the same strings, by breadth-first search of the tree — O(t^2r^{2t}) on one tape, O(t\,r^t) with two. Depth-first search can get stuck on an infinite branch.
Advice strings x\in\{1,\dots,r\}^* make the choices explicit; dovetailing tries all of length t for t steps, in O(t\,r^t) time with three tapes.
\textsf{NP} = languages with polynomial-time verifiers and certificates. Cook–Levin: \Phi_w with variables Q_{t,i,q}, T_{t,i,a} and five kinds of constraints has size O(N^2) and is satisfiable iff w\in L; so \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{P} implies \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP}.



                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Chapters 6–9 are tested on the final exam (Dec 11) only, and the final also covers the NP-hardness material of the algorithms half, which rests on the Cook–Levin theorem. From this chapter, know the definitions cold — they make good true/false items: “a nondeterministic machine rejects w if some branch rejects w” (false: every branch must); “swapping accept and reject in a nondeterministic decider for L gives a decider for \Sigma^*\setminus L” (false: see §9.2); “every language accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine is acceptable” (true: Theorem 1); “depth-first search would work just as well in Theorem 1” (false); “if \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP}, then \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{P}” (true, because \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{NP}). Rubric details: how exams are graded; review page: Turing machines and undecidability.


Sources for this page
Erickson, Models of Computation, Chapter 9 (§§9.1–9.6), summarized in our own words. The definitions, Theorem 1 with its queue simulation and bounds, the advice formulation, the \textsf{Dovetail} algorithm and its bounds, and the Cook–Levin construction (verifier definition of NP, variables Q_{t,i,q} and T_{t,i,a}, five kinds of constraints, O(N^2) size) follow the book. The machines N and N', the figures, the advice example, and the definitions of \textsf{P} and \textsf{NP} (which the book leaves implicit) are original. We state the rejection half of the advice view with an explicit length t, which keeps it correct when the tree has infinite branches, and we index the Cook–Levin tableau with cells 0, \dots, N+2 so that a run whose head reaches cell N+1 at time N is still represented; we also correct a few index typos in the printed constraints (every variable on the right of a transition constraint refers to time t-1, and the left boundary is cell 0). The computation tree and breadth-first order in the figures, the behavior of N, N' and the swapped machine, the advice example, the agreement of breadth-first search and dovetailing (on hundreds of random nondeterministic machines), the counting bounds, the advice view’s rejection half, and the Cook–Levin constraints (evaluated literally on two toy verifiers, with both cell windows) are checked by tools/checks/ch09.py.

1-models-of-computation/index.title: Part 1 · Models of Computation
1-models-of-computation/index.content:
What can be computed with a given amount of memory, and what cannot be computed at all? The chapters build the answer one model at a time. Strings are a recursive data type, so every proof about them is an induction (Ch 1). Regular languages have three descriptions — regular expressions (Ch 2), DFAs, which are one-pass algorithms with constant memory (Ch 3), and NFAs, which may guess (Ch 4) — and Kleene’s theorem says they describe the same languages; fooling sets prove that a language needs more than constant memory. Context-free grammars add recursion (Ch 5). Turing machines add an unbounded tape and capture everything computable (Ch 6) — and then diagonalization and reductions show that many natural questions about them have no algorithm at all (Ch 7). Chapter 8 shows how little it takes to be as powerful as a Turing machine, and Chapter 9 adds nondeterminism, which gives no more power but perhaps much more speed.
Midterm 1 (September 28) covered Chapters 1–5; the final exam (December 11) covers all nine. Every page follows the book’s sections in order, links the chapter PDF, and ends with a summary and an “On the exams” box.

concepts/acceptable-and-decidable.title: Acceptable and decidable languages
concepts/acceptable-and-decidable.content:
Definition — acceptable, decidable 
                  
                

Every input lands in exactly one of \textsf{Accept}(M), \textsf{Reject}(M) and \textsf{Diverge}(M) (crashing counts as diverging), and \textsf{Halt}(M) := \textsf{Accept}(M)\cup\textsf{Reject}(M).

L is acceptable (recognizable, semi-decidable, recursively enumerable) if L = \textsf{Accept}(M) for some Turing machine M.
L is decidable (computable, recursive) if L = \textsf{Accept}(M) and \textsf{Diverge}(M) = \varnothing for some M: a machine that halts on every input, accepting the strings in L and rejecting the rest.





                  
                  Lemma 5 
                  
                

An acceptable language L is decidable if and only if its complement \overline{L} = \Sigma^*\setminus L is acceptable. So if L is acceptable but undecidable, then \overline{L} is not acceptable.


Why it works. A decider with its answers swapped decides \overline{L}. Conversely, run an acceptor for L and one for \overline{L} in parallel, one step each in turn: every string is accepted by exactly one of them, so the combination always halts with the right answer. Hence decidable = acceptable and co-acceptable, and the classes are strictly nested: decidable \subsetneq acceptable \subsetneq all languages.


                  
                  Recipe — classifying a language 
                  
                


Acceptable: describe a machine that accepts exactly L — simulation with U, dovetailing, or nondeterministic guessing. Running forever on strings outside L is allowed.
Decidable: a machine that halts on every input; or show that L and \overline{L} are both acceptable; or combine decidable languages with \cup, \cap, \setminus (Lemma 2).
Undecidable: diagonalization, a reduction, or Rice’s theorem.
Not acceptable: \overline{L} is acceptable and L is undecidable (Lemma 5); a diagonal argument (Theorem 9); or Lemma 17 for properties that are not monotone (§7.12).



Example — the standard languages. Complements are taken among valid encodings; the strings that encode nothing form a decidable set and change none of the answers.







































































languageacceptable?decidable?reason\textsf{Accept} = \{\langle M,w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w\}yesnorun U; a decider would decide \textsf{SelfAccept}\textsf{Halt} = \{\langle M,w\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } w\}yesnorun U, accept if it halts; Theorem 12\overline{\textsf{Accept}}; \textsf{Diverge} = \overline{\textsf{Halt}}nonoLemma 5\textsf{SelfAccept}; \textsf{SelfReject}yesnoacceptable: Theorems 10, 11; undecidable: Theorems 7, 6\textsf{SelfHalt}yesnounion of those two (Lemma 4); Theorem 8\overline{\textsf{SelfAccept}}; \overline{\textsf{SelfReject}}nonoLemma 5\textsf{SelfDiverge} = \overline{\textsf{SelfHalt}}nonoTheorem 9 (diagonalization)\textsf{NeverAccept} = \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) = \varnothing\}nonoTheorem 13; Lemma 5, since its complement is acceptable\overline{\textsf{NeverAccept}}yesnodovetail M over all inputs\textsf{ThisIsSparta}: M accepts \mathtt{SPARTA} after exactly 300 stepsyesyessimulate 300 steps


                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Undecidable is not unacceptable: \textsf{Halt} is acceptable.
Acceptable languages are not closed under complement (\textsf{Halt} versus \textsf{Diverge}). They are closed under \cup and \cap (Lemma 4), but the union needs a parallel simulation, because the first acceptor may run forever.
“Decidable” is about existence: the language built from the binary digits of \pi in §7.2 is decidable though nobody knows its decider.



Where it appears. §6.2 (accepting versus deciding), §7.1 (the four languages of a machine), §7.2 (the \pi example), §7.3 (Lemmas 1–5), §7.8 (Theorems 10–11), §7.12 (which properties give acceptable languages), the big picture.
Practice. Acceptable and decidable languages (4 problems) — for example 7.1 Closure facts, true or false (easy), 7.6 Do two machines share a string (medium), 7.7 Accepts epsilon, rejects itself (hard).

concepts/chomsky-normal-form.title: Chomsky normal form
concepts/chomsky-normal-form.content:
Definition — Chomsky normal form (CNF) 
                  
                

A grammar is in Chomsky normal form if the start symbol S appears on no right side, the rule S\to\varepsilon is allowed, and every other rule has one of two forms: A\to BC (two nonterminals) or A\to a (one terminal).




                  
                  Theorem 5.7, and the 2n-1 fact
                  
                

Every context-free grammar of total length L can be converted into an equivalent grammar in CNF of length O(L^2), in O(L^2) time. In a CNF grammar, every parse tree of a string of length n\ge1 has exactly 2n-1 nonterminal nodes — n-1 using rules A\to BC and n using rules A\to a — so every derivation of it has exactly 2n-1 steps.


Why it is useful. In a general grammar, \varepsilon-rules and unit rules A\to B add steps that produce nothing, so a short string can have arbitrarily long derivations. In CNF every step either splits a piece in two or produces one symbol. So membership can be decided by trying every derivation of 2n-1 steps — or quickly by dynamic programming (standard: the CYK algorithm, O(n^3) time for a fixed grammar) — and inductions over derivations get just two cases.


                  
                  Recipe — the conversion (§5.9), in order 
                  
                


Add a new start symbol S' and the rule S'\to S.
Split long rules: replace A\to X\alpha, where X is one symbol and \lvert\alpha\rvert\ge2, by A\to XB and B\to\alpha with a new B, until every right side has length at most 2.
Find the nullable nonterminals (A\rightsquigarrow^*\varepsilon) with a fixed-point loop.
Remove \varepsilon-rules: delete every A\to\varepsilon, and add every non-empty variant of each rule with nullable symbols left out; add S'\to\varepsilon if S' is nullable.
Merge nonterminals that derive each other through unit rules (A\rightsquigarrow^*B\rightsquigarrow^*A).
Remove unit rules A\to B by copying B‘s rules to A, in reverse topological order.
Protect terminals: in every right side of length 2, replace each terminal a by a new nonterminal T_a with the rule T_a\to a.





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Split long rules before removing \varepsilon-rules: a right side with k nullable symbols has 2^k variants.
Removing \varepsilon-rules creates unit rules (A\to BC with B nullable gives the unit rule A\to C), so unit rules go after.
A\to aB, A\to BCD and A\to B are not CNF; only the start symbol may have an \varepsilon-rule, and only if \varepsilon is in the language.



Example. Palindromes: P\to\mathtt{0}P\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}P\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon. Steps 0–1 give S'\to P, P\to\mathtt{0}X\mid\mathtt{1}Y\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon, X\to P\mathtt{0} and Y\to P\mathtt{1}. The nullable nonterminals are P and S', so step 3 gives X\to P\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{0}, Y\to P\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1} and S'\to P\mid\varepsilon. Steps 5–6 then give
\begin{aligned}
S' &\to T_{\mathtt{0}}X \mid T_{\mathtt{1}}Y \mid \mathtt{0} \mid \mathtt{1} \mid \varepsilon, &
P &\to T_{\mathtt{0}}X \mid T_{\mathtt{1}}Y \mid \mathtt{0} \mid \mathtt{1},\\
X &\to PT_{\mathtt{0}} \mid \mathtt{0}, &
Y &\to PT_{\mathtt{1}} \mid \mathtt{1},\\
T_{\mathtt{0}} &\to \mathtt{0}, &
T_{\mathtt{1}} &\to \mathtt{1}.
\end{aligned}
For instance, 010 has one parse tree, with the 2\cdot3-1 = 5 nonterminal nodes S', T_{\mathtt{0}}, X, P, T_{\mathtt{0}}.
Where it appears. §5.8 (definition, binary parse trees), §5.9 (Theorem 5.7; the algorithm on the book’s running example), §5.3 (why \varepsilon-rules complicate proofs), §5.2 (parse trees).
Practice. Parse trees, ambiguity and Chomsky normal form (4 problems) — for example 5.1 Closure and ambiguity, true or false (easy), 5.6 The dangling else (medium).
