concepts/church-turing-thesis.title: Church–Turing thesis
concepts/church-turing-thesis.content:
The Church–Turing thesis 
                  
                

Every function that can be computed by an algorithm — any finite, mechanical procedure — can be computed by a Turing machine.
So “decidable” and “acceptable” mean the same thing for Turing machines, for Python programs, and for any other reasonable model of computation.


Why it is a thesis, not a theorem. “Algorithm” has no formal definition apart from the models themselves, so there is nothing to prove the claim against: it is a claim about the world. The evidence is that every reasonable model proposed since 1936 — Church’s λ-calculus, the recursive functions of Gödel and Herbrand, multi-tape and nondeterministic Turing machines, random-access machines, two-stack and counter machines, combinator calculus — computes exactly the same functions. Each of those equivalences is a theorem, proved by simulating each model in the other; the thesis extrapolates to every model anyone will propose.


                  
                  Using the thesis in proofs 
                  
                


Describe machines in pseudocode: “on input \langle M,w\rangle: write \langle M'\rangle; run \textsf{DecideL} on \langle M'\rangle; return its answer.”
Allowed steps: parse and modify encodings; simulate a machine with the universal machine, for a fixed number of steps or without limit; run several simulations in parallel, one step each in turn; count; call a hypothetical decider as a subroutine.
Not steps: “if M halts on w, …”, “if M accepts some string, …”, “try every input, then answer” — unless a decider for exactly that question is the hypothesis you are about to refute.

A simulation without a step limit may run forever: harmless in an acceptor, fatal in a decider.




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


The thesis cannot be proved, and it is not what shows two given models equivalent: that takes a simulation, as in §6.6 or §9.4.
It is about what can be computed, not how fast: one tape instead of two can cost a quadratic factor, and the known simulation of nondeterminism an exponential one.
It makes undecidability absolute: no program in any language decides \textsf{Halt} — not just no Turing machine.



Example — dovetailing. \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\ne\varnothing\} is acceptable. In pseudocode:
for k ← 1, 2, 3, …
    for each of the first k strings x (in length-lexicographic order)
        simulate M on x for k steps
        if M accepted x: accept

If M accepts the j-th string within s steps, the loop accepts by round \max\{j,s\} at the latest; if \textsf{Accept}(M) = \varnothing, it runs forever — allowed for an acceptor. By the thesis (or by hand, with the constructions of Chapter 6) this is a Turing machine. Running M to completion on one string at a time would get stuck on the first string where M runs forever.
Where it appears. Chapter 6 (the opening: Turing, Church and the thesis), §6.1 (simple enough to reason about, powerful enough to simulate everything), §6.7 (recursion and random-access memory), Chapter 8 (two stacks, counters, FRACTRAN, tiles and combinators are all universal), the big picture.
Related: turing-machines · universal-turing-machine · acceptable-and-decidable · nondeterministic-turing-machines · halting-problem

concepts/closure-properties.title: Closure properties
concepts/closure-properties.content:
Definition — closed under an operation 
                  
                

A class of languages is closed under an operation if applying the operation to languages in the class always gives a language in the class. A “yes” is a construction that works for an arbitrary input; a “no” needs only one counterexample.


Where it comes from. The constructions are expressions, product DFAs and NFAs for regular languages; new grammar rules for context-free ones; and for decidable and acceptable ones, Turing machines that run the given machines as subroutines — in parallel when one of them might run forever.
Below, R, R' are regular expressions and S_1, S_2 start symbols of grammars for L, L'; a homomorphism h replaces every symbol a by a fixed string h(a); \textsf{half}(L) = \{w \mid ww\in L\}; † marks a standard fact that the book does not prove.

























































































operationregularcontext-freedecidableacceptableL\cup L'yes: R+R'yes: {S\to S_1\mid S_2}yes: run bothyes: run both in parallelL\cap L'yes: product DFAno† (below)yes: run bothyes: run one, then the other\overline{L}yes: accept {Q\setminus A}no†: else De Morgan gives \capyes: swap accept and rejectno: not for \textsf{Halt}L\setminus L'yes: product DFAno†: {\Sigma^*\setminus L}yes: run bothno: {\Sigma^*\setminus\textsf{Halt}}LL'yes: RR'yes: {S\to S_1S_2}yes†: try every splityes†: all splits in parallelL^*yes: R^*yes: {S\to\varepsilon\mid S_1S}yes†: try every cuttingyes†: all cuttings in parallelL^Ryes: Lemma 4.4yes†: reverse every right sideyes†: reverse the inputyes†: reverse the inputh(L)yes†: h(a) for a in Ryes†: h(a) for a in the rulesno† (below)yes†: dovetail over preimagesh^{-1}(L)yes†: {\delta'(q,a) = \delta^*(q,h(a))}yes†yes†: compute h(w) firstyes†: compute h(w) firstL\cap R, R regularyes: product DFAyes†: product with a DFAyesyes\textsf{half}(L)yes: Lemma 4.5no† (below)yes†: decide wwyes†: run on ww
The witnesses. \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{2}^m\} (S\to AC, A\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon, C\to\mathtt{2}C\mid\varepsilon) and, symmetrically, \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{2}^n\} are context-free, but their intersection \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{2}^n\} is not (the proof is beyond this course). L = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}\,\mathtt{2}^*\mathtt{0}^*\,\{\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{2}^n\} is context-free, but \textsf{half}(L)\cap\mathtt{0}^+\mathtt{1}^+\mathtt{2}^+ = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{2}^n \mid n\ge1\} is not, so neither is \textsf{half}(L). And \{\langle M,w\rangle\#^t \mid M \text{ halts on } w \text{ within } t \text{ steps}\} is decidable, but erasing its \#s leaves \textsf{Halt}.


                  
                  Recipe — closure on an exam 
                  
                


L is regular: build it from known regular languages with closed operations — “contains 11, has even length, does not end in 0” is an intersection of three.
L is not regular: assume it is, combine it with regular languages by closed operations, and reach a known non-regular language — a contradiction.
A new closure property: give a construction that starts from an arbitrary DFA, grammar or machine (language transformations).





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Closure runs one way. If L\cap R is not regular (with R regular), then L is not regular; if L\cap R is regular, nothing follows. A regular union proves nothing either: {\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}\cup\overline{\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}} = \Sigma^*}.
Subsets and infinite unions are not closed operations: every language is a subset of \Sigma^* and a union of one-string languages.
Context-free ∩ context-free can fail; context-free ∩ regular (and so context-free minus regular, L\cap\overline{R}) cannot.
Acceptable languages are not closed under complement — which is why “decidable” means acceptable and co-acceptable (Lemma 5).



Example. L = \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m\ne n\} is not regular. If it were, \overline{L}\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* would be regular too (complement, then intersection with a regular language). But that language is \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}, which is not regular (Lemma 3.6).
Where it appears. §3.6 and §3.7 (boolean operations; Theorem 3.2, Corollaries 3.4–3.5), §4.9 (Lemmas 4.4–4.5), §5.5 (grammars for \cup, \bullet, ^*), §7.3 (Lemmas 2, 4 and 5); all classes at once in the big picture.
Practice. Product construction and closure properties (4 problems) — for example 3.1 Closure and fooling-set verdicts (easy), 3.6 A product, written formally (medium), 3.9 Three look-alike counting languages (hard).

concepts/context-free-grammars.title: Context-free grammars
concepts/context-free-grammars.content:
Definition — context-free grammar 
                  
                

A context-free grammar G has a finite set \Sigma of terminals, a finite set \Gamma of nonterminals disjoint from \Sigma, a start nonterminal S, and finitely many rules A\to\omega with A\in\Gamma and \omega\in(\Sigma\cup\Gamma)^*. Applying a rule is one derivation step, xAz\rightsquigarrow x\omega z; \rightsquigarrow^* means zero or more steps. Each nonterminal has a language L(A) = \{w\in\Sigma^* \mid A\rightsquigarrow^* w\}, and L(G) = L(S). A language is context-free if some grammar generates it.


Where it comes from. A grammar is a recursive definition: each nonterminal names a language, and each rule is one way to build its strings by concatenating smaller pieces, with \mid for union. Regular expressions are the special case that recurses only through the star — union, concatenation, and S\to\varepsilon\mid S_1S for star — so every regular language is context-free. Recursion adds matching, as in C\to\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}, which no DFA can do.


                  
                  Template — proving L(G) = L
                  
                

L\subseteq L(G). Let w\in L be arbitrary, and assume every shorter string of L is generated (or induct on a parameter such as n). Split w into pieces that match the right side of one rule, then derive w with that rule and the hypothesis for the pieces. 
L(G)\subseteq L. Let w\in L(G) be arbitrary and fix a shortest derivation of w; assume every string with a shorter derivation is in L. Case on the first rule of the derivation, and apply the hypothesis to the substrings derived from the nonterminals on its right side. 
Several nonterminals? State one claim per nonterminal and prove them all together (mutual induction).




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


\varepsilon-rules break “the pieces are shorter”: with S\to SS\mid\varepsilon, one piece may be empty. Induct on the length of a shortest derivation instead.
Describe the language of every nonterminal in a sentence that makes sense on its own.
The classic one-mistake error is a missing or extra \varepsilon: test \varepsilon and all strings of length 1 and 2.
Every left side is a single nonterminal; right sides may mix terminals and nonterminals freely.



Example. L = \{\mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b\mathtt{0}^c \mid b = a+c\} is generated by
S\to AB \qquad A\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon \qquad B\to\mathtt{1}B\mathtt{0}\mid\varepsilon
A generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}, B generates \{\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\}, and S concatenates one of each, because \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^{a+c}\mathtt{0}^c = \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^a\bullet\mathtt{1}^c\mathtt{0}^c. The same language is not regular: \mathtt{0}^* is a fooling set, with z = \mathtt{1}^i for x = \mathtt{0}^i, because every string in L has as many 1s as 0s.


                  
                  How grammars are graded 
                  
                

2 points for syntax and 8 for correctness, with exam deductions twice the homework ones: 2 for one mistake (typically \varepsilon), 4 for a few wrong strings, all 8 if infinitely many strings are wrong; a grammar for \varnothing or \Sigma^* earns nothing. Homework also requires an English description of every nonterminal’s language. Ambiguity costs nothing. On Midterm-1-style exams the grammar is paired with a fooling-set proof for the same language.


Where it appears. §5.1 (definitions; the running example \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m\ne n\}), §5.3 (Lemmas 5.1–5.4: both inclusions, \varepsilon pitfalls, mutual induction), §5.4 (a catalog of grammars), §5.5 and §5.6 (where context-free languages sit).
Practice. Designing context-free grammars (7 problems) · Proving what a grammar generates (1 problems) — for example 5.1 Closure and ambiguity, true or false (easy), 5.5 Two grammars with a separator (medium), 5.8 Enough 1s at the end (hard).

concepts/cook-levin-theorem.title: Cook–Levin theorem
concepts/cook-levin-theorem.content:
The Cook–Levin theorem (as stated in §9.6) 
                  
                

If \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{P}, then \textsf{P} = \textsf{NP}.
\textsf{SAT} is the set of satisfiable boolean formulas, and \textsf{P} is the set of languages decided by deterministic Turing machines in polynomial time. L\in\textsf{NP} if there are an integer k and a deterministic verifier M that halts within \max\{1,\lvert w\rvert^k\} steps on every input (w,x), such that M accepts (w,x) for some advice string x when w\in L, and rejects (w,x) for every x when w\notin L.


Where it comes from. Fix L\in\textsf{NP} with verifier M, and let N = \max\{1, n^k\} for an input w of length n. A run of M is a table with N+1 rows (times) and O(N) columns (cells). Boolean variables Q_{t,i,q} (“after t steps, M is in state q with its head on cell i”) and T_{t,i,a} (“after t steps, cell i holds a”) describe the table, and a formula \Phi_w says: row 0 is the start configuration on w followed by an unknown advice string, each advice cell holds exactly one symbol, each row follows from the previous one by \delta, and M reaches \textit{accept}. So \Phi_w is satisfiable iff some advice makes M accept iff w\in L. \Phi_w has size O(N^2) and is built in O(N^2) = O(n^{2k}) time, so a \textsf{SAT} algorithm running in O(m^c) time on formulas of size m would decide L in O(n^{2kc}) time.


                  
                  Recipe — the theorem as the algorithms half uses it 
                  
                


The proof is a reduction: w\mapsto\Phi_w is computable in polynomial time, and w\in L\iff\Phi_w\in\textsf{SAT}. In the vocabulary of the algorithms half, every language in \textsf{NP} reduces to \textsf{SAT}, so \textsf{SAT} is NP-hard; with \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{NP} (example below) it is NP-complete. Chapter 9 itself states only the implication above.
Hardness proofs start from \textsf{SAT}: to show that a problem X is NP-hard, reduce \textsf{SAT} (or another NP-hard problem) to X in polynomial time — the same direction rule as for undecidability.





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


The theorem does not say that \textsf{SAT}\notin\textsf{P} or that \textsf{P}\ne\textsf{NP}; both questions are open.
\textsf{NP} means nondeterministic polynomial time, not “not polynomial”: \textsf{P}\subseteq\textsf{NP}.
The time bound depends on \lvert w\rvert only, so the verifier reads at most polynomially many advice symbols: certificates are short.
Direction: every \textsf{NP} problem reduces to \textsf{SAT}. Reducing a new problem to \textsf{SAT} shows that it is no harder than \textsf{SAT}, not that it is hard.
The polynomial size of \Phi_w is essential; an exponentially long formula would prove nothing.



Example — \textsf{SAT}\in\textsf{NP}. The advice is an assignment, and the verifier evaluates the formula, in polynomial time. The formula (a\lor b)\land(\lnot a\lor\lnot b)\land(a\lor\lnot b) is satisfiable, with certificate a = \textsf{True}, b = \textsf{False} (the only one). Add the clause (\lnot a\lor b) and each of the four assignments falsifies some clause, so the verifier rejects every advice string: the new formula is not in \textsf{SAT}.
Where it appears. §9.6 (statement and proof), §9.3 (\textsf{P} and \textsf{NP}), §9.5 (advice strings), the algorithms half (NP-hardness and NP-completeness).
Related: nondeterministic-turing-machines · undecidability-reductions · turing-machines · church-turing-thesis

concepts/counting-arguments.title: Counting arguments
concepts/counting-arguments.content:
Countably many descriptions, uncountably many languages 
                  
                

Every regular expression, context-free grammar and Turing machine is a finite string over a finite alphabet, so there are only countably many of each. But the languages over a non-empty alphabet \Sigma — all subsets of \Sigma^* — form an uncountable set. So all but countably many languages are not regular, not context-free, and not even acceptable.


Why it works. Countable: list strings by length, and alphabetically within each length; every string gets a position, and so does every description (§2.8 instead reads a regular expression as a base-8 numeral). Uncountable: given any list L_1, L_2, \dots of languages and the list w_1, w_2, \dots of all strings, the diagonal language D = \{w_i \mid w_i\notin L_i\} differs from each L_i on the string w_i, so no list contains every language (Cantor). §2.8 instead pairs languages over \{\mathtt{1}\} with the real numbers in [0,1).


                  
                  Recipe — the argument in three lines 
                  
                


Each [regular expression / grammar / Turing machine] is a finite string over a finite alphabet, so there are countably many of them, and countably many languages that they describe.
There are uncountably many languages over \Sigma (Cantor’s diagonal argument).
So some language over \Sigma — in fact almost every one — has no such description.



What it does not tell you. It proves that non-regular, non-context-free and unacceptable languages exist, but it never names one, and it never shows that a given language is outside a class. For that you need a fooling set (not regular) or diagonalization and reductions (undecidable, unacceptable). Nor can it separate two countable classes, such as regular from context-free or decidable from acceptable.


                  
                  Trap
                  
                


“Infinite” is not “uncountable”: \Sigma^* is infinite but countable; the set of all languages over \Sigma is uncountable.
Every string and every description is finite, even when the language it describes is infinite.
A counting argument never proves that a specific language is not regular.



Example. Over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} the list of strings begins w_1 = \varepsilon, w_2 = \mathtt{0}, w_3 = \mathtt{1}, w_4 = \mathtt{00}, w_5 = \mathtt{01}, w_6 = \mathtt{10}; in general w_i is the binary numeral of i with its leading 1 deleted (6 is 110, so w_6 = \mathtt{10}). Against the list L_1 = \varnothing, L_2 = \mathtt{0}^*, L_3 = (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*, L_4 = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}, the diagonal language contains \varepsilon and \mathtt{00} but not \mathtt{0} or \mathtt{1}, so it differs from each L_i at w_i.
Where it appears. §2.8 (regular expressions as base-8 numerals; languages L_\alpha from real numbers), §5.6 (grammars as integers), §7.6 (Cantor’s theorem; not every language is acceptable), §7.5 (the same diagonal argument, aimed at Turing machines).
Related: diagonalization · acceptable-and-decidable · regular-languages · fooling-sets · halting-problem

concepts/dfa-minimization.title: DFA minimization
concepts/dfa-minimization.content:
Definition — distinguishable and equivalent states 
                  
                

States p and q of a DFA are distinguishable if some string z leads exactly one of them to an accepting state: exactly one of \delta^*(p,z) and \delta^*(q,z) is in A. Otherwise they are equivalent. Recursively, p and q are distinguishable if exactly one of them is accepting, or if \delta(p,a) and \delta(q,a) are distinguishable for some symbol a.


Why it works. Moore’s algorithm is dynamic programming on the length of a distinguishing string: after the initial marking and k passes, every pair distinguished by a string of length at most k is marked, and only distinguishable pairs are ever marked. Once a pass marks nothing, no later pass would either, so the unmarked pairs are equivalent. Equivalent states have equivalent successors, so merging them gives a well-defined DFA for the same language; by the Myhill–Nerode theorem its states are the classes of \equiv_L, so it is the smallest DFA, unique up to renaming.


                  
                  Moore's algorithm (table filling) 
                  
                


Delete the states that are unreachable from s.
Mark every pair \{p,q\} with exactly one accepting state.
In passes, mark \{p,q\} whenever \{\delta(p,a),\delta(q,a)\} is already marked for some symbol a. Stop after a pass that marks nothing (at most n passes, O(\sigma n^3) time for n states and \sigma symbols; Hopcroft’s algorithm needs only O(\sigma n\log n)).
Merge each group of mutually unmarked states; the merged state inherits the transitions and acceptance of its members.





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Step 1 matters: table filling never deletes a state, so unreachable states can survive as extra states. The brute-force design for “contains 11” in §3.5 has 14 possible states, 4 of them unreachable.
Start from the accepting/non-accepting split, not from “edges that look different”.
Keep making passes until one changes nothing; one pass is rarely enough.
The algorithm needs a real DFA: every transition present (keep the dump state) and no nondeterminism.
On exams, minimize only when asked: a larger DFA with clear state names earns full credit.



Example. Remembering a flag “seen 11” and the last symbol gives a 5-state DFA for “contains 11”, with states (\textsf{F},\varepsilon), (\textsf{F},\mathtt{0}), (\textsf{F},\mathtt{1}), (\textsf{T},\mathtt{0}), (\textsf{T},\mathtt{1}); the two \textsf{T} states accept. Step 2 marks the 6 pairs between the groups. Pass 1 marks \{(\textsf{F},\varepsilon),(\textsf{F},\mathtt{1})\} and \{(\textsf{F},\mathtt{0}),(\textsf{F},\mathtt{1})\}: reading 1 sends both to the marked pair \{(\textsf{F},\mathtt{1}),(\textsf{T},\mathtt{1})\}. Pass 2 marks nothing, because (\textsf{F},\varepsilon), (\textsf{F},\mathtt{0}) have identical successors, and so do (\textsf{T},\mathtt{0}), (\textsf{T},\mathtt{1}). Merging leaves the minimal 3-state DFA: “no 11, last symbol not 1”, “no 11, last symbol 1” and “seen 11”.
Where it appears. §3.10 (the algorithm and its running time), §3.9 (why the result is the smallest), §3.5 (brute-force designs, and why clarity beats minimality), §4.7 (a 9-state subset-construction DFA that minimizes to 4 states).
Practice. Myhill–Nerode and minimal DFAs (2 problems) — for example 3.3 Prefixes of a pattern (easy), 3.10 Shrink it, then prove it minimal (hard).
Related: myhill-nerode-theorem · dfa · fooling-sets · subset-construction · product-construction

concepts/dfa.title: DFA (deterministic finite automaton)
concepts/dfa.content:
Definition — DFA 
                  
                

A DFA is a tuple M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta): a finite alphabet \Sigma, a finite set Q of states, a start state s\in Q, a set A\subseteq Q of accepting states, and a total transition function \delta\colon Q\times\Sigma\to Q. The extended transition function follows the recursive definition of strings:
\delta^*(q,\varepsilon) := q,\qquad \delta^*(q,ax) := \delta^*\big(\delta(q,a),\,x\big).
M accepts w iff \delta^*(s,w)\in A, and its language is L(M) := \{w\in\Sigma^* \mid \delta^*(s,w)\in A\}.


Why it works. A DFA is an algorithm that reads its input once, left to right, and remembers only its current state: the states are the possible values of its memory, \delta is one iteration of the loop, and A is the final test. As a graph, every state has exactly one outgoing edge per symbol, so every string traces exactly one walk from s. Two identities, each a short string induction, do most of the work in proofs: \delta^*(q,xy) = \delta^*(\delta^*(q,x),y) and \delta^*(q,xa) = \delta(\delta^*(q,x),a). DFAs accept exactly the regular languages.


                  
                  Recipe — designing a DFA (the exam problem) 
                  
                


Write a one-pass loop whose variables take a fixed, finite set of values.
States = combinations of values; start = the initial values; \delta = one iteration; A = the final test.
Name each state after what it remembers (“last symbol was 0”, “seen 11”, “remainder 3”).
Complete \delta: one edge per state and symbol. Omitting the dump state is fine only if you say so.
Test \varepsilon, every short string, and one long string.





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


Missing transitions without a sentence about a dump state: an incomplete DFA. (An NFA where a DFA was asked for earns half credit.)
No start arrow, no double circles, or state names that say nothing — the names are graded.
“Remember how many 0s” is not a finite set of states, unless you count mod k or up to a cap.
Forgetting \varepsilon: the start state is accepting exactly when \varepsilon\in L.
Swapping accepting and non-accepting states complements a DFA, but not an NFA.



Example — strings that end in 01. Remember the longest suffix of the input so far that is a prefix of 01:

























state (what it remembers)on 0on 1\varepsilon — no progress (start)0\varepsilon0 — the input ends in 000101 — the input ends in 01 (accepting)0\varepsilon
On 1001 it visits \varepsilon,\varepsilon,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{0},\mathtt{01} and accepts. No DFA for this language has fewer states: \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{01}\} is a fooling set — the suffix 1 distinguishes \varepsilon from 0, and the suffix \varepsilon distinguishes 01 from each of the other two.
Where it appears. §3.1 (the multiples-of-5 machine), §3.2 (definition), §3.3 (correctness proofs), §3.5 (design), §3.6 (products), §3.10 (minimization). Every DFA is an NFA (§4.1), and language transformations start from a DFA (§4.9). Grading: how exams are graded.
Practice. Designing and proving DFAs (7 problems) — for example 3.2 A bounded counter (easy), 3.5 Read a DFA, then prove it (medium), 3.8 No 00 after an 11 (hard).
Related: nfa · product-construction · fooling-sets · dfa-minimization · myhill-nerode-theorem · kleenes-theorem

concepts/diagonalization.title: Diagonalization
concepts/diagonalization.content:
The diagonal argument 
                  
                

Cantor’s theorem: no function f\colon X\to 2^X is onto, because the set Y = \{x\in X \mid x\notin f(x)\} differs from every f(y) — at y itself: y\in Y \iff y\notin f(y).
For Turing machines, take X = \Sigma^* and f(\langle M\rangle) = \textsf{Accept}(M) (and f(w) = \varnothing for strings that encode no machine): then Y is a language that no Turing machine accepts. The same twist — run a machine on its own encoding and make it contradict itself — proves \textsf{SelfReject}, \textsf{SelfAccept} and \textsf{SelfHalt} undecidable (Theorems 6–8) and \textsf{SelfDiverge} unacceptable (Theorem 9).


Why “diagonal”. Write the machines M_1, M_2, \ldots as the rows of a table and their encodings \langle M_1\rangle, \langle M_2\rangle, \ldots as the columns; entry (i,j) says what M_i does on \langle M_j\rangle. A language defined by flipping the diagonal — \langle M_i\rangle belongs to it exactly when M_i does not accept \langle M_i\rangle — disagrees with row i in column i, so it is no machine’s language. Theorem 6 runs the same argument against a hypothetical decider \textsf{SR} for \textsf{SelfReject}: on its own encoding, \textsf{SR} would accept if and only if it rejects.


                  
                  Template — undecidability by diagonalization (graded 4 + 3 + 3) 
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{Dec} decides L. 
Build a new machine \textsf{Wrap} from \textsf{Dec}: [swap its accept and reject states / redirect its accepting transitions to a looping state / …]. 
Then for every Turing machine M: \textsf{Wrap} [accepts, or halts on] \langle M\rangle if and only if M [does not …] \langle M\rangle. 
In particular, take M = \textsf{Wrap}. 
If \textsf{Wrap} [accepts] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then by the line above \textsf{Wrap} does not [accept] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle — a contradiction. 
If \textsf{Wrap} does not [accept] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then by the line above \textsf{Wrap} [accepts] \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle — a contradiction. 
So \textsf{Dec} does not exist, and L is undecidable. \blacksquare
4 points for the wrapper machine and its behavior on \langle M\rangle, 3 for each of the two cases.




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Run the machine built from the decider on its own encoding; plugging in any other machine proves nothing.
Say why there are only two cases: \textsf{Wrap} halts because \textsf{Dec} does. With a mere acceptor there is a third case — running forever — and the contradiction must be “halts if and only if it diverges” (Theorem 9).
Check that the flip contradicts the definition of L. For \textsf{SelfReject} no flip is needed — \textsf{Dec} itself is the contradiction — and swapping its answers yields a consistent machine.
Diagonalization handles self-referential languages; for other languages, reduce from one of them.



Example — a doubled input. L := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \langle M\rangle\langle M\rangle\} is undecidable. Suppose \textsf{Dec} decides L. Let \textsf{Wrap}, on input x, reject unless x = \langle M\rangle\langle M\rangle for some machine M; in that case run \textsf{Dec} on \langle M\rangle and do the opposite — accept if \textsf{Dec} rejects, and reject if \textsf{Dec} accepts. \textsf{Wrap} halts on every input, and
\langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\in L \iff \textsf{Wrap} \text{ accepts } \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle \iff \textsf{Dec} \text{ rejects } \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle \iff \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\notin L,
a contradiction. The wrapper must contradict \textsf{Dec} on the input that the definition of L looks at — here \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, not \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle.
Where it appears. §7.5 (Theorem 6 and the diagonal table), §7.6 (Cantor’s theorem and the barber), §7.7 (Theorems 7–9 and the template), §2.8 and counting-arguments (the counting version: uncountably many languages).
Practice. Diagonalization (1 problems) — for example 7.7 Accepts epsilon, rejects itself (hard).
Related: halting-problem · undecidability-reductions · acceptable-and-decidable · counting-arguments · universal-turing-machine

concepts/fooling-sets.title: Fooling sets
concepts/fooling-sets.content:
Definition — distinguishing suffix, fooling set 
                  
                

A distinguishing suffix for strings x and y (with respect to L) is a string z such that exactly one of xz and yz is in L. A fooling set for L is a set F of strings in which every pair of distinct strings has a distinguishing suffix.
Fact. If F is a fooling set for L, every DFA for L has at least \lvert F\rvert states. So if L has an infinite fooling set, L is not regular.


Why it works. A DFA remembers nothing but its state. If distinct x, y\in F reached the same state, then xz and yz would reach the same state for every z, and the DFA would accept both or neither — but a distinguishing suffix puts exactly one of them in L. The Myhill–Nerode theorem adds the converse: every non-regular language has an infinite fooling set, so the method always works in principle.


                  
                  Template — fooling-set proof 
                  
                

Let F =  [an explicit infinite set]. 
Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F. 
The definition of F implies x =  […] and y =  […] for some integers i\ne j. 
Let z =  [a suffix that may depend on i and j]. 
Then xz =  […] \in L, because […]. 
And yz =  […] \notin L, because […]. 
So F is a fooling set for L. Because F is infinite, L cannot be regular. \blacksquare


Choosing F. Ask what any algorithm for L must remember without bound — a count, a prefix, a position — and let F list its values: \mathtt{0}^* for a count of 0s, \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} or all of \Sigma^* for a remembered prefix, sometimes L itself. Keep the strings simple; they need not belong to L. Finite fooling sets give lower bounds: \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{1},\mathtt{11}\} is one for “contains 11” (z = \mathtt{1} separates \varepsilon from 1, and z = \varepsilon separates 11 from both), so the 3-state DFA for that language is minimal.


                  
                  Trap
                  
                


One example pair is not a proof: argue for arbitrary distinct x, y\in F.
Prove both halves, each with a reason: one of xz, yz is in L, the other is not.
“Assume i<j” needs “without loss of generality” and a symmetric argument; a suffix built from x alone is usually not symmetric.
F must be infinite and explicit; a finite set proves only a lower bound.
z may depend on x and y, never on a hypothetical DFA.



Example. L = \{w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^* \mid \#(\mathtt{0},w) > \#(\mathtt{1},w)\} is not regular. Let F = \mathtt{0}^*, so distinct x, y\in F are x = \mathtt{0}^i and y = \mathtt{0}^j with i\ne j, and let z = \mathtt{1}^{\min(i,j)}. Whichever of xz, yz has \min(i,j) zeros has equally many 0s and 1s, so it is not in L; the other has \max(i,j) > \min(i,j) zeros, so it is in L. The naive z = \mathtt{1}^i fails when j<i: then neither xz nor yz is in L.


                  
                  How a fooling-set proof is graded 
                  
                

4 points for an explicit infinite set that really is a fooling set (a finite set earns nothing); 6 for the argument with arbitrary distinct x, y — 2 for an explicit suffix z, 2 for showing one of xz, yz is in L, 2 for showing the other is not. Midterm-1-style exams pair this proof with a grammar for the same language.


Where it appears. §3.8 (definitions, Lemmas 3.6–3.9, a table of standard fooling sets, the closure alternative), §3.9 (why an infinite fooling set always exists), §2.4 (\{ww\} is not regular), §5.5 (the language \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\} separates regular from context-free).
Practice. Fooling sets and non-regularity (8 problems) — for example 3.1 Closure and fooling-set verdicts (easy), 3.7 Squares need a marker (medium), 3.9 Three look-alike counting languages (hard).
Related: myhill-nerode-theorem · dfa-minimization · closure-properties · regular-languages · dfa · context-free-grammars

concepts/halting-problem.title: The halting problem
concepts/halting-problem.content:
Theorem 12 (the halting problem) 
                  
                

\textsf{Halt} := \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } w\}
is undecidable. It is acceptable — run the universal machine and accept as soon as the simulation halts — so its complement \textsf{Diverge} is not acceptable (Lemma 5).


Where it comes from. Turing proved it in 1936, and it is why Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem has no algorithmic solution. The book proves it in two steps. A diagonal argument shows that \textsf{SelfHalt} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } \langle M\rangle\} is undecidable (Theorem 8); then a decider \textsf{H} for \textsf{Halt} would decide \textsf{SelfHalt} — on input \langle M\rangle, run \textsf{H} on \langle M,\langle M\rangle\rangle. The same argument makes \textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Reject} and \textsf{Diverge} undecidable.


                  
                  Recipe — proving Theorem 12 from scratch, with one machine 
                  
                

Suppose \textsf{H} decides \textsf{Halt}. Build \textsf{Wrap}: on input \langle M\rangle, run \textsf{H} on \langle M,\langle M\rangle\rangle; if \textsf{H} accepts, loop forever; if \textsf{H} rejects, accept. (On strings that encode no machine, reject.) Since \textsf{H} always halts, \textsf{Wrap} halts on \langle M\rangle exactly when \textsf{H} rejects \langle M,\langle M\rangle\rangle.

If \textsf{Wrap} halts on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then \textsf{H} rejects \langle\textsf{Wrap},\langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\rangle, so \textsf{Wrap} does not halt on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle.
If \textsf{Wrap} does not halt on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then \textsf{H} accepts \langle\textsf{Wrap},\langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\rangle, so \textsf{Wrap} halts on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle.

Both cases are contradictions, so \textsf{H} does not exist. \blacksquare




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Undecidable is not unacceptable. \textsf{Halt} is acceptable; \textsf{Diverge} is not.
“Simulate M on w and see” is not a decider: if M runs forever, so does the simulation, and no computable time limit is correct for every \langle M,w\rangle — such a limit would decide \textsf{Halt}.
Mind the quantifier. Halting on a given w, on the blank tape, and on every input are three different languages (all undecidable).
Fixed versus given machine. For one fixed M the question may be easy — if M always halts, \textsf{Halt}(M) = \Sigma^*. The theorem says that no single machine answers it for every \langle M,w\rangle.
In a reduction, decide \textsf{Halt} using the decider for the new language — never the other way around.



Example — halting on the blank tape. \textsf{HaltBlank} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } \varepsilon\} is undecidable. Given \langle M,w\rangle, write \langle M_w\rangle, where M_w erases its input, writes w, and runs M. Then M_w halts on \varepsilon — indeed on every input — if and only if M halts on w. So a decider for \textsf{HaltBlank}, run on \langle M_w\rangle, would decide \textsf{Halt}, which is impossible. (Rice’s halting theorem gives the same result, with Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}} and N = M_{\textsf{Diverge}}.)
Where it appears. Chapter 6 (Turing’s 1936 paper), §7.7 (Theorem 8: \textsf{SelfHalt}), §7.9 (Theorem 12 and the direction of reductions), §7.11 (Rice’s theorem is proved by a reduction from \textsf{Halt}), §8.5 (undecidable problems far from Turing machines).
Practice. Undecidability by reduction (4 problems) — for example 7.3 A reduction that proves nothing (easy), 7.5 Two behaviors, two answers (medium), 7.8 Both languages infinite (hard).
Related: diagonalization · undecidability-reductions · acceptable-and-decidable · universal-turing-machine · rices-theorem

concepts/induction-on-strings.title: Induction on strings
concepts/induction-on-strings.content:
The pattern 
                  
                

To prove a claim P(w) for every string w: let w be an arbitrary string; assume P(x) for every string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert; and prove P(w) in cases that cover every string — usually w = \varepsilon and w = ax. In the second case \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert - 1 < \lvert w\rvert, so the hypothesis applies to x.


Why it works. If the claim failed for some string, it would fail for a shortest one, w. The hypothesis says that nothing shorter than w fails, and the cases show that w cannot fail either. The cases mirror the recursive definition of strings because that is how every function on strings unfolds. The hypothesis covers all shorter strings because that costs nothing, the graders expect it, and it still works when a proof needs a string two symbols shorter, or half as long.


                  
                  Template — induction on strings 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary string. 
Assume, for every string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, that [the claim holds for x]. 
There are two cases to consider. 
Case w = \varepsilon. … Therefore [the claim holds for w]. 
Case w = ax for some symbol a and string x. The induction hypothesis implies that [the claim holds for x]. … Therefore [the claim holds for w]. 
In both cases, [the claim holds for w]. \blacksquare


Variations. Induct on the argument that the definitions take apart (the left argument of {\bullet}) and keep the others fixed — or, if the proof applies the hypothesis with other values of them, quantify over them: “for all strings y, and every x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert”. Any other split works if it covers every string and only shrinks it: the last symbol (w = xa, natural for DFAs); w = a or w = uv with u, v non-empty (two base cases); or w = abx for a function defined two symbols at a time.


                  
                  Where induction proofs lose points 
                  
                


A weak hypothesis (“assume it for x, prove it for ax”): state it for every shorter string.
Applying the hypothesis to a string that is not shorter than w, or not saying why it is shorter.
Cases that miss strings: a definition with a case w = abx needs base cases \varepsilon and every single symbol.
Inducting on the wrong argument: the right argument of {\bullet} never gets smaller.
Steps justified by “clearly”: cite a definition, the hypothesis, or a lemma on every line.





                  
                  Example — \lvert w^R\rvert = \lvert w\rvert for every string w
                  
                

Recall \varepsilon^R := \varepsilon and (ax)^R := x^R\bullet a. Let w be an arbitrary string, and assume that \lvert x^R\rvert = \lvert x\rvert for every string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert. There are two cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. \lvert\varepsilon^R\rvert = \lvert\varepsilon\rvert, because \varepsilon^R = \varepsilon by the definition of {}^R.
Case w = ax for some symbol a and string x. Then \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to x, and
\begin{aligned}
\lvert (ax)^R\rvert &= \lvert x^R\bullet a\rvert && \text{by definition of } {}^R\\
&= \lvert x^R\rvert + \lvert a\rvert && \text{by Lemma 1.2}\\
&= \lvert x\rvert + 1 && \text{by the induction hypothesis, and } \lvert a\rvert = 1\\
&= \lvert ax\rvert && \text{by definition of } \lvert\cdot\rvert.
\end{aligned}
In both cases, \lvert w^R\rvert = \lvert w\rvert. \blacksquare


Where it appears. §1.3 (the template and Lemmas 1.1–1.3), §1.4 (other splits; quantifying the hypothesis), more recursive functions (a model exam answer and its rubric). The same pattern proves DFAs correct (§3.3) and the product lemma (§3.6); its cousin, structural induction, handles regular expressions (§2.6) and grammars (§5.3). Grading: how exams are graded.
Practice. Induction on strings and recursive functions (9 problems) — for example 1.1 Unfold an accumulator (easy), 1.4 Reversal with an accumulator (medium), 1.7 Complementing every other symbol (hard).
Related: strings · regular-expressions · dfa · context-free-grammars

concepts/kleenes-theorem.title: Kleene's theorem
concepts/kleenes-theorem.content:
Theorem 4.1 (Kleene) 
                  
                

A language can be described by a regular expression if and only if it is accepted by a DFA. With the constructions below, regular expressions, DFAs, NFAs and NFAs with \varepsilon-transitions all describe exactly the same class of languages: the regular languages. (Stated as Theorem 3.3 in Chapter 3, proved in Chapter 4.)


The cycle of conversions. Each arrow is an algorithm, so from any one description you can reach all the others:
\text{expression}\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{Thompson}\ }\ \varepsilon\text{-NFA}\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{subsets}\ }\ \text{DFA}\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{trivial}\ }\ \text{NFA}\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{elimination}\ }\ \text{expression}



































arrowconstructionsize of the resultexpression → \varepsilon-NFAThompson’s algorithm (Lemma 4.2)at most 2\times the length of the expression\varepsilon-NFA → NFA (optional)\varepsilon-removalthe same statesNFA → DFAsubset constructionup to 2^n states, sometimes necessaryDFA → NFAtrivial: \delta'(q,a) := \{\delta(q,a)\}the same statesNFA → expressionstate elimination (Lemma 4.3)length up to \Theta(4^n)
Why it matters. Each description is good at different things, and the theorem lets you switch freely. Expressions handle union, concatenation, star and reversal; DFAs handle complement and intersection (products) and lower bounds (fooling sets); NFAs handle guessing and transformations. Together they give Corollaries 3.4 and 3.5: regular languages are closed under every boolean operation, concatenation and star.


                  
                  Recipe — using the theorem 
                  
                


To prove that L is regular, give any one description — whichever is easiest.
To prove a closure property, transform the description that makes it easy: a DFA for L into an NFA for f(L), or an expression by structural recursion.
For a “convert” question, follow the construction literally and show the work: the gadgets, the subset table, each elimination.





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


The conversions preserve the language, not the size: subsets can cost 2^n states, elimination \Theta(4^n) symbols.
The theorem is about these models only. Regexen with back-references, grammars and Turing machines describe languages that are not regular.
It does not say that every language is regular; most languages are not.
No conversion is needed to treat a DFA as an NFA, and state elimination works on DFAs directly.



Example — one full turn (the book’s, plus the last arrow). Start with (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^*, the strings with an even number of 1s. Thompson’s algorithm gives a 14-state NFA. The incremental subset construction turns it into a 5-state DFA (instead of up to 2^{14} = 16384 states). Minimization merges that DFA’s three accepting states and its two rejecting states, leaving the 2-state parity DFA. State elimination on that DFA, removing the rejecting state first, gives back exactly (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^*. Section 4.7 repeats the exercise for (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*(\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{11})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*: a 26-state Thompson NFA (the book’s figure and table; its text says 18, the count you get by drawing each \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1} as one two-state gadget), a 9-state DFA, and a minimal DFA with 4 states.
Where it appears. §3.7 (stated as Theorem 3.3; its corollaries), §4.4 (Theorem 4.1 and the plan of the proof), then the arrows: §4.3 (\varepsilon-removal), §4.5, §4.6, §4.7, §4.8. The context-free analogue: grammars and recursive automata describe the same languages (§5.7). All the classes at once: the big picture.
Practice. Conversions: subset construction, Thompson, state elimination (4 problems) — for example 4.1 Six quick NFA facts (easy), 4.5 Subset construction by hand (medium).
Related: regular-languages · regular-expressions · dfa · nfa · thompsons-algorithm · subset-construction · state-elimination · closure-properties

concepts/language-transformations.title: Language transformations
concepts/language-transformations.content:
Definition — the two kinds of transformed language 
                  
                

For a function f from strings to strings and a language L:
\{w \mid f(w)\in L\} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \{f(w) \mid w\in L\}.
“Regular languages are closed under the transformation” means the new language is regular for every regular L. It is proved by a construction that starts from an arbitrary DFA M = (\Sigma,Q,s,A,\delta) for L.


Why it works. The input side gets the most structure — a DFA, one state per prefix — and the output side the most freedom: an NFA with \varepsilon-transitions. For \{w\mid f(w)\in L\}, the new machine reads w and simulates M on f(w), usually deterministically. For \{f(w)\mid w\in L\}, it reads the output and guesses a preimage w while simulating M on it: nondeterministic choices guess changed symbols, and \varepsilon-transitions guess deleted ones. The subset construction then turns the NFA into a DFA.


                  
                  Template — language transformation 
                  
                

Let M = (\Sigma,Q,s,A,\delta) be a DFA that accepts L. 
We construct an NFA M' = (\Sigma,Q',s',A',\delta') with \varepsilon-transitions that accepts [the new language]. 
In English: M' remembers [each component of its state, and what it means], guesses [what], and accepts when […]. 
Formally: Q' =  […], s' =  […], A' =  […], 
\delta'(q',a) =  […] for every state q' and symbol a, and \delta'(q',\varepsilon) =  […] (\varnothing if there are none).




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Start from an arbitrary DFA for L, never from a machine for one example language.
Keep the directions apart: \{w\mid f(w)\in L\} simulates M on f(w); \{f(w)\mid w\in L\} guesses w.
Define \delta' for every state and symbol, and \varepsilon; an unstated case is a missing transition.
Swapping the accepting states of an NFA does not complement its language — complement a DFA.
Test the edge cases L = \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^* and \Sigma^*.



Example. Let \textsf{del0}(w) delete every 0 from w, so \textsf{del0}(\mathtt{0110}) = \mathtt{11}, and let M be a DFA for L over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}. Both constructions keep the states, start state and accepting states of M.

\{w\mid\textsf{del0}(w)\in L\}: a DFA that ignores 0s, with \delta'(q,\mathtt{0}) = q and \delta'(q,\mathtt{1}) = \delta(q,\mathtt{1}).
\{\textsf{del0}(w)\mid w\in L\}: an NFA that guesses where the 0s were, with \delta''(q,\varepsilon) = \{\delta(q,\mathtt{0})\}, \delta''(q,\mathtt{1}) = \{\delta(q,\mathtt{1})\} and \delta''(q,\mathtt{0}) = \varnothing.



                  
                  How a transformation is graded 
                  
                

2 points for a formal, complete description of M' built from an arbitrary DFA M (say whether M' is a DFA or an NFA, and whether it has \varepsilon-transitions); 2 for an English explanation of its states and accepting states; 6 for correctness — 1 for the states, 1 for the start state, 1 for the accepting states and 3 for the transitions. Midterm-1-style exams ask for two such constructions.


Where it appears. §4.9 (the method; Lemma 4.4 reversal and Lemma 4.5 \textsf{half}(L) = \{w\mid ww\in L\}), §2.7 (the regular-expression route: reversal by structural recursion), §4.3 (\varepsilon-transitions), §3.6 (the product construction, the same idea with two machines).
Practice. Regular language transformations (3 problems) — for example 4.8 Rotating the first symbol (hard).
Related: nfa · dfa · closure-properties · subset-construction · product-construction

concepts/languages.title: Languages
concepts/languages.content:
Definition — language, concatenation, Kleene star 
                  
                

A language over \Sigma is any set L\subseteq\Sigma^* of strings, finite or infinite. Besides the set operations (\cup, \cap, \setminus, \oplus, and the complement \overline{L} := \Sigma^*\setminus L), two operations use the fact that the elements are strings:

concatenation A\bullet B := \{xy \mid x\in A \text{ and } y\in B\}, usually written AB;
Kleene star L^*: w\in L^* iff w = \varepsilon, or w = xy for some x\in L and y\in L^* — the concatenations of zero or more strings from L. The Kleene plus L^+ := L\bullet L^* allows one or more.



Why it matters. A language is a decision problem: given w, is w\in L? Every model in the course — regular expressions, DFAs, NFAs, grammars, Turing machines — is a finite description of a possibly infinite language, and the course asks which languages each kind of description can reach.
The algebra (Lemmas 2.1–2.3). \varnothing L = L\varnothing = \varnothing and \{\varepsilon\}L = L\{\varepsilon\} = L; concatenation is associative and distributes over \cup; L^* = \{\varepsilon\}\cup L^+ = L^*L^*; L^+ = L^* iff \varepsilon\in L; \varnothing^* = \{\varepsilon\}^* = \{\varepsilon\}, and every other L^* is infinite. Arden’s rule: if \varepsilon\notin A, then L = AL\cup B holds if and only if L = A^*B.


                  
                  Recipe — testing a claimed identity (true/false questions) 
                  
                


Try the extreme languages \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\} and \Sigma^*, then a one-string language such as \{\mathtt{0}\}.
List the short strings on each side; a counterexample, if there is one, usually has length at most 2.
If none turns up, prove both inclusions: an arbitrary w on the left is on the right, and conversely.





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


\varnothing (no strings), \{\varepsilon\} (one string) and \varepsilon (a string, not a language) are three different things: \varnothing\bullet L = \varnothing but \{\varepsilon\}\bullet L = L.
Concatenation is not commutative, and it does not distribute over \cap.
L^2 = LL is all concatenations of two strings of L, not \{ww \mid w\in L\}: for L = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}, LL has four strings, but \{ww \mid w\in L\} = \{\mathtt{00},\mathtt{11}\}.
AB can have fewer than \lvert A\rvert\cdot\lvert B\rvert strings: different pairs can glue to the same string.
The complement depends on the alphabet: \overline{L} = \Sigma^*\setminus L.



Example. Let A = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{01}\} and B = \{\mathtt{1},\mathtt{11}\}. Then AB = \{\mathtt{01},\mathtt{011},\mathtt{0111}\} has only three strings, because \mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{11} = \mathtt{01}\bullet\mathtt{1}, while BA = \{\mathtt{10},\mathtt{101},\mathtt{110},\mathtt{1101}\}; so AB\ne BA. The star A^* = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{00},\mathtt{01},\mathtt{000},\mathtt{001},\mathtt{010},\dots\} is exactly the set of binary strings in which every 1 is immediately preceded by a 0.
Where it appears. §2.1 (definition; the three “empty” things), §2.2 (operations, Lemmas 2.1–2.3, solving a DFA with Arden’s rule), §2.8 (uncountably many languages, only countably many descriptions). How the classes of languages fit together: the big picture.
Practice. Languages and their operations (3 problems) — for example 2.1 Empty things, products and stars (easy), 2.5 Equivalent or not (medium).
Related: strings · regular-languages · regular-expressions · closure-properties · counting-arguments

concepts/myhill-nerode-theorem.title: Myhill–Nerode theorem
concepts/myhill-nerode-theorem.content:
Definition — the relation \equiv_L
                  
                

For a language L, write x\equiv_L y if no suffix distinguishes x and y: xz\in L\iff yz\in L for every string z. This is an equivalence relation; its classes [x] group the strings that have the same possible futures.




                  
                  The Myhill–Nerode theorem 
                  
                

For every language L, these three numbers are equal (possibly all infinite):

the minimum number of states of a DFA for L;
the maximum size of a fooling set for L;
the number of equivalence classes of \equiv_L.

So L is regular if and only if \equiv_L has finitely many classes, if and only if every fooling set for L is finite.


Why it works. (1) ≥ (2): two strings of a fooling set cannot share a state. (2) = (3): a fooling set is exactly a set with at most one string from each class. (1) ≤ (3): the classes themselves are the states of a DFA, with start state [\varepsilon], accepting states \{[w] \mid w\in L\} and \delta([w],a) = [wa] — well defined because x\equiv_L y implies xa\equiv_L ya.
What it justifies. Fooling sets are complete: a non-regular language has infinitely many classes, and one string from each is an infinite fooling set, so a non-regularity proof by fooling set always exists. Minimization is canonical: in a DFA without unreachable states, two states are equivalent exactly when the strings reaching them lie in the same class, so merging equivalent states (Moore’s algorithm) yields the class DFA. The minimal DFA is unique up to renaming its states.


                  
                  Recipe — the exact number of states 
                  
                


Guess the classes: what must an algorithm for L remember? Pick one representative string per class.
Lower bound: show the representatives are pairwise distinguishable — a fooling set.
Upper bound: give a DFA with one state per class.

Either bound alone proves nothing exact.




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


The count includes the dump state: \{\mathtt{0}\} over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} has three classes, [\varepsilon], [\mathtt{0}] and [\mathtt{1}] (every string that is not a prefix of 0), so its minimal DFA has three states.
Classes are sets of strings; a non-minimal DFA may split one class over several states.
The theorem is about DFAs; an NFA can be exponentially smaller (example below).



Example. Let L_3 be the binary strings whose third symbol from the end is 1. Pad every string on the left with 0s to length 3; then x\equiv_{L_3} y exactly when x and y end in the same three padded symbols, so there are 2^3 = 8 classes. If two windows u\ne v first differ in position k, the suffix z = \mathtt{0}^{k-1} moves that position to third from the end, so exactly one of uz, vz is in L_3. The minimal DFA therefore has 8 states — but an NFA needs only 4: loop at the start, guess the 1, then read exactly two more symbols.
Where it appears. §3.9 (statement and proof), §3.8 (fooling sets), §3.10 (minimal automata), §4.5 (the subset construction, whose output can be exponentially larger).
Practice. Myhill–Nerode and minimal DFAs (2 problems) — for example 3.3 Prefixes of a pattern (easy), 3.10 Shrink it, then prove it minimal (hard).
Related: fooling-sets · dfa-minimization · dfa · nfa · subset-construction · regular-languages

concepts/nfa.title: NFA (nondeterministic finite automaton)
concepts/nfa.content:
Definition — NFA (with \varepsilon-transitions)
                  
                

An NFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) is like a DFA, except that \delta\colon Q\times(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\to 2^Q returns a set of states, possibly empty. The \varepsilon-reach of q is the set of states reachable from q by zero or more \varepsilon-transitions. M accepts w iff some walk from s to an accepting state spells w; formally, iff \delta^*(s,w)\cap A\ne\varnothing, where
\delta^*(q,\varepsilon) := \varepsilon\text{-reach}(q),\qquad \delta^*(q,ax) := \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)}\ \bigcup_{p\in\delta(r,a)}\delta^*(p,x).


Intuition. Three equivalent pictures: the machine guesses, always making a choice that leads to acceptance if one exists; it runs every choice as a parallel thread, a thread dying when it has no move, and accepts if any thread ends in A; or a prover supplies the choices and the machine only verifies them. Running an NFA by hand means tracking the set of current states — which is exactly the subset construction, so NFAs accept only regular languages. Their value is convenience: “guess where the pattern starts” and “glue two machines together with \varepsilon-edges” each take one line.
Removing \varepsilon-transitions needs no new states: keep Q and s, make q accepting iff \varepsilon\text{-reach}(q) meets A, and set \delta'(q,a) := \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(q)}\delta(r,a).


                  
                  Recipe — designing with nondeterminism 
                  
                


Decide what to guess: where a pattern starts, which of several cases holds, a symbol you never get to read.
Let wrong guesses die — only one thread has to accept.
Use \varepsilon-transitions to make a guess without reading anything, or to glue machines together.
Give \delta(q,a) and \delta(q,\varepsilon) as sets for every state, and say which transitions are \varepsilon-transitions.
Check both directions: every string in the language has an accepting walk, and no other string does.





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


Swapping accepting states does not complement an NFA (example below). Determinize first.
An NFA accepts if some walk accepts, not all; a string on which every thread dies is rejected.
\varepsilon-moves count before the first symbol and after the last one: always take the \varepsilon-reach.
Where a DFA is asked for, an NFA earns half credit.



Example — strings that end in 01. States s, a, b: s loops on 0 and 1, s\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}a, a\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}b, and A = \{b\}. The machine guesses which 0 is the second-to-last symbol. On 1001 the set of current states is \{s\},\{s\},\{s,a\},\{s,a\},\{s,b\}; the last set meets A, so it accepts. Making s and a accepting instead does not give the complement: that machine accepts 01, through the thread that stays in s.
Where it appears. §4.1 (definition), §4.2 (three intuitions), §4.3 (\varepsilon-transitions and their removal), §4.5 (NFA to DFA), §4.6 (expression to NFA), §4.9 (transformations: from a DFA to an NFA). Nondeterminism returns for Turing machines: nondeterministic-turing-machines.
Practice. NFAs and epsilon-transitions (8 problems) — for example 4.1 Six quick NFA facts (easy), 4.5 Subset construction by hand (medium), 4.8 Rotating the first symbol (hard).
Related: dfa · subset-construction · thompsons-algorithm · kleenes-theorem · language-transformations

concepts/nondeterministic-turing-machine.title: Nondeterministic Turing machines
concepts/nondeterministic-turing-machine.content:
Definition — nondeterministic Turing machine 
                  
                

Like a Turing machine, except that each \delta(p,a)\subseteq Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\} is a set of options: in state p reading a, the machine may perform any one of them, and if \delta(p,a) = \varnothing it rejects. Its possible runs on w form the computation tree, rooted at (\textit{start}, w, 0).

N accepts w if some branch reaches \textit{accept} — other branches may reject or run forever.
N rejects w if every branch reaches \textit{reject}; then the whole tree is finite.
Otherwise N neither accepts nor rejects w. N decides L if it accepts every string in L and rejects every other string.





                  
                  Theorem 1 (§9.4) 
                  
                

For every nondeterministic machine N there is a deterministic machine M that accepts exactly the strings N accepts and rejects exactly the strings N rejects. If every branch of N on w halts within t steps, then M halts within O(t^2r^{2t}) steps, where r is the size of the largest set \delta(p,a).


So nondeterministic machines accept exactly the acceptable languages and decide exactly the decidable ones.
Why it works. M explores the computation tree breadth-first, keeping a queue of encoded configurations on its tape; every level of the tree is finite, so an accepting leaf at depth d is found after finitely many steps. Depth-first search could follow one infinite branch forever. Equivalently (§9.5), the choices can be written in advance as an advice string, and dovetailing runs every advice string of length t for t steps, for t = 1, 2, 3, \ldots — O(t\,r^t) time with three tapes. Either way the simulation is exponential in t; whether polynomial-time nondeterminism can always be simulated in deterministic polynomial time is the \textsf{P} versus \textsf{NP} question.


                  
                  Recipe — guess, then verify 
                  
                


Guess a certificate one symbol per step — a divisor, an input string, a satisfying assignment — and write it on the tape.
Verify it deterministically; accept if the check succeeds.
For a decider, bound the guess (say, by the input length), so that every branch halts and the strings outside L are rejected.





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


One rejecting branch is not rejection. Every branch must reject; a single branch that runs forever means N does not reject.
Swapping accept and reject does not complement a nondeterministic machine: the swapped machine accepts whenever some branch rejects.
Simulate breadth-first, or by dovetailing — never depth-first.
Nondeterminism never decides an undecidable language: by Theorem 1 the decider could be made deterministic.



Example. The machine “guess a string x symbol by symbol, stopping whenever it likes; then run M on x and accept if M accepts” accepts \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\ne\varnothing\}. It rejects nothing — a branch that never stops guessing runs forever — which is fine for an acceptor; Theorem 1 turns it into a deterministic acceptor, much like the dovetailing loop on church-turing-thesis. By contrast, on input \mathtt{1}^n, the machine “guess d with 2\le d\le n-1 by marking one of the input cells; accept if d divides n, otherwise reject” halts on every branch, so it decides \{\mathtt{1}^n \mid n \text{ is composite}\}.
Where it appears. §9.1 (definition, computation tree), §9.2 (the asymmetry), §9.3 (\textsf{NTIME}, \textsf{NP}), §9.4 (Theorem 1), §9.5 (advice and dovetailing); for finite automata, §4.1, where the subset construction plays the role of Theorem 1.
Related: turing-machines · nfa · subset-construction · cook-levin-theorem · church-turing-thesis

concepts/parse-trees-and-ambiguity.title: Parse trees and ambiguity
concepts/parse-trees-and-ambiguity.content:
Definition — parse tree, ambiguity 
                  
                

A parse tree for a string w in a grammar G is a rooted ordered tree whose root is the start symbol, whose internal nodes are nonterminals, whose leaves are terminals or \varepsilon and spell w from left to right, and in which the children of every node A spell the right side of some rule A\to\omega. A string is ambiguous if it has more than one parse tree, and a grammar is ambiguous if some string is. A context-free language is inherently ambiguous if every grammar for it is ambiguous.


Where it comes from. A derivation fixes an order of rule applications; a parse tree keeps only which rule built which piece. Each parse tree corresponds to exactly one leftmost derivation (always expand the leftmost nonterminal), so “two parse trees” and “two leftmost derivations” mean the same thing. Ambiguity never changes L(G), but compilers read meaning off the tree: \mathtt{1}-\mathtt{1}-\mathtt{1} is -1 or 1 depending on the grouping.


                  
                  Recipe — showing and removing ambiguity 
                  
                


Ambiguous: exhibit one string and two different parse trees, or two different leftmost derivations.
Remove it: choose one canonical way to build each string and let the grammar allow only that one — produce optional pieces in a fixed order, use one nonterminal per precedence level (E\to E+T\mid T, T\to T\times F\mid F), and recurse on one side only to fix associativity.
Unambiguous: show by induction that at every step the string splits in only one way.





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Two different derivations are not enough — they may build the same tree. Compare trees, or leftmost derivations.
Ambiguity belongs to the grammar, not the language: the example below has both kinds of grammar. Inherently ambiguous languages do exist (a standard fact; for example \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{2}^k \mid i=j \text{ or } j=k\}).
The grading rubric does not penalize an ambiguous grammar.



Example. S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}S\mid\varepsilon generates \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m\ge n\}, ambiguously: 001 has two leftmost derivations,
S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001},
depending on which 0 is matched with the 1. (In general \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n has \binom{m}{n} parse trees.) Producing the unmatched 0s first removes the choice: S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid T, T\to\mathtt{0}T\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon generates the same language with exactly one parse tree per string.
Where it appears. §5.2 (definitions; S\to\mathtt{1}\mid S+S versus S\to\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}+S), §5.4 (balanced parentheses both ways; precedence in the expression grammar), §5.8 (parse trees of CNF grammars are full binary trees), §2.5 (expression trees).
Practice. Parse trees, ambiguity and Chomsky normal form (4 problems) — for example 5.1 Closure and ambiguity, true or false (easy), 5.6 The dangling else (medium).
Related: context-free-grammars · chomsky-normal-form · regular-expressions · recursive-automata

concepts/product-construction.title: Product construction
concepts/product-construction.content:
Definition — product of two DFAs 
                  
                

Given DFAs M_1 = (\Sigma, Q_1, s_1, A_1, \delta_1) and M_2 = (\Sigma, Q_2, s_2, A_2, \delta_2) over the same alphabet, the product has
Q := Q_1\times Q_2,\qquad s := (s_1,s_2),\qquad \delta\big((p,q),a\big) := \big(\delta_1(p,a),\,\delta_2(q,a)\big).
Only the accepting set depends on the operation:





























languageaccepting states AL_1\cap L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ and } q\in A_2\}L_1\cup L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ or } q\in A_2\}L_1\setminus L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ and } q\notin A_2\}L_1\oplus L_2\{(p,q) \mid p\in A_1 \text{ xor } q\in A_2\}\overline{L_1}no product needed: M_1 with accepting set Q_1\setminus A_1


Why it works. Lemma 3.1, a string induction: \delta^*((p,q),w) = (\delta_1^*(p,w),\delta_2^*(q,w)) for every string w. After reading w the product sits on the pair of states that the two machines reach separately, so it can accept on any boolean combination of ”M_1 accepts” and ”M_2 accepts”. Hence regular languages are closed under all boolean operations (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.4). The product has \lvert Q_1\rvert\cdot\lvert Q_2\rvert states, and products of products handle any finite number of machines.


                  
                  Template — writing up a product construction 
                  
                

Let M_1 = (\Sigma, Q_1, s_1, A_1, \delta_1) be a DFA for L_1: [its states and what each means, start, accepting states, transitions — or a drawing]. 
Let M_2 = (\Sigma, Q_2, s_2, A_2, \delta_2) be a DFA for L_2: [likewise]. 
Define M := (\Sigma,\ Q_1\times Q_2,\ (s_1,s_2),\ A,\ \delta) with \delta((p,q),a) := (\delta_1(p,a),\delta_2(q,a)), 
and with A := [the accepting pairs from the table]. 
By Lemma 3.1, M accepts w iff [the boolean combination], so L(M) = [the target language].




                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


A_1\times A_2 gives only \cap. For \cup a pair accepts when either component does, including pairs where the other component rejects.
Both factors must be complete DFAs over the same alphabet: if one factor has no move, the pair has none, and \cup, \setminus and \oplus lose strings.
“Run both machines in parallel” alone earns little: describe each factor completely, then the product’s states, start, transitions and accepting set.
A drawing may leave out unreachable pairs (say so), but every reachable pair needs all of its transitions.



Example. Let M_1 accept the strings that end in 01 (states \varepsilon, 0, 01, as on the DFA page) and let M_2 track the parity of the length (states \textsf{E}, \textsf{O}, start \textsf{E}). All six pairs are reachable, and the accepting sets are

\cap (ends in 01 and has even length): \{(\mathtt{01},\textsf{E})\};
\cup: \{(\varepsilon,\textsf{E}),(\mathtt{0},\textsf{E}),(\mathtt{01},\textsf{E}),(\mathtt{01},\textsf{O})\};
\setminus (ends in 01 and has odd length): \{(\mathtt{01},\textsf{O})\};
\oplus: \{(\varepsilon,\textsf{E}),(\mathtt{0},\textsf{E}),(\mathtt{01},\textsf{O})\}.

On 1101 the product visits (\varepsilon,\textsf{E}),(\varepsilon,\textsf{O}),(\varepsilon,\textsf{E}),(\mathtt{0},\textsf{O}),(\mathtt{01},\textsf{E}): the input ends in 01 and has even length, so the \cap machine accepts.
Where it appears. §3.6 (definition, Lemma 3.1, a parity example, grading), §3.7 (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.4), §3.8 (closure as a tool for non-regularity); “and” conditions in regular-expression design; machines that run several copies of a DFA at once, such as the one for \textsf{half}(L) (§4.9).
Practice. Product construction and closure properties (4 problems) — for example 3.1 Closure and fooling-set verdicts (easy), 3.6 A product, written formally (medium), 3.9 Three look-alike counting languages (hard).
Related: dfa · closure-properties · regular-languages · language-transformations · state-elimination

concepts/recursive-automata.title: Recursive automata
concepts/recursive-automata.content:
Definition — recursive automaton 
                  
                

A recursive automaton has an input alphabet \Sigma, a finite set N of module names disjoint from \Sigma with a main name S, and for each A\in N an NFA module M_A over \Sigma\cup N with start state s_A and a single accepting state t_A. A configuration is (remaining input, current state, stack of states). Besides reading symbols and following \varepsilon-edges, the automaton can

call A along an edge q\xrightarrow{A}q': push q' and jump to s_A, reading nothing;
return from t_A: pop a state and continue there.

It accepts w if it can go from (w, s_S, empty stack) to (\varepsilon, t_S, empty stack).


Where it comes from. It is a grammar drawn as flowcharts: an edge labeled A means “read some string that M_A accepts here”, exactly like a nonterminal on a right side, and the stack remembers where to resume. An NFA is the special case with one module and no calls; the unbounded stack is what lets it match \mathtt{0}^n with \mathtt{1}^n. (Other textbooks use the equivalent pushdown automata.)


                  
                  Lemmas 5.5 and 5.6 
                  
                

A language is context-free if and only if some recursive automaton accepts it.

Grammar → automaton: one module per nonterminal A, with a path from s_A to t_A for each rule A\to\omega that reads the terminals of \omega and calls its nonterminals, in order.
Automaton → grammar: one nonterminal [q] per state, generating the strings that lead from q to the accepting state of its module: [q]\to a[p] for p\in\delta(q,a), [q]\to[p] for p\in\delta(q,\varepsilon), [q]\to[s_B][p] for p\in\delta(q,B), and [t_A]\to\varepsilon; the start symbol is [s_S].





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


A call reads no input; the called module does. Acceptance needs the whole input read and an empty stack, in t_S.
The stack holds return states, not input symbols, and has no fixed bound; with a bounded stack the machine is just an NFA.
Each module has exactly one accepting state.
One stack gives exactly the context-free languages; two stacks already simulate a Turing machine.



Example. Balanced parentheses, S\to\mathtt{(}S\mathtt{)}S\mid\varepsilon, need one module with states s, a, b, c, t: a path s\xrightarrow{\mathtt{(}}a\xrightarrow{S}b\xrightarrow{\mathtt{)}}c\xrightarrow{S}t and an edge s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t. On () it reads (, calls S (pushing b), returns at once along s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t, reads ), calls S again (pushing t), returns, and stops in t with an empty stack: accepted. Lemma 5.6 turns the module back into a grammar:
[s]\to\mathtt{(}[a]\mid[t] \qquad [a]\to[s][b] \qquad [b]\to\mathtt{)}[c] \qquad [c]\to[s][t] \qquad [t]\to\varepsilon
Where it appears. §5.7 (definition, Lemmas 5.5–5.6, and a two-module automaton for {\{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m\ne n\}}), §4.1 (NFAs, the building blocks), §5.5 (regular languages are context-free), §8.2 (two stacks are as powerful as a Turing machine).
Related: context-free-grammars · nfa · chomsky-normal-form · turing-machines

concepts/regular-expressions.title: Regular expressions
concepts/regular-expressions.content:
Definition — regular expression and its language 
                  
                

A regular expression is \varnothing, a string w (possibly \varepsilon), or S+T, ST or S^* for regular expressions S and T, with parentheses for grouping. Its language is
L(\varnothing) = \varnothing,\quad L(w) = \{w\},\quad L(S+T) = L(S)\cup L(T),\quad L(ST) = L(S)\bullet L(T),\quad L(S^*) = L(S)^*.
Precedence: ^* binds tightest, then concatenation, then +. Two expressions are equivalent if they have the same language.


Where it comes from. It is the recursive definition of regular languages, written compactly. Every expression is really a tree whose root is the operation applied last; its subtrees are the subexpressions. So a proof about all regular expressions is a structural induction with five cases — \varnothing, a string, S+T, ST, S^* — whose hypothesis covers the proper subexpressions S and T (template). By Kleene’s theorem, expressions describe exactly the languages of DFAs.


                  
                  Recipe — designing a regular expression 
                  
                


List short examples in and out of the language, including \varepsilon and every string of length 1 and 2.
Cut a typical string into blocks that a star can repeat; handle the beginning and the end separately.
Write the expression piece by piece, and say in English what each piece does.
Test both directions: nothing extra is generated and nothing is missed; check \varepsilon explicitly.
“And” conditions are hard: refine the blocks, or build a product DFA and convert it by state elimination.





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


Precedence: \mathtt{10}^* is \mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}^*), not (\mathtt{10})^*; and \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}^* is not (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*.
Only the real syntax: no \cap, no complement, no counters like \mathtt{0}^n, no regex shortcuts (?, [01], + for “one or more”, back-references). Write RR^* for “one or more copies of R”.
\varepsilon versus \varnothing: L(\varnothing^*) = \{\varepsilon\}. A missing or extra \varepsilon is the typical one-mistake deduction.
A well-formed substring of R need not be a subexpression: induct on the tree, not on the characters.
In the S^* case of a structural induction, the hypothesis covers S, not S^*.





                  
                  Example — binary strings with no 00
                  
                

Idea. Every 0 except possibly the last symbol is followed by a 1, so the string splits into blocks 1 and 01, followed by at most one final 0.
Answer: (\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}). Cutting from the other end — every 0 except possibly the first symbol is preceded by a 1 — gives the equivalent (\varepsilon+\mathtt{0})(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{10})^*.
Test: \varepsilon, 0, 10, 0101 and 0110 match; 00, 100 and 1001 do not.
A wrong answer: (\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01})^* misses every string of the language that ends in 0 — 0, 10, 110, … — infinitely many, so it earns no correctness credit.


Where it appears. §2.3 (definition and the book’s table of examples), designing an expression (two worked examples; grading), §2.4 (regexen), §2.5 (trees), §2.6 (structural induction). Expressions become NFAs by Thompson’s algorithm (§4.6), and automata become expressions by state elimination (§4.8).
Practice. Regular expressions (9 problems) — for example 2.2 Read these expressions (easy), 2.4 Three regular expressions (medium), 2.7 Two careful regular expressions (hard).
Related: regular-languages · languages · kleenes-theorem · thompsons-algorithm · state-elimination

concepts/regular-languages.title: Regular languages
concepts/regular-languages.content:
Definition — regular language 
                  
                

A language L is regular if and only if

L is empty;
L contains exactly one string (which may be \varepsilon);
L is the union of two regular languages;
L is the concatenation of two regular languages; or
L is the Kleene star of a regular language.

Regular expressions are the notation for this definition. By Kleene’s theorem, L is regular if and only if some DFA accepts it (the book calls such languages automatic), if and only if some NFA accepts it.
