Why it matters. The regular languages are exactly the problems that a one-pass, constant-memory algorithm can solve. Every finite language is regular (a finite union of one-string languages), and so is \Sigma^*. But there are only countably many regular languages and uncountably many languages, and specific ones such as \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\} are not regular — fooling sets prove it.


                  
                  Recipe — three ways to prove that a language is regular 
                  
                


Give a regular expression for it.
Give a DFA or an NFA for it (\varepsilon-transitions allowed).
Build it from languages already known to be regular with closure properties — finitely many operations.

To prove something about every regular language, choose an expression R with L(R) = L and induct on R, or start from a DFA for L and build an NFA (language transformations). To prove that L is not regular, give an infinite fooling set, or use closure backwards: if L\cap R is not regular for some regular R, then L is not regular.


Closed under (with the construction that proves it): complement, \cup, \cap, \setminus and \oplus (product construction); concatenation, {}^* and {}^+ (expressions, or NFAs glued with \varepsilon-edges); reversal (Lemma 4.4); \textsf{half}(L) = \{w \mid ww\in L\} (Lemma 4.5); and many other transformations. Full table: closure-properties.


                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


A subset of a regular language need not be regular: \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}\subseteq(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*.
Closure covers finitely many operations. Every language is the union of its one-string subsets, so an infinite union of regular languages can be anything.
Closure arguments run one way: ”L\cap R is regular” or ”L\cup L' is regular” says nothing about L.
Regularity is a property of the language, not of how it is written: \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\le 374\} is finite, hence regular.
A language has no recursive structure to induct on — induct on an expression for it.



Example. L = \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n \mid m\ne n\} is not regular. If it were, then \overline{L}\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* would be regular too, by closure under complement and intersection; but that language is \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}, which is not regular (Lemma 3.6). In the other direction, the binary numerals of the multiples of 5 written least-significant bit first form a regular language, with no new design needed: they are the reversals of the usual numerals, which the 5-state DFA of §3.1 accepts, and regular languages are closed under reversal.
Where it appears. §2.3 (definition), §2.7 (proofs through an expression), §2.8 (counting), §3.7 (closure; the three ways), §3.8 (non-regularity), §4.4 (Kleene’s theorem), §4.9 (transformations), §5.5 (every regular language is context-free). The hierarchy of classes: the big picture.
Practice. Structural induction on regular expressions (2 problems) · Regular expressions (9 problems) — for example 2.2 Read these expressions (easy), 2.4 Three regular expressions (medium), 2.7 Two careful regular expressions (hard).
Related: regular-expressions · kleenes-theorem · closure-properties · fooling-sets · language-transformations · myhill-nerode-theorem

concepts/rices-theorem.title: Rice's theorem
concepts/rices-theorem.content:
Rice's theorem 
                  
                

Let \mathcal{L} be a set of languages (a property of languages). If \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L} for some Turing machine Y and \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L} for some Turing machine N, then
\textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\in\mathcal{L}\}
is undecidable.
Variants with the same proof: \textsf{Reject}, \textsf{Halt} or \textsf{Diverge} in place of \textsf{Accept} throughout (Rice’s rejection, halting and divergence theorems), and \textsf{DecideIn}(\mathcal{L}) := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ decides a language in } \mathcal{L}\}, with deciders Y and N (Rice’s decision theorem).


Why it works. One reduction from \textsf{Halt} handles every property at once. If \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L}, map \langle M,w\rangle to the machine \textsf{WTF}(x): “run M on w and ignore the result; then run Y on x.” If M halts on w, then \textsf{Accept}(\textsf{WTF}) = \textsf{Accept}(Y)\in\mathcal{L}; otherwise \textsf{Accept}(\textsf{WTF}) = \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L}. So a decider for \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) would decide \textsf{Halt}. If \varnothing\in\mathcal{L}, apply the same argument to the complementary property, with N in the role of Y.


                  
                  Recipe — three steps (graded 4 + 4 + 2) 
                  
                


Name the property. Write the language as \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) for an explicit set of languages \mathcal{L}, and check that membership of \langle M\rangle depends only on \textsf{Accept}(M): two machines with the same language are both in or both out. If it depends on \textsf{Halt}(M) instead, use that variant.
Give a machine Y whose language is in \mathcal{L}, concretely (4 points).
Give a machine N whose language is not in \mathcal{L} (4 points).

Conclude “by Rice’s theorem, \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is undecidable”, naming the variant (2 points for these details). Handy witnesses: M_{\textsf{Accept}} accepts every input (\textsf{Accept} = \Sigma^*); M_{\textsf{Reject}} rejects every input (\textsf{Accept} = \varnothing, \textsf{Halt} = \Sigma^*); M_{\textsf{Diverge}} moves right forever (\textsf{Accept} = \textsf{Halt} = \varnothing).




                  
                  When Rice's theorem does not apply 
                  
                


Behavior, not language. ”M accepts \mathtt{SPARTA} after exactly 300 steps” (\textsf{ThisIsSparta}) is decidable by simulation, and so is ”M never moves left on w” (Theorem 19); ”M moves left three times in a row on w” is undecidable (Theorem 20) — by a reduction.
Self-reference. \textsf{RevAccept} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \langle M\rangle^R\} depends on M‘s own encoding: undecidable, but by a reduction.
Trivial properties have no Y or no N: \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ is acceptable}\} is the set of all encodings — decidable.
Wrong variant. ”M halts on every input” is not a property of \textsf{Accept}(M): M_{\textsf{Reject}} and M_{\textsf{Diverge}} accept the same language \varnothing, but only M_{\textsf{Reject}} halts everywhere. Use Rice’s halting theorem with \mathcal{L} = \{\Sigma^*\}, Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}} and N = M_{\textsf{Diverge}}.
Undecidable only. Rice never proves “not acceptable” — \textsf{AcceptIn} of “non-empty” is acceptable. For that, see Lemma 17.



Example. \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ is infinite}\}: the property is \mathcal{L} = \{L \mid L \text{ is infinite}\}; take Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}}, since \Sigma^* is infinite, and N = M_{\textsf{Reject}}, since \varnothing is finite. By Rice’s theorem the language is undecidable. (By Corollary 18 neither it nor \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ is finite}\} is even acceptable; a direct reduction for the finite case is on undecidability-reductions.)
Where it appears. §7.11 (statement, proof, Corollary 15, the variants, \textsf{ThisIsSparta} and \textsf{RevAccept}), §7.12 (when \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) is acceptable: Lemma 17, Corollary 18), §7.13 (questions about behavior), how exams are graded.
Practice. Rice’s theorem and machine behavior (4 problems) — for example 7.2 Decidable, acceptable, or neither (easy), 7.4 Rice with the right variant (medium), 7.8 Both languages infinite (hard).
Related: undecidability-reductions · halting-problem · acceptable-and-decidable · diagonalization · turing-machines

concepts/state-elimination.title: State elimination
concepts/state-elimination.content:
Definition — expression automaton and the elimination rule 
                  
                

An expression automaton has a start state s with no incoming edges, a target state t\ne s with no outgoing edges, and a regular expression R(p\to q) on each edge (a missing edge means \varnothing). It accepts w if w = x_1x_2\cdots x_\ell for some walk s = q_0\to q_1\to\cdots\to q_\ell = t with each x_i\in L(R(q_{i-1}\to q_i)). To eliminate a state q\notin\{s,t\}, delete it and, for every pair of remaining states p, r (including p = r), set
R'(p\to r) := R(p\to r) + R(p\to q)\,R(q\to q)^*\,R(q\to r).
When only s and t are left, R(s\to t) is a regular expression for the language.


Why it works. A walk through q arrives from some p, loops at q zero or more times, and leaves to some r; the new term R(p\to q)R(q\to q)^*R(q\to r) matches exactly those detours. So the language does not change and the automaton loses a state (Lemma 4.3, by induction on the number of states). Any NFA becomes an expression automaton by adding a new start and a new target with \varepsilon-edges, so every NFA language is regular — the last arrow of Kleene’s theorem. The book presents the method as McNaughton and Yamada’s (1960), a modern form of Kleene’s 1951 argument.


                  
                  Recipe — automaton to regular expression by hand 
                  
                


Add a new start s with an \varepsilon-edge to the old start, and a new target t with an \varepsilon-edge from every accepting state.
Merge parallel edges with +; a missing edge is \varnothing.
Eliminate the old states one at a time, in any order (states with few edges first keep things small): for every predecessor p and successor r of q, add R(p\to q)R(q\to q)^*R(q\to r) to R(p\to r).
Simplify as you go: \varnothing terms vanish, \varepsilon R = R, and \varnothing^* = \varepsilon.
The answer is R(s\to t). Test \varepsilon and a few short strings.





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


Forgetting p = r: eliminating q also changes the self-loop of every state with edges both to and from q.
Dropping the old direct term R(p\to r).
Skipping the new s and t when the old start state has incoming edges or there are several accepting states.
Writing R(q\to q) instead of R(q\to q)^*; with no loop at q the factor is \varnothing^* = \varepsilon.
Different orders give different (equivalent) answers, and the expressions grow fast: by roughly a factor of 4 per elimination in the worst case, to length \Theta(4^n) for n states.



Example. The 2-state DFA for “an even number of 1s” has states \textsf{E} (start, accepting) and \textsf{O}, a loop on 0 at each, and 1-edges between them. Add s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\textsf{E} and \textsf{E}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t. Eliminating \textsf{O} (its only predecessor and successor is \textsf{E}) changes just the loop at \textsf{E}: R'(\textsf{E}\to\textsf{E}) = \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1}. Eliminating \textsf{E} then leaves R(s\to t) = \varepsilon(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^*\varepsilon = (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^*. The other order gives the longer, equivalent \mathtt{0}^*+\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{10}^*.
Where it appears. §4.8 (expression automata, Lemma 4.3, the multiples-of-3 example), §4.4 (Kleene’s theorem). Arden’s rule does the same job algebraically (§2.2), and the book derives its expression for the binary multiples of 3 (§2.3) by eliminating the states of the remainder-mod-3 DFA.
Practice. Conversions: subset construction, Thompson, state elimination (4 problems) — for example 4.1 Six quick NFA facts (easy), 4.5 Subset construction by hand (medium).
Related: kleenes-theorem · regular-expressions · nfa · dfa · thompsons-algorithm · product-construction

concepts/strings.title: Strings
concepts/strings.content:
Definition — alphabet, string, \Sigma^*
                  
                

An alphabet \Sigma is a finite set of symbols. A string over \Sigma is either the empty string \varepsilon, or a pair a\cdot x (written ax) of a symbol a\in\Sigma and a string x. \Sigma^* is the set of all strings over \Sigma: an infinite set (if \Sigma\ne\varnothing), but every string in it is finite. Length and concatenation follow the same two cases:
\lvert w\rvert := \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ 1 + \lvert x\rvert & \text{if } w = ax\end{cases}
\qquad\qquad
w\bullet z := \begin{cases} z & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ a\cdot(x\bullet z) & \text{if } w = ax.\end{cases}


Where it comes from. A string is built like a linked list: a first symbol and the rest. So every function on strings has a case for \varepsilon and a case for ax that recurses on the shorter string x, and every proof about strings is an induction on strings with the same two cases. Concatenation takes apart only its left argument, which is why proofs about w\bullet z induct on w. Lemmas 1.1–1.3 say w\bullet\varepsilon = w, \lvert w\bullet x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert + \lvert x\rvert, and (w\bullet x)\bullet y = w\bullet(x\bullet y): concatenation is associative (so dots and parentheses are dropped) but not commutative.


                  
                  The pieces of a string w of length n
                  
                































piece of wdefinitionhow manyprefixw = px for some string xexactly n+1suffixw = xs for some string xexactly n+1substringw = xyz for some strings x, z (contiguous)at most n(n+1)/2 non-empty onessubsequencedelete zero or more symbols, anywhereat most 2^n
A proper prefix, suffix, substring or subsequence is one other than w itself. Every substring is a subsequence, but not conversely.




                  
                  Recipe — a newly defined string function (an exam problem type) 
                  
                


Unfold it on two or three tiny inputs, case by case, exactly as the definition says (as in the example below).
Test the claim you are asked to prove on those inputs; a false “identity” usually fails on a two-symbol string.
Find the argument the definition takes apart — for {\bullet}, the left one. The induction goes on that argument.
Write the string-induction template, with a definition, the hypothesis, or one of Lemmas 1.1–1.3 cited on every line.





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


\varepsilon is a string; \{\varepsilon\} is a language with one string; \varnothing is the empty language (languages).
\Sigma^* contains no infinite strings: "\mathtt{000}\cdots" is not an element of \{\mathtt{0}\}^*.
Reversal flips the order: (wx)^R = x^Rw^R, not w^Rx^R (try w = \mathtt{0}, x = \mathtt{1}).
Substring is not subsequence: 0110 contains 00 as a subsequence but not as a substring. “Contains 00” means substring unless the problem says otherwise.
Formally the symbol a and the one-symbol string a\cdot\varepsilon differ; a\bullet z = a\cdot z uses both cases of the definition of {\bullet}.



Example. Unfolding the definition, \mathtt{ba}\bullet\mathtt{na} = \mathtt{b}\cdot(\mathtt{a}\bullet\mathtt{na}) = \mathtt{b}\cdot\big(\mathtt{a}\cdot(\varepsilon\bullet\mathtt{na})\big) = \mathtt{bana}. The string w = \mathtt{banana} has length 6, so it has 7 prefixes and 7 suffixes (counting \varepsilon and w). It has only 15 distinct non-empty substrings, not 6\cdot7/2 = 21, because some repeat — ana starts at positions 2 and 4 — and only 40 distinct subsequences, not 2^6 = 64. bnn is a subsequence of banana but not a substring.
Where it appears. §1.1 (definition), §1.2 (length and concatenation), §1.5 (indices and pieces), more recursive functions (\#(a,w), reversal, powers, complement). Later definitions recurse the same way, for example a DFA’s \delta^* (§3.2).
Practice. Induction on strings and recursive functions (9 problems) — for example 1.1 Unfold an accumulator (easy), 1.4 Reversal with an accumulator (medium), 1.7 Complementing every other symbol (hard).
Related: induction-on-strings · languages · dfa · regular-expressions

concepts/subset-construction.title: Subset construction
concepts/subset-construction.content:
Definition — subset construction (with \varepsilon-transitions)
                  
                

For an NFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta), possibly with \varepsilon-transitions, the DFA M' = (\Sigma, Q', s', A', \delta') has
Q' := 2^Q,\qquad s' := \{s\},\qquad A' := \{S\subseteq Q \mid \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S)\cap A\ne\varnothing\},
\delta'(S,a) := \bigcup_{p\in S}\ \bigcup_{r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(p)}\delta(r,a).
Without \varepsilon-transitions this is just A' = \{S \mid S\cap A\ne\varnothing\} and \delta'(S,a) = \bigcup_{p\in S}\delta(p,a).


Why it works. A DFA cannot guess, but it can remember every state the NFA might be in: all the parallel threads at once. By induction on w, \varepsilon\text{-reach}\big((\delta')^*(\{s\},w)\big) is exactly the set of states the NFA can be in after reading w, so M' accepts w iff some thread of M does. A set of NFA states is a finite amount of memory — one of 2^{\lvert Q\rvert} possibilities — so NFAs accept only regular languages.


                  
                  Recipe — the incremental subset construction (by hand) 
                  
                

Build only the subsets that are reachable, breadth-first from \{s\}, in a table with one row per DFA state and the columns S, \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S), “accepting?”, and \delta'(S,a) for each symbol.

Start with the row \{s\}.
In each row compute \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S); the row is accepting if that set meets A; for each symbol a, collect every \delta(r,a) with r\in\varepsilon\text{-reach}(S).
A subset that appears in a transition column for the first time gets a row of its own — \varnothing included (it is a dump state).
Stop when no new subset appears. The rows are the DFA’s states.





                  
                  The worst case is exponential — and sometimes necessary 
                  
                

M' has at most 2^{\lvert Q\rvert} states, and exponentially many can be needed. “The kth symbol from the end is 1” has an NFA with k+1 states (loop at the start, guess the position, then read k-1 more symbols), but every DFA for it has at least 2^k states: the 2^k strings of length k form a fooling set, because if x\ne y first differ at position i, the suffix \mathtt{0}^{i-1} makes that position the kth from the end.




                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


Taking the \varepsilon-reach only at the start: every row needs it, both for the moves and for the acceptance test.
Accepting a subset only if all its states accept: one accepting state in its \varepsilon-reach is enough.
Dropping \varnothing: if it is reachable, it is a state, with a loop on every symbol.
Listing all 2^{\lvert Q\rvert} subsets: build the reachable ones only. The result is correct but often not minimal (minimize it if asked).
To complement an NFA, determinize it first, then swap the accepting states.



Example (with an \varepsilon-transition). The NFA with states p (start, loop on 0) and q (accepting, loop on 1) and an \varepsilon-transition from p to q accepts \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*. The construction finds three DFA states:

































S\varepsilon\text{-reach}(S)accepting?on 0on 1\{p\} (start)\{p,q\}yes\{p\}\{q\}\{q\}\{q\}yes\varnothing\{q\}\varnothing\varnothingno\varnothing\varnothing
On the “ends in 01” NFA of the NFA page it finds the subsets \{s\}, \{s,a\}, \{s,b\} — 3 of the 2^3 = 8 — which form the 3-state DFA for that language. On Thompson’s 14-state NFA for (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^* it builds 5 states, not 2^{14} = 16384.
Where it appears. §4.5 (definition and the incremental version), §4.3 (\varepsilon-reach), §4.6 and §4.7 (applied to Thompson’s NFAs), §4.4 (its arrow in Kleene’s theorem). The same idea — simulate every choice — gives deterministic simulations of nondeterministic Turing machines (§9.4).
Practice. Conversions: subset construction, Thompson, state elimination (4 problems) — for example 4.1 Six quick NFA facts (easy), 4.5 Subset construction by hand (medium).
Related: nfa · dfa · kleenes-theorem · thompsons-algorithm · fooling-sets · dfa-minimization

concepts/thompsons-algorithm.title: Thompson's algorithm
concepts/thompsons-algorithm.content:
Definition — Thompson's algorithm (Lemma 4.2) 
                  
                

By recursion on the expression tree, build an NFA with exactly one accepting state t, different from its start state s:

\varnothing: states s and t, no transitions. \varepsilon: s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t. A symbol a: s\xrightarrow{a}t. (A longer string is a concatenation of symbols.)
ST, in series: add t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_T; the start is s_S and the accepting state is t_T.
S+T, in parallel: new s and t, with s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_S, s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_T, t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t and t_T\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t.
S^*: new s and t, with s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_S, t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}s_S (another copy), t_S\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t (stop), and s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t (zero copies).

The book closes the loop from the new t back to the new s instead of from t_S to s_S (§4.6). Both versions are correct and have the same number of states and edges; only some \varepsilon-reaches differ.


Why it works. Structural induction on the expression: in the finished NFA, every gadget is entered only at its start state and left only from its accepting state, so a walk through a gadget spells exactly a string of that gadget’s language. The single accepting state is what makes the gluing easy. The algorithm adds 2 states for each \varnothing, \varepsilon or symbol leaf and for each + and ^*, and none for a concatenation — at most twice the length of the expression. The NFAs are full of redundant states and \varepsilon-transitions; that is fine, because the next step is \varepsilon-removal or the subset construction.


                  
                  Recipe — Thompson's algorithm by hand 
                  
                


Parse the expression into its tree: ^* binds before concatenation, which binds before +.
Build bottom-up: a two-state gadget for each leaf, then glue at each internal node exactly as above.
Keep every sub-NFA’s start and accepting state labeled; new edges touch only those two states.
Count the states as a check: 2\times(\text{leaves} + \text{unions} + \text{stars}).





                  
                  Classic mistakes 
                  
                


Dropping the bypass s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t of the star gadget: then the NFA for S^* rejects \varepsilon unless \varepsilon\in L(S).
In ST, the accepting state of S stops being accepting; only t_T accepts.
The “shortcut” star — no new states, just make the old start state accepting and add an \varepsilon-edge back to it from the accepting state — fails when the start state has incoming edges. On the two-state NFA for \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} (the start loops on 0; a 1 leads to the accepting state) it accepts 0, which is not in (\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1})^*.
Expecting a small NFA: Thompson’s output is correct, not compact.



Example. For \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}: the star gadget around the 0 gadget has 4 states, the 1 gadget 2 more, and the concatenation adds only an \varepsilon-edge — 6 states, 5 \varepsilon-transitions and 2 symbol transitions. The subset construction turns it into a 4-state DFA (one of them the dump state \varnothing), and minimization into 3 states. For the book’s (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}^*\mathtt{1})^* the count is 2\times(4+1+2) = 14 states, the number in §4.6.
Where it appears. §4.6 (Lemma 4.2 and the 14-state example), §4.7 (a second example), §4.4 (its arrow in Kleene’s theorem), §4.3 (removing the \varepsilon-transitions afterwards). The same structural recursion turns an expression into a context-free grammar (§5.5).
Practice. Conversions: subset construction, Thompson, state elimination (4 problems) — for example 4.1 Six quick NFA facts (easy), 4.5 Subset construction by hand (medium).
Related: regular-expressions · nfa · subset-construction · kleenes-theorem · state-elimination

concepts/turing-machines.title: Turing machines
concepts/turing-machines.content:
Definition — Turing machine 
                  
                

A Turing machine M has a finite tape alphabet \Gamma with a blank \square\in\Gamma, an input alphabet \Sigma\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\square\}, a finite set of states Q containing three distinct states \textit{start}, \textit{accept}, \textit{reject}, and a transition function
\delta\colon \big(Q\setminus\{\textit{accept},\textit{reject}\}\big)\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}.
\delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta) means: in state p reading a, write b, move the head by \Delta, and enter state q. A configuration (q,x,i) records the state, the tape contents and the head position; on input w the machine starts in (\textit{start},w,0). It accepts w if it reaches \textit{accept}, rejects w if it reaches \textit{reject}, crashes if it moves left from cell 0, and otherwise runs forever.
M accepts a language L if it accepts exactly the strings in L, and decides L if it also rejects every string not in L — so it halts on every input.


Where it comes from. Turing (1936) wanted a definition of computation simple enough for one proof to reason about every machine, yet strong enough to run any algorithm — including other Turing machines (universal-turing-machine). It is a poor model of speed and the standard model of possibility: every reasonable variant — stay-put moves, more tapes, heads or tracks, a two-way infinite tape, nondeterminism — accepts and decides exactly the same languages.


                  
                  Recipe — writing a machine down 
                  
                


Describe the algorithm in English as a few passes: scan for something, mark or erase it, walk back.
Keep unbounded information on the tape, never in the state, and make sure the head cannot fall off cell 0 (mark the left end, or keep a blank sentinel there).
Turn each pass into one or two states with mnemonic names, give the table, and say that missing transitions reject.
Trace \varepsilon, a short member of the language, and a few near-misses.

In undecidability proofs, describe machines in pseudocode instead (church-turing-thesis); write a table only when one is asked for.




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


“Rejects” is not “does not accept.” A machine that does not accept w may reject it, crash, or run forever.
Accepting L is not deciding L. A decider halts on every input; an acceptor may run forever on strings outside L (acceptable-and-decidable).
A machine that matches symbols without checking their order accepts near-misses — for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}, strings such as 0110.



Example — a decider for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}. Erase the first 0 and the last 1, walk back, repeat; accept when nothing is left. \mathit{skip0} and \mathit{skip1} check the form \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* on every pass; — means reject.









































state\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}\square\textit{start}: erase a 0(\mathit{skip0},\square,+1)—(\textit{accept},\square,+1)\mathit{skip0}: scan the 0s(\mathit{skip0},\mathtt{0},+1)(\mathit{skip1},\mathtt{1},+1)(\mathit{erase1},\square,-1)\mathit{skip1}: scan the 1s—(\mathit{skip1},\mathtt{1},+1)(\mathit{erase1},\square,-1)\mathit{erase1}: erase the last 1—(\mathit{back},\square,-1)—\mathit{back}: return left(\mathit{back},\mathtt{0},-1)(\mathit{back},\mathtt{1},-1)(\textit{start},\square,+1)
Because erasing starts at the left end, a blank always sits just left of the remaining block, so \mathit{back} never falls off the tape. On 0011 the machine accepts after 15 steps; on 0101 it rejects when \mathit{skip1} meets a 0. On \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^k it makes k passes of at most 4k+1 steps each, so it runs in O(n^2) time on inputs of length n.
Where it appears. §6.2 (definitions), §6.3 (a decider for \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\}), §6.4 and §6.6 (variants, all equivalent), §6.5 (computing functions), §7.1 (the four languages), §9.1 (nondeterminism).
Practice. Turing machines: design, variants, simulation (6 problems) — for example 6.1 Deciding, crashing and variants (easy), 6.4 Palindromes by peeling both ends (medium), 6.6 A machine that doubles its input (hard).
Related: acceptable-and-decidable · church-turing-thesis · universal-turing-machine · nondeterministic-turing-machines · dfa

concepts/undecidability-reductions.title: Undecidability by reduction
concepts/undecidability-reductions.content:
The direction rule 
                  
                

To prove that L is undecidable, reduce a known undecidable language to L: assume that some machine \textsf{DecideL} decides L, and use it as a black-box subroutine in a machine that decides \textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Halt}, or another language already known to be undecidable. That is impossible, so \textsf{DecideL} does not exist.
Reducing L to \textsf{Halt} — deciding L with the help of a decider for \textsf{Halt} — proves nothing: every decidable language reduces to \textsf{Halt} too.


Why it works. A reduction from X to L proves “if L is decidable, so is X”; read backwards, if X is undecidable, so is L. Its heart is a translation: from \langle M,w\rangle, compute the encoding of a machine M' with \langle M'\rangle\in L exactly when \langle M,w\rangle\in X. Writing \langle M'\rangle down always halts, even if M' would run forever.


                  
                  Template — undecidability by reduction from \textsf{Accept} (graded 4 + 3 + 3)
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{DecideL} decides L. 
Consider the following machine \textsf{DecideAccept}. Given \langle M, w\rangle, it writes the encoding \langle M'\rangle of the machine 
\quad M'(x): [for example: ignore x; run M on w; then …] 
and then runs \textsf{DecideL} on \langle M'\rangle and returns its answer. 
\Rightarrow Suppose M accepts w. Then M' […], so \langle M'\rangle\in L. So \textsf{DecideL} accepts \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts \langle M, w\rangle. 
\Leftarrow Suppose M does not accept w — it rejects or diverges. Then M' […], so \langle M'\rangle\notin L. So \textsf{DecideL} rejects \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects \langle M, w\rangle. 
In both cases \textsf{DecideAccept} is correct, and it always halts. So \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept}, which is impossible. 
We conclude that \textsf{DecideL} does not exist: L is undecidable. \blacksquare
4 points for the reduction, 3 for each case. If \langle M'\rangle\in L exactly when M does not accept w, return the opposite of \textsf{DecideL}‘s answer.




                  
                  Trap
                  
                


Direction. The new language’s decider is the subroutine; the known undecidable language is the one you end up deciding.
Never run M'. \textsf{DecideAccept} only writes \langle M'\rangle down; it must halt on every input, so it cannot run M on w itself.
“Does not accept” means rejects or diverges, and the second case must handle both.
Say what M' does with its own input x, for every x: that is what determines \textsf{Accept}(M').
Name every machine — \textsf{DecideL}, \textsf{DecideAccept}, M, M' — and never write “it”.



Example — the input as a step budget. \textsf{FiniteAccept} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ is finite}\} is undecidable, by a reduction from \textsf{Halt}. Suppose \textsf{DecideFinite} decides it. Given \langle M,w\rangle, the machine \textsf{DecideHalt} writes the encoding of
M'(x)\colon\ \text{simulate } M \text{ on } w \text{ for } \lvert x\rvert \text{ steps; accept if } M \text{ has halted, otherwise reject},
runs \textsf{DecideFinite} on \langle M'\rangle, and returns the opposite answer. If M halts on w after s steps, then M' accepts every x with \lvert x\rvert\ge s — infinitely many strings — so \textsf{DecideFinite} rejects and \textsf{DecideHalt} accepts. If M never halts on w, then \textsf{Accept}(M') = \varnothing is finite, so \textsf{DecideFinite} accepts and \textsf{DecideHalt} rejects. (Rice’s theorem also gives this result.)
Where it appears. §7.9 (Theorem 12, the direction rule and the template), §7.10 (Theorems 13–14: \textsf{NeverAccept}, \textsf{DivergeSame}), §7.11 (one reduction for every property; \textsf{RevAccept}), §7.13 (Theorem 20), §8.6 (matrix mortality), proof templates.
Practice. Undecidability by reduction (4 problems) — for example 7.3 A reduction that proves nothing (easy), 7.5 Two behaviors, two answers (medium), 7.8 Both languages infinite (hard).
Related: halting-problem · rices-theorem · diagonalization · acceptable-and-decidable · cook-levin-theorem

concepts/universal-turing-machine.title: Universal Turing machine
concepts/universal-turing-machine.content:
Definition — universal Turing machine 
                  
                

A universal Turing machine U takes the encoding \langle M,w\rangle of a Turing machine M and a string w, and simulates M on w:
U \text{ accepts } \langle M,w\rangle \iff M \text{ accepts } w, \qquad U \text{ rejects } \langle M,w\rangle \iff M \text{ rejects } w.
If M runs forever on w, so does U. U is one fixed machine, with a fixed alphabet and a fixed number of states; M is just data on its tape.


How it works. Everything about M is written in binary: each symbol of \Gamma as \lceil\lg\lvert\Gamma\rvert\rceil bits and each state as \lceil\lg\lvert Q\rvert\rceil bits, with \textit{start} all 1s and \textit{reject} all 0s (U must also recognize \textit{accept}; the book leaves its code open, and this site uses \mathtt{0}\cdots\mathtt{01}). A string is [\langle a_1\rangle{\bullet}\langle a_2\rangle{\bullet}\cdots]. The machine is \langle M\rangle = [\langle\textit{reject}\rangle{\bullet}\langle\square\rangle] followed by a bracketed list of blocks [\langle p\rangle{\bullet}\langle a\rangle\,|\,\langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle b\rangle{\bullet}\langle\Delta\rangle], one for each transition \delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta) with q\ne\textit{reject}, where \langle -1\rangle = \mathtt{0} and \langle +1\rangle = \mathtt{1}. U keeps M‘s tape as a list of cells [\langle q\rangle{\bullet}\langle a\rangle], with q = \textit{reject} everywhere except in the cell under the head. One simulated step: find that cell; look up the block whose left half matches it (none: reject); copy in the new state and symbol (new state \textit{accept}: accept); move the state code one cell left or right, appending an encoded blank at the right end when needed.


                  
                  Using U in proofs
                  
                


“Run M on w” in pseudocode means “run U on \langle M,w\rangle”. This shows that \textsf{Accept} is acceptable; for \textsf{Halt}, accept whenever the simulation halts; for \textsf{SelfAccept}, run U on \langle M,\langle M\rangle\rangle (Theorem 10).
“Run M on w for k steps” — U with a step counter — always halts, so a decider may use it.
Run simulations in parallel, one step each in turn, whenever one of them might run forever.





                  
                  Trap
                  
                


U accepts \textsf{Accept} but does not decide it: on \langle M,w\rangle with M looping, U loops. No machine decides \textsf{Accept} (halting-problem).
A decider may call U only with a step limit, or on machines known to halt.
U does not grow with M; that is why states and symbols are encoded in binary.
\langle M\rangle is a string, M a machine: writing \langle M'\rangle down is finite work even if M' would run forever.



Example. Let \Gamma = \{\square,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}, Q = \{\textit{start},\textit{accept},\textit{reject}\}, and give M a single transition \delta(\textit{start},\mathtt{1}) = (\textit{accept},\mathtt{1},+1); all others reject, so M accepts the strings that begin with 1. With the 2-bit codes \langle\square\rangle = \mathtt{00}, \langle\mathtt{0}\rangle = \mathtt{01}, \langle\mathtt{1}\rangle = \mathtt{10} and \langle\textit{start}\rangle = \mathtt{11}, \langle\textit{accept}\rangle = \mathtt{01}, \langle\textit{reject}\rangle = \mathtt{00}:

\langle M\rangle is [00•00][[11•10|01•10•1]], and the input 10 is [10•01];
U‘s initial configuration is [[11•10][00•01]]. The head cell [11•10] matches the left half of the only block, whose new state 01 is \textit{accept}, so U accepts after one simulated step;
on input 01 the configuration is [[11•01][00•10]]; no block begins 11•01, so U rejects.

Where it appears. §6.8 (the encoding and the simulation), §7.4 (encodings are unique, modifiable, executable), §7.8 (Theorems 10–11), §7.9 (\textsf{Accept}, \textsf{Reject} and \textsf{Halt} are acceptable), §8.1 (and the much smaller universal systems of Chapter 8).
Related: turing-machines · church-turing-thesis · acceptable-and-decidable · halting-problem · diagonalization

index.title: CS/ECE 374 · Algorithms & Models of Computation
index.content:
Notes for CS/ECE 374 A — Algorithms and Models of Computation (University of Illinois, Fall 2026), written for review: the week before an exam, or when a homework problem needs the exact definition. They follow Jeff Erickson’s textbook Models of Computation section by section, with the book’s theorem numbers. They are not a replacement for the book — read it; come here to look things up, to review, and to practice.


                  
                  How this site is organized 
                  
                


Chapters (the spine, in book order) — one page per chapter with the book’s section numbers: definitions, numbered results, the exam templates, worked examples, traps, and an “On the exams” box. Each links its chapter PDF.
Concepts are the glossary: one short page per idea (fooling sets, the subset construction, Rice’s theorem, …) with the precise statement, how to use it, the traps, and links to every section that develops it.
Toolkit pages collect what is spread over the chapters: notation, every proof template on one page, the big picture of language classes, two exam reviews, how exams are graded, and errata in the book.
Worked problems are exam-style problems solved in full as model answers; the practice bank is where you do the work yourself — 60 problems tagged easy, medium or hard, each with a folded hint and a worked solution.

Hover a link for a preview, and use the graph view at the top right of any page to see what connects to what.


Course map
Toolkit — reference pages
Notation and conventions · Proof templates · The big picture · Review: Ch 1–5 · Review: Ch 6–9 · How exams are graded · Errata in the book
Part 1 · Models of Computation — Chapters 1–9 complete
Midterm 1 (Sep 28) covered Chapters 1–5; the final covers all nine.

Strings — recursive definitions and induction on strings
Regular languages — language operations, regular expressions, structural induction
Finite-state machines — DFAs, the product construction, fooling sets, Myhill–Nerode, minimization
Nondeterministic automata — NFAs, the subset construction, Thompson, state elimination, Kleene’s theorem, transformations
Context-free languages — grammars, ambiguity, proving L(G) = L, recursive automata, Chomsky normal form
Turing machines — the formal model, variants and their costs, the universal machine
Undecidability — diagonalization, the halting problem, reductions, Rice’s theorem
Universal models — two stacks, counters, FRACTRAN, Post’s correspondence problem, tiles, combinators
Nondeterministic Turing machines — computation trees, dovetailing, P and NP, Cook–Levin

Part 2 · Algorithms planned
Recursion, dynamic programming, graph algorithms and NP-hardness, following Erickson’s Algorithms — for Midterm 2 (Nov 9) and the final (Dec 11).
Practice problems — Chapters 1–7
Sixty problems, from two-minute true-or-false checks to full exam problems, each with a folded hint and a worked solution: by difficulty — easy · medium · hard — or by topic across chapters. Every chapter page links its own set.
Cross-cutting
Concept glossary · Worked problems · Practice problems
Conventions used throughout

The full list, with the book’s notation and the other names you will meet (acceptable = recognizable = semi-decidable = recursively enumerable, …), is on notation and conventions.
Callouts
The pages use a few recurring boxes, so you can skim for what you need:


                  
                  Definition 
                  
                

A formal definition — DFA, grammar, Turing machine, fooling set.




                  
                  Lemma or theorem 
                  
                

A result, numbered as in the book: Lemma 3.6, Theorem 4.1 (Kleene), Rice’s theorem.




                  
                  Template 
                  
                

Proof boilerplate to copy onto the exam, word for word, then fill in.




                  
                  Recipe 
                  
                

A construction or algorithm, step by step.




                  
                  Trap 
                  
                

A mistake that costs points, and how to avoid it.




                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

How the idea shows up on exams and how the rubric grades it.




                  
                  Intuition 
                  
                

The picture behind the formalism.




                  
                  Proof (click to expand) 
                  
                

Proofs are folded so the page stays readable. Expand when you want the details.


The practice pages add their own five: the problem statement sits in an easy, medium or hard box (the difficulty, followed by topic tags), and the hint and solution below it stay folded until you click them.
How the examples were checked
Every concrete example on the site — each regular expression, DFA, NFA, grammar, Turing machine, run trace, state count and fooling-set suffix — is checked by a script against a brute-force definition of its language (all strings up to length 10–14, and exactly by automaton equivalence wherever the language is regular); constructions such as language transformations are tested on hundreds of random DFAs. Each chapter page, concept page and worked problem was then reviewed independently against the book. The scripts are in the repository’s tools/ folder, and the slips found in the book along the way are on errata in the book.
Status: Part 1 (Models of Computation) is complete — 9 chapter pages, 32 concept pages, 7 toolkit pages, 11 worked problems and 60 practice problems. Part 2 (Algorithms) is planned. Source: Jeff Erickson, Models of Computation (December 2018), licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — summarized here in our own words, never copied.

practice/01-strings.title: Practice — Chapter 1: Strings
practice/01-strings.content:
Practice for Chapter 1 · concepts: strings · induction-on-strings · all practice: hub · by difficulty: easy · medium · hard · by topic
Work each problem on paper first. Open the hint only when stuck, and the solution only after you have an answer you would hand in. Every identity and every step of every proof in the solutions has been checked by a script on all short strings. In proofs you may cite Lemmas 1.1–1.3 and the facts listed under More recursive functions, as the exams allow.
Easy
1.1 Unfold an accumulator


                  
                  Easy · recursive functions 
                  
                

The function \textsf{rcat} takes two strings and recurses on its first argument:
\textsf{rcat}(x, y) := \begin{cases} y & \text{if } x = \varepsilon\\ \textsf{rcat}(z,\ a\cdot y) & \text{if } x = a\cdot z.\end{cases}
(a) Compute \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{011}, \varepsilon) by unfolding the definition one step at a time, and name the case used at each step.
(b) Compute \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{10}, \mathtt{01}).
(c) Guess a formula for \textsf{rcat}(x, y) in terms of x, y and the functions of Chapter 1, and a formula for \lvert\textsf{rcat}(x, y)\rvert. No proof is needed here; Problem 1.4 asks for one.
Source: classic.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Each step peels the first symbol off the first argument and puts it in front of the second argument with the small dot:
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{011}, \varepsilon) &= \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{11}, \mathtt{0}\cdot\varepsilon) = \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{11}, \mathtt{0}) && \text{second case: } a = \mathtt{0},\ z = \mathtt{11}\\
&= \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{1}, \mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{0}) = \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{1}, \mathtt{10}) && \text{second case: } a = \mathtt{1},\ z = \mathtt{1}\\
&= \textsf{rcat}(\varepsilon, \mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{10}) = \textsf{rcat}(\varepsilon, \mathtt{110}) && \text{second case: } a = \mathtt{1},\ z = \varepsilon\\
&= \mathtt{110} && \text{first case.}
\end{aligned}
(b) \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{10}, \mathtt{01}) = \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{101}) = \textsf{rcat}(\varepsilon, \mathtt{0101}) = \mathtt{0101}.
(c) The symbols of x arrive at the front of the second argument one at a time, so they end up in reverse order, in front of the untouched y: in (a), \mathtt{110} = (\mathtt{011})^R, and in (b), \mathtt{0101} = (\mathtt{10})^R\bullet\mathtt{01}. The guess is
\textsf{rcat}(x, y) = x^R\bullet y, \qquad \lvert\textsf{rcat}(x, y)\rvert = \lvert x\rvert + \lvert y\rvert.
Check: for x = \varepsilon the guess gives \varepsilon^R\bullet y = y, which is the first case of the definition.
Watch out: the recursive call changes both arguments — the first gets shorter, the second longer. A proof by induction on x must therefore allow any second argument in its hypothesis (Problem 1.4).
Answer. (a) \mathtt{110}. (b) \mathtt{0101}. (c) \textsf{rcat}(x, y) = x^R\bullet y, of length \lvert x\rvert + \lvert y\rvert.


1.2 Substrings, subsequences and prefixes


                  
                  Easy · true or false · substrings and subsequences 
                  
                

All strings are over \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\}. Answer each statement Yes (always true) or No (not always true), with a one-sentence justification; for a No, give a counterexample.
(a) If x is a substring of y\bullet z, then x is a substring of y or a substring of z.
(b) If x is a subsequence of y\bullet z, then x = u\bullet v for some subsequence u of y and some subsequence v of z.
(c) If p is a prefix of w, then p^R is a suffix of w^R.
(d) If x\bullet y = y\bullet x, then x = y.
(e) Every string of length n has at least n+1 distinct subsequences.
(f) The string \mathtt{0101} has exactly 11 distinct substrings, counting \varepsilon.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Every counterexample here needs at most three symbols. For (e), look for n+1 subsequences that are different for an obvious reason.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                


(a) No. A substring can straddle the boundary: x = \mathtt{01} is a substring of \mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{01}, but not of y = \mathtt{0} or of z = \mathtt{1}.
(b) Yes. A subsequence keeps some symbols of yz in order; the kept symbols that come from y form a subsequence u of y, those from z a subsequence v of z, and x = uv because every symbol of y comes before every symbol of z.
(c) Yes. If w = p\bullet x, then w^R = x^R\bullet p^R by the reversal fact (p\bullet x)^R = x^R\bullet p^R, so p^R is a suffix of w^R.
(d) No. x = \mathtt{0} and y = \mathtt{00} commute (\mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{00} = \mathtt{000} = \mathtt{00}\bullet\mathtt{0}) but are different; so do x = \varepsilon and any non-empty y.
(e) Yes. The n+1 prefixes w[1..0], w[1..1], \dots, w[1..n] are subsequences (a prefix is a substring, and a substring is a subsequence), and they are distinct because their lengths differ. The bound is reached: \mathtt{0}^n has exactly the n+1 subsequences \varepsilon, \mathtt{0}, \dots, \mathtt{0}^n.
(f) No. It has 8: \varepsilon, \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{01}, \mathtt{10}, \mathtt{010}, \mathtt{101}, \mathtt{0101}. Eleven — n(n+1)/2 non-empty substrings plus \varepsilon — is only an upper bound; here different positions give equal substrings (\mathtt{01} starts at positions 1 and 3).

Watch out: a Yes needs a reason that covers every case — one example proves nothing. A No needs one concrete counterexample, and a tiny one is best.
Answer. (a) No. (b) Yes. (c) Yes. (d) No. (e) Yes. (f) No: it has 8.


1.3 A proof with a missing case


                  
                  Easy · find the error · string induction 
                  
                

For a binary string w, w^c is its complement (every \mathtt{0} becomes \mathtt{1} and vice versa) and w^R its reversal. A student proves (w^R)^c = (w^c)^R, citing the facts (x\bullet y)^R = y^R\bullet x^R and (x\bullet y)^c = x^c\bullet y^c:
Let w be an arbitrary binary string, and assume that (x^R)^c = (x^c)^R for every string x with \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert. Case w = \varepsilon: (\varepsilon^R)^c = \varepsilon^c = \varepsilon = \varepsilon^R = (\varepsilon^c)^R. Case w = u\bullet v for non-empty strings u and v: then \lvert u\rvert, \lvert v\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, so
\big((uv)^R\big)^c = (v^Ru^R)^c = (v^R)^c(u^R)^c = (v^c)^R(u^c)^R = (u^cv^c)^R = \big((uv)^c\big)^R.
In both cases, (w^R)^c = (w^c)^R. \blacksquare
What is wrong with this proof? Repair it.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Which strings fall into neither case? Can such a string be written as u\bullet v with both pieces non-empty?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

The slip: the cases do not cover every string. A string of length 1 is neither \varepsilon nor a concatenation of two non-empty strings, so the proof says nothing about w = \mathtt{0} or w = \mathtt{1}. The u\bullet v step itself is correct: its five equalities use the reversal fact, the complement fact, the hypothesis for v and for u (both shorter than w), the reversal fact, and the complement fact.
The repair: add the case w = a for a single symbol a. By the definition of reversal, a^R = (a\cdot\varepsilon)^R = \varepsilon^R\bullet a = \varepsilon\bullet a = a: a one-symbol string is its own reversal. The complement a^c is again a single symbol, so (a^c)^R = a^c, and therefore (a^R)^c = a^c = (a^c)^R. With the three cases w = \varepsilon, w = a, and w = u\bullet v with u, v non-empty, every string is covered and the proof is complete.
Why the missing case matters. The same two cases “prove” the false claim \#(\mathtt{0}, w) = \#(\mathtt{1}, w): it holds for \varepsilon, and if it holds for u and v, then \#(\mathtt{0}, uv) = \#(\mathtt{0},u) + \#(\mathtt{0},v) = \#(\mathtt{1},u) + \#(\mathtt{1},v) = \#(\mathtt{1},uv). The claim fails exactly in the missing case: \#(\mathtt{0},\mathtt{0}) = 1\ne0 = \#(\mathtt{1},\mathtt{0}).
Watch out: the split w = u\bullet v always needs two base cases, \varepsilon and a single symbol (§1.4). On the exams, cases that miss some strings cost the 2 points for exhaustive cases.
Answer. Strings of length 1 are in neither case. Add the case w = a, where (a^R)^c = a^c = (a^c)^R because a one-symbol string is its own reversal.


Medium
1.4 Reversal with an accumulator


                  
                  Medium · string induction · recursive functions 
                  
                

Let \textsf{rcat} be the function of Problem 1.1: \textsf{rcat}(\varepsilon, y) := y and \textsf{rcat}(a\cdot z, y) := \textsf{rcat}(z, a\cdot y).
(a) Prove that \textsf{rcat}(x, y) = x^R\bullet y for all strings x and y.
(b) Conclude that \textsf{rcat}(x, \varepsilon) = x^R and \lvert\textsf{rcat}(x, y)\rvert = \lvert x\rvert + \lvert y\rvert.
Reversal is defined by \varepsilon^R := \varepsilon and (a\cdot z)^R := z^R\bullet a; you may also use \lvert w^R\rvert = \lvert w\rvert.
Source: classic.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Induct on x, the argument that shrinks. In the recursive case the second argument changes from y to a\cdot y, so the induction hypothesis must hold for every second argument, not only for y.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. \textsf{rcat} recurses on x, so induct on x. The recursive call has second argument a\cdot y instead of y; a hypothesis about the fixed y could not be applied to it, so the hypothesis quantifies over all second arguments.
(a) Let x be an arbitrary string. Assume that \textsf{rcat}(z, y') = z^R\bullet y' for every string z with \lvert z\rvert<\lvert x\rvert and every string y'. Let y be an arbitrary string. There are two cases.
Case x = \varepsilon. By the definitions of \textsf{rcat}, {\bullet} and {}^R: \textsf{rcat}(\varepsilon, y) = y = \varepsilon\bullet y = \varepsilon^R\bullet y.
Case x = a\cdot z for some symbol a and string z. Then \lvert z\rvert<\lvert x\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to z, with y' = a\cdot y:
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{rcat}(a\cdot z, y) &= \textsf{rcat}(z, a\cdot y) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{rcat}\\
&= z^R\bullet(a\cdot y) && \text{by the induction hypothesis, with } y' = a\cdot y\\
&= z^R\bullet(a\bullet y) && \text{because } a\bullet y = a\cdot y\\
&= (z^R\bullet a)\bullet y && \text{by Lemma 1.3}\\
&= (a\cdot z)^R\bullet y && \text{by definition of } {}^R.
\end{aligned}
In both cases, \textsf{rcat}(x, y) = x^R\bullet y. \blacksquare
(b) With y = \varepsilon, part (a) and Lemma 1.1 give \textsf{rcat}(x, \varepsilon) = x^R\bullet\varepsilon = x^R. By part (a), Lemma 1.2 and \lvert x^R\rvert = \lvert x\rvert: \lvert\textsf{rcat}(x, y)\rvert = \lvert x^R\rvert + \lvert y\rvert = \lvert x\rvert + \lvert y\rvert.
Check: \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{011}, \varepsilon) = \mathtt{110} = (\mathtt{011})^R and \textsf{rcat}(\mathtt{10}, \mathtt{01}) = \mathtt{0101} = \mathtt{01}\bullet\mathtt{01}, as computed in Problem 1.1.
Watch out: with the weaker hypothesis ”\textsf{rcat}(z, y) = z^R\bullet y for every shorter z” (the same y), the second line is not justified, because the call is \textsf{rcat}(z, a\cdot y). Graders count that as applying the hypothesis with the wrong value of the other argument (2 points on the induction rubric). Proving only the special case \textsf{rcat}(x, \varepsilon) = x^R by induction fails for the same reason — \textsf{rcat}(a\cdot z, \varepsilon) calls \textsf{rcat}(z, a), which is not of the form \textsf{rcat}(z', \varepsilon). Here the general statement is easier to prove than the special case.
Answer. (a) Induction on x, with the hypothesis for every second argument: \textsf{rcat}(az, y) = \textsf{rcat}(z, ay) = z^R\bullet(ay) = (z^Ra)\bullet y = (az)^R\bullet y. (b) \textsf{rcat}(x,\varepsilon) = x^R\bullet\varepsilon = x^R, and \lvert\textsf{rcat}(x,y)\rvert = \lvert x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert.


1.5 When subsequences are substrings


                  
                  Medium · substrings and subsequences 
                  
                

All strings are over \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\}.
(a) For integers a, b\ge1, how many distinct substrings and how many distinct subsequences does \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b have? Count \varepsilon.
(b) Prove that every subsequence of w is a substring of w if and only if w = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j or w = \mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{0}^j for some i, j\ge0.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) Deleting symbols from \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b never puts a \mathtt{1} before a \mathtt{0}. (b) For “only if”, find a symbol whose copies are not all next to each other, and look at its longest block of consecutive copies.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. A subsequence of \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b is a few 0s followed by a few 1s, and such a string sits around the boundary of \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b as a substring. A string of any other shape has a symbol that occurs in two separate blocks, and gluing copies from both blocks gives a subsequence that is too long to be a substring.
(a) A subsequence of \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b keeps some of the 0s and some of the 1s, in order, so it is \mathtt{0}^p\mathtt{1}^q with 0\le p\le a and 0\le q\le b; conversely each such string is a subsequence. Each of them is also a substring — the last p zeros and the first q ones, w[a-p+1\,..\,a+q] — and every substring is a subsequence. So the substrings and the subsequences are the same set \{\mathtt{0}^p\mathtt{1}^q \mid 0\le p\le a,\ 0\le q\le b\}, with (a+1)(b+1) elements (different pairs (p, q) give different strings).
(b) “If.” For w = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j this is the argument of (a), which also works when i = 0 or j = 0. For w = \mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{0}^j, exchange the roles of the two symbols.
“Only if”, by the contrapositive. Suppose w has neither form. Since w is not \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j, some \mathtt{1} of w comes before some \mathtt{0} (otherwise all 0s precede all 1s); since w is not \mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{0}^j, some \mathtt{0} comes before some \mathtt{1}. Let c be the first symbol of w and \bar c the other one. By one of the two facts (the first if c = \mathtt{0}, the second if c = \mathtt{1}), some \bar c comes before a later c; with the first symbol, w contains c, then \bar c, then c again, in that order. So the copies of c form at least two separate blocks (maximal runs of consecutive c‘s). Let m be the length of the longest block. The other block has at least one c, so \#(c, w)\ge m+1, and c^{m+1} is a subsequence of w. But it is not a substring: a substring made of m+1 copies of c would lie inside a single block, and every block has length at most m. \blacksquare
Check: \mathtt{0110} has neither form, and indeed \mathtt{00} is a subsequence but not a substring of it. \mathtt{0011} has (2+1)(2+1) = 9 substrings and 9 subsequences.
Answer. (a) (a+1)(b+1) substrings and (a+1)(b+1) subsequences — the two sets are equal. (b) “If”: every subsequence \mathtt{0}^p\mathtt{1}^q of \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j is a substring. “Only if”: otherwise some symbol c occurs in two blocks, and if its longest block has length m, then c^{m+1} is a subsequence but not a substring.


1.6 Rotating a string


                  
                  Medium · string induction · recursive functions 
                  
                

For symbols a, b and a string x, define
\textsf{rot}(w) := \begin{cases} w & \text{if } \lvert w\rvert\le1\\ b\cdot\textsf{rot}(a\cdot x) & \text{if } w = a\cdot b\cdot x.\end{cases}
(a) Compute \textsf{rot}(\mathtt{STAR}) by unfolding the definition.
(b) Prove directly from the definition, by induction on w, that \lvert\textsf{rot}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert for every string w.
(c) Prove that \textsf{rot}(a\cdot x) = x\bullet a for every symbol a and every string x.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(b) The definition has two cases, \lvert w\rvert\le1 and w = a\cdot b\cdot x, so the proof does too. The recursive call is on a\cdot x: is that string shorter than w, and does it matter that it is not the tail b\cdot x? (c) Here it is easier to induct on x and keep a fixed.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Each call moves the second symbol out to the front and keeps the first symbol inside the call, so the first symbol travels to the end: \textsf{rot} rotates the string by one position. For (b), the strong hypothesis (“every shorter string”) covers the call on a\cdot x; for (c), inducting on x makes the call an ordinary call on a shorter tail.
(a)
\textsf{rot}(\mathtt{STAR}) = \mathtt{T}\cdot\textsf{rot}(\mathtt{SAR}) = \mathtt{T}\cdot\mathtt{A}\cdot\textsf{rot}(\mathtt{SR}) = \mathtt{T}\cdot\mathtt{A}\cdot\mathtt{R}\cdot\textsf{rot}(\mathtt{S}) = \mathtt{TARS}.
(b) Let w be an arbitrary string, and assume that \lvert\textsf{rot}(y)\rvert = \lvert y\rvert for every string y with \lvert y\rvert<\lvert w\rvert. There are two cases.
Case \lvert w\rvert\le1. Then \textsf{rot}(w) = w, so \lvert\textsf{rot}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert.
Case w = a\cdot b\cdot x. The string a\cdot x has length \lvert x\rvert+1<\lvert x\rvert+2 = \lvert w\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to it:
\lvert\textsf{rot}(w)\rvert = \lvert b\cdot\textsf{rot}(a\cdot x)\rvert = 1 + \lvert\textsf{rot}(a\cdot x)\rvert = 1 + \lvert a\cdot x\rvert = 2 + \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert,
by the definition of \textsf{rot}, the definition of \lvert\cdot\rvert, the induction hypothesis, and the definition of \lvert\cdot\rvert twice more.
In both cases, \lvert\textsf{rot}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert. \blacksquare
The string a\cdot x is in general not a suffix of w — for w = \mathtt{STAR} it is \mathtt{SAR}. That does not matter: the hypothesis covers every string shorter than w.
(c) Let a be a symbol and x an arbitrary string. Assume that \textsf{rot}(a\cdot y) = y\bullet a for every string y with \lvert y\rvert<\lvert x\rvert. There are two cases.
Case x = \varepsilon. \textsf{rot}(a\cdot\varepsilon) = a = \varepsilon\bullet a, by the first case of \textsf{rot} and the definition of {\bullet}.
Case x = b\cdot y. Then \lvert y\rvert<\lvert x\rvert, and
\textsf{rot}(a\cdot b\cdot y) = b\cdot\textsf{rot}(a\cdot y) = b\cdot(y\bullet a) = (b\cdot y)\bullet a = x\bullet a,
by the definition of \textsf{rot}, the induction hypothesis for y, and the definition of {\bullet}.
In both cases, \textsf{rot}(a\cdot x) = x\bullet a. \blacksquare
Check: \textsf{rot}(\mathtt{STAR}) = \mathtt{TARS} = \mathtt{TAR}\bullet\mathtt{S}, as (c) predicts. And (b) also follows from (c): \lvert x\bullet a\rvert = \lvert x\rvert + 1 by Lemma 1.2.
Watch out: choosing what to induct on is part of the proof. Inducting on w in (c) works too, but then the hypothesis must be applied to a\cdot y, which is not a tail of w, and the bookkeeping is heavier.
Answer. (a) \mathtt{TARS}. (b) Two cases; for w = abx, the hypothesis applies to the shorter string a\cdot x, and \lvert b\cdot\textsf{rot}(ax)\rvert = 1 + \lvert ax\rvert = \lvert w\rvert. (c) Induction on x: \textsf{rot}(a\cdot b\cdot y) = b\cdot\textsf{rot}(a\cdot y) = b\cdot(y\bullet a) = (by)\bullet a.


Hard
1.7 Complementing every other symbol


                  
                  Hard · string induction · recursive functions 
                  
                

For a binary string w, the complement w^c is defined by \varepsilon^c := \varepsilon and (a\cdot x)^c := \bar a\cdot x^c, where \bar{\mathtt{0}} = \mathtt{1} and \bar{\mathtt{1}} = \mathtt{0}. Define
\textsf{zig}(w) := \begin{cases} \varepsilon & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ a\cdot\big(\textsf{zig}(x)\big)^c & \text{if } w = a\cdot x.\end{cases}
For example, \textsf{zig}(\mathtt{0000}) = \mathtt{0101} and \textsf{zig}(\mathtt{0110}) = \mathtt{0011}.
(a) Prove that \textsf{zig}(w^c) = \big(\textsf{zig}(w)\big)^c for every binary string w.
(b) Prove that \textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(w)) = w for every binary string w.
You may use (y^c)^c = y for every binary string y, and in (b) you may use (a).
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Write the boilerplate for both parts first. In (a), the case w = a\cdot x starts from w^c = \bar a\cdot x^c. In (b), unfolding \textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(a\cdot x)) twice produces \textsf{zig}\big(\textsf{zig}(x)^c\big): that is where (a) comes in, applied to the string \textsf{zig}(x).




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. \textsf{zig} keeps the first symbol and complements the result of the recursive call, so the second symbol is complemented once, the third twice, and so on: \textsf{zig} complements exactly the symbols in even positions, and doing that twice changes nothing. In the proof, a complement must be moved past \textsf{zig}; that is what (a) does.
(a) Let w be an arbitrary binary string. Assume that \textsf{zig}(y^c) = \textsf{zig}(y)^c for every binary string y with \lvert y\rvert<\lvert w\rvert. There are two cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. \textsf{zig}(\varepsilon^c) = \textsf{zig}(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon = \varepsilon^c = \textsf{zig}(\varepsilon)^c, by the definitions of {}^c and \textsf{zig}.
Case w = a\cdot x for a symbol a and a string x. Then \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to x, and
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{zig}(w^c) &= \textsf{zig}(\bar a\cdot x^c) && \text{by definition of } {}^c\\
&= \bar a\cdot\big(\textsf{zig}(x^c)\big)^c && \text{by definition of } \textsf{zig}\\
&= \bar a\cdot\big(\textsf{zig}(x)^c\big)^c && \text{by the induction hypothesis for } x\\
&= \big(a\cdot\textsf{zig}(x)^c\big)^c && \text{by definition of } {}^c\\
&= \textsf{zig}(a\cdot x)^c && \text{by definition of } \textsf{zig}.
\end{aligned}
In both cases, \textsf{zig}(w^c) = \textsf{zig}(w)^c. \blacksquare
(b) Let w be an arbitrary binary string. Assume that \textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(y)) = y for every binary string y with \lvert y\rvert<\lvert w\rvert. There are two cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. \textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(\varepsilon)) = \textsf{zig}(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon, by the definition of \textsf{zig} (twice).
Case w = a\cdot x for a symbol a and a string x. Then \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, and
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(a\cdot x)) &= \textsf{zig}\big(a\cdot\textsf{zig}(x)^c\big) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{zig}\\
&= a\cdot\Big(\textsf{zig}\big(\textsf{zig}(x)^c\big)\Big)^c && \text{by definition of } \textsf{zig}\\
&= a\cdot\Big(\big(\textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(x))\big)^c\Big)^c && \text{by (a), applied to the string } \textsf{zig}(x)\\
&= a\cdot\textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(x)) && \text{because } (y^c)^c = y\\
&= a\cdot x && \text{by the induction hypothesis for } x.
\end{aligned}
In both cases, \textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(w)) = w. \blacksquare
Check: \textsf{zig}(\mathtt{0110}) = \mathtt{0011} and \textsf{zig}(\mathtt{0011}) = \mathtt{0110}, as (b) says. For w = \mathtt{01}, (a) reads \textsf{zig}(\mathtt{10}) = \mathtt{11} = (\mathtt{00})^c = \textsf{zig}(\mathtt{01})^c.
Watch out: in the third line of (b) the induction hypothesis is of no use: it is about \textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(y)), not \textsf{zig}(y^c). Part (a) moves the complement out, and because (a) has been proved for every string, it may be applied to \textsf{zig}(x) with no question of length. The hypothesis of (b) is used once, for x, in the last line.
Answer. (a) Induction on w; for w = ax: \textsf{zig}(\bar ax^c) = \bar a\cdot\textsf{zig}(x^c)^c = \bar a\cdot(\textsf{zig}(x)^c)^c = (a\cdot\textsf{zig}(x)^c)^c = \textsf{zig}(ax)^c. (b) Induction on w, using (a) for \textsf{zig}(x) and the hypothesis for x: \textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(ax)) = a\cdot\textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(x)^c)^c = a\cdot\textsf{zig}(\textsf{zig}(x)) = ax.


1.8 Binary increment, low bit first


                  
                  Hard · string induction · recursive functions 
                  
                

Read a binary string as a number with its least significant bit first:
\textsf{val}(w) := \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ a + 2\cdot\textsf{val}(x) & \text{if } w = a\cdot x,\end{cases}
where the symbols \mathtt{0} and \mathtt{1} count as the numbers 0 and 1; for example, \textsf{val}(\mathtt{011}) = 0 + 2\big(1 + 2(1 + 2\cdot0)\big) = 6. The function
\textsf{inc}(w) := \begin{cases} \mathtt{1} & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ \mathtt{1}\cdot x & \text{if } w = \mathtt{0}\cdot x\\ \mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{inc}(x) & \text{if } w = \mathtt{1}\cdot x\end{cases}
adds one, the way you add one by hand: for example, \textsf{inc}(\mathtt{1101}) = \mathtt{0011}, that is, 11 + 1 = 12.
(a) Prove that \textsf{val}(\textsf{inc}(w)) = \textsf{val}(w) + 1 for every binary string w.
(b) Prove that \lvert\textsf{inc}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert + 1 if w = \mathtt{1}^n for some n\ge0, and \lvert\textsf{inc}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert otherwise.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

The definition of \textsf{inc} has three cases — \varepsilon, \mathtt{0}\cdot x, \mathtt{1}\cdot x — so both proofs do, and only the case \mathtt{1}\cdot x needs the induction hypothesis. In (b), split that case according to whether x is all 1s.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Adding one turns the leading block of 1s (the low-order bits) into 0s and the first 0 into a 1; the string gets longer only when there is no 0 to absorb the carry. Both proofs follow the three cases of the definition of \textsf{inc}.
(a) Let w be an arbitrary binary string, and assume that \textsf{val}(\textsf{inc}(x)) = \textsf{val}(x) + 1 for every binary string x with \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert. There are three cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. \textsf{val}(\textsf{inc}(\varepsilon)) = \textsf{val}(\mathtt{1}\cdot\varepsilon) = 1 + 2\cdot\textsf{val}(\varepsilon) = 1 = \textsf{val}(\varepsilon) + 1, by the definitions of \textsf{inc} and \textsf{val}.
Case w = \mathtt{0}\cdot x. \textsf{val}(\textsf{inc}(w)) = \textsf{val}(\mathtt{1}\cdot x) = 1 + 2\,\textsf{val}(x) = \big(0 + 2\,\textsf{val}(x)\big) + 1 = \textsf{val}(\mathtt{0}\cdot x) + 1, by the definitions of \textsf{inc} and \textsf{val}.
Case w = \mathtt{1}\cdot x. Then \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to x:
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{val}(\textsf{inc}(\mathtt{1}\cdot x)) &= \textsf{val}(\mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{inc}(x)) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{inc}\\
&= 0 + 2\,\textsf{val}(\textsf{inc}(x)) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{val}\\
&= 2\big(\textsf{val}(x) + 1\big) && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= \big(1 + 2\,\textsf{val}(x)\big) + 1 && \text{by arithmetic}\\
&= \textsf{val}(\mathtt{1}\cdot x) + 1 && \text{by definition of } \textsf{val}.
\end{aligned}
In all three cases, \textsf{val}(\textsf{inc}(w)) = \textsf{val}(w) + 1. \blacksquare
(b) A small fact first: \mathtt{1}\cdot x is of the form \mathtt{1}^n if and only if x is. Indeed, \mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{1}^m = \mathtt{1}^{m+1}; conversely, if \mathtt{1}\cdot x = \mathtt{1}^n, then n\ge1 (the string is not empty), so \mathtt{1}\cdot x = \mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{1}^{n-1} by the definition of powers, and x = \mathtt{1}^{n-1} because equal pairs have equal second parts.
Let w be an arbitrary binary string. Assume, for every binary string x with \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, that \lvert\textsf{inc}(x)\rvert = \lvert x\rvert + 1 if x is of the form \mathtt{1}^m, and \lvert\textsf{inc}(x)\rvert = \lvert x\rvert otherwise. There are three cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. Here w = \mathtt{1}^0, and \lvert\textsf{inc}(\varepsilon)\rvert = \lvert\mathtt{1}\rvert = 1 = \lvert\varepsilon\rvert + 1.
Case w = \mathtt{0}\cdot x. Here w is not of the form \mathtt{1}^n, because such a string is empty or starts with \mathtt{1}; and \lvert\textsf{inc}(w)\rvert = \lvert\mathtt{1}\cdot x\rvert = 1 + \lvert x\rvert = \lvert\mathtt{0}\cdot x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert.
Case w = \mathtt{1}\cdot x. By the definitions, \lvert\textsf{inc}(w)\rvert = \lvert\mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{inc}(x)\rvert = 1 + \lvert\textsf{inc}(x)\rvert, and \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, so the hypothesis applies to x.

If x = \mathtt{1}^m, then w = \mathtt{1}^{m+1}, and \lvert\textsf{inc}(w)\rvert = 1 + \lvert x\rvert + 1 = \lvert w\rvert + 1.
Otherwise, by the small fact, w is not of the form \mathtt{1}^n either, and \lvert\textsf{inc}(w)\rvert = 1 + \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert.

In all cases, the claim holds for w. \blacksquare
Check: \textsf{inc}(\mathtt{111}) = \mathtt{0001}: the value goes from 7 to 8, and the length from 3 to 4. \textsf{inc}(\mathtt{011}) = \mathtt{111}: the value goes from 6 to 7, and the length stays 3.
Grading notes. Each part is an induction proof of the exam type, graded out of 10: an arbitrary w (1), an explicit hypothesis for every shorter string (2), cases that cover every string — here the three of the definition (2), the base case (1), the hypothesis applied only to the shorter x (2), and justified details (2). See how exams are graded.
Watch out: the claim in (b) has two alternatives, so the hypothesis must state both: in the case w = \mathtt{1}\cdot x you do not know in advance which one applies to x.
Answer. (a) Three cases; only w = \mathtt{1}x uses the hypothesis: \textsf{val}(\mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{inc}(x)) = 2(\textsf{val}(x)+1) = \textsf{val}(\mathtt{1}x) + 1. (b) Three cases; for w = \mathtt{1}x, \lvert\textsf{inc}(w)\rvert = 1 + \lvert\textsf{inc}(x)\rvert, and w is all 1s exactly when x is.


Sources for this page
The problems are original or classic exercise types restated in our own words. Problems 1.1 and 1.4 use the classic accumulator version of reversal; 1.2 and 1.5 test the definitions of §1.5; 1.3 is built on the three-case split of §1.4; and the functions \textsf{rot}, \textsf{zig} and \textsf{inc} (1.6–1.8) are new, in the style of the book’s Chapter 1 exercises and of the exams’ induction problem. None is taken from a course exam or homework. Every identity, every line of every proof and every example is checked by brute force over all short strings (lengths up to 8–12) in tools/practice/checks/ch01.py.
