practice/02-regular-languages.content:
Practice for Chapter 2 · concepts: languages · regular-expressions · regular-languages · all practice: hub · by difficulty: easy · medium · hard · by topic
Work each problem on paper first. Open the hint only when stuck, and the solution only after you have an answer you would hand in. Every regular expression and every identity in the solutions has been checked by a script. All strings are over \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\}, and, as in regular expressions, a single string may stand for the language that contains just that string.
Easy
2.1 Empty things, products and stars


                  
                  Easy · true or false · languages · Kleene star 
                  
                

Answer each statement Yes (true for all languages involved) or No, with a one-sentence justification; for a No, give a counterexample.
(a) \varnothing\bullet\{\varepsilon\} = \{\varepsilon\}.
(b) \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{01}\}\bullet\{\mathtt{1},\mathtt{11}\} contains exactly four strings.
(c) (L^*)^* = L^* for every language L.
(d) (A\cup B)^* = A^*\cup B^* for all languages A and B.
(e) \varnothing^+ = \varnothing.
(f) If \varepsilon\in L, then L\bullet L = L.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Keep \varnothing (no strings), \{\varepsilon\} (one string) and \varepsilon (a string) apart: a concatenation needs a string from each factor. For the “for all” statements, try one-string languages such as \{\mathtt{0}\} and \{\mathtt{1}\} first.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                


(a) No. A concatenation needs a string from each factor and \varnothing has none, so \varnothing\bullet\{\varepsilon\} = \varnothing (Lemma 2.1(c)), which is not \{\varepsilon\}.
(b) No. It has three strings, \mathtt{01}, \mathtt{011} and \mathtt{0111}, because two different pairs give the same string: \mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{11} = \mathtt{01}\bullet\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{011}.
(c) Yes. L^*\subseteq(L^*)^* because every language is contained in its star, and (L^*)^*\subseteq L^* because a concatenation of concatenations of strings of L is itself a concatenation of strings of L.
(d) No. With A = \{\mathtt{0}\} and B = \{\mathtt{1}\}, the string \mathtt{01} is in (A\cup B)^* but neither in A^* = \mathtt{0}^* nor in B^* = \mathtt{1}^*. Only A^*\cup B^*\subseteq(A\cup B)^* holds.
(e) Yes. \varnothing^+ = \varnothing\bullet\varnothing^* = \varnothing\bullet\{\varepsilon\} = \varnothing by Lemma 2.1(c), even though \varnothing^* = \{\varepsilon\} — as Lemma 2.2(c) predicts, L^+\ne L^* when \varepsilon\notin L.
(f) No. L = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0}\} contains \varepsilon, but L\bullet L = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{00}\}\ne L. What does hold is L\subseteq L\bullet L, since x = x\bullet\varepsilon.

Answer. (a) No. (b) No. (c) Yes. (d) No. (e) Yes. (f) No.


2.2 Read these expressions


                  
                  Easy · regular expressions 
                  
                

For each regular expression, describe its language in one English sentence, and list every string of length at most 2 that it matches.
(a) (\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01})^*
(b) (\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*)^*
(c) (\mathtt{00}+\mathtt{000})^*
(d) (\mathtt{0}+\varnothing)^*\,\mathtt{1}\,\varnothing^*
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Ask what each starred block contributes, and what the empty sequence of blocks gives. In (d), find L(\mathtt{0}+\varnothing) and L(\varnothing^*) first.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                


(a) The blocks are \mathtt{1} and \mathtt{01}, so every \mathtt{0} is immediately followed by a \mathtt{1} (equivalently: no \mathtt{00}, and no final \mathtt{0}). Conversely, a string with that property splits into such blocks by cutting after every \mathtt{1}. Length at most 2: \varepsilon, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{01}, \mathtt{11}.
(b) Each block contains exactly two 1s, so every string matched has an even number of 1s; but each block contains at least one \mathtt{1}, so a non-empty string with no 1s is not matched. The language is \varepsilon together with the strings that have an even, positive number of 1s. Length at most 2: \varepsilon, \mathtt{11}.
(c) Strings of 0s whose length is 2i+3j for some i, j\ge0 — every length except 1. So the language is \{\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ne1\}, the same as L(\varepsilon+\mathtt{000}^*). Length at most 2: \varepsilon, \mathtt{00}.
(d) L(\mathtt{0}+\varnothing) = \{\mathtt{0}\}\cup\varnothing = \{\mathtt{0}\} and L(\varnothing^*) = \{\varepsilon\}, so the expression is equivalent to \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}: any number of 0s followed by a single 1. Length at most 2: \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{01}.

Watch out: (b) is not “an even number of 1s” — that language also contains \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{00}, \mathtt{000}, …, which have zero 1s. And in (d), \varnothing^* is \{\varepsilon\}, not \varnothing, so the expression does not describe the empty language.
Answer. (a) Every 0 is immediately followed by a 1: \varepsilon, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{01}, \mathtt{11}. (b) \varepsilon or an even, positive number of 1s: \varepsilon, \mathtt{11}. (c) \mathtt{0}^n with n\ne1: \varepsilon, \mathtt{00}. (d) \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}: \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{01}.


2.3 A missing empty string


                  
                  Easy · find the error · regular expressions 
                  
                

Let L be the set of binary strings in which every \mathtt{0} is followed, somewhere later in the string, by at least one \mathtt{1}. A student answers:
”(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1}. A string is in L exactly when its last symbol is a 1, since that final 1 comes after every 0; (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* is everything before it.”
Is the answer correct? If not, say exactly which strings it gets wrong, fix it, and say how the regular-expression rubric treats the slip.
Source: original.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

The slip: \varepsilon\in L, but \varepsilon does not match. The empty string contains no 0 at all, so “every 0 is followed by a 1” holds for it vacuously. The rest of the explanation is right: a non-empty string is in L if and only if it ends in \mathtt{1} (if it ends in \mathtt{0}, that last 0 has nothing after it; if it ends in \mathtt{1}, that 1 comes after every 0). So L = \{\varepsilon\}\cup L\big((\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1}\big), and \varepsilon is the only string the answer gets wrong.
Fix: \varepsilon+(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1}, or equivalently (\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1})^*: blocks of 0s each closed by a 1, where the empty sequence of blocks gives \varepsilon.
Grading: a single wrong string is the classic “one mistake” — typically a missing or extra \varepsilon — and costs the smallest correctness deduction (2 of the 8 correctness points on an exam). An answer that is wrong on infinitely many strings would lose all 8.
Watch out: test \varepsilon explicitly, every time. Conditions of the form “every … is …” are true for strings that contain no ”…” at all.
Answer. Not correct: it misses exactly one string, \varepsilon. A correct answer is \varepsilon+(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1} (or (\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1})^*).


Medium
2.4 Three regular expressions


                  
                  Medium · regular expressions 
                  
                

Give a regular expression for each language, with a one-sentence explanation of each part. No proof is required.
(a) Strings that contain both \mathtt{00} and \mathtt{11} as substrings.
(b) Strings in which the number of 0s between any two consecutive 1s is even. (Two 1s are consecutive if no 1 lies between them; 0s before the first 1 or after the last 1 are unrestricted.)
(c) Strings w with w_i = \mathtt{0} for every position i that is a multiple of 3. (Positions are numbered from 1, so the condition is on w_3, w_6, w_9 and so on.)
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) “And” is hard for regular expressions, but here you can split by which of the two substrings occurs first. (b) Describe the first 1, then each later 1 together with the gap of 0s before it. (c) Cut the string into blocks of three symbols; the last block may be incomplete.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Idea. An occurrence of \mathtt{00} and an occurrence of \mathtt{11} cannot overlap (they have no symbol in common), so one of them lies entirely before the other.
(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{11}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* + (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{11}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*
The first term is anything, then \mathtt{00}, then anything, then \mathtt{11}, then anything: an occurrence of \mathtt{00} before an occurrence of \mathtt{11}. The second term is the same with the order reversed. Every string of the language has one of the two orders, and every string matched contains both substrings. Check: \mathtt{0011}, \mathtt{1100} and \mathtt{10011} match; \mathtt{0110} (no \mathtt{00}), \mathtt{0101} and \varepsilon do not.
(b) Idea. The 0s before the first 1 and after the last 1 are free; only the gaps between consecutive 1s are constrained.
\mathtt{0}^* + \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\big((\mathtt{00})^*\mathtt{1}\big)^*\mathtt{0}^*
The term \mathtt{0}^* covers the strings with no 1, which have no gap to check. In the second term, \mathtt{0}^* is the 0s before the first 1; \mathtt{1} is the first 1; each (\mathtt{00})^*\mathtt{1} is an even gap of 0s followed by the next 1; and the final \mathtt{0}^* is the 0s after the last 1. Check: \varepsilon, \mathtt{000}, \mathtt{0110}, \mathtt{1001} and \mathtt{01001100} match; \mathtt{101}, \mathtt{10001} and \mathtt{11011} do not.
(c) Idea. Positions 3k-2, 3k-1, 3k form the kth block of three, and only the third symbol of a complete block is constrained.
\big((\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})\mathtt{0}\big)^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})
Each (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})\mathtt{0} is a complete block with a 0 in its third position, and the star allows any number of complete blocks; (\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}) is the incomplete last block, of length 0, 1 or 2, which contains no position divisible by 3. Check: \varepsilon, \mathtt{11}, \mathtt{110} and \mathtt{11011} match; \mathtt{111} and \mathtt{000001} do not.
Watch out: in (b), \mathtt{0}^*\big(\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{00})^*\big)^* looks plausible but forces an even number of 0s after the last 1, so it misses \mathtt{10}, \mathtt{1000}, …; in (c), leaving out the incomplete last block keeps only the strings whose length is divisible by 3. Each of these slips is wrong on infinitely many strings and loses all the correctness points.
Answer. (a) (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{11}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* + (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{11}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{00}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*. (b) \mathtt{0}^* + \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}((\mathtt{00})^*\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{0}^*. (c) ((\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})\mathtt{0})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}).


2.5 Equivalent or not


                  
                  Medium · regular expressions · languages 
                  
                

For each pair, decide whether the two regular expressions are equivalent. If they are, explain why; if not, give a shortest string that matches exactly one of them, and say whether one language contains the other.
(a) (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{0}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* and (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{01}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*
(b) \mathtt{1}(\mathtt{01})^* and (\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}
(c) (\mathtt{01}+\mathtt{10})^* and (\mathtt{01})^*(\mathtt{10})^*
(d) (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^* and \mathtt{0}^*(\mathtt{01})^*
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

List the short strings each side matches, in order of length, until the lists differ or a pattern appears. For an equivalence, argue both inclusions; in (a), look for a \mathtt{0} that is immediately followed by a \mathtt{1}.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Equivalence needs an argument for both inclusions; non-equivalence needs one string, checked against both expressions.
(a) Equivalent. Both describe the strings with a \mathtt{0} somewhere before a \mathtt{1}. Right \subseteq left: an occurrence of \mathtt{01} is a 0 before a 1. Left \subseteq right: if w = x\mathtt{0}y\mathtt{1}z, then the substring \mathtt{0}y\mathtt{1} begins with 0 and contains a 1; the symbol just before its first 1 is a 0, so w contains \mathtt{01}.
(b) Equivalent. The languages are \{\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{01})^n \mid n\ge0\} and \{(\mathtt{10})^n\mathtt{1} \mid n\ge0\}, and \mathtt{1}(\mathtt{01})^n = (\mathtt{10})^n\mathtt{1} for every n: both are the alternating string \mathtt{1010}\cdots\mathtt{01} of length 2n+1 (by associativity, \mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{01}\,\mathtt{01}\cdots\mathtt{01} regroups as \mathtt{10}\,\mathtt{10}\cdots\mathtt{10}\,\mathtt{1}). This is the “sliding” identity x(yx)^* = (xy)^*x.
(c) Not equivalent. Shortest witness: \mathtt{1001} = \mathtt{10}\bullet\mathtt{01} matches the left expression but not the right one, whose strings are some copies of \mathtt{01} followed by some copies of \mathtt{10}. Every string matched by the right expression is a sequence of \mathtt{01} and \mathtt{10} blocks, so L\big((\mathtt{01})^*(\mathtt{10})^*\big)\subsetneq L\big((\mathtt{01}+\mathtt{10})^*\big).
(d) Not equivalent. Shortest witness: \mathtt{010} = \mathtt{01}\bullet\mathtt{0} matches the left expression but not the right one, in which no \mathtt{0} can come after a \mathtt{01} block. Again L\big(\mathtt{0}^*(\mathtt{01})^*\big)\subsetneq L\big((\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^*\big): putting all the \mathtt{0} blocks first is one particular order of the blocks.
Check: in (c), both sides match exactly \varepsilon, \mathtt{01}, \mathtt{10} among the strings of length at most 3; of length 4, the left side matches \mathtt{0101}, \mathtt{0110}, \mathtt{1001}, \mathtt{1010} and the right side only \mathtt{0101}, \mathtt{0110}, \mathtt{1010}. In (d), the strings of length at most 2 agree (\varepsilon, \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{00}, \mathtt{01}), and \mathtt{010} is the only difference of length 3.
Watch out: “the two sides agree on every short string I tried” never proves equivalence — (c) agrees on everything shorter than 4.
Answer. (a) Equivalent. (b) Equivalent. (c) Not equivalent: \mathtt{1001}; the right language is a proper subset of the left. (d) Not equivalent: \mathtt{010}; the right language is a proper subset of the left.


2.6 Solving three language equations


                  
                  Medium · Arden's rule 
                  
                

The languages X, Y, Z satisfy
X = \mathtt{0}X\cup\mathtt{1}Y\cup\{\varepsilon\},\qquad Y = \mathtt{0}X\cup\mathtt{1}Z\cup\{\varepsilon\},\qquad Z = \mathtt{1}Z\cup\{\varepsilon\}.
(a) Use Arden’s rule to find regular expressions for Z, Y and X, and explain why the system has only one solution.
(b) Describe X in one English sentence.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Solve the last equation first, substitute the result into the second, and then substitute the second into the first. Each time you apply Arden’s rule, check that the language in front of the unknown does not contain \varepsilon.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Arden’s rule (Lemma 2.3, §2.2): if \varepsilon\notin A, then L = AL\cup B holds if and only if L = A^*B. Eliminate one unknown at a time, from the bottom up.
(a) Z. The equation Z = \mathtt{1}Z\cup\{\varepsilon\} has A = \{\mathtt{1}\}, and \varepsilon\notin A, so its only solution is Z = \mathtt{1}^*\{\varepsilon\} = \mathtt{1}^*.
Y in terms of X. Substituting, Y = \mathtt{0}X\cup\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\cup\{\varepsilon\} = \mathtt{0}X\cup\mathtt{1}^*, because \mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\cup\{\varepsilon\} = \mathtt{1}^+\cup\{\varepsilon\} = \mathtt{1}^* (Lemma 2.2(a)).
X. Substituting into the first equation and distributing (Lemma 2.1(f)),
X = \mathtt{0}X\cup\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}X\cup\mathtt{1}^*)\cup\{\varepsilon\} = (\mathtt{0}\cup\mathtt{10})X\cup(\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\cup\{\varepsilon\}) = (\mathtt{0}\cup\mathtt{10})X\cup\mathtt{1}^*.
Here A = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{10}\} does not contain \varepsilon, so Arden’s rule gives X = (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}^*, and then Y = \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}^* + \mathtt{1}^*.
Only one solution. If (X, Y, Z) is any solution, then Z must be \mathtt{1}^*, so Y must be \mathtt{0}X\cup\mathtt{1}^*, so X satisfies X = (\mathtt{0}\cup\mathtt{10})X\cup\mathtt{1}^* and must be (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}^*. Each “must” is the only if half of Arden’s rule, which needs \varepsilon\notin A.
(b) X is the set of strings that do not contain \mathtt{110}. In a string of (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^* every 1 is immediately followed by a 0, so it contains no \mathtt{11}; after it comes a final block of 1s, which has no 0 after it, so no \mathtt{110} can appear. Conversely, cut a string without \mathtt{110} just before its final block of 1s, so that the first part is empty or ends in \mathtt{0}. If some 1 in the first part were followed by another 1, the run of 1s containing them would be followed by a 0 (the first part ends in 0), and the last two 1s of that run together with this 0 would form \mathtt{110}. So every 1 of the first part is immediately followed by a 0, and the first part is in (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*.
Check: \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1011}, \mathtt{0101} and \mathtt{111} are in X; \mathtt{110} and \mathtt{01101} are not. The other two unknowns have meanings too: Y is the set of strings y such that \mathtt{1}y contains no \mathtt{110}, and Z the set of strings z such that \mathtt{11}z contains none — which is why Z = \mathtt{1}^*.
Watch out: Arden’s rule gives the only solution only when \varepsilon\notin A; with \varepsilon\in A it gives just the smallest one.
Answer. Z = \mathtt{1}^*, Y = \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}^*+\mathtt{1}^*, and X = (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}^*: the strings with no substring \mathtt{110}. The solution is unique because neither coefficient, \mathtt{1} or \mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10}, contains \varepsilon.


Hard
2.7 Two careful regular expressions


                  
                  Hard · regular expressions 
                  
                

Give a regular expression for each language, with an English explanation of every part, and test it on all strings of length at most 3. No proof is required.
(a) Strings that contain the substring \mathtt{11} exactly once. (Occurrences may overlap: \mathtt{111} contains \mathtt{11} twice.)
(b) Strings in which every \mathtt{0} has a \mathtt{1} as a neighbor: w_{i-1} = \mathtt{1} or w_{i+1} = \mathtt{1} for every position i with w_i = \mathtt{0}.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) Write the string as x\,\mathtt{11}\,y around its one occurrence. What must x and y avoid, and how may x end and y begin? (b) View the string as blocks of 1s separated by blocks of 0s: which blocks of 0s are allowed between two blocks of 1s, and which at the two ends?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Idea. Around its only occurrence the string is x\,\mathtt{11}\,y, where x and y contain no \mathtt{11}, x does not end in \mathtt{1}, and y does not begin with \mathtt{1} — otherwise a second, overlapping occurrence appears. The strings with no \mathtt{11} that are empty or end in \mathtt{0} are exactly the sequences of blocks \mathtt{0} and \mathtt{10}; symmetrically, those that are empty or begin with \mathtt{0} are the sequences of blocks \mathtt{0} and \mathtt{01}.
(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\,\mathtt{11}\,(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^*

(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^* is the part before the occurrence: every 1 in it is immediately followed by a 0, so it contains no \mathtt{11} and is empty or ends in \mathtt{0};
\mathtt{11} is the one occurrence;
(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^* is the part after it: every 1 in it is immediately preceded by a 0, so it contains no \mathtt{11} and is empty or begins with \mathtt{0}.

No other occurrence can straddle a boundary, because the symbol next to \mathtt{11} on either side is a 0, if there is one. Check: of the 15 strings of length at most 3, the expression matches exactly \mathtt{11}, \mathtt{011} and \mathtt{110}, which are exactly the ones with one occurrence (\mathtt{111} has two).
(b) Idea. A non-empty string with no 1 has a 0 without a 1 next to it, so \varepsilon is the only string of the language without a 1. Otherwise cut the string into blocks of 1s separated by blocks of 0s. A block of 0s between two blocks of 1s may have length 1 or 2, because then each of its 0s is next to one of the two surrounding 1s, while a block of three or more 0s has a middle 0 with no 1 next to it. A block of 0s at the beginning or the end touches a 1 on one side only, so it has length at most 1.
\varepsilon + (\varepsilon+\mathtt{0})\,\mathtt{1}\,(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01}+\mathtt{001})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0})

\varepsilon: the string with no 1 (there is no 0 to check);
(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}): at most one leading 0, which touches the first 1;
\mathtt{1}: the first 1;
(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01}+\mathtt{001})^*: each later 1, preceded by the zero, one or two 0s that separate it from the previous 1;
(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}): at most one trailing 0, which touches the last 1.

Check: of the strings of length at most 3, the expression matches \varepsilon, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{01}, \mathtt{10}, \mathtt{11}, \mathtt{010}, \mathtt{011}, \mathtt{101}, \mathtt{110} and \mathtt{111}, and rejects \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{00}, \mathtt{000}, \mathtt{001} and \mathtt{100} — each of which has a 0 with no 1 next to it. Longer: \mathtt{1001} matches, and \mathtt{10001} does not (its middle 0 is alone).
Grading notes. The exam rubric gives 2 points for syntax and 8 for correctness (how exams are graded). Typical losses here: in (a), (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{11}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^* means “at least once” and matches \mathtt{111}, \mathtt{1111}, …; and (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{11}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^* matches \mathtt{1110} (two occurrences) while missing \mathtt{1101}, \mathtt{110101} and many more. Both are wrong on infinitely many strings, so no correctness points. In (b), forgetting the term \varepsilon is a single wrong string (the small deduction), but allowing \mathtt{00} at either end matches \mathtt{001}, \mathtt{0011}, … and loses everything.
Answer. (a) (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{11}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^*. (b) \varepsilon+(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0})\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01}+\mathtt{001})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}).


2.8 An expression for all prefixes


                  
                  Hard · regex induction · regular expressions 
                  
                

For a language L, let \textsf{Pre}(L) := \{x \mid xy\in L \text{ for some string } y\} be the set of all prefixes of strings in L. For a regular expression R that does not use the symbol \varnothing, define the expression \textsf{pre}(R) by recursion on R:

\textsf{pre}(w) := \varepsilon + w_1 + w_1w_2 + \cdots + w_1w_2\cdots w_n if R is a string w = w_1w_2\cdots w_n (so \textsf{pre}(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon);
\textsf{pre}(S+T) := \textsf{pre}(S) + \textsf{pre}(T);
\textsf{pre}(ST) := \textsf{pre}(S) + S\,\textsf{pre}(T);
\textsf{pre}(S^*) := S^*\,\textsf{pre}(S).

(a) Compute \textsf{pre}\big((\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{1}\big) and describe its language in English.
(b) Prove that L(\textsf{pre}(R)) = \textsf{Pre}(L(R)) for every regular expression R that does not use \varnothing.
(c) Where does your proof use the assumption that R does not use \varnothing? Extend the definition by \textsf{pre}(\varnothing) := \varnothing, and give an expression R for which L(\textsf{pre}(R))\ne\textsf{Pre}(L(R)).
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Use the five-case template of §2.6 and prove a set equality in each case. A prefix of xy is either a prefix of x, or x followed by a prefix of y; a prefix of x_1x_2\cdots x_k is x_1\cdots x_{i-1} followed by a prefix of x_i. To go back from a prefix of x to a prefix of some xy, you need a string y\in L(T) — Lemma 2.4 provides one.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Follow the cases of the definition and describe, in each case, the prefixes of the strings that case builds. Lemma 2.4 (an expression without \varnothing has a non-empty language) is needed twice: to extend a prefix of x\in L(S) to a string xy\in L(S)L(T), and to get \varepsilon\in\textsf{Pre}(L(S)) in the star case.
(a) With S = (\mathtt{01})^* and T = \mathtt{1}:
\textsf{pre}\big((\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{1}\big) = \textsf{pre}\big((\mathtt{01})^*\big) + (\mathtt{01})^*\,\textsf{pre}(\mathtt{1}) = (\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01}) + (\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{1}),
which is equivalent to (\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}), because (\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{01} adds nothing to (\mathtt{01})^*. In English: some copies of \mathtt{01}, followed by at most one more symbol. Indeed, L\big((\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{1}\big) = \{\mathtt{1}, \mathtt{011}, \mathtt{01011}, \dots\}, and the prefixes of these strings are exactly the strings just described.
(b) Let R be an arbitrary regular expression that does not use \varnothing. Assume that L(\textsf{pre}(R')) = \textsf{Pre}(L(R')) for every proper subexpression R' of R; each of them is \varnothing-free too. There are five cases.

R = \varnothing. Impossible, because R does not use \varnothing.
R is a string w = w_1\cdots w_n. \textsf{Pre}(\{w\}) is the set of prefixes of w, which are exactly w[1..j] for 0\le j\le n (§1.5): the strings of L(\textsf{pre}(w)).
R = S+T. A string is a prefix of a string in L(S)\cup L(T) if and only if it is a prefix of a string in L(S) or of a string in L(T). So \textsf{Pre}(L(R)) = \textsf{Pre}(L(S))\cup\textsf{Pre}(L(T)) = L(\textsf{pre}(S))\cup L(\textsf{pre}(T)) = L(\textsf{pre}(R)), by the induction hypothesis for S and T.
R = ST. We show \textsf{Pre}(L(S)L(T)) = \textsf{Pre}(L(S))\cup L(S)\,\textsf{Pre}(L(T)); the hypothesis for S and T turns the right side into L(\textsf{pre}(S) + S\,\textsf{pre}(T)).

\subseteq: let zu = xy with x\in L(S) and y\in L(T). If \lvert z\rvert\le\lvert x\rvert, then z is the prefix of x of length \lvert z\rvert, so z\in\textsf{Pre}(L(S)). Otherwise z = xp, where p consists of the next \lvert z\rvert-\lvert x\rvert symbols; then xpu = xy gives pu = y by cancellation, so p\in\textsf{Pre}(L(T)) and z\in L(S)\,\textsf{Pre}(L(T)).
\supseteq: if zu = x\in L(S), then L(T) contains some string y, by Lemma 2.4 since T does not use \varnothing; so z(uy) = xy\in L(R) and z\in\textsf{Pre}(L(R)). If z = xp with x\in L(S) and pu = y\in L(T), then zu = xy\in L(R).


R = S^*. We show \textsf{Pre}(L(S)^*) = L(S)^*\,\textsf{Pre}(L(S)); the hypothesis for S turns the right side into L(S^*\,\textsf{pre}(S)).

\subseteq: let zu = x_1x_2\cdots x_k with every x_j\in L(S). If z = \varepsilon: L(S) is not empty (Lemma 2.4), and \varepsilon is a prefix of each of its strings, so z = \varepsilon\bullet\varepsilon\in L(S)^*\,\textsf{Pre}(L(S)). Otherwise let i be the smallest index with \lvert z\rvert\le\lvert x_1\cdots x_i\rvert; then z = x_1\cdots x_{i-1}\,p, where p is a prefix of x_i, so z\in L(S)^*\,\textsf{Pre}(L(S)).
\supseteq: if z = x_1\cdots x_{i-1}\,p with all x_j\in L(S) and pu = x_i\in L(S), then zu = x_1\cdots x_i\in L(S)^*.



In all five cases, L(\textsf{pre}(R)) = \textsf{Pre}(L(R)). \blacksquare
(c) The assumption is used through Lemma 2.4 in two places: in the case ST (\supseteq), to find a string y\in L(T), and in the case S^* (\subseteq, z = \varepsilon), to get \varepsilon\in\textsf{Pre}(L(S)). Both fail when the language may be empty. For R = \mathtt{0}\varnothing: L(R) = \varnothing, so \textsf{Pre}(L(R)) = \varnothing, but \textsf{pre}(\mathtt{0}\varnothing) = (\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}) + \mathtt{0}\varnothing denotes \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0}\}. For R = \varnothing^*: \textsf{Pre}(\{\varepsilon\}) = \{\varepsilon\}, but \textsf{pre}(\varnothing^*) = \varnothing^*\varnothing denotes \varnothing.
Check: in (a), the strings of length at most 3 of (\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}) are \varepsilon, \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{01}, \mathtt{010} and \mathtt{011} — exactly the prefixes of length at most 3 of the strings \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{011} and \mathtt{01011} of L\big((\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{1}\big) (longer strings of the language add no new short prefixes).
Watch out: in the star case the hypothesis covers S, not S^*; the argument about x_1x_2\cdots x_k is what handles the star. And since every non-empty regular language has a \varnothing-free expression (Lemma 2.5), the result shows that \textsf{Pre}(L) is regular for every regular language L (\textsf{Pre}(\varnothing) = \varnothing is regular too).
Answer. (a) (\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01}) + (\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{1})\equiv(\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}): some copies of \mathtt{01}, then at most one more symbol. (b) Structural induction with the set identities \textsf{Pre}(A\cup B) = \textsf{Pre}(A)\cup\textsf{Pre}(B), \textsf{Pre}(AB) = \textsf{Pre}(A)\cup A\,\textsf{Pre}(B) for B\ne\varnothing, and \textsf{Pre}(A^*) = A^*\,\textsf{Pre}(A) for A\ne\varnothing. (c) Through Lemma 2.4, in the cases ST and S^*; R = \mathtt{0}\varnothing and R = \varnothing^* break the extended definition.


Sources for this page
The problems are original or classic exercise types restated in our own words: identities from Lemmas 2.1–2.2 on small languages (2.1); reading and writing regular expressions in the style of §2.3 (2.2–2.4, 2.7); equivalence and non-equivalence with witnesses (2.5, where (b) is the classic sliding identity); a three-equation system solved with Arden’s rule (2.6); and a structural recursion on expressions in the spirit of the book’s reversal example and Lemmas 2.4–2.5 (2.8). None is taken from a course exam or homework. Every regular expression is compared exactly, by automaton equivalence, with an automaton built independently from the English description; every identity and counterexample is checked on all short strings; and the construction of 2.8 is verified on every \varnothing-free expression of size at most 6, all in tools/practice/checks/ch02.py.

practice/03-finite-state-machines.title: Practice — Chapter 3: Finite-state machines
practice/03-finite-state-machines.content:
Practice for Chapter 3 · concepts: dfa · product-construction · fooling-sets · dfa-minimization · all practice: hub · by difficulty: easy · medium · hard · by topic
Work each problem on paper first. Open the hint only when stuck, and the solution only after you have an answer you would hand in. Every automaton, regular expression and fooling set in the solutions has been checked by a script. All strings are over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}; in transition tables, → marks the start state and * the accepting states.
Easy
3.1 Closure and fooling-set verdicts


                  
                  Easy · true or false · closure properties · fooling sets 
                  
                

Let L, L', L_1, L_2 be languages over \Sigma = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}. Answer each statement Yes (always true) or No, with a one-sentence reason; for a No, give a counterexample.
(a) If L\oplus L' is regular, then L and L' are both regular.
(b) If L_1 is regular and L_2 is not, then L_1\oplus L_2 is not regular.
(c) If neither L nor L' is regular, then L\cap L' is not regular.
(d) Every DFA that accepts \{w\in\Sigma^* \mid \lvert w\rvert = 5\} has at least 7 states.
(e) If L is not regular, then L^* is not regular.
(f) If a DFA with n states accepts at least one string, then it accepts some string of length less than n.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Closure properties say nothing about non-regular inputs, so for a No look for a counterexample built from \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}, its complement, or \varnothing. For (b), write L_2 in terms of L_1 and L_1\oplus L_2.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) No. Take L = L' = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}, which is not regular (Lemma 3.6); then L\oplus L' = \varnothing, which is regular.
(b) Yes. L_2 = L_1\oplus(L_1\oplus L_2), so if L_1\oplus L_2 were regular, L_2 would be regular by closure under \oplus (Corollary 3.4).
(c) No. L = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\} and L' = \overline{L} are both non-regular (if \overline{L} were regular, so would be its complement L), but L\cap L' = \varnothing.
(d) Yes. The seven strings \varepsilon,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{0}^2,\dots,\mathtt{0}^6 form a fooling set: for 0\le i<j\le6 the suffix z = \mathtt{0}^{5-i} makes \mathtt{0}^iz exactly 5 symbols long and \mathtt{0}^jz longer. (Seven states also suffice: count the symbols up to 5, plus a dump state for longer strings.)
(e) No. L = \{\mathtt{0}^{2^n} \mid n\ge0\} is not regular (Lemma 3.8), but \mathtt{0} = \mathtt{0}^{2^0}\in L and L\subseteq\mathtt{0}^*, so L^* = \mathtt{0}^*, which is regular.
(f) Yes. The walk of a shortest accepted string never repeats a state (otherwise cutting out the loop between the two visits would leave a shorter accepted string), so it visits at most n states and reads at most n-1 symbols.
Watch out: in (a), (c) and (e) the closure theorems do not apply — they promise regular outputs only from regular inputs. The useful move is the one in (b): undo the operation with a language you know is regular.
Answer. (a) No (b) Yes (c) No (d) Yes (e) No (f) Yes.


3.2 A bounded counter


                  
                  Easy · DFA design 
                  
                

Let L be the set of strings w such that every prefix p of w (including \varepsilon and w itself) satisfies \lvert\#(\mathtt{0},p)-\#(\mathtt{1},p)\rvert\le2. For example, 0101 and 001101 are in L, but 0001 is not: its prefix 000 has three more 0s than 1s.
(a) Give a DFA for L with mnemonic state names, as a transition table with a column for the meaning of each state. No proof is required.
(b) In one sentence: why does the same idea not give a DFA for \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w)\}?
Source: textbook exercise style.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Write the algorithm first: one variable d = \#(\mathtt{0},p)-\#(\mathtt{1},p) for the prefix p read so far. Which values of d matter before the answer is certainly No?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Scan once, keeping d, the number of 0s minus the number of 1s read so far: a 0 adds 1 and a 1 subtracts 1. The first time \lvert d\rvert reaches 3, some prefix has failed and nothing later can repair that, so from then on the machine only needs to remember “failed”. That is five values of d plus a dump state.
(a)






















































statemeaning (input read so far)\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}*d_{-2}no prefix has failed; two more 1s than 0sd_{-1}\mathit{dead}*d_{-1}no prefix has failed; one more 1 than 0sd_{0}d_{-2}→ *d_{0}no prefix has failed; as many 0s as 1sd_{1}d_{-1}*d_{1}no prefix has failed; one more 0 than 1sd_{2}d_{0}*d_{2}no prefix has failed; two more 0s than 1s\mathit{dead}d_{1}\mathit{dead}some prefix has failed (dump state)\mathit{dead}\mathit{dead}
Check. 001101 visits d_0, d_1, d_2, d_1, d_0, d_1, d_0 and is accepted; 0001 visits d_0, d_1, d_2, \mathit{dead}, \mathit{dead} and is rejected. The empty string stays in d_0 and is accepted, as it should be: its only prefix is \varepsilon, with difference 0.
(b) There the difference is unbounded, so the counter would need a state for every integer; in fact \mathtt{0}^* is an infinite fooling set for that language (the suffix \mathtt{1}^i separates \mathtt{0}^i from \mathtt{0}^j).
Answer. Six states: d_{-2},\dots,d_{2} (no prefix has failed, and the subscript is the current value of d; all accepting; start d_0) and a dump state \mathit{dead}. Reading 0 moves d_k to d_{k+1}, reading 1 moves it to d_{k-1}, and stepping outside [-2,2] goes to \mathit{dead}.


3.3 Prefixes of a pattern


                  
                  Easy · fooling sets · Myhill–Nerode 
                  
                

Let L = \{w \mid w \text{ contains the substring } \mathtt{0110}\}.
(a) Prove that every DFA that accepts L has at least 5 states.
(b) A student adds 01101 to your five strings, hoping to prove that 6 states are needed. Why must this fail?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

A DFA hunting for 0110 must remember how much of the pattern it has just seen. Try the prefixes of 0110, and a suffix that completes the longer of the two strings.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Let F = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{01},\mathtt{011},\mathtt{0110}\}, the five prefixes of the pattern P = \mathtt{0110}. Let x and y be distinct strings in F, named so that \lvert x\rvert = i < j = \lvert y\rvert (a distinguishing suffix works for the pair in either order, so this loses nothing). Let z be the last 4-j symbols of P. Then yz = P\in L. And xz\notin L, because \lvert xz\rvert = i+4-j < 4 is too short to contain 0110. So F is a fooling set of size 5, and every DFA for L has at least 5 states.
For instance, z = \mathtt{10} distinguishes 0 and 01: 010 \notin L but 0110 \in L.
(b) 0110 and 01101 both contain the pattern, so \mathtt{0110}z and \mathtt{01101}z are both in L for every z: no suffix distinguishes them. In fact no fooling set for L has 6 strings, because the 5-state DFA below accepts L, and by the Myhill–Nerode theorem the largest fooling set is exactly as large as the smallest DFA. State q_u means “no 0110 yet, and u is the longest suffix of the input that is a prefix of 0110”:









































state\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}→q_\varepsilonq_{\mathtt{0}}q_\varepsilonq_{\mathtt{0}}q_{\mathtt{0}}q_{\mathtt{01}}q_{\mathtt{01}}q_{\mathtt{0}}q_{\mathtt{011}}q_{\mathtt{011}}\mathit{found}q_\varepsilon*\mathit{found}\mathit{found}\mathit{found}
Answer. (a) F = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{0},\mathtt{01},\mathtt{011},\mathtt{0110}\}: for \lvert x\rvert<\lvert y\rvert, the suffix that completes y to 0110 leaves xz shorter than 4. (b) 0110 and 01101 stay in L under every extension, so nothing distinguishes them; a 5-state DFA exists, so 5 is the exact minimum.


3.4 The forgotten second branch


                  
                  Easy · find the error · fooling sets · non-regularity 
                  
                

Let L = \{\mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b \mid a,b\ge0 \text{ and } (b = a \text{ or } b = 2a)\}. A student writes:
“Let F = \mathtt{0}^*. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F; then x = \mathtt{0}^i and y = \mathtt{0}^j for some integers i\ne j. Let z = \mathtt{1}^i. Then xz = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\in L, because b = a. And yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i\notin L, because j\ne i. So F is a fooling set for L, and since F is infinite, L is not regular.”
(a) Which sentence is wrong? Give a concrete pair x, y\in F that this z does not distinguish.
(b) Repair the proof. (Its conclusion is true.)
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Read the definition of L again: in how many ways can \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i belong to L?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) The slip is ”yz\notin L, because j\ne i”. That rules out only the branch b = a. The string yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i is also in L when i = 2j. For example, x = \mathtt{00} and y = \mathtt{0} (i = 2, j = 1) get z = \mathtt{11}, and both xz = \mathtt{0011} and yz = \mathtt{011} are in L. (The pair is still distinguishable — by z = \mathtt{1}, for instance: 001 \notin L but 01 \in L — but not by the suffix the proof chose.)
(b) Fix: shrink F so that the bad case cannot happen. Let F = \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{00})^*, the strings of 0s of odd length. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F; then x = \mathtt{0}^i and y = \mathtt{0}^j for some odd integers i\ne j. Let z = \mathtt{1}^i. Then xz = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\in L, because b = a. And yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i\notin L: the branch b = a would need i = j, and the branch b = 2a would need i = 2j, which is even, while i is odd. So F is a fooling set for L, and since F is infinite, L is not regular.
Another fix: keep F = \mathtt{0}^* and split cases. If i\ne 2j, the student’s z = \mathtt{1}^i works. If i = 2j, then j\ge1 (otherwise i = j = 0), and z = \mathtt{1}^j works: yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^j\in L, while xz = \mathtt{0}^{2j}\mathtt{1}^j\notin L, because j = 2j and j = 4j are both false for j\ge1.
Watch out: "yz\notin L" must rule out every way of being in L. When the definition contains an “or”, check each branch — a proof that skips one looks complete and still loses the points for that half.
Answer. (a) ”yz\notin L, because j\ne i” ignores the branch b = 2a: for x = \mathtt{00}, y = \mathtt{0}, z = \mathtt{11}, both 0011 and 011 are in L. (b) Use F = \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{00})^* with z = \mathtt{1}^i, where i = 2j is impossible because i is odd; or keep \mathtt{0}^* and use z = \mathtt{1}^j when i = 2j.


Medium
3.5 Read a DFA, then prove it


                  
                  Medium · DFA proof · string induction 
                  
                

For a string w, let \#(\mathtt{01},w) be the number of occurrences of 01 in w as a substring. The DFA M has start state A, accepting states \{A,B\} and this transition function:






























\delta\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}ABABBCCDCDDA
Prove that L(M) = \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{01},w)\text{ is even}\}:
(a) give each state q a meaning — a property P_q of the input read so far — such that \delta^*(A,w) = q exactly when w has P_q;
(b) prove your claim by induction on w, and conclude.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Two things matter: the parity of \#(\mathtt{01},\cdot) so far, and whether the last symbol read is a 0 (half of a possible new 01). Peel off the last symbol, w = xa, so that you need the claim only from the start state.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. The four states record two bits: the parity of \#(\mathtt{01},w), and whether w ends in 0. A new 01 appears exactly when a 1 is read right after a 0. The proof follows the template of §3.3.
(a) Meanings.






























stateP_q: the input w read so far …acceptingAhas an even \#(\mathtt{01},w) and does not end in 0 (it is empty or ends in 1)yesBhas an even \#(\mathtt{01},w) and ends in 0yesChas an odd \#(\mathtt{01},w) and does not end in 0noDhas an odd \#(\mathtt{01},w) and ends in 0no
Every string has exactly one of the four properties, so it is enough to prove: for every string w, \delta^*(A,w) is the state whose property w has.
(b) A fact first. For every string x and symbol a: \#(\mathtt{01},xa) = \#(\mathtt{01},x)+1 if x ends in 0 and a = \mathtt{1}, and \#(\mathtt{01},xa) = \#(\mathtt{01},x) otherwise. Indeed, an occurrence of 01 in xa either lies inside x or uses the last two symbols, and those two symbols are 01 exactly when x ends in 0 and a = \mathtt{1}.
Proof. Let w be an arbitrary string, and assume that for every string x shorter than w, \delta^*(A,x) is the state whose property x has. There are two cases.

w = \varepsilon. \delta^*(A,\varepsilon) = A by the definition of \delta^*, and \varepsilon has P_A: \#(\mathtt{01},\varepsilon) = 0 is even, and \varepsilon does not end in 0.
w = xa for some string x and symbol a. Then \delta^*(A,w) = \delta(\delta^*(A,x),a), and by the induction hypothesis \delta^*(A,x) = q, where x has P_q. The fact gives the property of xa in each of the eight combinations of q and a, and in each one \delta(q,a) is the matching state:




























































x hasaso xa has\delta(q,a)P_A0even, ends in 0: P_BB ✓P_A1even (no new 01: x does not end in 0), ends in 1: P_AA ✓P_B0even, ends in 0: P_BB ✓P_B1odd (one new 01), ends in 1: P_CC ✓P_C0odd, ends in 0: P_DD ✓P_C1odd (no new 01), ends in 1: P_CC ✓P_D0odd, ends in 0: P_DD ✓P_D1even (one new 01), ends in 1: P_AA ✓
In both cases \delta^*(A,w) is the state whose property w has. \blacksquare
Conclusion. w\in L(M)\iff\delta^*(A,w)\in\{A,B\}\iff w has P_A or P_B\iff\#(\mathtt{01},w) is even.
Check. 00110 contains one 01: M visits A,B,B,C,C,D and rejects. 0101 contains two: M visits A,B,C,D,A and accepts.
Watch out: peeling the first symbol (w = ax) would need the claim from every state, because \delta^*(A,ax) = \delta^*(\delta(A,a),x) runs x from \delta(A,a). And \#(\mathtt{01},\cdot) is not additive: \#(\mathtt{01},xy) is one more than \#(\mathtt{01},x)+\#(\mathtt{01},y) when the seam is a 01 — that is exactly what the fact keeps track of.
Answer. A: even and not ending in 0; B: even and ending in 0; C: odd and not ending in 0; D: odd and ending in 0 (parity of \#(\mathtt{01},w)). Induction on w = xa, using that reading a adds a 01 exactly when x ends in 0 and a = \mathtt{1}, proves these meanings; since A and B are the accepting states, L(M) = \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{01},w)\text{ is even}\}.


3.6 A product, written formally


                  
                  Medium · product construction · closure properties · DFA design 
                  
                

Let L_1 be the set of strings that start with 1, let L_2 = \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{1},w)\text{ is even}\}, and let L = L_1\cap L_2.
(a) Give DFAs M_1 for L_1 and M_2 for L_2 with mnemonic state names.
(b) Describe the product DFA M = (\Sigma,Q,s,A,\delta) for L formally. Then give the transition table of its reachable states, and run it on 1001 and on 0110.
(c) Changing only the accepting set, give DFAs for L_1\cup L_2 and for L_1\setminus L_2.
(d) Two reachable states of M can be merged without changing L(M). Which two, and why?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

A product state is a pair (state of M_1, state of M_2), and M runs both machines in lockstep. Only the accepting set depends on whether you want \cap, \cup or \setminus. For (d), look for states from which no accepting state can be reached.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. M_1 remembers what the first symbol was, M_2 the parity of the number of 1s. Run both at once (§3.6) and accept when both accept.
(a) M_1 = (\Sigma,\{\mathit{new},\mathit{good},\mathit{bad}\},\mathit{new},\{\mathit{good}\},\delta_1) and M_2 = (\Sigma,\{\mathit{even},\mathit{odd}\},\mathit{even},\{\mathit{even}\},\delta_2):

































M_1meaning\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}→\mathit{new}nothing read yet\mathit{bad}\mathit{good}*\mathit{good}the first symbol was 1\mathit{good}\mathit{good}\mathit{bad}the first symbol was 0\mathit{bad}\mathit{bad}


























M_2meaning\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}→ *\mathit{even}an even number of 1s so far\mathit{even}\mathit{odd}\mathit{odd}an odd number of 1s so far\mathit{odd}\mathit{even}
(b) The product.
Q := \{\mathit{new},\mathit{good},\mathit{bad}\}\times\{\mathit{even},\mathit{odd}\},\qquad s := (\mathit{new},\mathit{even}),\qquad A := \{(\mathit{good},\mathit{even})\},
\delta\big((p,q),a\big) := \big(\delta_1(p,a),\,\delta_2(q,a)\big)\quad\text{for every } (p,q)\in Q \text{ and } a\in\Sigma.
Q has six states, but (\mathit{new},\mathit{odd}) is unreachable: M_1 is in \mathit{new} only before anything is read, when the number of 1s is 0. The other five:















































statemeaning\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}→(\mathit{new},\mathit{even})nothing read yet(\mathit{bad},\mathit{even})(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd})*(\mathit{good},\mathit{even})starts with 1, even number of 1s(\mathit{good},\mathit{even})(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd})(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd})starts with 1, odd number of 1s(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd})(\mathit{good},\mathit{even})(\mathit{bad},\mathit{even})starts with 0, even number of 1s(\mathit{bad},\mathit{even})(\mathit{bad},\mathit{odd})(\mathit{bad},\mathit{odd})starts with 0, odd number of 1s(\mathit{bad},\mathit{odd})(\mathit{bad},\mathit{even})
Check. On 1001, M visits (\mathit{new},\mathit{even}), (\mathit{good},\mathit{odd}) three times, then (\mathit{good},\mathit{even}) and accepts: the string starts with 1 and has two 1s. On 0110 it visits (\mathit{new},\mathit{even}), (\mathit{bad},\mathit{even}), (\mathit{bad},\mathit{odd}), (\mathit{bad},\mathit{even}), (\mathit{bad},\mathit{even}) and rejects: two 1s, but it starts with 0. The empty string stays in (\mathit{new},\mathit{even}) and is rejected, correctly, since it does not start with 1.
(c) Keep Q, s and \delta, and change A:

L_1\cup L_2: A := \{(p,q) \mid p = \mathit{good} \text{ or } q = \mathit{even}\} = \{(\mathit{new},\mathit{even}),(\mathit{good},\mathit{even}),(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd}),(\mathit{bad},\mathit{even})\};
L_1\setminus L_2: A := \{(p,q) \mid p = \mathit{good} \text{ and } q = \mathit{odd}\} = \{(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd})\}.

(d) (\mathit{bad},\mathit{even}) and (\mathit{bad},\mathit{odd}). Neither is accepting, and every transition out of them stays between the two, so from either one no string leads to an accepting state: both accept the same set of continuations, namely none. Merging them into a single dump state leaves a 4-state DFA for L, which Moore’s algorithm confirms is minimal. (For L_1\cup L_2 the two must stay apart, because there (\mathit{bad},\mathit{even}) accepts.)
Watch out: the product construction gives a correct DFA, not a minimal one. Define Q as the whole product Q_1\times Q_2 with \delta on every pair; tabulating only the reachable states is fine, but the formal definition must not leave transitions undefined.
Grading notes. A product construction earns its description points only if each factor is described completely (states, start, accepting states, transitions) and the product’s accepting set is given explicitly; “run both machines in parallel” alone earns little (how exams are graded).
Answer. Q = \{\mathit{new},\mathit{good},\mathit{bad}\}\times\{\mathit{even},\mathit{odd}\}, s = (\mathit{new},\mathit{even}), \delta((p,q),a) = (\delta_1(p,a),\delta_2(q,a)), A = \{(\mathit{good},\mathit{even})\}; five states are reachable. For L_1\cup L_2: A = \{(\mathit{new},\mathit{even}),(\mathit{good},\mathit{even}),(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd}),(\mathit{bad},\mathit{even})\}; for L_1\setminus L_2: A = \{(\mathit{good},\mathit{odd})\}. The two \mathit{bad} states merge into one dump state.


3.7 Squares need a marker


                  
                  Medium · fooling sets · non-regularity 
                  
                

Prove that L = \{ww \mid w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*\}, the set of strings that consist of two copies of the same string, is not regular. Use a fooling set, and write the proof in full.
Source: classic.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Let every string of F end with a marker 1, and try the suffix z = x. To show yz\notin L, count the 1s: how many does each half of a string in L get?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. A DFA reading the first half must remember all of it. The suffix z = x copies x, so xz = xx\in L for free; a single 1 at the end of each string of F marks where the copy starts, which makes yz easy to rule out.
Proof. Let F = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} = \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} \mid i\ge0\}. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F; then x = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} and y = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1} for some integers i\ne j. Let z = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}.
Then xz = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} = ww for w = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}, so xz\in L.
And yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}\notin L. Suppose instead that yz = uu for some string u. The two copies of u contain the same number of 1s, and yz contains exactly two, so u contains exactly one 1. The string yz ends in 1, so u ends in 1; therefore u = \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1} for some k, and yz = \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}. Comparing the numbers of 0s before the first 1 and between the two 1s gives j = k and i = k, so i = j, a contradiction.
So z distinguishes x and y, and F is a fooling set for L. Because F is infinite, L is not regular. \blacksquare
Check. For i = 1, j = 2: xz = \mathtt{0101}\in L, and yz = \mathtt{00101} has odd length, so it is not in L. For i = 1, j = 3: yz = \mathtt{000101} has halves 000 and 101.
Watch out: with F = \mathtt{0}^* the suffix z = x fails: then yz = \mathtt{0}^{i+j}, which is in L whenever i+j is even. (\mathtt{0}^* can still be made to work, with z = \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} and the same counting argument.)
Grading notes. 4 points for an explicit infinite set that really is a fooling set, then 2 each for an explicit z, for xz\in L and for yz\notin L — and yz\notin L needs an argument for arbitrary i\ne j, not an example.
Answer. F = \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1} with z = x: for x = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} and y = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}, xz = (\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1})(\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1})\in L, while yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} would have to be \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}, forcing i = j.


Hard
3.8 No 00 after an 11


                  
                  Hard · DFA design · regular expressions 
                  
                

Let L be the set of strings w that have no substring of the form \mathtt{11}x\mathtt{00} with x\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*. In words: once 11 has appeared, 00 never appears afterwards. For example, 0010110 and 110101 are in L, but 0110100 is not.
(a) Give a DFA for L with mnemonic state names. No proof is required.
(b) Give a regular expression for L, with a one-sentence explanation of each part.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) Before the first 11, remember whether the last symbol was 1; after it, whether the last symbol was 0. (b) Cut w just before the first 11. What can the part before the cut look like, and the part after it?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. The scan has two phases. Before the first 11, a 00 is harmless and the machine watches for 11; from then on it watches for 00, which is fatal. Note that 00 before the first 11 is allowed, as in 0010110.
(a)















































statemeaning: the input read so far …\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}→ *\mathit{before}has no 11, and is empty or ends in 0\mathit{before}\mathit{before1}*\mathit{before1}has no 11, and ends in 1\mathit{before}\mathit{after1}*\mathit{after1}has a 11 and no 00 after it, and ends in 1\mathit{after0}\mathit{after1}*\mathit{after0}has a 11 and no 00 after it, and ends in 0\mathit{dead}\mathit{after1}\mathit{dead}has a 00 after a 11 (dump state)\mathit{dead}\mathit{dead}
(b)
(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*\,(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01})^*\,(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0})

(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^* is the part before the first 11: every 1 in it is followed by a 0, so it contains no 11 and does not end in 1 (a 1 just before the first 11 would make an earlier 11).
(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01})^* is the part from the first 11 on: every 0 in it is followed by a 1, so it contains no 00. (If w has no 11 at all, this part is empty or a single final 1.)
(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}) allows one final 0 — the only 0 after the first 11 that need not be followed by a 1.

Check. 0010110 splits as 0010 · 11 · 0, and the DFA visits \mathit{before},\mathit{before},\mathit{before},\mathit{before1},\mathit{before},\mathit{before1},\mathit{after1},\mathit{after0} and accepts. 110101 is \varepsilon · 110101 · \varepsilon, since 110101 = 1·1·01·01. On 0110100 the DFA reaches \mathit{after1} after 011 and falls into \mathit{dead} at the final 00; the expression cannot match it either, because after the first 11 every 0 but a final one must be followed by a 1.
Watch out: (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01})^* without the final (\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}) looks right but misses 110, 1110, … — infinitely many strings, which on an exam costs all of the correctness points. And “no 00 and no 11 anywhere” describes a much smaller language: 00 is fine before the first 11.
Grading notes. For the DFA: a start arrow, marked accepting states and a sentence about the dump state if you omit it from a drawing (2 points), correctness (6), mnemonic state names (2). For the expression: syntax (2) and correctness (8) (how exams are graded).
Answer. (a) Five states: \mathit{before} (start), \mathit{before1}, \mathit{after1}, \mathit{after0}, all accepting, and the dump state \mathit{dead}, as in the table. (b) (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{01})^*(\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}).


3.9 Three look-alike counting languages


                  
                  Hard · non-regularity · closure properties · fooling sets 
                  
                

For strings u and w, let \#(u,w) be the number of occurrences of u in w as a substring; overlapping occurrences count, so \#(\mathtt{00},\mathtt{000}) = 2. For each language below, decide whether it is regular, and prove your answer: a regular expression with a short justification if it is regular, a proof if it is not.
(a) L_a = \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{00},w) = \#(\mathtt{11},w)\}
(b) L_b = \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{01},w) = \#(\mathtt{10},w)\}
(c) L_c = \{w \mid \#(\mathtt{01},w) = \#(\mathtt{11},w)\}
Source: original; part (b) is a classic exercise.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) Intersect with \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* and count 00 and 11 in \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b. (b) Cut w into maximal runs of equal symbols; where can 01 and 10 occur? (c) Extra 0s at the front of a string change neither count — so build the fooling set from 1s.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. All three definitions compare two substring counts, but only some comparisons need an unbounded counter. Before trying to prove anything, ask what a one-pass algorithm would have to remember — and test the definition on short strings.
(a) Not regular — by closure. Suppose L_a were regular. Since \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* is regular, L_a\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* would be regular too (Corollary 3.4). The string \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b contains \max(a-1,0) copies of 00 and \max(b-1,0) copies of 11; these are equal when a = b, and otherwise only when a\le1 and b\le1. So
L_a\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}\cup\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}.
The finite language \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} is regular, so (L_a\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*)\setminus\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\} would be regular as well, contradicting Lemma 3.6. So L_a is not regular.
(A fooling set works too, but not \mathtt{0}^* with z = \mathtt{1}^i: that suffix fails for the pair \varepsilon, 0, which are both in L_a. With F = \{\mathtt{0}^i \mid i\ge1\} and z = \mathtt{1}^i, the string yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i has j-1 copies of 00 but i-1 copies of 11.)
(b) Regular. L_b is the language of the expression
\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1},
the strings that are empty or start and end with the same symbol: \varepsilon, 0 and 1 are the strings of length at most 1, and the last two terms are the longer strings that start and end with 0, respectively 1. Why this is L_b: cut a non-empty w into its maximal runs of equal symbols, w = r_1r_2\cdots r_k (for example 0110 = 0·11·0). Inside a run adjacent symbols are equal, so the occurrences of 01 and 10 are exactly the k-1 seams between consecutive runs. The runs alternate between 0s and 1s, so the seams alternate between 01 and 10. Hence \#(\mathtt{01},w) = \#(\mathtt{10},w) exactly when k-1 is even, that is, when r_1 and r_k consist of the same symbol — when w starts and ends with the same symbol. And \varepsilon\in L_b, since 0 = 0.
(c) Not regular — by a fooling set. First, \mathtt{0}^* is useless here: for i,j\ge1 and every z, the strings \mathtt{0}^iz and \mathtt{0}^jz have the same numbers of 01 and 11, because the extra 0s create only copies of 00. So no suffix distinguishes \mathtt{0}^i and \mathtt{0}^j. The quantity a DFA would have to count is the number of 11s, so use 1s.
Let F = \{\mathtt{1}^i \mid i\ge1\}. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F; then x = \mathtt{1}^i and y = \mathtt{1}^j for some integers i,j\ge1 with i\ne j. Let z = (\mathtt{01})^{i-1}. For any m\ge1, in \mathtt{1}^mz the copies of 11 are the m-1 inside \mathtt{1}^m (z alternates and starts with 0), and the copies of 01 are the i-1 inside z (there are none inside \mathtt{1}^m, and the seam is 10). So:

xz = \mathtt{1}^i(\mathtt{01})^{i-1} has i-1 copies of each, so xz\in L_c;
yz = \mathtt{1}^j(\mathtt{01})^{i-1} has j-1 copies of 11 but i-1\ne j-1 copies of 01, so yz\notin L_c.

So F is a fooling set for L_c, and since it is infinite, L_c is not regular. \blacksquare
Check. (b): 0110 has one 01 and one 10; 011 has one 01 and no 10. (c) with i = 2, j = 3: xz = \mathtt{1101} has one 11 and one 01; yz = \mathtt{11101} has two 11s and one 01.
Watch out: three definitions that look alike, three different arguments — never decide “not regular” from the shape of a definition. In (a) the closure argument must run in the right direction (assume L_a regular and derive a known non-regular language; a regular intersection would prove nothing), and the intersection must be computed exactly: forgetting 0 and 1 is a real error. More on this trick in §3.8.
Answer. (a) Not regular: (L_a\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*)\setminus\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}. (b) Regular: \varepsilon+\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{1}. (c) Not regular: F = \{\mathtt{1}^i \mid i\ge1\} with z = (\mathtt{01})^{i-1}.


3.10 Shrink it, then prove it minimal


                  
                  Hard · minimization · Myhill–Nerode · fooling sets 
                  
                

The DFA M has start state A, accepting states \{E,G\} and this transition function:













































\delta\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}ADBBCBCDEDABEGEGGEHAC
(a) Which states are unreachable from A?
(b) Run Moore’s algorithm on the reachable states: list the pairs marked initially and in each pass. (In pass k, mark \{p,q\} if, for some symbol a, the pair \{\delta(p,a),\delta(q,a)\} was marked before pass k began; stop after a pass that marks nothing.)
(c) Give the minimal DFA with mnemonic state names, and describe L(M) in one sentence.
(d) Prove with a fooling set that no DFA with fewer states accepts L(M).
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Pass k marks exactly the pairs whose shortest distinguishing string has length k (the initial marks are the length-0 pairs). For (d), take one string that leads to each state of your minimal DFA.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Moore’s algorithm (§3.10) is dynamic programming on “some string of length at most k distinguishes p and q”. Whatever is never marked can be merged; a fooling set then certifies that the result cannot be shrunk further.
(a) From A we reach D and B, then C, then E, then G; no transition enters H. So H is unreachable, and we delete it.
(b) Six states give 15 pairs.

Initially: the 8 pairs with exactly one accepting state, \{X,Y\} for X\in\{A,B,C,D\} and Y\in\{E,G\}.
Pass 1: \{A,C\}, \{B,C\}, \{C,D\}. In each, reading 1 leads to the marked pair \{B,E\}, because \delta(A,\mathtt{1}) = \delta(B,\mathtt{1}) = \delta(D,\mathtt{1}) = B and \delta(C,\mathtt{1}) = E.
Pass 2: \{A,B\} (reading 0 gives \{D,C\}, marked in pass 1) and \{B,D\} (reading 0 gives \{C,A\}, marked in pass 1).
Pass 3: nothing. The remaining pairs only lead to themselves or to a single state: \{A,D\} goes to \{D,A\} on 0 and to B on 1; \{E,G\} goes to G on 0 and to E on 1. Stop.

The pass that marked each pair (0 = initially, – = never):





















































ABCDEB2C11D–21E0000G0000–
(c) Merge A with D, and E with G:








































statemeaning: the input read so far …\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}→ADhas no 101, and does not end in 1 or 10ADBBhas no 101, and ends in 1CBChas no 101, and ends in 10ADEG*EGcontains 101EGEG
So L(M) is the set of strings that contain 101 as a substring.
(d) Let S = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{1},\mathtt{10},\mathtt{101}\}, one string for each state of the minimal DFA. Every pair has a distinguishing suffix z (shown with the string of the pair that z puts into L(M)):















































pairzin L(M)not in L(M)\varepsilon, 10110101\varepsilon, 10110111, 10110111\varepsilon, 101\varepsilon101\varepsilon1, 101\varepsilon101110, 101\varepsilon10110
So S is a fooling set of size 4: every DFA for L(M) has at least 4 states, and the DFA in (c) is minimal.
Check. The pass numbers agree with shortest distinguishing strings: 1 distinguishes A and C (\delta^*(A,\mathtt{1}) = B rejects, \delta^*(C,\mathtt{1}) = E accepts), while A and B need two symbols: 01 takes A to B (reject) and B to E (accept), and no single symbol separates them.
Watch out: if marks made earlier in the same pass are allowed to count, the pass numbers can change (checking pairs in alphabetical order, \{B,D\} is then marked in pass 1, because \{A,C\} was marked earlier in that pass), but the final partition cannot. And do not skip step 1: H is equivalent to no other state, so leaving it in the table produces a 5-state “minimal” DFA.
Answer. (a) H. (b) Initially the 8 pairs between \{A,B,C,D\} and \{E,G\}; pass 1: \{A,C\},\{B,C\},\{C,D\}; pass 2: \{A,B\},\{B,D\}; pass 3: nothing. (c) Four states AD, B, C, EG; L(M) is the set of strings containing 101. (d) S = \{\varepsilon,\mathtt{1},\mathtt{10},\mathtt{101}\} is a fooling set of size 4.


Sources for this page
All ten problems were written for this page in the style of the course’s exams; none is taken from a course exam or homework. Problem 3.7 (the squares \{ww\} are not regular) and part (b) of 3.9 (equally many 01s and 10s is a regular condition) are classic textbook exercises, and 3.2 is a standard bounded-counter design, all in our own words; the rest are original. The methods are those of the book’s Chapter 3: the correctness template (§3.3), DFAs as algorithms (§3.5), the product construction and closure properties (§§3.6–3.7), fooling sets and the closure trick (§3.8), the Myhill–Nerode theorem (§3.9) and Moore’s algorithm (§3.10). Every DFA, regular expression, fooling-set suffix and Moore pass on this page is checked by tools/practice/checks/ch03.py.
