practice/05-context-free-languages.title: Practice — Chapter 5: Context-free languages
practice/05-context-free-languages.content:
Practice for Chapter 5 · concepts: context-free-grammars · parse-trees-and-ambiguity · chomsky-normal-form · recursive-automata · all practice: hub · by difficulty: easy · medium · hard · by topic
Work each problem on paper first. Open the hint only when stuck, and the solution only after you have an answer you would hand in. Every automaton, expression and grammar in the solutions has been checked by a script. Strings are over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} unless a problem says otherwise, \#(a,w) is the number of a‘s in w, and rules with the same left side are combined with \mid.
Easy
5.1 Closure and ambiguity, true or false


                  
                  Easy · true or false · context-free closure · ambiguity 
                  
                

All languages are over \Sigma = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}. Answer each statement Yes (always true) or No, with a one-sentence reason; for a No, give a counterexample. You may use the fact (§5.6) that \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\} is not context-free.
(a) If L_1\cup L_2 is context-free, then L_1 and L_2 are both context-free.
(b) If L is context-free and R is regular, then L\setminus R is context-free.
(c) If L is context-free and R is regular, then R\setminus L is context-free.
(d) If L is context-free but not regular, then \overline{L} is not regular.
(e) If a grammar G is ambiguous, then L(G) is infinite.
(f) Every regular language is generated by some unambiguous grammar.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Closure under union says nothing about the pieces of a union. For (b) and (c), write each difference as an intersection with a complement, and ask which language gets complemented. For (f), think of the grammar you get from a DFA.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) No. Take L_1 = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\} and L_2 = \overline{L_1}: their union is \Sigma^*, generated by S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid\mathtt{1}S\mid\varepsilon, but L_1 is not context-free.
(b) Yes. L\setminus R = L\cap\overline{R}, the complement of a regular language is regular, and the intersection of a context-free language with a regular language is context-free (construction below).
(c) No. Take R = \Sigma^* and L = \overline{\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\}}, which is context-free (grammar below); then R\setminus L = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\} is not.
(d) Yes. If \overline{L} were regular, then L = \overline{\overline{L}} would be regular too, because regular languages are closed under complement (Corollary 3.4).
(e) No. S\to A\mid B, A\to\mathtt{0}, B\to\mathtt{0} is ambiguous — 0 has two parse trees — but its language is \{\mathtt{0}\}.
(f) Yes. The grammar of a DFA — one nonterminal [q] per state, rules [q]\to a\,[\delta(q,a)], and [q]\to\varepsilon for every accepting q — gives each accepted string exactly one parse tree, which traces the DFA’s unique run (Problem 5.2 builds one).
The grammar for (c). A string is not of the form \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n exactly when it has a 1, a later 0 and a still later 1 (so it is not in \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*), or it is \mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b\mathtt{0}^c with a\ne b, or with b\ne c:
\begin{aligned}
&S\to N\mid UZ\mid ZV && N\to X\mathtt{1}X\mathtt{0}X\mathtt{1}X && X\to\mathtt{0}X\mid\mathtt{1}X\mid\varepsilon\\
&U\to\mathtt{0}U\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}Z\mid Y\mathtt{1} && V\to\mathtt{1}V\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}Y\mid Z\mathtt{0} && Z\to\mathtt{0}Z\mid\varepsilon \qquad Y\to\mathtt{1}Y\mid\varepsilon
\end{aligned}
Here U generates \{\mathtt{0}^a\mathtt{1}^b \mid a\ne b\}, V generates \{\mathtt{1}^b\mathtt{0}^c \mid b\ne c\}, Z and Y generate \mathtt{0}^* and \mathtt{1}^*, and X generates every string.
The construction for (b). Given a grammar for L and a DFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta), use nonterminals B_{pq} for every nonterminal B and states p, q, meaning “the strings of L(B) that drive M from p to q”. For every rule B\to X_1\cdots X_k and every choice of states p = r_0, r_1, \dots, r_k = q, add B_{pq}\to Y_1\cdots Y_k, where Y_i = (X_i)_{r_{i-1}r_i} if X_i is a nonterminal, and Y_i = X_i if X_i is a terminal with \delta(r_{i-1},X_i) = r_i (if it is a terminal without that transition, skip this choice); a rule B\to\varepsilon gives B_{pp}\to\varepsilon. A new start symbol with S'\to S_{sf} for every f\in A generates L\cap L(M). For (b), let M be a DFA for \overline{R}.
Watch out: (b) and (c) differ only in which language is complemented. Context-free languages survive intersection with a regular language but not complementation, and R\setminus L = R\cap\overline{L} needs \overline{L}.
Answer. (a) No (b) Yes (c) No (d) Yes (e) No (f) Yes.


5.2 A grammar from a DFA


                  
                  Easy · grammar design · parse trees 
                  
                

The DFA M with states 0, 1, 2, start state 0, accepting states \{0\} and \delta(q,a) = (2q+a)\bmod 3 accepts the binary representations of the multiples of 3 (reading \varepsilon as the number 0).
(a) Turn M into a context-free grammar with one nonterminal R_q for each state q, and describe the language of each R_q in a self-contained sentence.
(b) Give the derivation of 1001 (nine in binary) and compare it with the run of M.
(c) Explain in one or two sentences why your grammar is unambiguous.
Source: textbook exercise style.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

A rule R_q\to a\,R_p says “read a, then continue from state p” — the construction of Lemma 5.6 for an automaton with a single module. Where must a derivation be allowed to stop?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. R_q generates “the rest of the input” when M is in state q: the strings that lead from q to an accepting state. One rule per transition, and one \varepsilon-rule per accepting state.
(a) The transitions are \delta(0,\mathtt{0}) = 0, \delta(0,\mathtt{1}) = 1, \delta(1,\mathtt{0}) = 2, \delta(1,\mathtt{1}) = 0, \delta(2,\mathtt{0}) = 1, \delta(2,\mathtt{1}) = 2. With start symbol R_0:
R_0\to\mathtt{0}R_0\mid\mathtt{1}R_1\mid\varepsilon \qquad R_1\to\mathtt{0}R_2\mid\mathtt{1}R_0 \qquad R_2\to\mathtt{0}R_1\mid\mathtt{1}R_2
Write \textsf{val}(x) for the number whose binary representation is x. A prefix of value v leaves M in state q = v\bmod 3, and reading x after it gives the value v\cdot2^{\lvert x\rvert}+\textsf{val}(x), whose remainder mod 3 depends on v only through q. So R_q generates the strings x for which q\cdot2^{\lvert x\rvert}+\textsf{val}(x) is a multiple of 3; for q = 0, 1, 2 that number is the value of x, of \mathtt{1}x and of \mathtt{10}x:

R_0 generates the binary representations of the multiples of 3;
R_1 generates the strings x such that \mathtt{1}x represents a multiple of 3;
R_2 generates the strings x such that \mathtt{10}x represents a multiple of 3.

(b) R_0\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}R_1\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{10}R_2\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{100}R_1\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1001}R_0\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1001}. The nonterminals R_0, R_1, R_2, R_1, R_0 are exactly the states 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 that M visits on 1001, and the last step, R_0\to\varepsilon, is allowed because the run ends in the accepting state 0.
(c) Every sentential form has a single nonterminal, at its end, and each R_q has one rule per next symbol (plus R_0\to\varepsilon, which can only finish the derivation), so every step of a derivation of w is forced by the next symbol of w. Hence w has at most one derivation, so at most one parse tree — the run of M on w.
Check: 11 (three): R_0\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}R_1\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{11}R_0\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{11}. 10 (two): R_0\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}R_1\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{10}R_2, and R_2 has no \varepsilon-rule, so the derivation cannot finish. \varepsilon is generated, as the number 0 should be.
Watch out: the \varepsilon-rules are where acceptance lives. Without R_0\to\varepsilon no derivation ever ends and the grammar generates \varnothing; an \varepsilon-rule on a non-accepting state adds wrong strings (R_1\to\varepsilon would generate 1).
Answer. R_0\to\mathtt{0}R_0\mid\mathtt{1}R_1\mid\varepsilon, R_1\to\mathtt{0}R_2\mid\mathtt{1}R_0, R_2\to\mathtt{0}R_1\mid\mathtt{1}R_2, start R_0; R_q generates the strings that take M from q to state 0, i.e. the x for which x, \mathtt{1}x, \mathtt{10}x (for q = 0, 1, 2) represents a multiple of 3. It is unambiguous because each derivation step is forced by the next symbol.


5.3 Find the error, a union


                  
                  Easy · find the error · grammar design 
                  
                

A student is asked for a context-free grammar for
L = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}\cup\{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^{2n} \mid n\ge0\},
the strings of 0s followed by either equally many or twice as many 1s, and answers:
”S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\mid\varepsilon. Each rule adds one 0 together with one or two 1s, so every 0 is matched with one 1 or with two 1s.”
(a) What is wrong? Give a shortest string that shows it.
(b) Fix the grammar, and describe the language of every nonterminal.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Does the student’s sentence describe L? Try a derivation that uses both rules.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) The slip: the shape is chosen at every step instead of once. One derivation may mix the two rules, so the grammar generates every \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^m with n\le m\le 2n. The shortest wrong string is 00111:
S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{111}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00111},
with two 0s and three 1s — neither equally many nor twice as many. Every \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^{n+1} with n\ge2 is wrong too, so there are infinitely many wrong strings, which on an exam costs all the correctness points. (Nothing is missing: every string of L is generated.) The student’s sentence describes each 0 separately, but L needs all the 0s to be matched the same way.
(b) Choose the shape once, at the top:
S\to A\mid B \qquad A\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon \qquad B\to\mathtt{0}B\mathtt{11}\mid\varepsilon

A generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\};
B generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^{2n} \mid n\ge0\};
S generates L(A)\cup L(B) = L.

Check: 0011 comes from A and 011 from B; 00111 comes from neither. The empty string has two parse trees (through A and through B), so the fixed grammar is ambiguous — which costs nothing.
Watch out: the student’s grammar is a correct answer to a different question — it generates \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j \mid i\le j\le 2i\}, Example 1 of §5.4. For a union of two shapes, branch once, with S\to A\mid B.
Answer. (a) One derivation can mix the two rules; the shortest wrong string is 00111, and there are infinitely many more. (b) S\to A\mid B, A\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon, B\to\mathtt{0}B\mathtt{11}\mid\varepsilon.


5.4 Recursive automaton to grammar


                  
                  Easy · recursive automata · grammar design 
                  
                

A recursive automaton over \Sigma = \{\mathtt{1},{+},\mathtt{(},\mathtt{)}\} has main module E and one more module T; an edge labeled with a module name calls that module.























modulestartacceptingedgesEs_Et_Es_E\xrightarrow{T}x, \ x\xrightarrow{+}s_E, \ x\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t_ETs_Tt_Ts_T\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}t_T, \ s_T\xrightarrow{\mathtt{(}}y, \ y\xrightarrow{E}z, \ z\xrightarrow{\mathtt{)}}t_T
(a) Write the grammar of Lemma 5.6, with one nonterminal [q] for each state q.
(b) Describe the language of every nonterminal.
(c) Simplify the grammar to two nonterminals, and decide whether (1+1)+1, 1+ and () are accepted.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Each edge gives one rule: reading a on an edge from q to p gives [q]\to a\,[p], an \varepsilon-edge gives [q]\to[p], and a call of module A gives [q]\to[s_A]\,[p] — run all of A, then continue at p. The accepting state of each module gets the return rule [t_A]\to\varepsilon.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) One rule per edge plus one return rule per module (Lemma 5.6), with start symbol [s_E]:
\begin{aligned}
&[s_E]\to[s_T]\,[x] && [x]\to{+}\,[s_E]\mid[t_E] && [t_E]\to\varepsilon\\
&[s_T]\to\mathtt{1}\,[t_T]\mid\mathtt{(}\,[y] && [y]\to[s_E]\,[z] && [z]\to\mathtt{)}\,[t_T] \qquad [t_T]\to\varepsilon
\end{aligned}
(b) Call a string an expression if it is t_1{+}t_2{+}\cdots{+}t_k for some k\ge1, where each term t_i is 1 or \mathtt{(}e\mathtt{)} for an expression e. Then

[s_E] generates the expressions, and [s_T] the terms;
[x] generates \varepsilon and the strings that consist of + followed by an expression — what may follow a term inside an expression;
[y] generates the strings that consist of an expression followed by ) — what must follow an opening parenthesis;
[z] generates only ), and [t_E] and [t_T] generate only \varepsilon.

(c) The nonterminals [t_E], [t_T] and [z] each generate a single string, so substitute it for them; then [y] becomes [s_E] followed by ), and [x] becomes \varepsilon or + followed by [s_E]. Renaming [s_E], [s_T] to E, T gives
E\to T\mid T{+}E \qquad T\to\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{(}E\mathtt{)}
(1+1)+1 is accepted: E\rightsquigarrow T{+}E\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{(}E\mathtt{)}{+}E\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{(}T{+}E\mathtt{)}{+}E\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{(1{+}1){+}}E\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{(1{+}1){+}}T\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{(1{+}1){+}1}. 1+ is not: a + must be followed by an expression, and expressions are non-empty. () is not: between the parentheses there must be an expression.
Watch out: a call edge is not a terminal. s_E\xrightarrow{T}x becomes [s_E]\to[s_T]\,[x] — run module T to its end, then continue at x — and not [s_E]\to T\,[x]. And without the return rules [t_E]\to\varepsilon, [t_T]\to\varepsilon no derivation ever finishes.
Answer. (a) The nine rules above (seven nonterminals). (b) [s_E]: expressions; [s_T]: terms; [x]: the empty string or + followed by an expression; [y]: an expression followed by ); [z]: only ); [t_E], [t_T]: only \varepsilon. (c) E\to T\mid T{+}E, T\to\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{(}E\mathtt{)}; (1+1)+1 is accepted, 1+ and () are not.


Medium
5.5 Two grammars with a separator


                  
                  Medium · grammar design 
                  
                

Let \Sigma = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{\#}\}. Give a context-free grammar for each language, and describe the language of every nonterminal in a self-contained sentence. No proof is required.
(a) L_a = \{u\mathtt{\#}v \mid u,v\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*,\ \#(\mathtt{1},u) = \#(\mathtt{1},v)\}: the two sides of the # contain equally many 1s.
(b) L_b = \{x\mathtt{\#}y \mid x,y\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*,\ y \text{ is a substring of } x^R\}. For example, 0110#1 and 01#10 are in L_b, but 01#01 is not.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) Only the 1s need partners: pair the first 1 of u with the last 1 of v, and let 0s appear anywhere. (b) y is a substring of x^R exactly when x = u\,y^R\,v for some strings u and v. Write p = y^R; then x\mathtt{\#}y = u\cdot p\,v\mathtt{\#}p^R, and in the second part p and p^R are nested around v\mathtt{\#}.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Idea. Match the 1s of u with the 1s of v from the outside in. The 0s are unconstrained, so they can be added at either end at any time.
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid S\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{\#}
S is the only nonterminal, and it generates exactly L_a. Every rule keeps the numbers of 1s on the two sides equal. Conversely, a string u\mathtt{\#}v\in L_a can be taken apart by the rules: if u starts with 0 or v ends with 0, remove that 0; otherwise either u = v = \varepsilon (the string is #), or u = \mathtt{1}u' and v = v'\mathtt{1} with u'\mathtt{\#}v'\in L_a.
Check: S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{01}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1\#01}. 1#0 is not generated, because every 1 is created together with a partner on the other side.
(b) Idea. y is a substring of x^R if and only if y^R is a substring of x, that is, x = u\,p\,v with p = y^R. Then x\mathtt{\#}y = u\cdot\big(p\,v\mathtt{\#}p^R\big): the prefix u is arbitrary, and the rest nests the symbols of p around v\mathtt{\#}.
S\to ZT \qquad T\to\mathtt{0}T\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}T\mathtt{1}\mid Z\mathtt{\#} \qquad Z\to\mathtt{0}Z\mid\mathtt{1}Z\mid\varepsilon

Z generates all strings over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}.
T generates the strings x\mathtt{\#}y with x,y\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^* such that y^R is a prefix of x — equivalently, y is a suffix of x^R.
S generates L_b: a string of T with an arbitrary string added in front.

Check: 01#10 has u = v = \varepsilon and p = \mathtt{01}: S\rightsquigarrow ZT\rightsquigarrow T\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}T\mathtt{0}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{01}T\mathtt{10}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{01}Z\mathtt{\#10}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{01\#10}. For 0110#1 take u = \mathtt{0}, p = \mathtt{1}, v = \mathtt{10}. And 01#01 is not generated: p = (\mathtt{01})^R = \mathtt{10} is not a substring of 01.
Watch out: the Z in T\to Z\mathtt{\#} is easy to forget. Without it, T generates only the strings p\mathtt{\#}p^R, and the grammar finds y only at the start of x^R: it misses 10#1, whose y = \mathtt{1} is a substring of x^R = \mathtt{01} but not a prefix.
Answer. (a) S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid S\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{\#}. (b) S\to ZT, T\to\mathtt{0}T\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}T\mathtt{1}\mid Z\mathtt{\#}, Z\to\mathtt{0}Z\mid\mathtt{1}Z\mid\varepsilon.


5.6 The dangling else


                  
                  Medium · ambiguity · parse trees 
                  
                

The grammar S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S\mid\mathtt{0}S\mid\varepsilon generates the set P of strings in which every prefix has at least as many 0s as 1s (Problem 5.10 proves this). Read 0 as if and 1 as else.
(a) Find a shortest string with two different parse trees, and give both as leftmost derivations.
(b) Give an unambiguous grammar for P, describe the language of every nonterminal, and explain why every string of P has exactly one parse tree.
Source: classic.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) An else after two ifs can belong to either of them. (b) Let every 1 belong to the nearest unmatched 0 before it: in a rule S\to\mathtt{0}M\mathtt{1}S, let M generate only balanced strings (equally many 0s and 1s, and every prefix with at least as many 0s as 1s).




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) 001. Every string of length at most 2 has at most one parse tree, and among the strings of length 3 only 001 has two:
\begin{aligned}
&S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001} && \text{(the 1 belongs to the first 0)}\\
&S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001} && \text{(the 1 belongs to the second 0)}
\end{aligned}
As trees: S(\mathtt{0},\,S(\mathtt{0},S(\varepsilon)),\,\mathtt{1},\,S(\varepsilon)) and S(\mathtt{0},\,S(\mathtt{0},S(\varepsilon),\mathtt{1},S(\varepsilon))). This is the dangling else: in if if … else … the grammar does not say which if the else belongs to.
(b) Idea. Let every 1 close the nearest unmatched 0, by requiring the part between a 0 and its 1 to be balanced.
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid\mathtt{0}M\mathtt{1}S\mid\varepsilon \qquad M\to\mathtt{0}M\mathtt{1}M\mid\varepsilon

M generates the balanced strings: equally many 0s and 1s, and every prefix with at least as many 0s as 1s.
S generates P.

Why there is one parse tree. Let w\in P be non-empty; it starts with 0. The rule S\to\mathtt{0}M\mathtt{1}S produces strings \mathtt{0}m\mathtt{1}s whose prefix \mathtt{0}m\mathtt{1} is balanced while every shorter non-empty prefix, \mathtt{0}m' with m' a prefix of m, has more 0s than 1s; so \mathtt{0}m\mathtt{1} must be the shortest non-empty balanced prefix of the string. The rule S\to\mathtt{0}S produces strings with no non-empty balanced prefix. Hence:

if w has a non-empty balanced prefix, only S\to\mathtt{0}M\mathtt{1}S fits, and the split w = \mathtt{0}m\mathtt{1}s is forced: cut after the shortest such prefix;
otherwise only S\to\mathtt{0}S fits, with w = \mathtt{0}s.

Either way the first rule and the pieces are determined, and the same argument works for M (a non-empty balanced string must be cut after its shortest non-empty balanced prefix). By induction on the length, every string of P has exactly one parse tree. The language is still P: the two cases are exactly those of the proof in Problem 5.10.
Check: 001 now has only S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}M\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001} — the else belongs to the nearest if, the rule of C and Java. Another unambiguous grammar puts the unmatched 0s at the top level instead: S\to M\mid M\mathtt{0}S with the same M.
Watch out: to show ambiguity you need one string with two parse trees — two leftmost derivations; two derivations that only expand the nonterminals in another order build the same tree. And the unambiguous grammar must still generate all of P: test it on strings such as 0101 and 0010.
Answer. (a) 001: S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001} and S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}. (b) S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid\mathtt{0}M\mathtt{1}S\mid\varepsilon, M\to\mathtt{0}M\mathtt{1}M\mid\varepsilon, where M generates the balanced strings.


5.7 A small CNF conversion


                  
                  Medium · Chomsky normal form 
                  
                

Consider the grammar
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid AB \qquad A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\varepsilon \qquad B\to\mathtt{1}B\mid\varepsilon
(a) What language does it generate?
(b) Convert it to Chomsky normal form with the algorithm of §5.9, showing the grammar after each step.
(c) How many steps does every derivation of 0011 take in your final grammar, and why?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Every step except step 4 changes something. When you look for nullable nonterminals, do not stop at the \varepsilon-rules: S\to AB makes S nullable, and then the new start symbol too. In step 5, copy the rules of A and B as they are after step 3.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) A generates \mathtt{0}^* and B generates \mathtt{1}^*, so AB generates \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*; the rule S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1} wraps a string of \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* in one more 0…1, which stays in \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*. So the language is \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* — regular, which makes every step easy to test.
(b) The grammar after each step:













































stepwhat happensgrammar0S is on a right side and nullable: new start symbol S'S'\to S; \ S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid AB; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\varepsilon; \ B\to\mathtt{1}B\mid\varepsilon1split S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1} into S\to\mathtt{0}C and C\to S\mathtt{1}S'\to S; \ S\to\mathtt{0}C\mid AB; \ C\to S\mathtt{1}; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\varepsilon; \ B\to\mathtt{1}B\mid\varepsilon2nullable: A and B (\varepsilon-rules), then S (by S\to AB), then S'; not C (its rule contains the terminal 1)unchanged3add the variants without a nullable occurrence; drop the \varepsilon-rules, but add S'\to\varepsilonS'\to S\mid\varepsilon; \ S\to\mathtt{0}C\mid AB\mid A\mid B; \ C\to S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}; \ A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}; \ B\to\mathtt{1}B\mid\mathtt{1}4the unit rules S'\to S, S\to A, S\to B form no cycle: nothing to mergeunchanged5copy the rules of A and B into S, then the new rules of S into S'S'\to\mathtt{0}C\mid AB\mid\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}B\mid\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon; \ S\to\mathtt{0}C\mid AB\mid\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}B\mid\mathtt{1}; \ C, A, B as in step 36T_0\to\mathtt{0} and T_1\to\mathtt{1} replace the terminals in rules of length 2below
The final grammar, in Chomsky normal form with start symbol S':
\begin{aligned}
S'&\to T_0C\mid AB\mid T_0A\mid T_1B\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon\\
S&\to T_0C\mid AB\mid T_0A\mid T_1B\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}\\
C&\to ST_1\mid\mathtt{1} \qquad A\to T_0A\mid\mathtt{0} \qquad B\to T_1B\mid\mathtt{1} \qquad T_0\to\mathtt{0} \qquad T_1\to\mathtt{1}
\end{aligned}
From step 3 on, S generates \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* without \varepsilon; only S' still generates all of \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*.
(c) Seven. In Chomsky normal form, a parse tree of a string of length n\ge1 has exactly 2n-1 nonterminal nodes — n nodes X\to a above the leaves and n-1 nodes X\to YZ — and each derivation step expands one node. For 0011, n = 4; for example
S'\rightsquigarrow AB\rightsquigarrow T_0AB\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}AB\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}B\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}T_1B\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}B\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0011}.
(0011 has three parse trees here, exactly as in the original grammar: the conversion does not remove ambiguity.)
Check: S' generates \varepsilon, 0, 1 and 0011, but not 10. Every rule has the form X\to YZ or X\to a, except S'\to\varepsilon, and S' appears on no right side. The old start symbol S does (in C\to ST_1), which is why it could not stay the start symbol.
Watch out:

Step 3 adds S\to A and S\to B, but never S\to\varepsilon: the empty string survives only through S'\to\varepsilon.
In step 5, copy the rules of A and B as they are after step 3 (A\to\mathtt{0}A\mid\mathtt{0}), not the original ones — otherwise S\to\varepsilon comes back.
Keep S': the book drops the new start symbol after step 2 only when it is not nullable, and here it is.

Answer. (a) \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*. (b) S'\to T_0C\mid AB\mid T_0A\mid T_1B\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon, S\to T_0C\mid AB\mid T_0A\mid T_1B\mid\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}, C\to ST_1\mid\mathtt{1}, A\to T_0A\mid\mathtt{0}, B\to T_1B\mid\mathtt{1}, T_0\to\mathtt{0}, T_1\to\mathtt{1}. (c) 2\cdot4-1 = 7 steps.


Hard
5.8 Enough 1s at the end


                  
                  Hard · fooling sets · grammar design 
                  
                

Let L be the set of binary strings whose last \#(\mathtt{0},w) symbols are all 1s:
L = \{w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^* \mid w = x\,\mathtt{1}^{\#(\mathtt{0},w)} \text{ for some string } x\}.
For example, 0011, 101 and 11 are in L, but 0101 and 10 are not.
(a) Prove that L is not regular.
(b) Give a context-free grammar for L, describe the language of every nonterminal, and explain briefly why the grammar generates exactly L.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) A DFA would have to count the 0s; try F = \mathtt{0}^*. (b) Look at the first symbol. Removing a leading 1 keeps a string in L. If a string of L starts with 0, what must its last symbol be, and what is left if you remove both?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Idea. An algorithm for L must remember how many 0s it has read, to know how many 1s to demand at the end.
Proof. Let F = \mathtt{0}^*. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F; then x = \mathtt{0}^i and y = \mathtt{0}^j for some integers i\ne j. A suffix that distinguishes x from y also distinguishes y from x, so we may name the two strings so that i<j. Let z = \mathtt{1}^i.
Then xz = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\in L, because it has i 0s and its last i symbols are 1s.
And yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i\notin L, because it has j 0s, but its last j symbols are \mathtt{0}^{j-i}\mathtt{1}^i, which contain a 0 because j>i.
So z distinguishes x and y, and F is a fooling set for L. Because F is infinite, L is not regular. \blacksquare
(b) Idea. Decide by the first symbol: a leading 1 is harmless, and a leading 0 must be paid for with a 1 at the very end.
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mid\varepsilon
S is the only nonterminal, and it generates exactly L:

Every rule stays inside L. \varepsilon\in L. Let x\in L have k 0s, so \lvert x\rvert\ge k and the last k symbols of x are 1s. Then \mathtt{1}x has the same k 0s and the same last k symbols, so \mathtt{1}x\in L; and \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} has k+1 0s, and its last k+1 symbols are the last k symbols of x followed by 1, all 1s, so \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}\in L.
Every string of L is built this way. Let w\in L be non-empty, with k 0s. If w = \mathtt{1}x, then x has the same k 0s and the same last k symbols, so x\in L. If w starts with 0, then k\ge1, so the last symbol of w is 1 and w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}; now x has k-1 0s, and its last k-1 symbols are the symbols just before the final 1 of w, all 1s, so x\in L. In both cases x is shorter than w, so by induction on the length x is generated, and then so is w. (Problem 5.10 shows how such an argument is written out in full.)

Check: S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0011} and S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{10}S\mathtt{1}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{101}. 0101 starts with 0 and ends with 1, but the middle 10 is not in L, so 0101 is not generated — as it should be.
Watch out: the reflex answer S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid S\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon generates only strings of the form \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n with n\ge m. It misses 101, 1101, 11101, … — infinitely many strings, because in L some 1s may come before the 0s.
Grading notes. Fooling set: 4 points for an explicit infinite fooling set, 6 for the argument with arbitrary x\ne y (2 for the suffix, 2 for each membership claim). Grammar: 2 for syntax and 8 for correctness (how exams are graded).
Answer. (a) F = \mathtt{0}^*: for \mathtt{0}^i and \mathtt{0}^j with i<j, the suffix \mathtt{1}^i gives \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\in L and \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}^i\notin L. (b) S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mid\varepsilon.


5.9 A 1 in the first half


                  
                  Hard · fooling sets · grammar design 
                  
                

Let L be the set of binary strings of even length whose first half contains a 1:
L = \{xy \mid x,y\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*,\ \lvert x\rvert = \lvert y\rvert,\ \#(\mathtt{1},x)\ge1\}.
For example, 10, 0100 and 1000 are in L, but 01, 0010 and 101 are not.
(a) Prove that L is not regular.
(b) Give a context-free grammar for L, and describe the language of every nonterminal.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) With F = \mathtt{0}^*, put a single 1 into the suffix, so that it lands in the first half of xz but not of yz — and let the parity of \lvert yz\rvert help you. (b) Fix one 1 in the first half and write the string as u\mathtt{1}v. How must \lvert u\rvert and \lvert v\rvert be related? Generate u together with the last \lvert u\rvert symbols of v.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Idea. After reading \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}, an algorithm must remember i: the 1 lies in the first half exactly when at least i+1 more symbols follow (and the total length is even).
Proof. Let F = \mathtt{0}^*. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F; then x = \mathtt{0}^i and y = \mathtt{0}^j for some integers i\ne j. A suffix that distinguishes x from y also distinguishes y from x, so we may name the two strings so that i<j. Let z = \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^{i+1}.
Then xz = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^{i+1} has length 2i+2, and its first half \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1} contains a 1, so xz\in L.
And yz = \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^{i+1}\notin L, which has length i+j+2. If i+j is odd, that length is odd. If i+j is even, then j\ge i+2 (because j-i is even and positive), so the first half has length \frac{i+j}{2}+1\le j and lies inside the block \mathtt{0}^j: it contains no 1.
So z distinguishes x and y, and F is a fooling set for L. Because F is infinite, L is not regular. \blacksquare
(b) Idea. Pick a 1 in the first half and write the string as u\mathtt{1}v. The length \lvert u\rvert+\lvert v\rvert+1 must be even and the 1, at position \lvert u\rvert+1, must be in the first half; together these say that \lvert v\rvert-\lvert u\rvert is odd and positive. So wrap u and the last \lvert u\rvert symbols of v around a 1 followed by a string of odd length.
S\to XSX\mid\mathtt{1}O \qquad O\to X\mid XXO \qquad X\to\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}

X generates the one-symbol strings 0 and 1.
O generates the binary strings of odd length.
S generates the strings u\mathtt{1}v in which \lvert v\rvert-\lvert u\rvert is odd and positive, and these are exactly the strings of L. If \lvert v\rvert = \lvert u\rvert+2m+1, the length is 2(\lvert u\rvert+m+1) and the 1 sits at position \lvert u\rvert+1\le\lvert u\rvert+m+1, in the first half. Conversely, a 1 at position k of a string of length 2n with k\le n gives \lvert u\rvert = k-1 and \lvert v\rvert = 2n-k, whose difference 2(n-k)+1 is odd and positive.

Check: S\rightsquigarrow XSX\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}SX\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{01}OX\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{01}XX\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{010}X\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0100}, and 1000 is \mathtt{1}O with O\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{000}. 0010 is not generated: its only 1 is at position 3 of 4.
Watch out:

S\to XSX\mid\mathtt{1}X looks natural, but it only finds a 1 at the last position of the first half: it misses 1000, 1010 and every \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^{2k-1} with k\ge2 — infinitely many strings.
S\to XSX\mid\mathtt{1}Z, with Z generating all strings, forgets the parity: it generates 1 and 100.

Answer. (a) F = \mathtt{0}^*: for \mathtt{0}^i and \mathtt{0}^j with i<j, the suffix \mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^{i+1} gives \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^{i+1}\in L and \mathtt{0}^j\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^{i+1}\notin L. (b) S\to XSX\mid\mathtt{1}O, O\to X\mid XXO, X\to\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{1}.


5.10 Prefixes of balanced strings, a proof


                  
                  Hard · grammar proof 
                  
                

Let P be the set of strings w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^* in which every prefix (including \varepsilon and w itself) has at least as many 0s as 1s. Prove that the grammar
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S\mid\mathtt{0}S\mid\varepsilon
generates exactly P: prove L(S)\subseteq P and P\subseteq L(S), each by induction, in full.
Source: textbook exercise style.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Write \textsf{bal}(x) := \#(\mathtt{0},x)-\#(\mathtt{1},x); then \textsf{bal}(xy) = \textsf{bal}(x)+\textsf{bal}(y), and the prefixes of xy are the prefixes of x and the strings xq for prefixes q of y. For P\subseteq L(S), take a non-empty w\in P and look for its shortest non-empty prefix with balance 0. If there is one, it has the form \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Cut w where its first 0 is “closed”: after the shortest non-empty prefix with equally many 0s and 1s. If there is such a prefix, w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}y (rule S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S); if not, the first 0 is never closed and w = \mathtt{0}x (rule S\to\mathtt{0}S).
Notation. \textsf{bal}(x) := \#(\mathtt{0},x)-\#(\mathtt{1},x), so \textsf{bal}(xy) = \textsf{bal}(x)+\textsf{bal}(y), and P = \{w \mid \textsf{bal}(p)\ge0 \text{ for every prefix } p \text{ of } w\}. The prefixes of xy are the prefixes of x and the strings xq for prefixes q of y.
Claim 1: L(S)\subseteq P. Let w be an arbitrary string in L(S), fix a derivation S\rightsquigarrow^* w, and assume that every string in L(S) shorter than w is in P. Every rule other than S\to\varepsilon puts terminals next to its copies of S, so the pieces below are strictly shorter than w; unlike Lemma 5.3, no shortest-derivation trick is needed. There are three cases, by the first rule of the derivation.

S\to\varepsilon. Then w = \varepsilon, whose only prefix has balance 0.
S\to\mathtt{0}S. Then w = \mathtt{0}x with S\rightsquigarrow^* x and \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert, so x\in P by the induction hypothesis. A prefix of w is \varepsilon, or \mathtt{0}q for a prefix q of x, and \textsf{bal}(\mathtt{0}q) = 1+\textsf{bal}(q)\ge1.
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S. Then w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}y with S\rightsquigarrow^* x and S\rightsquigarrow^* y, both shorter than w, so x, y\in P by the induction hypothesis. A prefix of w is \varepsilon; or \mathtt{0}q for a prefix q of x, with balance 1+\textsf{bal}(q)\ge1; or \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}q for a prefix q of y, with balance 1+\textsf{bal}(x)-1+\textsf{bal}(q) = \textsf{bal}(x)+\textsf{bal}(q)\ge0, because x is a prefix of itself and x, y\in P.

In every case every prefix of w has non-negative balance, so w\in P.
Claim 2: P\subseteq L(S). Let w be an arbitrary string in P, and assume that every string in P shorter than w is in L(S). If w = \varepsilon, then S\rightsquigarrow\varepsilon. Otherwise the first symbol of w is 0, because the one-symbol prefix has balance at least 0. There are two cases.

Some non-empty prefix of w has balance 0. Let p be the shortest one; \lvert p\rvert\ge2, because \textsf{bal}(\mathtt{0}) = 1. Deleting the last symbol of p leaves a non-empty prefix of w shorter than p, whose balance is \ge0 (as w\in P) and \ne0 (by the choice of p), hence \ge1; one more symbol brings it to 0, so it was exactly 1 and the last symbol of p is 1. So p = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} and w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}y for some strings x and y. Then x\in P: for a prefix q of x, \mathtt{0}q is a non-empty prefix of w shorter than p, so \textsf{bal}(\mathtt{0}q)\ge1 and \textsf{bal}(q)\ge0. And y\in P: for a prefix q of y, pq is a prefix of w, so 0\le\textsf{bal}(pq) = \textsf{bal}(p)+\textsf{bal}(q) = \textsf{bal}(q). Both x and y are shorter than w, so the induction hypothesis gives S\rightsquigarrow^* x and S\rightsquigarrow^* y, and therefore S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}y = w.
No non-empty prefix of w has balance 0. Write w = \mathtt{0}x. For a prefix q of x, \mathtt{0}q is a non-empty prefix of w, so \textsf{bal}(\mathtt{0}q)\ge1 and \textsf{bal}(q)\ge0; hence x\in P. Since x is shorter than w, the induction hypothesis gives S\rightsquigarrow^* x, and S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}x = w.

In every case w\in L(S). Together the two claims give L(S) = P. \blacksquare
Check: \varepsilon, 0, 01, 001, 0011 and 010 are in P and are generated (010 = \mathtt{0}\cdot\varepsilon\cdot\mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{0} by the first case); 1, 10 and 011 are not in P, and are not generated.
Watch out: the cut must be after the shortest balanced prefix. After the longest one, 0101 would split as \mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{10}\cdot\mathtt{1}, and \mathtt{10}\notin P.
Grading notes. Each inclusion is an induction and is graded like one: an arbitrary string, an explicit strong induction hypothesis, exhaustive cases (one per rule for L(S)\subseteq P, the two cases above for P\subseteq L(S)), the base case, and every use of the hypothesis on a string that is visibly shorter (how exams are graded).
Answer. Strong induction on \lvert w\rvert in both directions. L(S)\subseteq P: one case per rule, checking every prefix. P\subseteq L(S): cut a non-empty w\in P after its shortest non-empty balanced prefix \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}, giving w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1}y with x, y\in P; if there is none, w = \mathtt{0}x with x\in P.


Sources for this page
All ten problems were written for this page in the style of the course’s exams; none is taken from a course exam or homework. The dangling-else ambiguity (5.6), the grammar for prefixes of balanced strings (5.6, 5.10) and the grammar of a DFA (5.2) are classic textbook material, and the intersection of a grammar with a DFA in 5.1(b) is the standard construction (not in the book’s chapter); all are in our own words. The methods are those of the book’s Chapter 5: parse trees and ambiguity (§5.2), proving L(G) = L by induction (§5.3), designing grammars (§5.4), regular languages are context-free (§5.5), closure properties and the non-context-free language \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\} (§5.6), recursive automata and Lemma 5.6 (§5.7), and Chomsky normal form (§§5.8–5.9); the fooling sets are those of Chapter 3. Every grammar, derivation, parse-tree count, conversion step and fooling-set suffix on this page is checked by tools/practice/checks/ch05.py.

practice/06-turing-machines.title: Practice — Chapter 6: Turing machines
practice/06-turing-machines.content:
Practice for Chapter 6 · concepts: turing-machines · acceptable-and-decidable · all practice: hub · by difficulty: easy · medium · hard · by topic
Work each problem on paper first. Open the hint only when stuck, and the solution only after you have an answer you would hand in. Every Turing machine in the solutions has been checked by a script. Machines follow §6.2 unless a problem says otherwise: one tape, infinite to the right; every step moves the head one cell left (-1) or right (+1); a move left from cell 0 crashes; and missing transitions go to \textit{reject}. A table entry (q, b, \Delta) in row p and column a means \delta(p,a) = (q,b,\Delta).
Easy
6.1 Deciding, crashing and variants


                  
                  Easy · true or false · TM variants 
                  
                

Answer each statement Yes (always true) or No, with a one-sentence reason; for a No, give a counterexample. “Standard” means the model of §6.2.
(a) A Turing machine that never moves its head to the left can accept a language that is not regular.
(b) If a Turing machine M halts on every input and accepts every string in L, then M decides L.
(c) If a Turing machine M crashes on at least one input, then M decides no language at all.
(d) Every Turing machine that may also stay put (\Delta = 0) can be simulated by a standard Turing machine that takes at most twice as many steps.
(e) Every Turing machine whose tape is infinite in both directions can be simulated by a standard Turing machine with only a constant-factor slowdown.
(f) If a two-tape Turing machine decides L in O(n) time, then some standard Turing machine decides L in O(n) time.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

For (a): can the machine ever look again at a cell it has left? For (b) and (c), go back to the exact definitions of accepts L and decides L. For (f), §6.6 names a language with a quadratic gap.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) No. Such a machine reads each input symbol exactly once, left to right, and after the input it reads only blanks, so its state at the end of the input determines everything that follows: it is a DFA in disguise, and \textsf{Accept}(M) is regular. (Concretely: a DFA with states Q\cup\{\textit{ACC},\textit{REJ}\} follows M‘s state symbol by symbol, and accepts in \textit{ACC} and in every state from which M‘s walk over blanks reaches \textit{accept} — a walk that depends on the state alone.)
(b) No. “Accepts every string in L” still allows accepting more. The machine M_{\textsf{Accept}} that accepts at once halts on every input and accepts every string in L = \{\varepsilon\}, but it also accepts 0; it decides \Sigma^*, not \{\varepsilon\}. With "\textsf{Accept}(M) = L" instead, the statement would be true.
(c) Yes. A decider must accept or reject every input, and on an input where M crashes it does neither: a crash is not a rejection.
(d) Yes. The construction of §6.4 with states Q\times\{0,1\} replaces each stay-put step by a step right and a step back, and every other step by one step, so t steps become at most 2t.
(e) Yes. Fold the tape at cell 0 onto two tracks — the upper track of cell i\ge0 holds cell i, the lower track holds cell -i-1 — mark cell 0, and keep the current track in the state; each simulated step costs one step, or two when the head crosses between cells 0 and -1 (plus two steps at the start to mark cell 0).
(f) No. The marked palindromes \{w\,\mathtt{\#}\,w^R \mid w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*\}: two tapes decide them in O(n) steps — copy w onto tape 2, then compare it backwards with the part after the \mathtt{\#} — but every standard one-tape machine needs \Omega(n^2) time (§6.6). What is true is the simulation bound: one tape can always do it in O(n^2) steps.
Watch out: (b) and (c) are pure definitions, and that is where exam points go. M accepts L means M accepts exactly the strings of L; M decides L means, in addition, that M halts — accepts or rejects, never crashes or runs forever — on every input.
Answer. (a) No (b) No (c) Yes (d) Yes (e) Yes (f) No.


6.2 Four ways a run ends


                  
                  Easy · TM simulation 
                  
                

The machine M below has input alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}, tape alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\square\} and states \textit{start}, \mathit{look}, \textit{accept}, \textit{reject}; the blank entry is a missing transition.























\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}\square\textit{start}(\mathit{look},\mathtt{1},+1)(\mathit{look},\mathtt{1},-1)\mathit{look}(\mathit{look},\mathtt{0},-1)(\textit{start},\mathtt{1},+1)(\textit{accept},\mathtt{1},-1)
(a) Write the run of M on input 000 as a sequence of configurations (q, x, i), and say how it ends.
(b) On each of the inputs \varepsilon, 1, 01 and 011, does M accept, reject, crash, or run forever? Justify each answer.
(c) Does M decide any language?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

A configuration (q,x,i) lists the state, the tape without trailing blanks, and the head position. On 011, write configurations until one of them comes back.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) The run on 000:









































stepconfigurationstepconfiguration0(\textit{start},\mathtt{000},0)5(\mathit{look},\mathtt{110},1)1(\mathit{look},\mathtt{100},1)6(\textit{start},\mathtt{110},2)2(\mathit{look},\mathtt{100},0)7(\mathit{look},\mathtt{111},3)3(\textit{start},\mathtt{100},1)8(\textit{accept},\mathtt{1111},2)4(\mathit{look},\mathtt{110},2)
M accepts after 8 steps. In state \textit{start} it overwrites a 0 with 1 and steps right; \mathit{look} sees another 0, steps back onto the 1 it just wrote, and steps forward again in state \textit{start} — three steps per cell. After the last 0, \mathit{look} reads the blank, writes 1 and accepts.
(b)

\varepsilon: reject. \textit{start} reads \square and has no transition for it, so (\textit{start},\varepsilon,0)\Rightarrow(\textit{reject},\varepsilon,0).
1: crash. \textit{start} reads 1 on cell 0 and moves left; there is no next configuration.
01: reject. (\textit{start},\mathtt{01},0)\Rightarrow(\mathit{look},\mathtt{11},1)\Rightarrow(\textit{start},\mathtt{11},2), and \textit{start} reads \square.
011: runs forever. (\textit{start},\mathtt{011},0)\Rightarrow(\mathit{look},\mathtt{111},1)\Rightarrow(\textit{start},\mathtt{111},2)\Rightarrow(\mathit{look},\mathtt{111},1). The configuration of step 1 has come back at step 3. A Turing machine is deterministic, so from then on it alternates between these two configurations forever.

(c) No. A machine that decides a language halts on every input, and M crashes on 1 and runs forever on 011.
Going further. Following the head on every input gives the complete picture. In state \textit{start} on a 0, the machine uses up that 0 if the next symbol is 0, and the block 01 if it is 1 (\mathit{look} steps over the 1). So it reads the input as a sequence of blocks 0 and 01: it accepts if a lone 0 ends the input, rejects if a block 01 ends it, and loops as soon as a block 01 is followed by a 1:
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{Accept}(M) &= (\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{0}, & \textsf{Reject}(M) &= \varepsilon+(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{01},\\
\text{crashes on } &\mathtt{1}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*, & \text{runs forever on } &(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{011}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*.
\end{aligned}
\textsf{Accept}(M) is regular, so it is decidable — just not by M. Decidable describes a language; decides relates one machine to one language.
Answer. (a) Accepts after 8 steps, ending in (\textit{accept},\mathtt{1111},2). (b) \varepsilon: reject; 1: crash; 01: reject; 011: runs forever (a configuration repeats). (c) No: it crashes on 1 and runs forever on 011.


6.3 A decider that only accepts


                  
                  Easy · find the error · Turing machine design 
                  
                

Let E = \{w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^* \mid \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w)\}. A student designs a Turing machine for E and writes:
“The first symbol is overwritten with {\vdash}, which marks the left end and remembers one symbol still waiting for a partner. Then repeat: find an unmarked partner of the opposite kind to the right and mark it \mathtt{x}; walk back to the {\vdash}; find the first unmarked symbol, mark it \mathtt{x}, and look for its partner. When no unmarked symbol is left, accept. In the table, — means ‘write back the symbol read’, and missing transitions reject. My machine decides E.“














































































































statereadwritemovenext state\textit{start}\mathtt{0}{\vdash}+1\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{1}{\vdash}+1\mathit{seek0}\square—+1\textit{accept}\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{x}—+1\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{1}\mathtt{x}-1\mathit{rewind}\square—+1\mathit{seek1}\mathit{seek0}\mathtt{1}, \mathtt{x}—+1\mathit{seek0}\mathtt{0}\mathtt{x}-1\mathit{rewind}\mathit{rewind}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{x}—-1\mathit{rewind}{\vdash}—+1\mathit{next}\mathit{next}\mathtt{x}—+1\mathit{next}\mathtt{0}\mathtt{x}+1\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{1}\mathtt{x}+1\mathit{seek0}\square—+1\textit{accept}
(a) Run the machine on 100. (b) What is wrong with the claim “my machine decides E”, and which entry causes it? Fix the machine. (c) Does the student’s machine accept E?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

On 100, the first 1 finds its partner. What happens to the second 0?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) The first 1 is matched with the first 0; then the second 0 looks for a partner that does not exist:
\begin{aligned}
&(\textit{start},\mathtt{100},0)\Rightarrow(\mathit{seek0},{\vdash}\mathtt{00},1)\Rightarrow(\mathit{rewind},{\vdash}\mathtt{x0},0)\Rightarrow(\mathit{next},{\vdash}\mathtt{x0},1)\\
&\Rightarrow(\mathit{next},{\vdash}\mathtt{x0},2)\Rightarrow(\mathit{seek1},{\vdash}\mathtt{xx},3)\Rightarrow(\mathit{seek1},{\vdash}\mathtt{xx},4)\Rightarrow(\mathit{seek1},{\vdash}\mathtt{xx},5)\Rightarrow\cdots
\end{aligned}
From step 5 on, \mathit{seek1} reads a blank, moves right, and reads another blank: the machine runs forever.
(b) The slip is the entry \delta(\mathit{seek1},\square) = (\mathit{seek1},\square,+1) — “keep looking for a 1” after the input has ended. Every cell past the input is blank, so once \mathit{seek1} reaches the end it never halts. That happens on every string with more 0s than 1s (each round marks one 0 and one 1, so eventually a 0 is left without a partner), and a decider must halt on every input. Fix: delete that entry. Reaching the blank in \mathit{seek1} means “this 0 has no partner”, so w\notin E, and the missing transition rejects — exactly what \mathit{seek0} already does when it reaches a blank. With this change the machine decides E.
(c) Yes. The bad entry is used only when \mathit{seek1} reaches the blank; on every other input the student’s machine and the fixed one behave identically. So the student’s machine accepts exactly E, rejects the strings with more 1s than 0s, and runs forever on the strings with more 0s than 1s: it accepts E but does not decide it.
Watch out: every “scan for something” state needs an answer to what if I reach the blank? “Skip every symbol that is not a 1” is exactly the thought that produces this bug.
Answer. (a) It runs forever: after matching the 1, \mathit{seek1} walks right over blanks forever. (b) \delta(\mathit{seek1},\square) = (\mathit{seek1},\square,+1) makes it loop on every string with more 0s than 1s; delete it, so that the blank rejects. (c) Yes: \textsf{Accept}(M) = E, but M is not a decider.


Medium
6.4 Palindromes by peeling both ends


                  
                  Medium · Turing machine design 
                  
                

Design a Turing machine that decides \textsf{Pal} = \{w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^* \mid w = w^R\}. Give
(a) the algorithm in English, as passes over the tape;
(b) a transition table with a one-line meaning for every state;
(c) an argument that your machine never crashes and halts on every input of length n within O(n^2) steps.
Source: classic.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

A string of length at least 2 is a palindrome exactly when its first and last symbols agree and the part between them is a palindrome. Remember the first symbol in the state, and erase symbols as you use them: the blank left behind at the front also tells the machine where to stop when it walks back.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Peel off the two ends: erase the first remaining symbol, remembering it in the state; walk to the end; compare and erase the last remaining symbol; walk back. Nothing left, or a lone middle symbol, means accept.
(a) Algorithm. Repeat:

If the current cell is blank, nothing is left: accept. Otherwise erase the current symbol a and remember it.
Walk right to the first blank, and step back onto the last remaining symbol.
If that cell is blank, the erased a was the middle symbol: accept. If it holds the other symbol, reject. If it holds a, erase it.
Walk left to the first blank, step right, and start over.

(b) Transition table (”—” means “write back the symbol read”; missing transitions reject):





















































































































statereadwritemovenext statemeaning\textit{start}\mathtt{0}\square+1\mathit{have0}erase the first remaining symbol, a 0 …\mathtt{1}\square+1\mathit{have1}… or a 1\square—+1\textit{accept}nothing left: every pair matched\mathit{have0}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}—+1\mathit{have0}the first symbol was 0; walk to the end\square—-1\mathit{last0}step back onto the last remaining symbol\mathit{have1}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}—+1\mathit{have1}the first symbol was 1; walk to the end\square—-1\mathit{last1}\mathit{last0}\mathtt{0}\square-1\mathit{back}the ends agree: erase the last symbol\square—+1\textit{accept}nothing after the erased 0: it was the middle\mathit{last1}\mathtt{1}\square-1\mathit{back}the ends agree\square—+1\textit{accept}the erased 1 was the middle\mathit{back}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}—-1\mathit{back}walk left over the remaining symbols\square—+1\textit{start}the blank in front of them: next round
The rejections are the missing transitions \delta(\mathit{last0},\mathtt{1}) and \delta(\mathit{last1},\mathtt{0}): the ends differ.
(c) No crash. The first step erases cell 0, so from then on cell 0 is blank and \mathit{back} stops there at the latest, moving right. The other left moves step from a blank onto the last remaining symbol, or from the last remaining symbol (which lies to the right of the erased first one) one cell left, never past cell 0. Running time. Each round erases two symbols (one in the final round of an odd-length input), so there are at most n/2+1 rounds, and each round walks across the remaining symbols and back, at most 2n+1 steps: O(n^2) in all. Exactly, on a palindrome of length n the machine takes (n+1)(n+2)/2 steps (a round on m\ge2 remaining symbols costs 2m+1 steps); on other inputs it rejects sooner.
Check. On 0110: round 1 erases both 0s and walks back to cell 0; round 2 erases both 1s; then \textit{start} reads \square and accepts — 15 steps = 5\cdot6/2. On 0100: round 1 erases the outer 0s, then \mathit{last1} reads 0 and rejects (13 steps). On 010: after round 1, \textit{start} erases the 1, \mathit{have1} reads \square at once, and \mathit{last1} reads the blank where the 1 was: accept. On \varepsilon: accept in one step.
Answer. The six-state machine above (erase the first symbol, remember it, compare with the last, erase, walk back); it never crashes and takes (n+1)(n+2)/2 = O(n^2) steps on palindromes of length n.


6.5 Two tapes, linear time


                  
                  Medium · TM variants · Turing machine design 
                  
                

A two-tape Turing machine has one finite control and two tapes, each with its own head. Its transition function has the form \delta(p,(a_1,a_2)) = (q,(b_1,b_2),(\Delta_1,\Delta_2)): it reads the symbols a_1, a_2 under the two heads, writes b_1 and b_2, and moves each head by \Delta_k\in\{-1,0,+1\} (in this problem a head may also stay put). The input is on tape 1, tape 2 is blank, both heads start on cell 0, and a head moving left from cell 0 crashes the machine.
(a) Design a two-tape machine that decides Z = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\} within O(\lvert w\rvert) steps on every input w. Describe it in English and give its transition table with a meaning for every state.
(b) Exactly how many steps does your machine take on \mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k? Compare with the one-tape machine of §6.3, which takes 4k^2+9k+1 steps.
(c) What running time does the simulation of §6.6 give for a one-tape machine built from yours? Does your machine show that two tapes can decide languages that one tape cannot?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Use tape 2 as a unary counter: one mark per 0 of the first block. Then walk tape 2’s head back over the marks while tape 1 reads the 1s, and forward again while tape 1 reads the last block. Make the mark in tape 2’s cell 0 special, so that its head knows where to stop.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. One left-to-right pass over the input, with tape 2 counting: write one mark per 0 of the first block (the first one is {\vdash}, so that cell 0 of tape 2 is recognizable); match the 1s against the marks walking tape 2 left, then match the last block against the marks walking tape 2 right.
Construction. Missing transitions reject; ”—” means “write back the symbols read”.













































































stateread (a_1,a_2)writemovenext statemeaning\textit{start}(\mathtt{0},\square)(\mathtt{0},{\vdash})(+1,+1)\mathit{copy}first 0: mark tape 2’s cell 0 with {\vdash}(\square,\square)—(+1,+1)\textit{accept}\varepsilon\in Z\mathit{copy}(\mathtt{0},\square)(\mathtt{0},\mathtt{x})(+1,+1)\mathit{copy}one mark per further 0 of block 1(\mathtt{1},\square)—(0,-1)\mathit{match1}block 1 is over: tape 2 steps back onto the last mark\mathit{match1}(\mathtt{1},\mathtt{x})—(+1,-1)\mathit{match1}pair a 1 with a mark, walking tape 2 left(\mathtt{1},{\vdash})—(+1,0)\mathit{match0}this 1 pairs with {\vdash}; tape 2 stays put\mathit{match0}(\mathtt{0},{\vdash}), (\mathtt{0},\mathtt{x})—(+1,+1)\mathit{match0}pair a 0 of block 3 with a mark, walking tape 2 right(\square,\square)—(+1,+1)\textit{accept}input and marks run out together
Every way to fail is a missing transition: \textit{start} reading a 1 (no first block), \mathit{copy} reading (\square,\square) (no 1s), \mathit{match1} reading a 0 or \square on tape 1 (too few 1s), and \mathit{match0} reading a 1 (too many 1s, or a fourth block), (\mathtt{0},\square) (block 3 too long), or (\square,\mathtt{x}) or (\square,{\vdash}) (block 3 too short). The tape-2 head moves left only from a cell holding \mathtt{x}, which is never cell 0, so the machine never crashes. Tape 1’s head moves right in every step but one, so the machine halts within \lvert w\rvert+2 steps.
(b) For k\ge1: 1 step in \textit{start}, k-1 in \mathit{copy} on the remaining 0s, 1 more when \mathit{copy} meets the first 1, k in \mathit{match1}, k in \mathit{match0}, and 1 to accept — 3k+2 steps (and 1 step for k=0). Against 4k^2+9k+1: for k = 100, 302 steps instead of 40,901.
(c) One tape simulates t steps of a two-tape machine in O(t^2) steps when t\ge n (two tracks per tape — contents and head mark — and one sweep over the used cells per simulated step). Here t = O(n), so the simulation decides Z in O(n^2) steps on one tape, the same order as the machine of §6.3. No: every two-tape machine can be simulated by a one-tape machine, so both models decide exactly the same languages; the second tape saves time, not power.
Check. On 010: \textit{start} writes {\vdash}; \mathit{copy} meets the 1 and backs tape 2 onto {\vdash}; \mathit{match1} pairs the 1 with {\vdash}; \mathit{match0} pairs the last 0 with {\vdash}, then reads (\square,\square): accept after 5 steps = 3\cdot1+2. On 0110, \mathit{match0} reads (\mathtt{1},{\vdash}) and rejects; on 00110, \mathit{match0} reads (\square,\mathtt{x}) and rejects.
Answer. (a) The four-state machine above: count block 1 on tape 2, match block 2 walking tape 2 left, block 3 walking it right. (b) 3k+2 steps, against 4k^2+9k+1 with one tape. (c) O(n^2) by simulation; two tapes decide no new languages, they only run faster.


Hard
6.6 A machine that doubles its input


                  
                  Hard · Turing machine design · TM simulation 
                  
                

A Turing machine computes a function as in §6.5: it has a single halting state \textit{halt}, and its output is the tape contents when it halts, without trailing blanks. Design a one-tape Turing machine that computes the doubling function D(w) = ww for w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*; for example D(\mathtt{10}) = \mathtt{1010} and D(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon.
(a) Describe your algorithm in English as passes over the tape. You may add tape symbols.
(b) Give the transition table, with a one-line meaning for every state, and explain why your machine never moves left from cell 0.
(c) Trace your machine on input 10 (every configuration).
(d) Find the exact number of steps your machine takes on an input of length n, and conclude that it runs in \Theta(n^2) time.
Source: textbook exercise style.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Copy one symbol per round, left to right: mark it, carry it to the end in the state, write it there, and walk back. Write the copies as new symbols until the very end (what goes wrong otherwise?). And mark only the symbol you are copying right now: then the walk back always stops at that mark, and the machine never needs to find cell 0.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Round i copies the ith symbol: the state carries it to the right end. Two kinds of temporary symbols: copies are written as \mathtt{a} (a copy of 0) and \mathtt{b} (a copy of 1), so the machine can see where the original ends; and the one symbol being copied is written as \hat{\mathtt{0}} or \hat{\mathtt{1}}, which is where the walk back stops.
(a) Algorithm.

(\mathit{next}) If the current cell holds an original symbol c, overwrite it with \hat{c} and carry c to the right. If it holds a copy, every symbol has been copied: go to step 4. If it is blank (only when w = \varepsilon), halt.
(\mathit{carry0}, \mathit{carry1}) Move right over originals and copies to the first blank, write the copy of c there, and step left.
(\mathit{back}) Move left to the hatted cell, restore it to c, step right, and go to step 1.
(\mathit{clean}) Walk right turning \mathtt{a} into 0 and \mathtt{b} into 1; halt at the blank.

(b) Transition table (tape alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\hat{\mathtt{0}},\hat{\mathtt{1}},\mathtt{a},\mathtt{b},\square\}; ”—” means “write back the symbol read”):





































































































































statereadwritemovenext statemeaning\mathit{next} (start)\mathtt{0}\hat{\mathtt{0}}+1\mathit{carry0}mark the symbol to copy, a 0 …\mathtt{1}\hat{\mathtt{1}}+1\mathit{carry1}… or a 1\mathtt{a}\mathtt{0}+1\mathit{clean}the first copy: every original is copied\mathtt{b}\mathtt{1}+1\mathit{clean}\square—+1\textit{halt}empty input: D(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon\mathit{carry0}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}—+1\mathit{carry0}carrying a 0 to the end …\square\mathtt{a}-1\mathit{back}… append its copy\mathit{carry1}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}—+1\mathit{carry1}carrying a 1 to the end …\square\mathtt{b}-1\mathit{back}… append its copy\mathit{back}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}, \mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}—-1\mathit{back}walk left to the hatted cell\hat{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{0}+1\mathit{next}restore it; the next cell is the next to copy\hat{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{1}+1\mathit{next}\mathit{clean}\mathtt{a}\mathtt{0}+1\mathit{clean}turn the copies into ordinary symbols\mathtt{b}\mathtt{1}+1\mathit{clean}\square—+1\textit{halt}done: the tape holds ww
The pairs not listed never occur. No crash: there are two kinds of left moves. \mathit{carry} steps left from the blank it has just filled, which lies to the right of the hatted cell; \mathit{back} walks left only until it reads the hatted cell, and exactly one cell — the one being copied — is hatted whenever \mathit{back} runs, so it turns right there, at cell 0 at the earliest.
(c) Trace on 10 (hats and copies as they stand on the tape):





















































stepconfigurationstepconfiguration0(\mathit{next},\mathtt{10},0)7(\mathit{carry0},\mathtt{1}\hat{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{b},3)1(\mathit{carry1},\hat{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{0},1)8(\mathit{back},\mathtt{1}\hat{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{ba},2)2(\mathit{carry1},\hat{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{0},2)9(\mathit{back},\mathtt{1}\hat{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{ba},1)3(\mathit{back},\hat{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{0b},1)10(\mathit{next},\mathtt{10ba},2)4(\mathit{back},\hat{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{0b},0)11(\mathit{clean},\mathtt{101a},3)5(\mathit{next},\mathtt{10b},1)12(\mathit{clean},\mathtt{1010},4)6(\mathit{carry0},\mathtt{1}\hat{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{b},2)13(\textit{halt},\mathtt{1010},5)
It halts after 13 steps with output 1010.
(d) Step count. Let n = \lvert w\rvert. The round that copies the symbol in cell i takes: 1 step in \mathit{next}; n-1 steps of \mathit{carry} over cells i+1,\dots,n+i-1 (the n-1-i remaining originals and the i copies so far); 1 step writing the copy in cell n+i; n-1 steps of \mathit{back} over cells n+i-1,\dots,i+1; and 1 step restoring cell i. That is 2n+1 steps per round, n(2n+1) for all n rounds. The finish takes 1 step in \mathit{next} on the first copy, n-1 steps of \mathit{clean} and 1 step at the blank: n+1 more. In total
T(n) = n(2n+1) + n + 1 = 2n^2+2n+1,
which is also right for n = 0 (one step). Since 2n^2\le T(n)\le 5n^2 for n\ge1, the machine runs in \Theta(n^2) time. Check: T(2) = 13, as in (c).
Watch out:

Writing each copy as a plain 0 or 1 breaks termination: after the last original, \mathit{next} sees the first copy, copies it, and the machine keeps copying its own copies forever.
Keeping every copied original hatted, and planning to unhat them all at the end while walking left, crashes: walking left over hatted symbols, the machine cannot tell when it has reached cell 0. Either hat only the current symbol (as here) or give cell 0 a mark of its own.
The final head position does not matter: the output is the tape contents.

Answer. (a)–(b) The five-state machine above (mark the current symbol, carry it to the end, append a temporary copy, walk back to the mark; finally clean up the copies). (c) 13 steps, ending in (\textit{halt},\mathtt{1010},5). (d) Exactly 2n^2+2n+1 steps, so \Theta(n^2).


Sources for this page
Problems 6.1, 6.2, 6.3 and 6.5 are original; 6.4 (palindromes, decided by peeling off both ends) and 6.6 (the doubling function, computed by copying one symbol per round) are classic textbook exercises, written here in our own words. The facts behind 6.1 and 6.5 — removing stay-put moves, folding a two-way infinite tape onto two tracks, the quadratic one-tape simulation of several tapes, and the marked palindromes — are from §§6.4 and 6.6 of the book, and 6.5 revisits the language \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}^n\} of §6.3. None is taken from a course exam or homework. Every machine, trace and step count on this page is checked by tools/practice/checks/ch06.py: the one- and two-tape machines on all inputs of length up to 12–14, the four outcomes of 6.2 on every input up to length 12, and the constructions behind 6.1 (right-moving machines are DFAs, stay-put removal, two-track folding) on hundreds of random machines.

practice/07-undecidability.content:
Practice for Chapter 7 · concepts: acceptable-and-decidable · diagonalization · undecidability-reductions · rices-theorem · all practice: hub · by difficulty: easy · medium · hard · by topic
Work each problem on paper first. Open the hint only when stuck, and the solution only after you have an answer you would hand in. Every concrete machine in the solutions has been checked by a script. Conventions as in §7.1: ”M does not accept w” means that M rejects w or diverges on it (a crash counts as diverging), and \overline{L} = \Sigma^*\setminus L. M_{\textsf{Accept}}, M_{\textsf{Reject}} and M_{\textsf{Diverge}} are the machines of §7.11 that accept at once, reject at once, and move right forever.
Easy
7.1 Closure facts, true or false


                  
                  Easy · true or false · closure of decidable languages · acceptable vs decidable 
                  
                

All languages are over a fixed alphabet \Sigma. Answer each statement Yes (always true) or No, with a one-sentence reason; for a No, give a counterexample.
(a) If L is decidable, then \overline{L} is decidable.
(b) If L is acceptable, then every subset of L is acceptable.
(c) If L_1 and L_2 are decidable, then their concatenation L_1\bullet L_2 is decidable.
(d) If L_1\cup L_2 is decidable, then L_1 and L_2 are both decidable.
(e) If L and \overline{L} are both acceptable, then L is decidable.
(f) If L is undecidable and L' is decidable, then L\setminus L' is undecidable.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

\Sigma^* and \varnothing are decidable, \textsf{Halt} is acceptable but undecidable, and \textsf{SelfDiverge} is not even acceptable. Most of the No’s need nothing more.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Yes. Swap the accept and reject states of a decider for L (Lemma 1(a)); the new machine still halts on every input, and it decides \overline{L}.
(b) No. \Sigma^* is acceptable (even decidable), but its subset \textsf{SelfDiverge} is not acceptable (Theorem 9).
(c) Yes. Given w, try all \lvert w\rvert+1 ways to write w = xy, running the decider for L_1 on x and the decider for L_2 on y, and accept if some split passes both tests; there are finitely many splits and every test halts, so this machine halts on every input.
(d) No. \textsf{Halt}\cup\overline{\textsf{Halt}} = \Sigma^* is decidable, but \textsf{Halt} is not (Theorem 12).
(e) Yes. This is Lemma 5: run an acceptor for L and one for \overline{L} in parallel on w; exactly one of them eventually accepts, and which one tells you whether w\in L.
(f) No. Take L' = \Sigma^*: then L\setminus L' = \varnothing, which is decidable whatever L is. (Corollary 3 runs the other way: if L' is decidable and L\setminus L' is undecidable, then L is undecidable.)
Watch out: “try every split” in (c) works because each test halts. For two acceptable languages the concatenation is still acceptable, but the splits must be tested in parallel, one step at a time — a test that runs forever would block the rest.
Answer. (a) Yes (b) No (c) Yes (d) No (e) Yes (f) No.

(b) \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts no string}\} is acceptable.
(c) By Rice’s theorem, \{\langle M\rangle \mid \text{some transition of } M \text{ writes the symbol } \mathtt{\#}\} is undecidable.
(d) \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } w \text{ within } \lvert w\rvert^2 \text{ steps}\} is decidable.
(e) \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on every input of length } 3\} is decidable.
(f) \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ is finite}\} is undecidable.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

An acceptor only has to say yes on the yes-instances; it may run forever on the others. So “acceptable” asks: is there a search that succeeds exactly when the answer is yes? For a language that is not acceptable, use Lemma 5 or Corollary 18.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

(a) Yes. Dovetail: in round t = 1, 2, 3, \dots, run M for t steps on each of the first t strings of \Sigma^*, and accept as soon as one of these runs accepts; if M accepts the ith string within s steps, this happens by round \max(i,s). (c) No. Whether some transition writes \mathtt{\#} can be read off the encoding \langle M\rangle by scanning its list of transitions, so the language is decidable. Rice’s theorem does not apply because this is a property of the transition table, not of \textsf{Accept}(M): adding a new state that is never entered, with a transition that writes \mathtt{\#}, changes membership but not the language.
(d) Yes. Simulate M on w for \lvert w\rvert^2 steps with the universal machine, counting steps; accept if M has halted, otherwise reject. Decidable.
