7.3 A reduction that proves nothing


                  
                  Easy · find the error · reductions 
                  
                

Let \textsf{EvenAccept} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts at least one string of even length}\}. A student writes:
“Claim: \textsf{EvenAccept} is undecidable. Proof: Suppose some machine \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept}. Given \langle M\rangle, build the machine M' that ignores its own input and runs M on all strings of even length in parallel (dovetailing), accepting as soon as M accepts one of them. Then M' accepts \varepsilon if and only if \langle M\rangle\in\textsf{EvenAccept}. So the machine that writes \langle M', \varepsilon\rangle and runs \textsf{DecideAccept} on it decides \textsf{EvenAccept}. Since \textsf{Accept} is undecidable, \textsf{EvenAccept} is undecidable.”
Every step of the construction is correct. What is wrong with the proof? Fix it.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Which language does the student’s argument assume can be decided, and which one does it then decide? Compare with the boxed rule in §7.9.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

The slip: the reduction goes in the wrong direction. The student decides \textsf{EvenAccept} using a decider for \textsf{Accept} — a reduction from \textsf{EvenAccept} to \textsf{Accept}. That proves only “if \textsf{Accept} were decidable, \textsf{EvenAccept} would be decidable too”, which says nothing, because \textsf{Accept} is not decidable. The same kind of argument “reduces” decidable languages to \textsf{Accept} — for example \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ has three states}\} — so it cannot prove undecidability.
The fix: reduce \textsf{Accept} to \textsf{EvenAccept}. Suppose for the sake of argument that \textsf{DecideEven} decides \textsf{EvenAccept}. Build \textsf{DecideAccept}: given \langle M, w\rangle, write the encoding of the machine
M_w(x)\colon\ \text{ignore } x;\ \text{run } M \text{ on } w;\ \text{accept if } M \text{ accepts},
then run \textsf{DecideEven} on \langle M_w\rangle and return its answer.

If M accepts w, then M_w accepts every string, in particular \varepsilon, which has even length; so \langle M_w\rangle\in\textsf{EvenAccept}, \textsf{DecideEven} accepts, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts.
If M does not accept w (it rejects or runs forever), then M_w accepts no string at all; so \langle M_w\rangle\notin\textsf{EvenAccept}, \textsf{DecideEven} rejects, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects.

So \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept}, which is impossible; hence \textsf{DecideEven} does not exist. (Rice’s theorem gives the same in one line: \mathcal{L} = \{L \mid L \text{ contains a string of even length}\}, Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}}, N = M_{\textsf{Reject}}.)
What the student did prove. Running the universal machine on \langle M', \varepsilon\rangle accepts \textsf{EvenAccept}. So \textsf{EvenAccept} is acceptable — and, by the fix, undecidable.
Answer. The reduction goes from \textsf{EvenAccept} to \textsf{Accept}, which proves nothing; reduce \textsf{Accept} to \textsf{EvenAccept} instead, with M_w (“ignore the input, run M on w”).


Medium
7.4 Rice with the right variant


                  
                  Medium · Rice's theorem 
                  
                

Prove that each language is undecidable, using Rice’s theorem or one of its variants for rejection, halting, divergence or deciding (§7.11). For each, write the language as \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}), \textsf{RejectIn}(\mathcal{L}), \textsf{HaltIn}(\mathcal{L}), … with an explicit property \mathcal{L}, and give concrete machines Y and N. Machines have input alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}.
(a) \textsf{RevClosed} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \text{for every string } w, \text{ if } M \text{ accepts } w \text{ then } M \text{ accepts } w^R\}.
(b) \textsf{RejectOne} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ rejects exactly one string}\}.
(c) \textsf{AcceptEqualsReject} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) = \textsf{Reject}(M)\}.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) needs a machine whose language contains some string but not its reversal. In (b), whether \langle M\rangle belongs depends on \textsf{Reject}(M): two machines with the same \textsf{Accept}(M) can disagree. In (c), what is \textsf{Accept}(M)\cap\textsf{Reject}(M)?




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Rice’s theorem applies to a property of one of the four languages of a machine. First find which one decides membership, then exhibit one machine whose language has the property and one whose language does not.
(a) Rice’s theorem. \textsf{RevClosed} = \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}_a) with \mathcal{L}_a = \{L \mid w^R\in L \text{ for every } w\in L\}: membership depends only on \textsf{Accept}(M).

Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}}: \textsf{Accept}(Y) = \Sigma^* contains every reversal, so it is in \mathcal{L}_a.
N accepts exactly \{\mathtt{01}\}: \delta(\textit{start},\mathtt{0}) = (\mathit{saw0},\mathtt{0},+1), \delta(\mathit{saw0},\mathtt{1}) = (\mathit{saw01},\mathtt{1},+1), \delta(\mathit{saw01},\square) = (\textit{accept},\square,+1), all other transitions reject. \mathtt{01}\in\textsf{Accept}(N) but \mathtt{10}\notin\textsf{Accept}(N), so \textsf{Accept}(N)\notin\mathcal{L}_a.

By Rice’s theorem, \textsf{RevClosed} is undecidable.
(b) Rice’s rejection theorem. \textsf{RejectOne} = \textsf{RejectIn}(\mathcal{L}_b) with \mathcal{L}_b = \{L \mid L \text{ has exactly one element}\}.

Y: \delta(\textit{start},\square) = (\textit{reject},\square,+1) and \delta(\textit{start},a) = (\textit{accept},a,+1) for a\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}. It rejects \varepsilon and accepts everything else: \textsf{Reject}(Y) = \{\varepsilon\}\in\mathcal{L}_b.
N = M_{\textsf{Accept}}: \textsf{Reject}(N) = \varnothing, which has no element, so it is not in \mathcal{L}_b.

By Rice’s rejection theorem, \textsf{RejectOne} is undecidable. The plain (accepting) version does not fit: change Y to move right forever on \square instead of rejecting. The new machine accepts the same strings as Y, but rejects none, so it is not in \textsf{RejectOne} — membership is not determined by \textsf{Accept}(M).
(c) Rice’s halting theorem. No machine both accepts and rejects the same string, so \textsf{Accept}(M)\cap\textsf{Reject}(M) = \varnothing, and the two sets can be equal only if both are empty — that is, if M halts on no input. So \textsf{AcceptEqualsReject} = \textsf{HaltIn}(\{\varnothing\}).

Y = M_{\textsf{Diverge}}: \textsf{Halt}(Y) = \varnothing.
N = M_{\textsf{Accept}}: \textsf{Halt}(N) = \Sigma^*\ne\varnothing.

By Rice’s halting theorem, \textsf{AcceptEqualsReject} is undecidable.
Check. N on 01 goes \textit{start}\to\mathit{saw0}\to\mathit{saw01} and accepts at the blank; on 10, \textit{start} reads 1 and has no transition, so it rejects; on 011, \mathit{saw01} reads 1 and rejects. Y in (b) reads \square at once on \varepsilon and rejects, and accepts every other input in one step. In (c), M_{\textsf{Diverge}} accepts and rejects nothing (\varnothing = \varnothing), while M_{\textsf{Accept}} accepts \Sigma^*\ne\varnothing.
Watch out: the rubric gives 2 of the 10 points for the details, including the right variant. Citing the plain theorem in (b) or (c) — and describing Y and N by the strings they accept — proves nothing there, because membership is not decided by \textsf{Accept}(M).
Answer. (a) \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}_a), Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}}, N accepts exactly \{\mathtt{01}\}. (b) \textsf{RejectIn}(\{L : \lvert L\rvert = 1\}), Y rejects exactly \varepsilon, N = M_{\textsf{Accept}}. (c) \textsf{HaltIn}(\{\varnothing\}), Y = M_{\textsf{Diverge}}, N = M_{\textsf{Accept}}.


7.5 Two behaviors, two answers


                  
                  Medium · TM behavior · reductions 
                  
                

Decide whether each language is decidable, and prove your answer. Machines have input alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\} and any finite tape alphabet; \mathtt{\#} is a fixed symbol that may or may not belong to a machine’s tape alphabet.
(a) \textsf{Reach374} := \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M, \text{ run on input } w, \text{ at some time has its head on cell } 374\}.
(b) \textsf{WritesHash} := \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M, \text{ run on input } w, \text{ writes the symbol } \mathtt{\#} \text{ in some step}\}.
Why does Rice’s theorem settle neither question?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) A run that never reaches cell 374 lives inside a box of 374 cells. How many different configurations fit in that box? (b) Modify M so that it writes \mathtt{\#} exactly when it is about to accept — and think about what happens if M‘s step into \textit{accept} moves left from cell 0.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. A behavior that confines the machine to finitely many configurations is decidable by bounded simulation; a behavior that a simulation can avoid, and then perform on purpose, is undecidable by reduction (§7.13).
(a) Decidable. Let Q and \Gamma be M‘s states and tape alphabet. As long as the head stays among cells 0,\dots,373, the cells from 374 on are never read or written, so they keep their initial contents, and the configuration is determined by the state, the head position, and the contents of cells 0,\dots,373: at most
N := \lvert Q\rvert\cdot374\cdot\lvert\Gamma\rvert^{374}
possibilities. The decider simulates M on w for up to N steps. It accepts as soon as the head is on cell 374, and rejects if M halts or crashes first. If N steps pass with neither, it rejects: two of the N+1 configurations seen so far are equal (pigeonhole), and since M is deterministic, the run cycles through the same configurations forever and never reaches cell 374. The decider halts after at most N simulated steps and is right in all three cases.
(b) Undecidable, by a reduction from \textsf{Accept}. Suppose for the sake of argument that \textsf{DecideHash} decides \textsf{WritesHash}. Build \textsf{DecideAccept}: given \langle M, w\rangle, it modifies M‘s transition table into a machine M':

if \mathtt{\#} is in M‘s tape alphabet, rename it to a new symbol everywhere in the table;
add a new state \mathit{fin}, and redirect every transition into \textit{accept} to \mathit{fin} instead (same symbol written, same move);
for every tape symbol c, let \delta'(\mathit{fin}, c) = (\textit{accept}, \mathtt{\#}, +1).

Then it runs \textsf{DecideHash} on \langle M', w\rangle and returns its answer. Editing a finite table always terminates, and \textsf{DecideHash} halts, so \textsf{DecideAccept} halts on every input.

Suppose M accepts w. M' makes exactly the same steps as M until M would enter \textit{accept}; it enters \mathit{fin} instead and then writes \mathtt{\#}. So \langle M',w\rangle\in\textsf{WritesHash}, \textsf{DecideHash} accepts, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts.
Suppose M does not accept w: it rejects, crashes or runs forever. M' does the same and never enters \mathit{fin}, and step 1 guarantees that it writes no \mathtt{\#} along the way. So \langle M',w\rangle\notin\textsf{WritesHash}, \textsf{DecideHash} rejects, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects.

So \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept}, which is impossible; \textsf{WritesHash} is undecidable. (It is acceptable: simulate and wait for a \mathtt{\#}.)
Rice does not apply to either language, because both are about behavior, not about \textsf{Accept}(M). M_{\textsf{Accept}} accepts every input after one step, never reaching cell 374 and never writing \mathtt{\#}; a machine that first walks 374 cells to the right, writing \mathtt{\#} as it goes, and then accepts, has the same language and belongs to both.
Check. Try the decider of (a) on three machines. M_{\textsf{Accept}} moves to cell 1 and accepts: reject. A machine that moves right forever in one state is on cell 374 after 374 steps: accept. A machine that, on the empty input, steps right onto a blank and back left forever repeats its first configuration after two steps: reject, since it will never get further. In (b), if M accepts w after t steps, M' writes \mathtt{\#} in step t+1; if M rejects w after t steps, so does M', without writing \mathtt{\#}.
Watch out: it is tempting to write \mathtt{\#} in the step into \textit{accept} itself. If that step moves left from cell 0, M crashes instead of accepting — yet the \mathtt{\#} has been written. The extra state \mathit{fin}, which always moves right, avoids this (the same trick is behind Theorem 20).
Answer. (a) Decidable: simulate \lvert Q\rvert\cdot374\cdot\lvert\Gamma\rvert^{374} steps; a run that has not reached cell 374 by then has repeated a configuration and never will. (b) Undecidable: from M build M' that writes \mathtt{\#} (in one extra step) exactly when M accepts w. Rice’s theorem is about \textsf{Accept}(M), and these are properties of the run.


7.6 Do two machines share a string


                  
                  Medium · acceptable vs decidable · reductions 
                  
                

Let \textsf{Overlap} := \{\langle M_1\rangle\langle M_2\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M_1)\cap\textsf{Accept}(M_2)\ne\varnothing\}: some string is accepted by both machines.
(a) Show that \textsf{Overlap} is acceptable: describe an acceptor, and explain why “for each string x in turn, run M_1 on x and then M_2 on x” does not work.
(b) Show that \textsf{Overlap} is undecidable.
(c) Is \textsf{Disjoint} := \{\langle M_1\rangle\langle M_2\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M_1)\cap\textsf{Accept}(M_2) = \varnothing\} acceptable? Is it decidable?
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) Interleave both the strings and the step counts. (b) Fix one of the two machines so that \textsf{Overlap} turns into a language you already know. (c) Lemma 5.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. A yes-instance has a finite certificate — a string x and two accepting runs — so a patient search finds it; that makes \textsf{Overlap} acceptable. Fixing M_2 = M_{\textsf{Accept}} turns it into ”M_1 accepts something”, which is undecidable, and then Lemma 5 rules out the complement.
(a) An acceptor (dovetailing). On input \langle M_1\rangle\langle M_2\rangle (reject anything else): for t = 1, 2, 3, \dots, for each of the first t strings x of \Sigma^*, run M_1 on x for t steps and M_2 on x for t steps; if both accept, accept. If the ith string is accepted by M_1 within s_1 steps and by M_2 within s_2 steps, the acceptor accepts by round \max(i, s_1, s_2). If no string is accepted by both, it runs forever — which an acceptor may do. So it accepts exactly \textsf{Overlap}.
The serial search gets stuck on the first string on which M_1 or M_2 runs forever. Let M_1 accept 0, reject 1, and run forever on \varepsilon, and let M_2 = M_{\textsf{Accept}}. The pair is in \textsf{Overlap}, because both machines accept 0, but the serial search runs M_1 on \varepsilon forever and never gets to 0. Dovetailing accepts in round 2.
(b) Undecidable, by a reduction from \textsf{NeverAccept} (Theorem 13). Suppose for the sake of argument that \textsf{DecideOverlap} decides \textsf{Overlap}. Build \textsf{DecideNA}: given a string, reject it if it is not an encoding \langle M\rangle; otherwise run \textsf{DecideOverlap} on \langle M\rangle\langle M_{\textsf{Accept}}\rangle and return the opposite answer. Since \textsf{Accept}(M)\cap\Sigma^* = \textsf{Accept}(M):

If \textsf{Accept}(M) = \varnothing, the intersection is empty, \textsf{DecideOverlap} rejects, and \textsf{DecideNA} accepts \langle M\rangle.
If M accepts some string x, then M_{\textsf{Accept}} accepts x too, \textsf{DecideOverlap} accepts, and \textsf{DecideNA} rejects \langle M\rangle.

So \textsf{DecideNA} decides \textsf{NeverAccept}, which is impossible; \textsf{Overlap} is undecidable.
(c) Not acceptable, so not decidable. The complement of \textsf{Overlap} is \textsf{Disjoint} together with the strings that do not have the form \langle M_1\rangle\langle M_2\rangle, which form a decidable set. If \textsf{Disjoint} were acceptable, then so would be this union (Lemma 4), so both \textsf{Overlap} (by (a)) and its complement would be acceptable, and Lemma 5 would make \textsf{Overlap} decidable — contradicting (b).
Check. On the pair in (a), round 1 runs both machines on \varepsilon for one step (M_1 is still running); round 2 runs them on \varepsilon and 0 for two steps each, and both accept 0 in their first step: accept. The serial search, in contrast, never gets past \varepsilon.
Answer. (a) Dovetail over strings and step counts; the serial search hangs on a string where M_1 or M_2 runs forever. (b) Undecidable: \langle M\rangle\langle M_{\textsf{Accept}}\rangle\in\textsf{Overlap} exactly when \textsf{Accept}(M)\ne\varnothing. (c) \textsf{Disjoint} is not acceptable (Lemma 5), hence not decidable.


Hard
7.7 Accepts epsilon, rejects itself


                  
                  Hard · diagonalization · acceptable vs decidable 
                  
                

Let \textsf{EpsSelfReject} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \varepsilon \text{ and } M \text{ rejects } \langle M\rangle\}.
(a) Prove that \textsf{EpsSelfReject} is undecidable by diagonalization (not by a reduction).
(b) Prove that \textsf{EpsSelfReject} is acceptable.
(c) Is the complement of \textsf{EpsSelfReject} acceptable?
(d) Explain why Rice’s theorem cannot be used here: give two machines that accept the same language, exactly one of them in \textsf{EpsSelfReject}, and two machines that reject the same language, exactly one of them in \textsf{EpsSelfReject}.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

Build the wrapper so that it certainly accepts \varepsilon. On encodings, should it copy the decider’s answer or flip it? Try both on the wrapper’s own encoding, and keep the one that gives a contradiction in both cases.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Run a wrapper built from the hypothetical decider on its own encoding. The wrapper must make the side condition “accepts \varepsilon” true for itself, and on encodings it must copy the decider’s answer — the language is about rejecting, as in Theorem 6.
(a) Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{Dec} decides \textsf{EpsSelfReject}. Build the machine \textsf{Wrap}: on input x,

if x = \varepsilon, accept;
if x = \langle M\rangle for some machine M, run \textsf{Dec} on x and return its answer (accept if \textsf{Dec} accepts, reject if \textsf{Dec} rejects);
otherwise reject.

\textsf{Wrap} halts on every input, because \textsf{Dec} does, and it accepts \varepsilon. So \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\in\textsf{EpsSelfReject} if and only if \textsf{Wrap} rejects \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle. Run \textsf{Dec} on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle; it halts, so there are two cases.

If \textsf{Dec} accepts \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then \textsf{Wrap} accepts \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, so \textsf{Wrap} does not reject \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, so \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\notin\textsf{EpsSelfReject} — yet \textsf{Dec} accepted it. Contradiction.
If \textsf{Dec} rejects \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, then \textsf{Wrap} rejects \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, and it accepts \varepsilon, so \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\in\textsf{EpsSelfReject} — yet \textsf{Dec} rejected it. Contradiction.

Both cases are impossible, so \textsf{Dec} does not exist: \textsf{EpsSelfReject} is undecidable. \blacksquare
(b) \textsf{EpsSelfReject} = \textsf{AccEps}\cap\textsf{SelfReject}, where \textsf{AccEps} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } \varepsilon\}. \textsf{AccEps} is acceptable (on \langle M\rangle, run M on \varepsilon with the universal machine), \textsf{SelfReject} is acceptable (Theorem 11), and the intersection of two acceptable languages is acceptable (Lemma 4). Concretely: reject non-encodings; run M on \varepsilon; if it accepts, run M on \langle M\rangle and accept if that run rejects. If M runs forever on \varepsilon, so does this acceptor — which is fine, since then \langle M\rangle\notin\textsf{EpsSelfReject}.
(c) No. \textsf{EpsSelfReject} is acceptable by (b) and undecidable by (a), so by Lemma 5 its complement is not acceptable.
(d) Let M_1 accept if its input is empty and reject otherwise, and M_2 accept if its input is empty and run forever otherwise. Both accept exactly \{\varepsilon\}. But M_1 rejects every non-empty string — its own encoding included — so \langle M_1\rangle\in\textsf{EpsSelfReject}, while M_2 rejects nothing, so \langle M_2\rangle\notin\textsf{EpsSelfReject}. Next, let M_3 run forever if its input is empty and reject otherwise: it rejects the same strings as M_1, but it does not accept \varepsilon, so \langle M_3\rangle\notin\textsf{EpsSelfReject}. Membership is decided neither by \textsf{Accept}(M) nor by \textsf{Reject}(M), so neither Rice’s theorem nor its rejection version applies. (The pair M_1, M_{\textsf{Accept}} — both halt on every input, but M_{\textsf{Accept}} rejects nothing — rules out the halting and divergence versions too.)
Watch out:

Flipping is the wrong reflex here. If \textsf{Wrap} returned the opposite of \textsf{Dec}‘s answer, both cases would be consistent: \textsf{Dec} accepts \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle, so \textsf{Wrap} rejects it and \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle\in\textsf{EpsSelfReject} — no contradiction; similarly for rejection. Work out both cases before committing to a wrapper.
Forgetting the \varepsilon clause breaks the proof too: a wrapper that does not accept \varepsilon is never in the language, so ”\textsf{Dec} rejects \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle” is perfectly consistent.
Say why the run of \textsf{Dec} on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle halts; otherwise there is a third case.

Grading. Out of 10: 4 for the wrapper (built from \textsf{Dec}, with its behavior on \varepsilon and on encodings stated) and 6 for the contradiction, 3 for each case.
Answer. (a) \textsf{Wrap} accepts \varepsilon and copies \textsf{Dec}‘s answer on encodings; on \langle\textsf{Wrap}\rangle both answers of \textsf{Dec} are wrong. (b) \textsf{AccEps}\cap\textsf{SelfReject} is acceptable by Lemma 4. (c) No, by Lemma 5. (d) M_1 and M_2 accept \{\varepsilon\}, but only M_1 is in the language; M_1 and M_3 reject every non-empty string, but only M_1 is in the language.


7.8 Both languages infinite


                  
                  Hard · reductions · Rice's theorem 
                  
                

Let \textsf{BothInfinite} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M) \text{ and } \textsf{Reject}(M) \text{ are both infinite}\}, for machines with input alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}.
(a) Show that neither Rice’s theorem nor Rice’s rejection theorem applies directly: give two machines that accept the same language, exactly one of them in \textsf{BothInfinite}, and two machines that reject the same language, exactly one of them in \textsf{BothInfinite}.
(b) Prove that \textsf{BothInfinite} is undecidable by a reduction, written out in full with both directions.
Source: original.




                  
                  Hint 
                  
                

(a) Accept the strings of even length; decide what happens to the odd ones. (b) Build M' that first runs M on w and then, only if M accepted, behaves like your machine from (a) that is in \textsf{BothInfinite}.




                  
                  Solution 
                  
                

Idea. Membership depends on \textsf{Accept}(M) and \textsf{Reject}(M) together, so no single-language version of Rice fits; but the reduction behind Rice still works, with a target machine that both accepts and rejects infinitely many strings.
(a) Three parity machines, with start state \mathit{even}: on 0 or 1, \mathit{even} and \mathit{odd} swap and move right; on the blank they do this:





































machine\mathit{even} reads \square\mathit{odd} reads \square\textsf{Accept}\textsf{Reject}in \textsf{BothInfinite}?Pacceptrejecteven-length stringsodd-length stringsyesP'acceptmove right, stay in \mathit{odd}even-length strings\varnothingnoP''move right, stay in \mathit{even}reject\varnothingodd-length stringsno
(P' runs forever on odd-length inputs, walking right over blanks; P'' does the same on even-length ones.) \textsf{Accept}(P) = \textsf{Accept}(P') but only P is in \textsf{BothInfinite}, so it is not \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) for any \mathcal{L}; \textsf{Reject}(P) = \textsf{Reject}(P'') but only P is in it, so it is not \textsf{RejectIn}(\mathcal{L}) either.
(b) Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{DecideBI} decides \textsf{BothInfinite}. Consider the machine \textsf{DecideAccept} that, given \langle M, w\rangle, writes the encoding \langle M'\rangle of the machine
M'(x)\colon\ \text{run } M \text{ on } w;\ \text{if } M \text{ accepts } w\text{: accept } x \text{ if } \lvert x\rvert \text{ is even, reject } x \text{ if } \lvert x\rvert \text{ is odd}
(if M rejects w, M' runs forever; if M runs forever or crashes on w, so does M'), and then runs \textsf{DecideBI} on \langle M'\rangle and returns its answer. Writing \langle M'\rangle always terminates and \textsf{DecideBI} always halts, so \textsf{DecideAccept} halts on every input.

Suppose M accepts w. Then on every input x, M' finishes running M on w and accepts x if \lvert x\rvert is even and rejects it if \lvert x\rvert is odd. So \textsf{Accept}(M') is the set of even-length strings and \textsf{Reject}(M') the set of odd-length strings, both infinite: \langle M'\rangle\in\textsf{BothInfinite}. So \textsf{DecideBI} accepts \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts \langle M, w\rangle.
Suppose M does not accept w. If M rejects w, then M' runs forever on every input by construction; if M runs forever on w, then M' never finishes its first phase. Either way M' halts on no input, so \textsf{Accept}(M') = \textsf{Reject}(M') = \varnothing: \langle M'\rangle\notin\textsf{BothInfinite}. So \textsf{DecideBI} rejects \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects \langle M, w\rangle.

In both cases \textsf{DecideAccept} is correct, so it decides \textsf{Accept} — which is impossible. Hence \textsf{DecideBI} does not exist, and \textsf{BothInfinite} is undecidable. \blacksquare
Check. P is what M' turns into when M accepts w. On 01 it goes \mathit{even}\to\mathit{odd}\to\mathit{even} and accepts at the blank; on 0, \mathit{odd} reads the blank and rejects; on \varepsilon it accepts at once. P' on 0 walks right over blanks in state \mathit{odd} forever.
Watch out: the clause “if M rejects w, M' runs forever” matters. If M' went on to the parity phase whenever M halts on w, then a rejection of w would put \langle M'\rangle in \textsf{BothInfinite}, and the second direction would fail. That version is a correct reduction from \textsf{Halt} instead; what breaks the proof is mixing the two.
Grading. Out of 10: 4 for the reduction (\textsf{DecideAccept} and M' described, in the right direction), 3 for ”M accepts w ⇒ accept”, 3 for ”M rejects or diverges ⇒ reject”.
Answer. (a) P (accept even, reject odd) and P' (accept even, run forever on odd) accept the same language; P and P'' (reject odd, run forever on even) reject the same language; only P is in \textsf{BothInfinite}. (b) Reduce \textsf{Accept}: M' runs M on w and, if M accepts, accepts even-length and rejects odd-length inputs.


Sources for this page
All eight problems are original, written in the formats of the course’s true-or-false and undecidability problems; none is taken from a course exam or homework. They use the results of the book’s Chapter 7: the closure lemmas and Lemma 5 (§7.3), diagonalization (§§7.5–7.7), the halting problem and reductions (§§7.9–7.10), Rice’s theorem with its rejection and halting variants (§7.11), Corollary 18 (§7.12), and the two principles of §7.13 — bounded simulation, as in Theorem 19, and the extra-steps construction behind Theorem 20. The grading notes paraphrase the course’s undecidability rubrics. Undecidability itself cannot be tested by a program, but everything concrete around the proofs is checked by tools/practice/checks/ch07.py: every witness machine on all short inputs, the bounded-simulation decider of 7.5(a) against long simulations of 400 random machines, the construction of 7.5(b) on 400 random machines, the dovetailing acceptor of 7.6 against the serial search on 300 random pairs, the case analysis of the diagonal argument in 7.7 (including the failure of the flipping wrapper), and the parity machines of 7.8.

practice/index.content:
Knowing the definitions and being able to produce a DFA, a fooling set or a reduction under time pressure are different skills, and only the second one is tested. This bank has 60 problems for Chapters 1–7: quick true-or-false checks, standard exam parts, and full exam-length problems in the formats of the course’s exams. None of them is copied from a course exam or homework.


                  
                  How to use the bank 
                  
                


Pick a chapter you have read and do its easy problems first — a few minutes each, one idea per problem.
Work on paper, the way you will on the exam. Open the hint only after you have been stuck for a few minutes, and the solution only once you have an answer you would hand in.
Compare with the Answer. line, then read the solution’s Check: it shows how to test your own answer (run the DFA on a few strings, try \varepsilon, try the shortest strings in and out of the language).
Move on to medium (one exam part), then hard (a whole exam problem, about 20 minutes).
A day later, redo every problem you got wrong, without looking.





                  
                  Before the final 
                  
                

Go chapter by chapter: read the chapter’s definition, template and trap boxes, then do its easy problems and one medium. Leave the hard problems for a second pass, and write your handwritten cheat sheet from the proof templates and the exam review pages.

problems/a-product-construction-written-.title: Worked problem — A product construction, written formally
problems/a-product-construction-written-.content:
Problem · a DFA built by the product construction, as in a Midterm 1 DFA problem, plus a minimality question · uses §3.6, §3.10 · concepts: product-construction, fooling-sets, dfa-minimization


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let L be the set of binary strings w such that \#(\mathtt{1},w), the number of 1s in w, is divisible by 3, and w does not contain the substring 00. For example, \varepsilon, 0, 111, 0111 and 10101 are in L; 1, 11, 00 and 1001 are not.
(a) Give DFAs M_1 and M_2, with mnemonic state names, for the two conditions separately.
(b) Describe a DFA for L formally by the product construction: its states, start state, transition function and accepting states.
(c) How many states does your product DFA have? Is it minimal? Find the number of states of a minimal DFA for L, and prove that no DFA with fewer states accepts L.


(a) The two factors
Idea. One condition is a counter, the other a pattern. M_1 remembers the number of 1s mod 3. M_2 remembers just enough about the end of the input to notice 00: whether the last symbol was a 0 — and, once 00 has appeared, that it has.


                  
                  Answer (a) 
                  
                

M_1: Q_1 = \{0, 1, 2\}, s_1 = 0, A_1 = \{0\}, \delta_1(r,\mathtt{0}) = r and \delta_1(r,\mathtt{1}) = (r+1)\bmod 3. State r means: the number of 1s read so far is \equiv r\pmod 3.
M_2: Q_2 = \{\textsf{safe},\textsf{zero},\textsf{dead}\}, s_2 = \textsf{safe}, A_2 = \{\textsf{safe},\textsf{zero}\}, and





























statemeaning: the input read so far …on \mathtt{0}on \mathtt{1}→ \textsf{safe} *contains no 00, and is empty or ends in 1\textsf{zero}\textsf{safe}\textsf{zero} *contains no 00, and ends in 0\textsf{dead}\textsf{safe}\textsf{dead}contains 00\textsf{dead}\textsf{dead}



left: three-state cycle counting 1s mod 3; right: three-state DFA safe, zero, deadM₁: number of 1s mod 3M₂: no 0000011110100,1012safezerodeadThe two factors. M₁ keeps the number of 1s mod 3 and accepts 0. M₂ keeps safe (no 00 yet, and the input is empty or ends in 1), zero (no 00 yet, ends in 0) or dead (00 has appeared, a dump state); it accepts safe and zero. The product's states are the nine pairs (r, p).
Both factors are minimal on their own: three remainders need three states, and \textsf{safe} and \textsf{zero} differ on the suffix 0.
(b) The product, formally
Idea. Run both machines in parallel on the same input. A state of the product is a pair — one state of each machine — and by Lemma 3.1 the product is in state (\delta_1^*(s_1,w), \delta_2^*(s_2,w)) after reading w. For \cap, accept when both components accept.


                  
                  Answer (b) 
                  
                

M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) with
Q = Q_1\times Q_2 = \{0,1,2\}\times\{\textsf{safe},\textsf{zero},\textsf{dead}\},\qquad s = (s_1, s_2) = (0,\textsf{safe}),
\delta\big((r,p),a\big) = \big(\delta_1(r,a),\ \delta_2(p,a)\big),\qquad A = A_1\times A_2 = \{(0,\textsf{safe}),\ (0,\textsf{zero})\}.
State (r,p) means: the number of 1s read so far is \equiv r\pmod 3, and the input so far is in situation p of M_2. Written out:























































stateon \mathtt{0}on \mathtt{1}→ (0,\textsf{safe}) *(0,\textsf{zero})(1,\textsf{safe})(1,\textsf{safe})(1,\textsf{zero})(2,\textsf{safe})(2,\textsf{safe})(2,\textsf{zero})(0,\textsf{safe})(0,\textsf{zero}) *(0,\textsf{dead})(1,\textsf{safe})(1,\textsf{zero})(1,\textsf{dead})(2,\textsf{safe})(2,\textsf{zero})(2,\textsf{dead})(0,\textsf{safe})(0,\textsf{dead})(0,\textsf{dead})(1,\textsf{dead})(1,\textsf{dead})(1,\textsf{dead})(2,\textsf{dead})(2,\textsf{dead})(2,\textsf{dead})(0,\textsf{dead})


Check. On 0111: (0,\textsf{safe})\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}(0,\textsf{zero})\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(1,\textsf{safe})\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(2,\textsf{safe})\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(0,\textsf{safe}): accept. On 1001: (0,\textsf{safe})\to(1,\textsf{safe})\to(1,\textsf{zero})\to(1,\textsf{dead})\to(2,\textsf{dead}): reject — and once the second component is \textsf{dead}, no continuation can make the product accept.


                  
                  Where product answers lose points 
                  
                


“Run M_1 and M_2 in parallel” and nothing else. The rubric wants each factor completely and then the product’s states, start state, transitions and accepting set. The accepting set is the only part that knows whether you mean \cap, \cup or \setminus.
The wrong accepting set. \{(r,p) \mid r = 0 \text{ or } p\ne\textsf{dead}\} is the union: it accepts 1, which has no 00 but one 1.
Pairs without meanings. (2,\textsf{zero}) is a mnemonic name because each component is; names like q_7 are not.



(c) Nine states, but seven are enough
The count. The product has 3\times3 = 9 states, and all 9 are reachable: \mathtt{1}^r reaches (r,\textsf{safe}), \mathtt{1}^r\mathtt{0} reaches (r,\textsf{zero}), and \mathtt{1}^r\mathtt{00} reaches (r,\textsf{dead}). Reachable does not mean necessary, though. The three states (0,\textsf{dead}), (1,\textsf{dead}), (2,\textsf{dead}) are non-accepting and lead only to each other, so from none of them does any suffix lead to acceptance. No suffix distinguishes them: they are equivalent, and merging them into one dump state gives a 7-state DFA for L. Moore’s algorithm agrees — it marks every pair of states except the pairs of dead states.
The lower bound. Seven states are also necessary. Take one string for each state of the merged DFA,
F = \{\varepsilon,\ \mathtt{1},\ \mathtt{11},\ \mathtt{0},\ \mathtt{10},\ \mathtt{110},\ \mathtt{00}\},
which reach (0,\textsf{safe}), (1,\textsf{safe}), (2,\textsf{safe}), (0,\textsf{zero}), (1,\textsf{zero}), (2,\textsf{zero}) and the dump state. For a string x without 00, let t_x\in\{0,1,2\} be the number of 1s that x lacks to a multiple of 3: t_x = (3-\#(\mathtt{1},x))\bmod 3.


                  
                  Proof that F is a fooling set
                  
                

Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F. Whether a suffix distinguishes x and y does not depend on which of the two is called x, so it suffices to consider three cases.

One of them is 00; call it y. Let z = \mathtt{1}^{t_x}. Then xz contains no 00 (x contains none, and appending 1s creates none), and its number of 1s is \#(\mathtt{1},x)+t_x\equiv0\pmod 3, so xz\in L. But yz contains 00, so yz\notin L.
Neither is 00, and they contain different numbers of 1s. In F these numbers are among 0, 1, 2, so they differ mod 3. Let z = \mathtt{1}^{t_x}. As before, xz\in L. And yz contains no 00, but \#(\mathtt{1},yz) = \#(\mathtt{1},y)+t_x\not\equiv\#(\mathtt{1},x)+t_x\equiv0\pmod 3, so yz\notin L.
Neither is 00, and they contain equally many 1s. These are the pairs \varepsilon/\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}/\mathtt{10} and \mathtt{11}/\mathtt{110}; call x the one that is empty or ends in 1, and y the one that ends in 0. Let z = \mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}^{t_x}. Then x\mathtt{0} contains no 00, because x does not end in 0, and neither does xz; its number of 1s, \#(\mathtt{1},x)+t_x, is divisible by 3; so xz\in L. But in yz the last 0 of y is followed by the first 0 of z, so yz\notin L.

Every two distinct strings of F have a distinguishing suffix, so F is a fooling set of size 7, and every DFA for L has at least 7 states. \blacksquare




                  
                  Answer (c) 
                  
                

The product DFA has 9 states, all reachable, but it is not minimal: (0,\textsf{dead}), (1,\textsf{dead}) and (2,\textsf{dead}) are equivalent. Merging them gives a 7-state DFA, and the 7-element fooling set F shows that 7 is the minimum.


Which operations let the dead states merge. After a 00, the fate of a string under \cap no longer depends on its number of 1s: it is out of L whatever follows. That is why the three dead states merge. The same happens for every combination whose answer, once 00 has appeared, ignores the count — L_2\setminus L_1, or the complement of L_1\cap L_2, also need only 7 states. For L_1\cup L_2, L_1\setminus L_2 or L_1\oplus L_2 the count still matters after a 00, and the 9-state product is already minimal. So the product of two minimal DFAs need not be minimal, and whether it is depends on the boolean operation: mn states always suffice, and sometimes fewer do.


                  
                  How a product construction is graded 
                  
                

On a DFA problem, a product construction is graded with the DFA rubric (out of 10): 2 for an unambiguous, complete description — which for a product means each factor completely, then the product’s states, start state, transitions and accepting states; 6 for correctness; 2 for mnemonic state names (pairs named by their components, like (2,\textsf{zero}), qualify). Minimality is not required: the 9-state product earns full credit. Statements like “the product of two minimal DFAs is minimal” (false, as (c) shows) are natural true/false items. See how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
An original problem. The product construction, Lemma 3.1, fooling sets and Moore’s algorithm are from Erickson, Models of Computation, §§3.6–3.10, described in our own words. Checked by tools/checks/problems_1.py: both factors and their state meanings, the product against the definition of L on all strings of length at most 14, the 9-row table entry by entry, reachability, the equivalent states (only the three dead states merge), the 7-state minimum, the fooling-set suffix rule on all 21 pairs, the example strings and runs, the union trap, and the minimal state counts for the other boolean combinations (9 for \cup, L_1\setminus L_2 and \oplus; 7 for L_2\setminus L_1 and the complement of \cap).

problems/cnf-conversion-step-by-step.title: Worked problem — CNF conversion, step by step
problems/cnf-conversion-step-by-step.content:
Problem · a conversion exercise on Chomsky normal form · uses §5.8, §5.9 · concepts: chomsky-normal-form, context-free-grammars


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

The grammar
S\to SS\mid P\mid\varepsilon\qquad\qquad P\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}
generates the balanced strings: read 0 as ”(” and 1 as ”)”; a string w is balanced if \#(\mathtt{0},w) = \#(\mathtt{1},w) and every prefix of w has at least as many 0s as 1s. S generates all balanced strings, and P those of the form \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} with x balanced. The grammar has an \varepsilon-rule (S\to\varepsilon), a unit rule (S\to P) and a long rule (P\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}).
(a) Convert the grammar to Chomsky normal form with the algorithm of §5.9, showing the grammar after every step.
(b) Check the result.


The target. A grammar is in Chomsky normal form if its start symbol appears on no right side, the only allowed \varepsilon-rule is (start symbol) \to\varepsilon, and every other rule is A\to BC (two nonterminals) or A\to a (one terminal). Each step of the algorithm removes one kind of violation without changing the language; the order of the steps matters.
(a) The conversion
Step 0 — new start symbol. S appears on right sides (S\to SS, P\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}) and the language contains \varepsilon, so S cannot be the start symbol of a CNF grammar. Add S'\to S:
S'\to S\qquad S\to SS\mid P\mid\varepsilon\qquad P\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}
Step 1 — split long rules. Only P\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1} has a right side longer than 2. Keep its first symbol and hand the rest to a new nonterminal B:
S'\to S\qquad S\to SS\mid P\mid\varepsilon\qquad P\to\mathtt{0}B\qquad B\to S\mathtt{1}
B generates the strings x\mathtt{1} with x balanced. (A rule of length k becomes k-1 rules of length 2.)
Step 2 — find the nullable nonterminals. S is nullable (S\to\varepsilon), and therefore so is S' (S'\to S). P and B are not: each of their rules contains a terminal. Nullable: \{S, S'\}. Because S' is nullable, the final grammar will keep S'\to\varepsilon.
Step 3 — remove \varepsilon-rules. For each rule, add every variant with some nullable occurrences deleted (never an empty right side); then delete S\to\varepsilon and add S'\to\varepsilon.

S\to SS: deleting one S gives S\to S; deleting both would give \varepsilon, which is not added.
B\to S\mathtt{1}: deleting S gives B\to\mathtt{1}.
S'\to S: deleting S would leave \varepsilon; instead S'\to\varepsilon is added, since S' is nullable.

S'\to S\mid\varepsilon\qquad S\to SS\mid S\mid P\qquad P\to\mathtt{0}B\qquad B\to S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}
From now on S generates the non-empty balanced strings; only S' still generates \varepsilon.


                  
                  Step 3 
                  
                


B\to\mathtt{1} is easy to miss, and fatal. Without it every P needs a B, every B needs a non-empty S, and every non-empty S needs a P: the grammar generates nothing but \varepsilon.
Do not put S\to\varepsilon back “because S is nullable”. Only the start symbol may keep an \varepsilon-rule; the variants now do the work of the deleted rule.
Removing \varepsilon-rules creates unit rules — here S\to S, from S\to SS. That is why unit rules are removed after \varepsilon-rules.



Step 4 — merge equivalent nonterminals. The unit rules are S'\to S, S\to S and S\to P. The only cycle among them is the self-loop S\to S, which says nothing: delete it. No two different nonterminals derive each other by unit rules, so nothing is merged.
S'\to S\mid\varepsilon\qquad S\to SS\mid P\qquad P\to\mathtt{0}B\qquad B\to S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}
Step 5 — remove unit rules. The unit rules form the chain S'\to S\to P. Work from its end backward (reverse topological order): P has no unit rule; replace S\to P by P‘s rule, giving S\to SS\mid\mathtt{0}B; then replace S'\to S by S‘s rules as they are now:
S'\to SS\mid\mathtt{0}B\mid\varepsilon\qquad S\to SS\mid\mathtt{0}B\qquad P\to\mathtt{0}B\qquad B\to S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}
P is no longer reachable from S', so delete it. (CNF does not forbid useless nonterminals, but there is no reason to keep one.)


                  
                  Step 5 
                  
                

The order matters. Processing S' before S copies S‘s rules while S\to P is still among them: S'\to SS\mid P\mid\varepsilon, and the unit rule S'\to P survives into the “final” grammar — same language, but not in CNF.


Step 6 — protect terminals. In each right side of length 2, replace a terminal a by a new nonterminal T_a with the rule T_a\to a. Rules A\to a stay as they are (B\to\mathtt{1}).


                  
                  Answer (a) — the grammar in Chomsky normal form, start symbol S'
                  
                

\begin{aligned}
S'&\to SS\mid T_{\mathtt{0}}B\mid\varepsilon & S&\to SS\mid T_{\mathtt{0}}B & B&\to ST_{\mathtt{1}}\mid\mathtt{1}\\
T_{\mathtt{0}}&\to\mathtt{0} & T_{\mathtt{1}}&\to\mathtt{1}
\end{aligned}
S' generates the balanced strings, S the non-empty balanced strings, and B the strings x\mathtt{1} with x balanced.















































stepwhat changedgrammar afterwards0new start symbolS'\to S; \ S\to SS\mid P\mid\varepsilon; \ P\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}1P\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1} splitS'\to S; \ S\to SS\mid P\mid\varepsilon; \ P\to\mathtt{0}B; \ B\to S\mathtt{1}2nullable: S, S'unchanged3\varepsilon-rules removedS'\to S\mid\varepsilon; \ S\to SS\mid S\mid P; \ P\to\mathtt{0}B; \ B\to S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}4self-loop S\to S deletedS'\to S\mid\varepsilon; \ S\to SS\mid P; \ P\to\mathtt{0}B; \ B\to S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}5unit rules removed, P deletedS'\to SS\mid\mathtt{0}B\mid\varepsilon; \ S\to SS\mid\mathtt{0}B; \ B\to S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}6terminals protectedthe answer above
(b) Checking the result
Syntax. S' appears on no right side; S'\to\varepsilon is the only \varepsilon-rule; every other rule is two nonterminals or one terminal. ✓
Language. S'\to\varepsilon gives \varepsilon; S'\to T_{\mathtt{0}}B gives \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} with x balanced; S'\to SS gives the concatenations of two non-empty balanced strings. These are all the balanced strings: cut a non-empty balanced string after its shortest non-empty balanced prefix; if that prefix is the whole string, the string is \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{1} with x balanced, and otherwise it is a concatenation of two non-empty balanced strings. The same argument shows that S generates the non-empty ones. ✓
Short strings. Test a few strings in each intermediate grammar as you go: \varepsilon, 01, 0011, 0101 must be generated, 0, 10, 0110 must not. A step that changes the language usually fails one of them at once — forgetting B\to\mathtt{1} fails 01.
A derivation. In CNF, every derivation of a string of length n\ge1 has exactly 2n-1 steps. For 0011:
S'\rightsquigarrow T_{\mathtt{0}}B\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}B\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}ST_{\mathtt{1}}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}T_{\mathtt{0}}BT_{\mathtt{1}}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}BT_{\mathtt{1}}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{001}T_{\mathtt{1}}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0011},
seven steps, 2\cdot4-1. ✓


                  
                  How a conversion is checked 
                  
                

No standard rubric targets CNF conversions. A conversion goes wrong in one of two visible ways: the result is not in CNF (a leftover unit rule, an \varepsilon-rule for a nonterminal other than the start symbol, a terminal in a rule of length 2), or it generates a different language — and a forgotten variant in step 3 usually changes infinitely many strings, as B\to\mathtt{1} does here. On the grammar rubric’s scale (2 for syntax, 8 for correctness), infinitely many wrong strings cost all the correctness points. Writing down every intermediate grammar is what lets you test each step on short strings.


Sources for this page
The grammar is a variant, with an explicit unit rule, of the balanced-parentheses grammar of Erickson, Models of Computation, §5.4, and the algorithm is the book’s §5.9, in our own words; the problem, the intermediate grammars, the traps and their consequences are ours. Checked by tools/checks/problems_2.py: every intermediate grammar generates exactly the balanced strings of length at most 12, the nullable set, the CNF test for the final grammar, the languages of S and B, the decomposition of balanced strings, the derivation of 0011, and both trap scenarios (no B\to\mathtt{1}; the wrong order in step 5).

problems/designing-a-turing-machine.title: Worked problem — Designing a Turing machine
problems/designing-a-turing-machine.content:
Problem · a Turing-machine design exercise (Chapter 6 material, on the final exam) · uses §6.2, §6.3, §6.6 · concepts: turing-machines, acceptable-and-decidable


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let \textsf{Copy} = \{w\mathtt{\#}w \mid w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^*\} over the input alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{\#}\}. For example, 01#01 and # are in \textsf{Copy}; 01#10, 0#0# and \varepsilon are not.
(a) Describe a single-tape Turing machine that decides \textsf{Copy}: the algorithm in English, the states with their meanings, and the full transition table.
(b) Trace your machine on 01#01, and say where it rejects 01#00.
(c) Explain why it halts on every input, and show that its running time is \Theta(n^2) for inputs of length n.


(a) The machine
Idea. \textsf{Copy} is not even context-free (a classic fact whose proof is beyond this course), so no grammar or stack can check it — but a Turing machine can, by comparing the two halves one symbol at a time and zigzagging across the #. It cannot remember w, but it can remember one symbol in its state and mark the symbols it has finished with.


                  
                  The algorithm in English 
                  
                

Repeat rounds. In each round:

Take the leftmost unmarked symbol of the left half, overwrite it with x, and remember it in the state. If the # comes first instead, the left half is used up: go to step 5.
Carry it right, past the rest of the left half, to the #.
Seek past the marked symbols to the right of the # to the first unmarked one. It must be the remembered symbol: mark it with x. Anything else — the other symbol, a blank, a second # — means reject.
Walk back left, past the marked symbols and the #, then past the unmarked rest of the left half to the rightmost x; step right and start the next round.
Check that every symbol right of the # is marked: scan right over xs, accept at the first blank, reject at anything else.

If the input has no #, step 2 runs into a blank: reject.


The tape alphabet is \Gamma = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{\#},\mathtt{x},\square\}. The states and what each one knows:





































statemeaning\textit{start}the head is on the leftmost unmarked symbol of the left half, or on the # if there is none\mathit{carry0}, \mathit{carry1}just marked a 0 (a 1) of the left half; moving right to the #\mathit{seek0}, \mathit{seek1}right of the #, skipping marked symbols; the next unmarked symbol must be a 0 (a 1)\mathit{backR}just marked the match; moving left through the right half to the #\mathit{backL}moving left through the unmarked part of the left half to the rightmost x\mathit{check}the left half is used up; every symbol right of the # must be marked\textit{accept}, \textit{reject}halting states
In the table, ”—” means “write back the symbol that was read”. Missing transitions reject.





















































































































































statereadwritemovenext statecomment\textit{start}\mathtt{0}\mathtt{x}+1\mathit{carry0}take a 0\mathtt{1}\mathtt{x}+1\mathit{carry1}take a 1\mathtt{\#}—+1\mathit{check}left half used up\mathit{carry0}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}—+1\mathit{carry0}through the left half\mathtt{\#}—+1\mathit{seek0}\mathit{carry1}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}—+1\mathit{carry1}\mathtt{\#}—+1\mathit{seek1}\mathit{seek0}\mathtt{x}—+1\mathit{seek0}skip matched symbols\mathtt{0}\mathtt{x}-1\mathit{backR}a match: mark it\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{x}—+1\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{1}\mathtt{x}-1\mathit{backR}\mathit{backR}\mathtt{x}—-1\mathit{backR}back to the #\mathtt{\#}—-1\mathit{backL}\mathit{backL}\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}—-1\mathit{backL}back to the last x\mathtt{x}—+1\textit{start}next round\mathit{check}\mathtt{x}—+1\mathit{check}\square—+1\textit{accept}everything matched
That is 20 transitions. The rejections are exactly the missing ones: \textit{start} on \square (the empty input has no #); \mathit{carry0} or \mathit{carry1} on \square (no #); \mathit{seek0} on 1 or \mathit{seek1} on 0 (a mismatch); either \mathit{seek} state on \square (the right half is too short) or on # (a second #); \mathit{check} on 0 or 1 (the right half is too long) or on # (a second #).

state diagram with states start, carry0, carry1, seek0, seek1, backR, backL, check, acceptmissing transitions go to reject0/x,+11/x,+1#;+10,1;+10,1;+1#;+1#;+1x;+1x;+10/x,−11/x,−1x;−1#;−10,1;−1x;+1x;+1□;+1startcarry0seek0carry1seek1backLbackRcheckacceptA Turing machine that decides {w#w}. Each round crosses off the next symbol of the left half (start), carries it across the # in the state (carry0/carry1), crosses off the matching symbol of the right half (seek0/seek1), and walks back (backR, then backL). A label a/b,±1 means read a, write b, move; 0,1;−1 means read 0 or 1, leave it, move left.


                  
                  Design traps 
                  
                


Falling off the left end. \mathit{backL} walks left until it sees an x, and that x always exists: cell 0 holds x from the machine’s first move on (an input that starts with # never reaches \mathit{backL}). A machine that walks left “to the beginning of the tape” cannot see the beginning — it crashes there (§6.2).
Junk inputs. “Decides” means halting with the right answer on every input: \varepsilon, 0#, ##, 0#0#, 01, not just strings with mismatched halves. Here each of them ends in a missing transition; list the cases, as above, and test them.
Silent missing transitions. They reject only if you say so. Write “missing transitions go to reject” (the book’s convention) — or give every transition.
One mark for both halves. Using the same x on both sides works because the # separates them and the marks of the left half form a prefix: the first x that \mathit{backL} meets is the last symbol taken.



(b) Traces


                  
                  Trace on 01#01
                  
                

The underlined symbol is the one under the head. The machine accepts after 18 steps.





























































































stepstatetapestepstatetape0\textit{start}\underline{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{1\#01}10\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{xx\#x}\underline{\mathtt{1}}1\mathit{carry0}\mathtt{x}\underline{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{\#01}11\mathit{backR}\mathtt{xx\#}\underline{\mathtt{x}}\mathtt{x}2\mathit{carry0}\mathtt{x1}\underline{\mathtt{\#}}\mathtt{01}12\mathit{backR}\mathtt{xx}\underline{\mathtt{\#}}\mathtt{xx}3\mathit{seek0}\mathtt{x1\#}\underline{\mathtt{0}}\mathtt{1}13\mathit{backL}\mathtt{x}\underline{\mathtt{x}}\mathtt{\#xx}4\mathit{backR}\mathtt{x1}\underline{\mathtt{\#}}\mathtt{x1}14\textit{start}\mathtt{xx}\underline{\mathtt{\#}}\mathtt{xx}5\mathit{backL}\mathtt{x}\underline{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{\#x1}15\mathit{check}\mathtt{xx\#}\underline{\mathtt{x}}\mathtt{x}6\mathit{backL}\underline{\mathtt{x}}\mathtt{1\#x1}16\mathit{check}\mathtt{xx\#x}\underline{\mathtt{x}}7\textit{start}\mathtt{x}\underline{\mathtt{1}}\mathtt{\#x1}17\mathit{check}\mathtt{xx\#xx}\underline{\square}8\mathit{carry1}\mathtt{xx}\underline{\mathtt{\#}}\mathtt{x1}18\textit{accept}\mathtt{xx\#xx}\square\underline{\square}9\mathit{seek1}\mathtt{xx\#}\underline{\mathtt{x}}\mathtt{1}


Rejecting 01#00. The first round matches the two 0s exactly as above (steps 0–7, ending with \textit{start} on cell 1 and tape \mathtt{x1\#x0}). In the second round \mathit{carry1} crosses the #, \mathit{seek1} skips the x in cell 3 and reads 0 in cell 4 at step 10, where it needs a 1. There is no transition for (\mathit{seek1}, 0), so step 11 goes to \textit{reject}.
(c) Halting and running time
It halts on every input. Each round marks one more symbol to the left of the first #, so there are at most n rounds. Within a round, every phase moves in one direction and stops at a symbol that is guaranteed to be there, or rejects: \mathit{carry} and \mathit{seek} move right and reject on a blank, so they never pass cell n, the first blank; \mathit{backR} stops at the # it crossed on the way right; \mathit{backL} stops at an x. The final \mathit{check} moves right and stops by cell n as well.
At most O(n^2) steps. A round sweeps right from its starting cell to at most cell n and back, at most 2n+2 steps; with at most n rounds and a final scan of at most n+2 steps, the machine halts within 2n^2+3n+2 steps on every input of length n.
Exactly 2(k+1)^2 steps on w\mathtt{\#}w. Let \lvert w\rvert = k, so n = 2k+1. Round i (1\le i\le k) starts on cell i-1:

\textit{start} marks w_i, and \mathit{carry} crosses the other k-i unmarked symbols of the left half and the #: k-i+2 steps;
\mathit{seek} crosses the i-1 marked symbols right of the # and marks the next one: i steps;
\mathit{backR} crosses those i-1 marks and the #: i steps;
\mathit{backL} crosses the k-i unmarked symbols and reads the x on cell i-1: k-i+1 steps.

Every round therefore takes 2k+3 steps, whatever i is. The last phase — \textit{start} reads the #, \mathit{check} crosses k marks and reads the blank — takes k+2. In all,
k(2k+3) + k + 2 = 2k^2+4k+2 = 2(k+1)^2 = \frac{(n+1)^2}{2}\ \text{steps}.
For 01#01 (k = 2) that is 18, as in the trace: rounds of 7 steps end at steps 7 and 14. Even lengths have no string w\mathtt{\#}w, but w\mathtt{\#}w\mathtt{0} (n = 2k+2) runs the same k rounds and is rejected when \mathit{check} reads the final 0: again 2(k+1)^2 = n^2/2 steps.


                  
                  Answer (c) 
                  
                

The machine halts on every input of length n within 2n^2+3n+2 steps, and on w\mathtt{\#}w with \lvert w\rvert = k it takes exactly 2(k+1)^2 = (n+1)^2/2 steps (for even n, w\mathtt{\#}w\mathtt{0} takes n^2/2). So its worst-case running time is \Theta(n^2).


Could a cleverer one-tape machine do better? Not asymptotically. Every one-tape machine for \textsf{Copy} needs \Omega(n^2) steps in the worst case — the classic crossing-sequence argument, the same one behind the book’s remark about marked palindromes in §6.6 — while a machine with two tapes decides it in O(n) time: copy w to the second tape, then compare. The quadratic time is the price of a single head, not of a careless design.


                  
                  Time-analysis traps 
                  
                


Counting rounds only. There are about n/2 rounds, and each one walks across the # and back, about n steps: \Theta(n) rounds of \Theta(n) steps.
\Theta needs both bounds. The O(n^2) upper bound alone is not \Theta(n^2); the exact count on w\mathtt{\#}w supplies the matching lower bound.
n is the whole input length, # included: n = 2k+1 for w\mathtt{\#}w.





                  
                  On the exams 
                  
                

Turing machines (Chapter 6) are tested on the final exam only. The course’s standard rubrics have no separate entry for Turing-machine design, so take the DFA rubric’s demands as the guide: a complete, unambiguous description — every state with its meaning, every transition or an explicit “missing transitions reject” — plus a check of the edge cases (\varepsilon, no #, two #s, halves of different lengths). Describe the algorithm in English first; the table is then routine.


Sources for this page
\{w\mathtt{\#}w\} is a classic example language for Turing machines (and a standard example of a decidable language that is not context-free); the machine, its table, the traces and the exact step count are ours, in the conventions of Erickson, Models of Computation, §§6.2–6.3. The \Omega(n^2) lower bound for one-tape machines is a classic crossing-sequence result, cited here and not proved; the book states the analogous fact for marked palindromes in §6.6. Checked by tools/checks/problems_2.py: the machine accepts exactly \textsf{Copy} and halts on all 88,573 inputs over \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{\#}\} of length at most 10, within the stated bound; it takes 2(k+1)^2 steps on every w\mathtt{\#}w with k\le7, in rounds of 2k+3 steps, and as many on every w\mathtt{\#}w\mathtt{0}; and both traces are as shown.

problems/fooling-set-and-grammar-for-one.title: Worked problem — A fooling set and a grammar for one language
problems/fooling-set-and-grammar-for-one.content:
Problem · style of the Midterm 1 non-regularity-and-grammar problem · uses §3.8, §5.3 · concepts: fooling-sets, context-free-grammars


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let L = \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{0}^k \mid i, j, k\ge0 \text{ and } j = i+k\}: a run of 0s, a run of 1s and a run of 0s (each possibly empty), with exactly as many 1s as 0s in total. For example, \varepsilon, 01, 10, 0110 and 001110 are in L; 0, 1, 0101 and 1001 are not.
(a) Prove that L is not regular.
(b) Give a context-free grammar for L. Describe the language of each nonterminal, and argue briefly that the grammar generates exactly L.


What any algorithm for L must remember. Reading 0000…, a machine for L has to remember how many 0s it has seen: after \mathtt{0}^m the continuation \mathtt{1}^m must be accepted, and \mathtt{1}^n for n\ne m must not. An unbounded count is exactly what a fooling set exploits. A grammar, on the other hand, can match symbols from the outside in, and every string of L splits into two such nested pieces:
\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^{j}\mathtt{0}^k = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^{i+k}\mathtt{0}^k = \big(\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\big)\big(\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k\big).
(a) Not regular: a fooling set
Idea. Take F = \mathtt{0}^*: different numbers of leading 0s need different numbers of 1s. For x = \mathtt{0}^m, the suffix z = \mathtt{1}^m completes x to a string of L (with k = 0). To show that yz is not in L, do not fight with the decomposition of yz into runs; use a property that every string of L has: equally many 0s and 1s, since \#(\mathtt{0},w) = i+k = j = \#(\mathtt{1},w).


                  
                  Proof of (a) — model answer 
                  
                

Let F = \mathtt{0}^* = \{\mathtt{0}^n \mid n\ge0\}. Let x and y be arbitrary distinct strings in F. Then x = \mathtt{0}^m and y = \mathtt{0}^n for some integers m, n\ge0 with m\ne n. Let z = \mathtt{1}^m.

xz = \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^m\in L: take i = m, j = m and k = 0; then j = i+k.
yz = \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^m\notin L: every string \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{0}^k of L contains i+k 0s and j = i+k 1s, equally many; but yz contains n 0s and m\ne n 1s.

So z distinguishes x and y, and F is a fooling set for L. Because F is infinite, L is not regular. \blacksquare




                  
                  Where (a) loses points 
                  
                


Ruling out one decomposition instead of all of them. ”yz = \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^m\mathtt{0}^0 and m\ne n+0” checks just one way to write yz as \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{0}^k. When m = 0, yz = \mathtt{0}^n splits as \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^0\mathtt{0}^k in n+1 ways, and the proof must show that none of them has j = i+k (each has j = 0 < n = i+k). The counting argument handles every decomposition at once.
Reusing the statement’s letters. Writing x = \mathtt{0}^i and y = \mathtt{0}^j collides with the i and j in the definition of L, and "j = i+k" then means two different things. Pick fresh names.
One example pair. “0 and 00 are distinguished by 1” proves nothing about the other pairs; the argument must work for arbitrary m\ne n.
A finite set. \{\varepsilon, \mathtt{0}, \mathtt{00}\} is a fooling set, but it only proves that every DFA for L has at least 3 states — and earns no credit as a non-regularity proof.



An alternative: closure. If L were regular, then L\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* would be regular too (Corollary 3.4). A string of L with no 0 after a 1 has k = 0 (or it has no 1 at all, and then i = k = 0), so L\cap\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^* = \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n \mid n\ge0\}, which is not regular by Lemma 3.6. That proof is correct too — but when the exam asks for a fooling set, give the fooling set.
(b) A grammar: two nested halves side by side
Idea. Split the run of 1s: the first i 1s match the leading 0s, and the last k match the trailing 0s. Each half is a nested language like the book’s \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n\}, and one start rule puts the halves next to each other.


                  
                  Answer (b) 
                  
                

S\to AB\qquad\qquad A\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\mid\varepsilon\qquad\qquad B\to\mathtt{1}B\mathtt{0}\mid\varepsilon

A generates \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i \mid i\ge0\}: some 0s followed by equally many 1s.
B generates \{\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k \mid k\ge0\}: some 1s followed by equally many 0s.
S generates L: a string generated by A followed by a string generated by B.




parse tree: S with children A and B; A derives 0 0 epsilon 1 1, B derives 1 epsilon 000εA1A1A1εB0BSA ⇝* 0011 = 0²1²B ⇝* 10 = 1¹0¹The parse tree of 001110 = 0²1³0¹. S → AB cuts the string into 0i1i = 0011 (from A) and 1k0k = 10 (from B); the middle run 111 is shared between the two halves. Leaves read left to right spell the string (ε contributes nothing).
Why the grammar is right.

The nonterminals. A is the book’s grammar C\to\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{0}C\mathtt{1} under another name, so L(A) = \{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i \mid i\ge0\} by Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2. B is the same grammar with 0 and 1 exchanged, so the same two lemmas (with the symbols exchanged) give L(B) = \{\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k \mid k\ge0\}.
L(S)\subseteq L. Every derivation from S begins S\rightsquigarrow AB, and from then on A and B derive their parts independently; so L(S) = L(A)\bullet L(B). Each such string is \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\bullet\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^{i+k}\mathtt{0}^k, which is in L with j = i+k.
L\subseteq L(S). If w = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{0}^k\in L, then j = i+k, so w = \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\bullet\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k, and S\rightsquigarrow AB\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^iB\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^i\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k = w.

Check. \varepsilon: both halves empty. 10: A\rightsquigarrow\varepsilon and B\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{1}B\mathtt{0}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{10}. 0110 = 01·10. And 0101 cannot be generated: every generated string has the shape \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*.


                  
                  Where (b) loses points 
                  
                


Nesting instead of concatenating. S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid T, T\to\mathtt{1}T\mathtt{0}\mid\varepsilon puts the \mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k block inside the \mathtt{0}^i\cdots\mathtt{1}^i block, so it generates \mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k\mathtt{1}^i: it produces 0101 \notin L and misses 0110 \in L. Wrong on infinitely many strings, so no correctness credit.
Losing the empty halves. With A\to\mathtt{0}A\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{01} and B\to\mathtt{1}B\mathtt{0}\mid\mathtt{10} neither half can be empty, so the grammar misses \varepsilon, 01, 10 and every \mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^n — again infinitely many strings.
A grammar for a bigger language. S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{1}\mid\mathtt{1}S\mathtt{0}\mid SS\mid\varepsilon generates every string with equally many 0s and 1s, including 0101 and 1001. Equal counts are necessary for L, not sufficient: the shape \mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^* matters too.
Descriptions that are not self-contained. ”B does the second part” says nothing. ”B generates exactly the strings \mathtt{1}^k\mathtt{0}^k with k\ge0” does.





                  
                  How the problem is graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams pair a non-regularity proof with a grammar for the same language. The fooling-set proof (out of 10): 4 for an explicit infinite set that really is a fooling set — a finite set earns nothing — and 6 for the argument with arbitrary distinct x and y: 2 for an explicit suffix z, 2 for showing that one of xz, yz is in L, and 2 for showing that the other is not. The grammar (out of 10): 2 for syntax and 8 for correctness, with the same deductions as for regular expressions (one mistake, a few wrong strings, or all 8 points for infinitely many wrong strings). Homework also requires a self-contained description of every nonterminal’s language; ambiguity is not penalized. See how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
\{\mathtt{0}^i\mathtt{1}^j\mathtt{0}^k \mid j = i+k\} is a classic textbook-style example, worked here in our own words (the course’s practice exams use a different three-run language). The fooling-set template and Lemma 3.6 are from Erickson, Models of Computation, §3.8, and Lemmas 5.1–5.2 from §5.3. Checked by tools/checks/problems_1.py: the grammar and both nonterminals’ languages on all strings of length at most 12; every fooling-set pair \mathtt{0}^m, \mathtt{0}^n with m\ne n up to 18, including the case m = 0; the equal-count fact and the closure identity on all strings of length at most 14; the examples and the parse tree’s split; and each wrong grammar’s witnesses.

problems/index.title: Worked problems
problems/index.content:
Each problem page states the problem, solves it the way a strong student would write it on the exam — structure first, then the construction or proof, then a check — and calls out the trap at each step and how the rubric would grade it. They are original problems in the style of the course’s exams; none is copied from an exam, a homework or the book. Every automaton, expression, grammar and Turing machine on them is checked by a script, and every page was re-solved from its statement by an independent reviewer.

Four of the five problem types of the Midterm 1 format — language transformations, induction, fooling set plus grammar, DFA plus regular expression — have a worked counterpart above; the fifth, true or false with a one-sentence justification, is drilled by the quick checks that open every practice page.
