problems/induction-on-a-recursive-string.title: Worked problem — Induction on a recursive string function
problems/induction-on-a-recursive-string.content:
Problem · style of the Midterm 1 induction problem (a newly defined recursive string function) · uses §1.3, more recursive functions · concepts: induction-on-strings, strings


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

For every binary string w, define
\textsf{sort}(w) := \begin{cases} \varepsilon & \text{if } w = \varepsilon\\ \mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(x) & \text{if } w = \mathtt{0}x\\ \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1} & \text{if } w = \mathtt{1}x\end{cases}
for every string x. For example, \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{0110}) = \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1010}) = \mathtt{0011}. You may use Lemmas 1.1–1.3 without proof.
(a) Prove that \lvert\textsf{sort}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert for every binary string w.
(b) Prove that \textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(w)) = \textsf{sort}(w) for every binary string w.


Unfold the definition before proving anything. On a short string:
\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{101}) = \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{01})\bullet\mathtt{1} = \big(\mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1})\big)\bullet\mathtt{1} = \Big(\mathtt{0}\cdot\big(\textsf{sort}(\varepsilon)\bullet\mathtt{1}\big)\Big)\bullet\mathtt{1} = (\mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{1})\bullet\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{011}.
A 0 at the front stays in front (second case); a 1 at the front is taken off and re-attached at the very end, after the rest has been sorted (third case). So \textsf{sort}(w) is w with every 0 moved before every 1, \textsf{sort}(w) = \mathtt{0}^{\#(\mathtt{0},w)}\mathtt{1}^{\#(\mathtt{1},w)}, and both claims are believable. The job is to prove them from the definition. Notice the two different dots: the second case puts one symbol in front (\cdot, a pair), the third glues two strings (\bullet, concatenation) — that difference is what each proof has to handle.
(a) Sorting keeps the length
Idea. The definition has three cases, so the proof has three cases. The cases w = \varepsilon and w = \mathtt{0}x unfold with the definitions alone. The case w = \mathtt{1}x ends in a concatenation, and the definition of length peels the first symbol of a string, not the last — so it needs Lemma 1.2, \lvert y\bullet z\rvert = \lvert y\rvert + \lvert z\rvert.


                  
                  Proof of (a) — model answer 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary binary string. Assume that \lvert\textsf{sort}(x)\rvert = \lvert x\rvert for every binary string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert. There are three cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. \textsf{sort}(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon by definition, so \lvert\textsf{sort}(w)\rvert = \lvert\varepsilon\rvert = \lvert w\rvert.
Case w = \mathtt{0}x for some string x. Then \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert - 1 < \lvert w\rvert, so the induction hypothesis applies to x, and
\begin{aligned}
\lvert\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{0}x)\rvert &= \lvert\mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(x)\rvert && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}\\
&= 1 + \lvert\textsf{sort}(x)\rvert && \text{by definition of } \lvert\cdot\rvert\\
&= 1 + \lvert x\rvert && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= \lvert\mathtt{0}x\rvert && \text{by definition of } \lvert\cdot\rvert.
\end{aligned}
Case w = \mathtt{1}x for some string x. Again \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, and
\begin{aligned}
\lvert\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1}x)\rvert &= \lvert\textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}\rvert && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}\\
&= \lvert\textsf{sort}(x)\rvert + \lvert\mathtt{1}\rvert && \text{by Lemma 1.2}\\
&= \lvert x\rvert + 1 && \text{by the induction hypothesis, and } \lvert\mathtt{1}\rvert = 1 + \lvert\varepsilon\rvert = 1\\
&= \lvert\mathtt{1}x\rvert && \text{by definition of } \lvert\cdot\rvert.
\end{aligned}
The three cases cover every binary string, and in each case \lvert\textsf{sort}(w)\rvert = \lvert w\rvert. \blacksquare




                  
                  Where (a) loses points 
                  
                


Two cases where the definition has three. Writing “case w = ax” is fine only if you then split on a = \mathtt{0} and a = \mathtt{1}: \textsf{sort} does different things in the two cases, and an argument that treats them together proves nothing about either.
Treating \bullet like \cdot. ”\lvert\textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}\rvert = 1 + \lvert\textsf{sort}(x)\rvert by definition of length” cites the wrong reason: the definition peels the first symbol, and this \mathtt{1} is the last. Cite Lemma 1.2.
A vague hypothesis. “Assume it works for smaller strings” does not say what works. Write the claim out for every string shorter than w; that sentence is worth two rubric points by itself.



(b) Sorting twice changes nothing
Idea — and where the obvious attempt gets stuck. Try the same three cases. The first two go through (they are written out in the proof below). The third does not:
\textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1}x)) = \textsf{sort}\big(\textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}\big) = \ ?
The definition of \textsf{sort} looks at the first symbol of its argument, and the first symbol of \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1} is not the \mathtt{1} just attached (unless x = \varepsilon). The induction hypothesis does not help either: it is about \textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(y)), not about \textsf{sort}(y\bullet\mathtt{1}), and the string \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1} has length \lvert x\rvert + 1 = \lvert w\rvert (by part (a) and Lemma 1.2), so it is not even shorter than w. What is missing is a fact about sorting a string that ends in \mathtt{1} — a final \mathtt{1} is already where \textsf{sort} would put it. State that fact as a lemma, prove it first, and the stuck case becomes one line.


                  
                  Lemma 
                  
                

\textsf{sort}(y\bullet\mathtt{1}) = \textsf{sort}(y)\bullet\mathtt{1} for every binary string y.




                  
                  Proof of the lemma 
                  
                

Let y be an arbitrary binary string. Assume that \textsf{sort}(z\bullet\mathtt{1}) = \textsf{sort}(z)\bullet\mathtt{1} for every binary string z with \lvert z\rvert < \lvert y\rvert. There are three cases.
Case y = \varepsilon. By the definition of \bullet, \varepsilon\bullet\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{1} = \mathtt{1}\cdot\varepsilon, so the third case of the definition of \textsf{sort} (with x = \varepsilon) gives \textsf{sort}(\varepsilon\bullet\mathtt{1}) = \textsf{sort}(\varepsilon)\bullet\mathtt{1}.
Case y = \mathtt{0}z for some string z. Then \lvert z\rvert < \lvert y\rvert, and
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{0}z\bullet\mathtt{1}) &= \textsf{sort}\big(\mathtt{0}\cdot(z\bullet\mathtt{1})\big) && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}\\
&= \mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(z\bullet\mathtt{1}) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}\\
&= \mathtt{0}\cdot\big(\textsf{sort}(z)\bullet\mathtt{1}\big) && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= \big(\mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(z)\big)\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}\\
&= \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{0}z)\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}.
\end{aligned}
Case y = \mathtt{1}z for some string z. Then \lvert z\rvert < \lvert y\rvert, and
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1}z\bullet\mathtt{1}) &= \textsf{sort}\big(\mathtt{1}\cdot(z\bullet\mathtt{1})\big) && \text{by definition of } {\bullet}\\
&= \textsf{sort}(z\bullet\mathtt{1})\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}\\
&= \big(\textsf{sort}(z)\bullet\mathtt{1}\big)\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1}z)\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}.
\end{aligned}
In all three cases, \textsf{sort}(y\bullet\mathtt{1}) = \textsf{sort}(y)\bullet\mathtt{1}. \blacksquare




                  
                  Proof of (b) — model answer 
                  
                

Let w be an arbitrary binary string. Assume that \textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(x)) = \textsf{sort}(x) for every binary string x with \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert. There are three cases.
Case w = \varepsilon. \textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(\varepsilon)) = \textsf{sort}(\varepsilon), because \textsf{sort}(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon.
Case w = \mathtt{0}x for some string x. Then \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, and
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{0}x)) &= \textsf{sort}\big(\mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(x)\big) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}\\
&= \mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(x)) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}\\
&= \mathtt{0}\cdot\textsf{sort}(x) && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{0}x) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}.
\end{aligned}
Case w = \mathtt{1}x for some string x. Then \lvert x\rvert < \lvert w\rvert, and
\begin{aligned}
\textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1}x)) &= \textsf{sort}\big(\textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}\big) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}\\
&= \textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(x))\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by the lemma, with } y = \textsf{sort}(x)\\
&= \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1} && \text{by the induction hypothesis}\\
&= \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1}x) && \text{by definition of } \textsf{sort}.
\end{aligned}
In all three cases, \textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(w)) = \textsf{sort}(w). \blacksquare


Look at how the two tools split the work. The induction hypothesis is applied only to x, which is shorter than w. The lemma is applied with y = \textsf{sort}(x), to the string \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}, which is exactly as long as w — but the lemma holds for every string y, so no length condition is needed.


                  
                  Where (b) loses points 
                  
                


Applying the hypothesis to \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}. That string is as long as w, so the hypothesis does not cover it — and even for a shorter string the hypothesis would only give \textsf{sort}(\textsf{sort}(y)) = \textsf{sort}(y), which is not the step needed. This is the rubric’s “correct use of the hypothesis” item.
Asserting the lemma. “A 1 at the end is already in place” is the right intuition and not a proof. The lemma is not a result from lecture, so it needs its own induction; on an exam, prove it right before you use it.
Proving a false lemma. Test a lemma on a two-symbol example first. The look-alike \textsf{sort}(y\bullet\mathtt{0}) = \textsf{sort}(y)\bullet\mathtt{0} fails at y = \mathtt{1}: \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{10}) = \mathtt{01}, but \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{1})\bullet\mathtt{0} = \mathtt{10}. The same example refutes \textsf{sort}(x\bullet y) = \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\textsf{sort}(y).



Another route, and why it is not shorter. You could first prove the closed form \textsf{sort}(w) = \mathtt{0}^{\#(\mathtt{0},w)}\mathtt{1}^{\#(\mathtt{1},w)} and then \textsf{sort}(\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n) = \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^n. That is two inductions as well, plus facts about powers such as \mathtt{1}^n\bullet\mathtt{1} = \mathtt{1}^{n+1}. When a direct induction gets stuck, ask: what fact about the stuck expression would let me continue? The answer is usually a lemma as small as the one above — and it is usually proved by the same kind of induction.


                  
                  How this problem is graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams devote a whole problem to a newly defined string function like \textsf{sort}. A proof is graded with the induction rubric, out of 10: 1 for starting from an arbitrary string; 2 for an explicitly stated strong hypothesis (weak induction is discouraged); 2 for cases that cover every string — three here, mirroring the definition; 1 for the base case; 2 for applying the hypothesis correctly — to x, never to \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}; 2 for the remaining details, with every line justified by a definition, a lemma or the hypothesis. A lemma you need is part of your proof and is graded with it; results from lecture, the course notes, labs or homework solutions (Lemmas 1.1–1.3, for instance) may be cited without proof. “Clearly” draws scrutiny. See how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
An original problem in the style of the Midterm 1 induction problem; the function \textsf{sort}, both proofs, the lemma and the traps are ours (the course’s practice exams use other functions). The proof template and Lemma 1.2 are from Erickson, Models of Computation, §1.3. Checked by tools/checks/problems_1.py: the examples and the unfolding, part (a), the lemma, part (b) and the closed form on every binary string of length at most 14, the length of \textsf{sort}(x)\bullet\mathtt{1}, and the counterexamples in the traps.

problems/proving-what-a-grammar-generate.title: Worked problem — Proving what a grammar generates
problems/proving-what-a-grammar-generate.content:
Problem · a grammar-correctness proof: two inductions, graded with the induction rubric · uses §5.3 · concepts: context-free-grammars, induction-on-strings, parse-trees-and-ambiguity


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let G be the grammar with one nonterminal S and the rules
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\mid\mathtt{0}S\mid\varepsilon ,
and let L = \{\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} \mid m\ge n\ge 0\}: a block of 0s followed by an even number of 1s, with at least one 0 for every two 1s.
(a) Prove that L\subseteq L(G).
(b) Prove that L(G)\subseteq L.
(c) Is G ambiguous? Does that matter for (a) and (b)?


Test the claim before proving it. The strings of length at most 6 that G generates are \varepsilon, 0, 00, 011, 000, 0000, 0011, 00000, 00011, 000000, 000011, 001111 — exactly the strings \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} with m\ge n of that length. 0111 (an odd number of 1s) and 01111 (too few 0s) are correctly missing. Reading the rules explains why: S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11} adds one 0 and two 1s, and S\to\mathtt{0}S adds an extra 0, always on the outside.
(a) Everything in L is generated
Idea. Build a derivation from the outside in. If the string has 1s, peel off a 0 in front and 11 at the back (rule S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}); if it has none, peel off one 0 (rule S\to\mathtt{0}S). Induct on m, the number of 0s.


                  
                  Proof of (a) — model answer 
                  
                

Claim. S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} for all integers m\ge n\ge 0.
Let m and n be arbitrary integers with m\ge n\ge 0, and assume that S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^{m'}\mathtt{1}^{2n'} for all integers m'\ge n'\ge 0 with m'<m. There are three cases.
Case m = 0. Then n = 0, because 0\le n\le m. So \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} = \varepsilon, and S\rightsquigarrow\varepsilon by the rule S\to\varepsilon.
Case m\ge1 and n = 0. The pair (m-1, 0) satisfies m-1\ge0 and m-1<m, so the induction hypothesis gives S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^{m-1}. Hence
S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{0}^{m-1} = \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n},
by the rule S\to\mathtt{0}S and then the hypothesis, applied inside the context \mathtt{0}\,\underline{\ \ }.
Case m\ge1 and n\ge1. The pair (m-1, n-1) satisfies m-1\ge n-1\ge0 and m-1<m, so the hypothesis gives S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^{m-1}\mathtt{1}^{2n-2}. Hence
S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}\bullet\mathtt{0}^{m-1}\mathtt{1}^{2n-2}\bullet\mathtt{11} = \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n},
by the rule S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11} and then the hypothesis inside the context \mathtt{0}\,\underline{\ \ }\,\mathtt{11}.
The three cases cover every pair with m\ge n\ge0, and in each case S\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n}. \blacksquare


For m = 3, n = 1 the proof builds S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{000}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00011}: one \mathtt{0}\ldots\mathtt{11} layer, then the two extra 0s, then S\to\varepsilon.


                  
                  Where (a) loses points 
                  
                


Missing the case n = 0. The rule S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11} cannot produce a string without 1s, so \mathtt{0}^m needs its own case and its own rule. Inducting on n alone has the same hole: its base case n = 0 is the whole family \mathtt{0}^m, which needs a second induction.
Using the hypothesis without checking that it applies. Say why (m-1, n-1) is a legal pair: m-1\ge n-1 because m\ge n, n-1\ge0 because n\ge1, and m-1<m.
Only describing the derivation. “Use S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11} n times, then S\to\mathtt{0}S m-n times, then S\to\varepsilon” is the right idea; the induction is what turns it into a proof.



(b) Everything generated is in L
Idea. Take an arbitrary derivation apart at its first step — one case per rule. The string derived from the inner S is shorter than w, so the hypothesis applies to it.


                  
                  Proof of (b) — model answer 
                  
                

Claim. Every string w\in L(G) equals \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} for some integers m\ge n\ge0.
Let w be an arbitrary string in L(G), and fix a derivation S\rightsquigarrow^* w. Assume that every string x\in L(G) with \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert is in L. The derivation starts with one of the three rules for S.
Case S\to\varepsilon. Then the derivation is S\rightsquigarrow\varepsilon, so w = \varepsilon = \mathtt{0}^0\mathtt{1}^0, with m = n = 0.
Case S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}. Then the derivation is S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow^* w. The 0 and the 11 are terminals, so every later step rewrites the middle S or a symbol derived from it; hence w = \mathtt{0}x\mathtt{11} for some string x with S\rightsquigarrow^* x. So x\in L(G) and \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert-3<\lvert w\rvert, and the induction hypothesis gives x = \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} for some m\ge n\ge0. Then w = \mathtt{0}^{m+1}\mathtt{1}^{2(n+1)} with m+1\ge n+1\ge0, so w\in L.
Case S\to\mathtt{0}S. In the same way w = \mathtt{0}x with S\rightsquigarrow^* x and \lvert x\rvert = \lvert w\rvert-1<\lvert w\rvert, so x = \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} with m\ge n\ge0 by the hypothesis. Then w = \mathtt{0}^{m+1}\mathtt{1}^{2n} with m+1>m\ge n, so w\in L.
In all three cases, w\in L. \blacksquare


Where the \varepsilon-rule needs care. Two details make this induction work, and both concern \varepsilon.

The inner string may be empty. 011 has the derivation S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{011}, with x = \varepsilon. The hypothesis covers x = \varepsilon because it is about every shorter string, \varepsilon included; the base case is not a separate assumption but the case S\to\varepsilon of the same argument.
The inner string is strictly shorter — because every rule except S\to\varepsilon puts at least one terminal next to S. This is exactly what fails for a rule whose right side has only nonterminals: with S\to SS, one of the two halves can derive \varepsilon, the other is then all of w, and the hypothesis says nothing about it. For such grammars, fix a shortest derivation (a half that derives \varepsilon could then be cut out) or induct on the length of the derivation — see Careful with those epsilons and Lemma 5.3. (Here, adding S\to SS would also break the claim itself: S\rightsquigarrow SS\rightsquigarrow^*\mathtt{011}\bullet\mathtt{0} = \mathtt{0110}\notin L.)



                  
                  Where (b) loses points 
                  
                


Reading the rule off the string. ”w ends in 11, so its derivation starts with S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}” is false: 0011 also has the derivation S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0}S\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{00}S\mathtt{11}\rightsquigarrow\mathtt{0011}. Split into cases on the derivation you fixed, not on what w looks like.
Weak induction. A hypothesis only for strings of length \lvert w\rvert-1 does not cover the case S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11}, where x is three symbols shorter. Assume the claim for every shorter string.
Not justifying \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert — true here, but it is the reason the hypothesis applies, so say it; fatal in grammars with rules like S\to SS.
Checking only half of the definition of L. Membership of w = \mathtt{0}^{m+1}\mathtt{1}^{2(n+1)} needs both the shape (0s, then an even number of 1s) and the inequality m+1\ge n+1.



(c) Ambiguity
G is ambiguous: 0011 has two parse trees. In one, the root uses S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11} and the inner S uses S\to\mathtt{0}S and then S\to\varepsilon; in the other, the root uses S\to\mathtt{0}S and the inner S uses S\to\mathtt{0}S\mathtt{11} and then S\to\varepsilon. In general \mathtt{0}^m\mathtt{1}^{2n} has exactly \binom{m}{n} parse trees: a parse tree is a chain of m rules that each add one 0, followed by S\to\varepsilon, and any n of those m rules can be the ones that also add 11.
It does not matter. L(G) is a set of strings; (a) needs some derivation of each string of L, and (b) works for any derivation of each generated string. The grading rubrics do not penalize ambiguity either. If you want an unambiguous grammar anyway, produce the extra 0s first:
S\to\mathtt{0}S\mid T\qquad T\to\mathtt{0}T\mathtt{11}\mid\varepsilon .
Here T generates \{\mathtt{0}^n\mathtt{1}^{2n}\mid n\ge0\} and S puts the m-n extra 0s in front; every string of L has exactly one parse tree.


                  
                  How a proof like this is graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams ask for a grammar without a proof (homework also asks for a description of each nonterminal). A correctness proof like this one consists of two inductions, each graded with the standard induction rubric, out of 10: 1 for starting from an arbitrary object (an arbitrary pair m\ge n\ge0; an arbitrary string with a fixed derivation), 2 for an explicitly stated strong induction hypothesis, 2 for cases that cover everything (three in each direction here), 1 for the base case, 2 for using the hypothesis correctly — only on legal, smaller objects, which is what the checks m-1\ge n-1 and \lvert x\rvert<\lvert w\rvert are for — and 2 for the remaining details. “Clearly” draws scrutiny. See how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
A classic textbook-style exercise, written in our own words; the problem statement, both proofs, the traps, the parse-tree count and the unambiguous grammar are ours, and the proof pattern follows Lemmas 5.1–5.3 of Erickson, Models of Computation, §5.3. Checked by tools/checks/problems_2.py: L(G) = L on all strings of length at most 14, the derivation built in (a) for every m\ge n with m+2n\le16, the facts used in each case of (b), the alternative derivation of 0011, the S\to SS counterexample, the count \binom{m}{n} of parse trees, and the language and unambiguity of the second grammar.

problems/regular-expression-and-dfa-for-.title: Worked problem — A regular expression and a DFA for one language
problems/regular-expression-and-dfa-for-.content:
Problem · style of the Midterm 1 DFA-and-regular-expression problem · uses §2.3, §3.5 · concepts: dfa, regular-expressions


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let L be the set of binary strings in which the substring \mathtt{01} occurs exactly twice. For example, 0101, 01010, 1001101 and 00110011 are in L; \varepsilon, 01, 0110, 1100 and 010101 are not.
(a) Give a DFA that accepts L. Use mnemonic state names; no proof is required.
(b) Give a regular expression for L, and explain each part in English; no proof is required.


Look at a typical string first. Cut it into maximal runs: 1001101 = 1|00|11|0|1. An occurrence of 01 is exactly a place where a run of 0s ends and a run of 1s begins: two occurrences cannot overlap, and nothing else creates one. So w\in L exactly when w has two such boundaries — an optional run of 1s, then a run of 0s, a run of 1s, a run of 0s, a run of 1s, and an optional run of 0s:
w = \mathtt{1}^{a}\,\mathtt{0}^{b}\,\mathtt{1}^{c}\,\mathtt{0}^{d}\,\mathtt{1}^{e}\,\mathtt{0}^{f}\qquad\text{with } a, f\ge0 \text{ and } b, c, d, e\ge1 .
Both answers come from this picture: the DFA keeps track of which run it is in, and the regular expression writes the runs down one after the other.
(a) A DFA that counts the occurrences
Idea. Scan left to right with two variables: the number k of occurrences of 01 so far (0, 1, 2, or “too many”), and whether the last symbol read was a 0 — a 0 that the next 1 would turn into one more occurrence. That is 3\times2 states plus one for “too many”. Name each state by what it remembers: \textsf{ones}_k and \textsf{zeros}_k, where the subscript is the count.


                  
                  Answer (a) 
                  
                

Start state \textsf{ones}_0 (→); accepting states \textsf{ones}_2 and \textsf{zeros}_2 (*).





















































statemeaning: the input read so far …on \mathtt{0}on \mathtt{1}→ \textsf{ones}_0contains no 01, and is empty or ends in 1\textsf{zeros}_0\textsf{ones}_0\textsf{zeros}_0contains no 01, and ends in 0\textsf{zeros}_0\textsf{ones}_1\textsf{ones}_1contains 01 once, and ends in 1\textsf{zeros}_1\textsf{ones}_1\textsf{zeros}_1contains 01 once, and ends in 0\textsf{zeros}_1\textsf{ones}_2\textsf{ones}_2 *contains 01 twice, and ends in 1\textsf{zeros}_2\textsf{ones}_2\textsf{zeros}_2 *contains 01 twice, and ends in 0\textsf{zeros}_2\textsf{dead}\textsf{dead}contains 01 three or more times\textsf{dead}\textsf{dead}



seven-state DFA drawn as a chain: ones0, zeros0, ones1, zeros1, ones2, zeros2, then dead1001100110010,1ones0zeros0ones1zeros1ones2zeros2deadExactly two occurrences of 01. The subscript counts the occurrences of 01 read so far; ones means the input so far is empty or ends in 1, zeros that it ends in 0. A 0 moves from ones to zeros, and a 1 after a 0 completes one more 01. The accepting states are the two with subscript 2; a third 01 leads to the dump state dead.
The machine is a chain. A 0 moves from \textsf{ones}_k to \textsf{zeros}_k and then keeps it there; a 1 read in \textsf{zeros}_k completes an occurrence and moves on to \textsf{ones}_{k+1}. The third occurrence sends the machine to \textsf{dead}, which never leaves and never accepts.
Check. On 1001101 the machine visits \textsf{ones}_0, \textsf{ones}_0, \textsf{zeros}_0, \textsf{zeros}_0, \textsf{ones}_1, \textsf{ones}_1, \textsf{zeros}_1, \textsf{ones}_2 and accepts. On 010101 the third 1 arrives in \textsf{zeros}_2 and goes to \textsf{dead}: reject. On \varepsilon it stays in \textsf{ones}_0: reject, correctly — the empty string contains 01 zero times.
Is it minimal? Yes, although the problem does not ask. The strings \varepsilon, 0, 01, 010, 0101, 01010, 010101 reach the seven states in the order of the table, and every two of them have a distinguishing suffix — for example, 101 distinguishes \varepsilon from 0 (0101 \in L, 101 \notin L), and 1 distinguishes 01 from 010. So they form a fooling set of size 7, and no DFA for L has fewer states.


                  
                  Where DFA answers lose points 
                  
                


No dump state, and no sentence about it. Leaving out \textsf{dead} is fine only together with “all missing transitions go to a dump state”. Without that sentence, \textsf{zeros}_2 has no transition on 1 and the drawing is not a DFA.
An accepting sink. Merging \textsf{ones}_2, \textsf{zeros}_2 and \textsf{dead} into one accepting state that loops on everything is the DFA for “at least twice”: it accepts 010101.
Counting symbol changes. A machine that counts every switch between 0 and 1 counts 10 boundaries too: 0110 has two switches but only one 01.
States without meanings. Names like q_0,\dots,q_6 lose the mnemonic-name points even when the machine is right — and make your own mistakes harder to find.



(b) A regular expression, run by run
Idea. Write the runs of the typical string from left to right: an optional run of 1s, then (a run of 0s, a run of 1s) twice, then an optional run of 0s. “A run of 0s” means at least one 0, which is \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^* — in a regular expression, + means union, so there is no \mathtt{0}^+ shorthand.


                  
                  Answer (b) 
                  
                

\mathtt{1}^*\ \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\ \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\ \mathtt{0}^*

\mathtt{1}^* — the leading 1s, if any. No 0 comes before them, so they contain no 01. (The DFA sits in \textsf{ones}_0.)
\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^* — a non-empty run of 0s followed by a non-empty run of 1s; the boundary between the two runs is the first 01. (\textsf{zeros}_0, then \textsf{ones}_1.)
\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^* again — the second 01. (\textsf{zeros}_1, then \textsf{ones}_2.)
\mathtt{0}^* — the trailing 0s, if any. No 1 follows them, so they create no third 01. (\textsf{zeros}_2.)



Check, both directions. Nothing extra: inside a run there is no 01, and every other run boundary is a 10, so a matching string contains exactly the two marked occurrences. Nothing missing: the run decomposition above writes every string of L in exactly this shape. On examples: 1001101 matches as 1·00·11·0·1·\varepsilon; 0101 as \varepsilon·0·1·0·1·\varepsilon; \varepsilon does not match (the middle needs at least four symbols), and neither does 010101.


                  
                  Four tempting wrong answers 
                  
                































expressionwhat it actually describeswrong on(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{01}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*\mathtt{01}(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{1})^*01 occurs at least twice010101, and every (\mathtt{01})^n with n\ge3\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*01 occurs at most twice\varepsilon, and every \mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}^*the strings of L that start with 0misses 10101, and every \mathtt{1}^n\mathtt{0101}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*the strings of L that end in 1misses 01010, and every \mathtt{0101}\mathtt{0}^n
Each one is wrong on infinitely many strings, so each would get no correctness credit at all. The second is the ”\mathtt{0}^* where \mathtt{0}\mathtt{0}^* is needed” slip: a run of length zero is no run, and its “boundary” is no occurrence. The last two each leave out one of the optional runs at the ends.




                  
                  How the two answers are graded 
                  
                

On Midterm-1-style exams this is one problem: a DFA and a regular expression for the same language, with mnemonic state names and no proof. The DFA (rubric out of 10): 2 for an unambiguous, complete description — start arrow, double circles, every transition, or an explicit sentence about the omitted dump state; 6 for correctness; 2 for mnemonic state names. An NFA where a DFA was asked earns half credit. The regular expression (rubric out of 10): 2 for syntax and 8 for correctness, with exam deductions twice the homework ones — 2 for one mistake (typically a missing or extra \varepsilon), 4 for a few wrong strings, and all 8 when infinitely many strings are wrong, as for every expression in the trap above; \varnothing or \Sigma^* earns nothing. On homework, the English explanation of each part is required as well. See how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
An original problem in the style of the Midterm 1 DFA-and-regular-expression problem (the course’s practice exams use other languages). The DFA follows the design method of Erickson, Models of Computation, §3.5 (one state for each combination of values of a left-to-right scan’s variables), in our own words; the run-by-run regular expression is ours, in the style of the book’s examples in §2.3. Checked by tools/checks/problems_1.py: the DFA against a brute-force count of 01 on all strings of length at most 14 and exactly against a counting automaton built from the statement; every state meaning; the regular expression by exact equivalence; minimality and the 7-string fooling set; the example strings and runs; and the language of each wrong expression (exactly) with its witnesses.

problems/state-elimination-by-hand.title: Worked problem — State elimination by hand
problems/state-elimination-by-hand.content:
Problem · the regular-expression half of a Midterm-1-style DFA problem, done mechanically · uses §4.8 · concepts: state-elimination, regular-expressions, dfa


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let L = \{w\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}^* \mid \#(\mathtt{0},w)-\#(\mathtt{1},w)\text{ is divisible by } 3\}. For example, 0011, 000 and 1100 are in L; 0 and 011 are not.
(a) Give a DFA for L with mnemonic state names (no proof required).
(b) Turn your DFA into a regular expression for L by state elimination. Show the expression automaton after every elimination.
(c) Sanity-check the expression.
(d) Eliminate the states in a different order. What changes?


(a) A DFA that tracks the difference mod 3
Idea. Reading left to right, an algorithm only needs the difference \#(\mathtt{0})-\#(\mathtt{1}) of the prefix read so far, and only modulo 3: a 0 adds 1 and a 1 subtracts 1. A variable with three values is a DFA with three states.


                  
                  Answer (a) 
                  
                

States q_0, q_1, q_2, where q_i means “the prefix read so far has \#(\mathtt{0})-\#(\mathtt{1})\equiv i \pmod 3”. Start state q_0; accepting states \{q_0\}; \delta(q_i,\mathtt{0}) = q_{(i+1)\bmod 3} and \delta(q_i,\mathtt{1}) = q_{(i-1)\bmod 3}:





























statemeaning: difference so far\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}→ q_0 *\equiv 0q_1q_2q_1\equiv 1q_2q_0q_2\equiv 2, that is, \equiv -1q_0q_1


Check. 0011 visits q_0, q_1, q_2, q_1, q_0 and is accepted; 011 ends in q_2 and is rejected; the empty string stays in q_0 and is accepted (0-0 = 0).
(b) State elimination
The tool is state elimination (§4.8): give the automaton a start state s with no incoming edges and a target t with no outgoing edges, then remove the other states one at a time. Removing q replaces, for every remaining pair p, r — including p = r —
R(p\to r)\quad\text{by}\quad R(p\to r) + R(p\to q)\,R(q\to q)^*\,R(q\to r),
where a missing edge is \varnothing. When only s and t are left, R(s\to t) is the answer. We eliminate q_1, then q_2, then q_0: the state adjacent to s and t goes last (part (d) shows why).
Step 0 — new start and target. q_0 cannot serve as either: it has incoming edges, and it is accepting with outgoing edges. Add s\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}q_0 and q_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}t.

expression automaton: s, epsilon to q0, triangle q0 q1 q2 with 0-edges one way and 1-edges the other, q0 epsilon to tεε010101stq₀q₁q₂Step 0: the DFA as an expression automaton. State qi means “#0 − #1 ≡ i (mod 3)”: a 0 moves one step around the triangle, a 1 one step back. The new start s and target t are joined to q0 by ε-edges, so no edge enters s and none leaves t.


                  
                  Skipping step 0 
                  
                

If you eliminate q_1 and q_2 in the DFA itself, you are left with q_0 and a loop label R, and nothing tells you whether the answer is R, R^* or R^+. With s and t in place, the last elimination produces the right star by itself. Add them whenever the start state has incoming edges or the accepting state is not a single state without outgoing edges — that is, almost always.


Step 1 — eliminate q_1. There is no loop at q_1, so R(q_1\to q_1)^* = \varnothing^* = \varepsilon. The predecessors of q_1 are q_0 (label 0) and q_2 (label 1); its successors are q_2 (label 0) and q_0 (label 1). That gives four pairs:



































edge p\to rold labeldetour p\to q_1\to rnew labelq_0\to q_0\varnothing\mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{1}\mathtt{01}q_0\to q_2\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00}q_2\to q_0\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11}q_2\to q_2\varnothing\mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{0}\mathtt{10}
Step 2 — eliminate q_2. Its only predecessor and only successor is q_0, and it now has the loop 10, which gets starred:
R(q_0\to q_0) = \mathtt{01} + (\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11}).
Step 3 — eliminate q_0. Its predecessor is s and its successor is t, both by \varepsilon, and its loop is the label just computed:
R(s\to t) = \varepsilon\,\big(\mathtt{01}+(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11})\big)^*\,\varepsilon .

three expression automata: after eliminating q1, after eliminating q2, after eliminating q0after eliminating q₁after eliminating q₂after eliminating q₀(01+(1+00)(10)*(0+11))*ε01101+000+11εεε01+(1+00)(10)*(0+11)sq₀q₂tsq₀tstSteps 1–3: one state fewer each time. Eliminating q1 turns every detour through it into an edge label — including the round trips q0 → q1 → q0 (the loop 01) and q2 → q1 → q2 (the loop 10). Eliminating q2 folds its loop into a star; eliminating q0 leaves one edge, whose label is the answer.


                  
                  Answer (b) 
                  
                

L = L\Big(\big(\mathtt{01}+(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11})\big)^*\Big)




                  
                  Where elimination steps go wrong 
                  
                


Forgetting p = r. Two of the four new labels in step 1 are loops: the round trips q_0\to q_1\to q_0 and q_2\to q_1\to q_2. Drop them and the same steps produce \big((\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11})\big)^*, which misses 01, 0101, 010101, …
Dropping the old label. R(q_0\to q_2) becomes \mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00}, not \mathtt{00}: the direct edge stays.
Starring the wrong loop. In step 2 the loop of the state being removed (q_2) is starred; the loop at q_0 gets its star only when q_0 itself goes, in step 3.
“Simplifying” without a rule. Rewrite only with identities you can name (Lemmas 2.1–2.2). A longer correct expression earns full credit; a shorter wrong one does not.



(c) Sanity check
Three quick tests, each of which catches a different kind of slip.

The empty string. The expression is a star, so it matches \varepsilon; and \varepsilon\in L. ✓
Everything it matches is in L. The block 01 has difference 0. In the block (\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11}), the first piece contributes -1 or +2, both \equiv -1; each 10 contributes 0; the last piece contributes +1 or -2, both \equiv +1. So every block has difference \equiv 0, and so does every concatenation of blocks. ✓
Short strings of L are matched. Length 2: 01 (one block 01) and 10 = \mathtt{1}\cdot(\mathtt{10})^0\cdot\mathtt{0}. Length 3: only 000 = \mathtt{00}\cdot\mathtt{0} and 111 = \mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{11} are in L. Length 4: the strings of L are the six with two 0s and two 1s, and all six match: 0011 = \mathtt{00}\cdot\mathtt{11}, 0101 = \mathtt{01}\cdot\mathtt{01}, 0110 = \mathtt{01}\cdot\mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{0}, 1001 = \mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{01}, 1010 = \mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{1}\,\mathtt{0}, 1100 = \mathtt{1}\cdot\mathtt{10}\cdot\mathtt{0}. ✓

Test 3 is what catches the forgotten loops of the trap above: \big((\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11})\big)^* passes tests 1 and 2, but not 01.


                  
                  Why the answer looks like this 
                  
                

Each block is a walk that leaves q_0 and returns to it for the first time: either through q_1 (reading 01), or into q_2 (by 1, or by 00 via q_1), any number of round trips q_2\to q_1\to q_2 (each reading 10), and back to q_0 (by 0, or by 11 via q_1). A string is in L exactly when its walk ends in q_0, that is, when it splits into first returns — hence the outer star.


(d) A different order
Now eliminate q_0 first, then q_1, then q_2. q_0 is the only state joined to s and t, so removing it hands edges from s and to t to both remaining states, and every later step must carry them along.
Step 1 — eliminate q_0 (predecessors s, q_1, q_2; successors q_1, q_2, t; no loop):





























to q_1to q_2to tfrom s\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}\varepsilonfrom q_1\mathtt{10}\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11}\mathtt{1}from q_2\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00}\mathtt{01}\mathtt{0}
Step 2 — eliminate q_1 (loop 10): R(s\to q_2) = \mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11}), \ R(s\to t) = \varepsilon+\mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}, \ R(q_2\to q_2) = \mathtt{01}+(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11}), \ R(q_2\to t) = \mathtt{0}+(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}.
Step 3 — eliminate q_2:
\begin{aligned}
R(s\to t) = {}&\varepsilon+\mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}\\
&+\big(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11})\big)\,\big(\mathtt{01}+(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11})\big)^*\\
&\qquad\quad\big(\mathtt{0}+(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})(\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}\big).
\end{aligned}
This expression is exactly equivalent to the answer of (b) — every order is correct — but it has 28 symbol occurrences instead of 10. It spells out separately the walks that end in q_0 without ever visiting q_2 (\varepsilon + \mathtt{0}(\mathtt{10})^*\mathtt{1}), the walk up to the first visit to q_2, the round trips from q_2, and the walk after the last visit to q_2. Over all six orders, the expression has 10 symbols when q_0 goes last, 22 when it goes second, and 28 when it goes first; the order q_2, q_1, q_0 gives the mirror image \big(\mathtt{10}+(\mathtt{0}+\mathtt{11})(\mathtt{01})^*(\mathtt{1}+\mathtt{00})\big)^* (swap the roles of 0 and 1).


                  
                  Choosing an elimination order 
                  
                

Eliminate first the states with the fewest edges, and keep the states joined to s and t for last. No order is wrong, but sizes differ, and in the worst case they grow by about a factor of 4 per elimination (\Theta(4^n) in all).




                  
                  How this would be graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams ask for a DFA and a regular expression for the same language (no proof needed); state elimination is one reliable way to get the expression from your DFA when it does not come by inspection. The expression is graded 2 for syntax and 8 for correctness, with exam deductions doubled: 2 for one mistake (often a missing or extra \varepsilon), 4 for a few wrong strings, and all 8 if infinitely many strings are wrong — which is what a forgotten loop or a dropped term usually costs. Hence the sanity checks. Homework answers also need a one-sentence explanation of each piece, like the intuition box above.


Sources for this page
Original problem. The method is state elimination as in Erickson, Models of Computation, §4.8 (Lemma 4.3), in our own words; the DFA, both eliminations, the first-return reading and the comparison of orders are ours. Every expression automaton (as a language and edge by edge), both final expressions (exact equivalence with the DFA), all six orders, the forgotten-loop expression and the sample strings are checked by tools/checks/problems_2.py.

problems/subset-construction-by-hand.title: Worked problem — The subset construction by hand
problems/subset-construction-by-hand.content:
Problem · an NFA-to-DFA conversion by hand, the computation behind many Midterm 1 answers · uses §4.3, §4.5 · concepts: subset-construction, nfa, dfa-minimization


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

The NFA N has alphabet \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}, states s, p, q, t, start state s, accepting states \{t\}, and the transitions below (empty cells are \varnothing).



































\delta\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}\varepsilon→ s\{s\}\{p\}p\{q\}\{t\}q\{p\}t *\{t\}
(a) Describe L(N).
(b) Convert N to a DFA with the incremental subset construction. Show the full table: for each DFA state S, its \varepsilon-reach, whether it is accepting, and its transitions.
(c) Is the resulting DFA minimal? If not, find the number of states of a minimal DFA, and prove your answer.



NFA with states s, p, q, t; epsilon edges s to p and p to t; p to q on 0 and q to p on 101εε01sptqAn NFA for 0*(01)*1*. s reads the leading 0s, the cycle p → q → p reads one block 01, and t reads the trailing 1s. The two ε-transitions move from one phase to the next without reading anything. Missing transitions lead nowhere (the thread dies).
(a) The language: three phases
Idea. The \varepsilon-transitions only go forward, s\to p\to t, so every run of N has three phases and never returns to an earlier one: in s it reads 0s; around the cycle p\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}q\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}p it reads blocks 01; in t it reads 1s.


                  
                  Answer (a) 
                  
                

L(N) = \mathtt{0}^*(\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{1}^* = \{\mathtt{0}^i(\mathtt{01})^j\mathtt{1}^k \mid i, j, k\ge0\}. For example 0011 = \mathtt{0}\cdot\mathtt{01}\cdot\mathtt{1}, \varepsilon, 0 and 1 are in L(N); 010 and 10 are not.


(b) The incremental subset construction
The recipe, as in the book. A DFA state is a set S of NFA states, and everything is computed from its \varepsilon-reach, the set of states reachable from S by \varepsilon-transitions alone:

the start state is \{s\} itself (its \varepsilon-reach goes in its own column);
S is accepting iff \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S) contains an accepting state of N;
\delta'(S,a) = \bigcup_{r\,\in\,\varepsilon\text{-reach}(S)}\delta(r,a): slide along \varepsilon-moves first, then read a.

Start a table with the row \{s\}. Whenever a set appears in a transition column that has no row yet, give it the next row. Stop when every set in the transition columns has a row. Here the \varepsilon-reaches of single states are \varepsilon\text{-reach}(s) = \{s,p,t\}, \varepsilon\text{-reach}(p) = \{p,t\}, \varepsilon\text{-reach}(q) = \{q\} and \varepsilon\text{-reach}(t) = \{t\}.
Row 1, in full. \varepsilon\text{-reach}(\{s\}) = \{s,p,t\}, which contains t, so \{s\} is accepting. Then
\begin{aligned}
\delta'(\{s\},\mathtt{0}) &= \delta(s,\mathtt{0})\cup\delta(p,\mathtt{0})\cup\delta(t,\mathtt{0}) = \{s\}\cup\{q\}\cup\varnothing = \{s,q\},\\
\delta'(\{s\},\mathtt{1}) &= \delta(s,\mathtt{1})\cup\delta(p,\mathtt{1})\cup\delta(t,\mathtt{1}) = \varnothing\cup\varnothing\cup\{t\} = \{t\}.
\end{aligned}
Both sets are new, so they become rows 2 and 3, in that order. The other rows are computed the same way:


                  
                  Answer (b) 
                  
                






































































rowS\varepsilon\text{-reach}(S)accepting?\delta'(S,\mathtt{0})\delta'(S,\mathtt{1})1→ \{s\}\{s,p,t\}yes\{s,q\}\{t\}2\{s,q\}\{s,p,q,t\}yes\{s,q\}\{p,t\}3\{t\}\{t\}yes\varnothing\{t\}4\{p,t\}\{p,t\}yes\{q\}\{t\}5\varnothing\varnothingno\varnothing\varnothing6\{q\}\{q\}no\varnothing\{p\}7\{p\}\{p,t\}yes\{q\}\{t\}
The DFA has these 7 states (of the 2^4 = 16 subsets of \{s,p,q,t\}, only these are reachable), start state \{s\}, the five accepting states marked “yes”, and the transitions in the last two columns. \varnothing is a genuine state — the dump state, reached when no thread of N survives.



seven-state DFA whose states are sets of NFA states0101010110010,1{s}{s,q}{p,t}{p}{q}{t}∅The DFA found by the subset construction. Seven of the 16 subsets are reachable; five are accepting because their ε-reach contains t. ∅ is the dump state. The two highlighted states {p,t} and {p} have the same ε-reach {p,t}, hence identical rows: they are equivalent, and merging them gives the 6-state minimal DFA.
Check. On 0011: \{s\}\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}\{s,q\}\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}\{s,q\}\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}\{p,t\}\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}\{t\}, accept. On 010: \{s\}\to\{s,q\}\to\{p,t\}\to\{q\}, reject — halfway through a block. On 10: \{s\}\to\{t\}\to\varnothing, reject — after a trailing 1, a 0 kills every thread.


                  
                  Where subset constructions go wrong 
                  
                


Accepting S only when S itself contains an accepting state. Acceptance looks at \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S). Without it, rows 1, 2 and 7 become non-accepting, and the DFA rejects \varepsilon, 0, 00 and 0101 — all in L(N).
Reading before sliding. \delta'(\{s\},\mathtt{1}) is not \delta(s,\mathtt{1}) = \varnothing: the NFA can slide s\to p\to t by \varepsilon-moves and then read the 1. Forgetting the \varepsilon-reach in the transitions sends 1 and 01 to \varnothing.
Dropping the \varnothing row. The empty set is reachable (on 10), and a DFA needs a transition from every state on every symbol. Keep the row, or say explicitly that missing transitions go to a dump state.
Tabulating all 16 subsets. Only reachable sets get rows; the incremental construction never creates the other nine. (A table of all 16 still describes a correct DFA, with nine unreachable states, but it is not what was asked and it wastes exam time.)



A second convention. Some textbooks name each DFA state by its \varepsilon-reach instead: the start state is \varepsilon\text{-reach}(\{s\}) = \{s,p,t\} and \delta'(S,a) = \varepsilon\text{-reach}\big(\bigcup_{r\in S}\delta(r,a)\big). That also gives a correct DFA — here a 6-state one, because rows 4 and 7 have the same \varepsilon-reach and become a single state. On this site, as in the book, the table keeps S and its \varepsilon-reach in separate columns.
(c) Not minimal: two twin rows
Idea. Look for rows that agree in everything. Rows 4 and 7, \{p,t\} and \{p\}, are both accepting, both go to \{q\} on 0, and both go to \{t\} on 1. States with identical rows are equivalent: both accept or both reject the empty suffix, and after any first symbol the two are in the same state. They agree because they have the same \varepsilon-reach \{p,t\}, and the construction computes everything from the \varepsilon-reach. In terms of the language: 01 reaches \{p,t\} and 0101 reaches \{p\}, and both mean “a block 01 has just been completed; more blocks or the trailing 1s may follow”.
Merging the twins leaves 6 states. To show that no DFA for L(N) has fewer, take one string reaching each of them:
F = \{\varepsilon,\ \mathtt{0},\ \mathtt{1},\ \mathtt{01},\ \mathtt{10},\ \mathtt{010}\},\quad\text{which reach } \{s\},\ \{s,q\},\ \{t\},\ \{p,t\},\ \varnothing,\ \{q\}.
For each pair, the table gives a distinguishing suffix z — exactly one of xz and yz is in L(N) (row x, column y):





















































\mathtt{0}\mathtt{1}\mathtt{01}\mathtt{10}\mathtt{010}\varepsilon10100\varepsilon\varepsilon\mathtt{0}00\varepsilon\varepsilon\mathtt{1}01\varepsilon\varepsilon\mathtt{01}\varepsilon\varepsilon\mathtt{10}1
For instance, 101 separates \varepsilon from 0: 0101 \in L(N) but 101 \notin L(N). And 1 separates the dump state from \{q\}: 0101 \in L(N) but 101 \notin L(N). Every \varepsilon entry pairs a string of L(N) with one outside it.


                  
                  Answer (c) 
                  
                

Not minimal: \{p\} and \{p,t\} are equivalent. Merging them gives a 6-state DFA, and the 6-element fooling set F shows that 6 is the minimum.




                  
                  How this is graded 
                  
                

Midterm-1-style exams have no separate subset-construction problem; the construction is a tool — for turning an NFA you designed into the DFA a problem asks for (an NFA where a DFA was asked earns half credit), and for true/false items about state counts. A DFA built this way is graded like any DFA: a complete description (start state, accepting states, every transition, including those into \varnothing), correctness, and mnemonic names. A set like \{s,q\} is a meaningful name only if you have said what each NFA state means — “still among the leading 0s, or halfway through a block”. See how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
An original example. The incremental subset construction and its table — sets S, acceptance and transitions through \varepsilon\text{-reach}(S) — follow Erickson, Models of Computation, §4.5, described in our own words. Checked by tools/checks/problems_1.py: the NFA’s language against a brute-force predicate on all strings of length at most 12 and exactly against \mathtt{0}^*(\mathtt{01})^*\mathtt{1}^*; the \varepsilon-reach of each state; the 7-row table, row by row and in discovery order, as computed by the library’s implementation of the book’s construction; the runs; the minimal DFA (only \{p\} and \{p,t\} merge); every entry of the suffix table (each a shortest one); the two wrong constructions in the trap; and the 6-state result of the other convention.

problems/two-language-transformations.title: Worked problem — Two language transformations
problems/two-language-transformations.content:
Problem · style of the Midterm 1 language-transformation problem · uses §4.9, §4.3 · concepts: language-transformations, nfa


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let L be an arbitrary regular language over \Sigma = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}. Prove that the following languages are regular.
(a) \textsf{Insert1}(L) := \{x\mathtt{1}y \mid x, y\in\Sigma^* \text{ and } xy\in L\} — the strings obtained from a string of L by inserting one 1, anywhere.
(b) \textsf{Delete1}(L) := \{xy \mid x, y\in\Sigma^* \text{ and } x\mathtt{1}y\in L\} — the strings obtained from a string of L by deleting one of its 1s.
In each part, give a formal description of an NFA (\varepsilon-transitions allowed) in terms of an arbitrary DFA M = (\Sigma, Q, s, A, \delta) that accepts L, and explain in English what its states mean.


Which kind of transformation? In both parts the input w is the result of an edit applied to some string of L, and the machine must check that some string of L produces w. That is the “transforms of strings in L” kind of transformation: an NFA reads w, guesses where the edit happened, and simulates M on the unedited string. Both NFAs need one extra bit of memory — has the edit been handled yet? — so their states are pairs (q, f) with q\in Q and f\in\{0, 1\}: two copies of M, a “before” copy and an “after” copy, and the only way down is the guess.

two NFAs, each two copies of a two-state parity DFA, joined by highlighted 1-edges (left) and epsilon-edges (right)Insert1: skip one input 1Delete1: feed M one extra 1110011001100110011εεE,0O,0E,1O,1E,0O,0E,1O,1Two copies of M, one guess. Here M accepts the strings with an odd number of 1s (E/O: even/odd so far). Top row: phase 0, the extra 1 has not been handled yet; bottom row: phase 1, it has. Left: reading a 1 may drop to phase 1 without moving M — that 1 is the inserted one. Right: an ε-move drops to phase 1 while M reads a 1 that is not in the input (so E,0 drops to O,1). Only (O, 1) accepts. The left machine accepts an even, positive number of 1s; the right one an even number of 1s.
(a) Inserting a 1
Idea. M' reads w = x\mathtt{1}y and runs M on xy: it must skip exactly one input 1 without showing it to M. Before the skip (f = 0) every symbol goes to M. On reading a 1, M' may guess “this is the inserted 1”: it leaves M‘s state alone and sets f = 1. After that every symbol goes to M again.


                  
                  Answer (a) 
                  
                

M' = (\Sigma, Q', s', A', \delta'), an NFA without \varepsilon-transitions:
Q' = Q\times\{0,1\},\qquad s' = (s,0),\qquad A' = \{(q,1) \mid q\in A\},
\begin{aligned}
\delta'\big((q,0),\mathtt{0}\big) &= \big\{(\delta(q,\mathtt{0}),0)\big\}\\
\delta'\big((q,0),\mathtt{1}\big) &= \big\{(\delta(q,\mathtt{1}),0),\ (q,1)\big\}\\
\delta'\big((q,1),a\big) &= \big\{(\delta(q,a),1)\big\}\qquad\text{for each } a\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}.
\end{aligned}
In English. (q,0): the inserted 1 has not been read yet, and M, run on the input read so far, is in state q. (q,1): the inserted 1 has been read and skipped, and M, run on the input read so far without that 1, is in state q. The transition (q,0)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(q,1) is the guess. M' accepts if the skip has happened (f = 1) and M accepts what is left (q\in A).


Why it works. A short induction on the input, of the kind behind Lemma 3.1, shows: M' can be in (q,0) after reading w iff q = \delta^*(s,w), and it can be in (q,1) iff w = x\mathtt{1}y for some strings x, y with q = \delta^*(s, xy). So M' accepts w iff some way of writing w = x\mathtt{1}y has xy\in L — which is the definition of \textsf{Insert1}(L).
Example. In the figure (left), M accepts the strings with an odd number of 1s. On input 0110, M' can go (\textsf{E},0)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}(\textsf{E},0)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(\textsf{O},0)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(\textsf{O},1)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}(\textsf{O},1), skipping the second 1, and accept: 0110 is 01·1·0, and 010 has one 1. In general this M' accepts exactly the strings with an even, positive number of 1s.


                  
                  Where (a) loses points 
                  
                


Accepting before the insertion. With A' = A\times\{0,1\} the machine also accepts the strings of L themselves, with nothing inserted. For L = \{\varepsilon\} it accepts \varepsilon, but \textsf{Insert1}(\{\varepsilon\}) = \{\mathtt{1}\}.
Guessing on the wrong symbol. An extra (q,0)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{0}}(q,1) inserts an arbitrary symbol: for L = \{\varepsilon\} it accepts 0.
Showing the inserted 1 to M. (q,0)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(\delta(q,\mathtt{1}),1) instead of (q,1) just reads a 1 of a string of L: for L = \{\varepsilon\} the machine accepts nothing at all, not even 1.
No flag. One copy of M with an extra loop q\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}q at every state skips any number of 1s, including none: for L = \{\varepsilon\} it accepts all of \mathtt{1}^*.



(b) Deleting a 1
Idea. Now M'' reads w = xy and runs M on x\mathtt{1}y: somewhere — between two input symbols, or before the first, or after the last — it must feed M one 1 that is not in the input. That is what an \varepsilon-transition is for: it changes M‘s state as if a 1 had been read, without consuming any input, and sets f = 1 so that it happens exactly once.


                  
                  Answer (b) 
                  
                

M'' = (\Sigma, Q'', s'', A'', \delta''), an NFA with \varepsilon-transitions: Q'' = Q\times\{0,1\}, s'' = (s,0), A'' = \{(q,1) \mid q\in A\}, and for every q\in Q and a\in\{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}
\begin{aligned}
\delta''\big((q,0),a\big) &= \big\{(\delta(q,a),0)\big\}, & \delta''\big((q,0),\varepsilon\big) &= \big\{(\delta(q,\mathtt{1}),1)\big\},\\
\delta''\big((q,1),a\big) &= \big\{(\delta(q,a),1)\big\}, & \delta''\big((q,1),\varepsilon\big) &= \varnothing.
\end{aligned}
In English. (q,0): the deleted 1 has not been put back yet, and M, run on the input read so far, is in state q. (q,1): it has been put back, and M, run on the input read so far with that 1 inserted where the \varepsilon-move happened, is in state q. The \varepsilon-move (q,0)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}(\delta(q,\mathtt{1}),1) is the guess “the deleted 1 was here”. M'' accepts if the 1 has been put back and M accepts.


Why it works. The same kind of induction shows that M'' can be in (q,1) after reading w iff w = xy for some strings x, y with q = \delta^*(s, x\mathtt{1}y). An \varepsilon-move may be taken at any time, including before the first symbol (x = \varepsilon) and after the last one (y = \varepsilon), so every position of the deleted 1 is covered.
Example. In the figure (right), the \varepsilon-move from (\textsf{E},0) goes to (\textsf{O},1), not to (\textsf{E},1): M sees the extra 1. On input \varepsilon, M'' takes that \varepsilon-move and accepts, correctly — deleting the only 1 of 1 \in L gives \varepsilon. In general this M'' accepts exactly the strings with an even number of 1s.


                  
                  Where (b) loses points 
                  
                


Reading the 1 instead of inventing it. (q,0)\xrightarrow{\mathtt{1}}(\delta(q,\mathtt{1}),1) consumes an input 1, so nothing is deleted: the machine accepts the strings of L that contain a 1. For L = \mathtt{1}^* it rejects \varepsilon, but \varepsilon\in\textsf{Delete1}(\mathtt{1}^*).
Forgetting to feed the 1 to M. (q,0)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}(q,1) only flips the flag, and the machine accepts L itself. For L = \{\varepsilon\} it accepts \varepsilon, but \textsf{Delete1}(\{\varepsilon\}) = \varnothing: the empty string has no 1 to delete.
No flag. One copy of M with \varepsilon-moves q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\delta(q,\mathtt{1}) deletes any number of 1s, including none. For L = \{\mathtt{11}\} it accepts \varepsilon, 1 and 11, but \textsf{Delete1}(\{\mathtt{11}\}) = \{\mathtt{1}\}.
Unstated \varepsilon-transitions. The description must list exactly which \varepsilon-transitions exist; “\varepsilon-moves where needed” describes no machine.



Edge cases
Run both constructions on the languages the graders try first. Each line below is what the NFAs above actually accept:









































L\textsf{Insert1}(L)\textsf{Delete1}(L)why\varnothing\varnothing\varnothingA = \varnothing, so no state of either NFA accepts\{\varepsilon\}\{\mathtt{1}\}\varnothing\varepsilon has no 1 to delete\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{1}^*\mathtt{1}^*deleting the only 1 of 1 gives \varepsilon\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{0}^*\mathtt{1}\mathtt{0}^*\varnothingno string of \mathtt{0}^* contains a 1\Sigma^*\Sigma^*\mathtt{1}\Sigma^*\Sigma^*every xy comes from x\mathtt{1}y\in\Sigma^*
The two operations are not inverses: \textsf{Delete1}(\textsf{Insert1}(L)) always contains L (delete the 1 you inserted), but it can be larger — \textsf{Delete1}(\textsf{Insert1}(\{\mathtt{01}\})) = \textsf{Delete1}(\{\mathtt{101},\mathtt{011}\}) = \{\mathtt{01},\mathtt{10}\}.


                  
                  How a transformation problem is graded 
                  
                

The standard rubric, out of 10 for a construction: 2 for a formal, complete description of M' built from an arbitrary DFA M — say whether it is a DFA or an NFA, and list its \varepsilon-transitions; 2 for an English explanation of the states and of the accepting states; 6 for correctness: 1 for the states, 1 for the start state, 1 for the accepting states, 3 for the transitions. Graders test the edge cases \varnothing, \{\varepsilon\}, \mathtt{1}^* and \Sigma^*, so run your construction on them before handing it in, as in the table above. A construction for one particular DFA, like the parity example above, proves nothing about other regular languages. See how exams are graded.


Sources for this page
An original problem in the style of the Midterm 1 transformation problem; inserting and deleting one symbol are classic textbook-style transformations, worked here in our own words. The method — guess, simulate M on the unedited string, use \varepsilon-transitions for symbols that are not in the input — follows Erickson, Models of Computation, §4.9. Checked by tools/checks/problems_1.py: both constructions implemented as functions of an arbitrary DFA and compared with the definitions of \textsf{Insert1} and \textsf{Delete1} on 300 random DFAs with 2–4 states (exactly, on every string of length at most 8); the edge-case table and the parity example by exact DFA equivalence; the run on 0110; and every wrong construction in the traps on its counterexample.

problems/undecidability-by-reduction-and.title: Worked problem — Undecidability by reduction and by Rice's theorem
problems/undecidability-by-reduction-and.content:
Problem · style of an undecidability problem (Chapter 7 material, on the final exam) · uses §7.9, §7.11, §7.12 · concepts: undecidability-reductions, rices-theorem, acceptable-and-decidable


                  
                  Problem 
                  
                

Let \textsf{AtLeastTwo} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts at least two different strings}\}, that is, the encodings of Turing machines M with \lvert\textsf{Accept}(M)\rvert\ge2.
(a) Prove that \textsf{AtLeastTwo} is undecidable by a reduction from \textsf{Accept} = \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w\}.
(b) Prove it again with Rice’s theorem.
(c) Show that \textsf{Quick374} := \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on input } \varepsilon \text{ within 374 steps}\} is decidable, and explain why Rice’s theorem does not apply to it.
(d) Is \textsf{AtLeastTwo} acceptable? Is its complement?


Machines have input alphabet \Sigma = \{\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\}, and “halts” means “reaches \textit{accept} or \textit{reject}”.
(a) A reduction from Accept
Idea. Given \langle M, w\rangle, build a machine M' whose language is huge — all of \Sigma^*, so certainly two strings — if M accepts w, and empty otherwise. M' ignores its own input: the only thing that decides what it does is whether M accepts w. This is the standard shape of a reduction (§7.9).


                  
                  Proof of (a) — model answer 
                  
                

Suppose for the sake of argument that some Turing machine \textsf{DecideAtLeastTwo} decides \textsf{AtLeastTwo}.
Consider the following machine \textsf{DecideAccept}. Given \langle M, w\rangle, it writes the encoding \langle M'\rangle of the machine
M'(x)\colon\ \text{erase } x;\ \text{write } w;\ \text{run } M \text{ on } w;\ \text{if } M \text{ accepts, accept; if } M \text{ rejects, reject},
then runs \textsf{DecideAtLeastTwo} on \langle M'\rangle and returns its answer.
\Rightarrow Suppose M accepts w. Whatever the input x is, M' erases it and then does exactly what M does on w, so M' accepts every input: \textsf{Accept}(M') = \Sigma^*, which contains the two different strings 0 and 1. So \langle M'\rangle\in\textsf{AtLeastTwo}, \textsf{DecideAtLeastTwo} accepts \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} accepts \langle M, w\rangle.
\Leftarrow Suppose M does not accept w: it rejects w or diverges on w. In the first case M' rejects every input; in the second, M' diverges on every input. Either way \textsf{Accept}(M') = \varnothing, which has fewer than two strings. So \langle M'\rangle\notin\textsf{AtLeastTwo}, \textsf{DecideAtLeastTwo} rejects \langle M'\rangle, and \textsf{DecideAccept} rejects \langle M, w\rangle.
In both cases \textsf{DecideAccept} answers correctly, and it always halts: writing \langle M'\rangle is a finite edit of \langle M\rangle and w, and \textsf{DecideAtLeastTwo} always halts. So \textsf{DecideAccept} decides \textsf{Accept}, which is impossible, because \textsf{Accept} is undecidable. Therefore \textsf{DecideAtLeastTwo} does not exist: \textsf{AtLeastTwo} is undecidable. \blacksquare


Four machines, four names: the hypothetical decider \textsf{DecideAtLeastTwo}; the decider we build from it, \textsf{DecideAccept}; its input machine M; and M', whose encoding \textsf{DecideAccept} writes down but never runs.


                  
                  Where reductions go wrong 
                  
                


An M' that does not land in the property. ”M'(x): run M on x” gives \textsf{Accept}(M') = \textsf{Accept}(M), which has nothing to do with w. ”M'(x): if x = \varepsilon, run M on w; otherwise reject” gives \textsf{Accept}(M')\subseteq\{\varepsilon\} — never two strings — so the \Rightarrow direction fails. In the yes-case the language must have the property; \Sigma^* has two strings to spare.
Running M' (or M). \textsf{DecideAccept} only writes \langle M'\rangle. If it ran M on w itself, it could run forever, and a decider must halt.
Forgetting divergence. “Does not accept” includes running forever. Then M' runs forever on every input, so \textsf{Accept}(M') = \varnothing — do not write ”M' rejects”.
The wrong direction. Deciding \textsf{AtLeastTwo} with the help of a decider for \textsf{Accept} proves nothing.



(b) The same result by Rice’s theorem


                  
                  Proof of (b) — model answer 
                  
                

Let \mathcal{L} := \{L\subseteq\Sigma^* \mid \lvert L\rvert\ge2\}, the set of languages with at least two strings. Then \textsf{AtLeastTwo} = \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) = \{\langle M\rangle \mid \textsf{Accept}(M)\in\mathcal{L}\}: whether \langle M\rangle belongs depends only on the language \textsf{Accept}(M).

Y := M_{\textsf{Accept}}, with \delta(\textit{start}, a) = (\textit{accept}, a, +1) for every a\in\Gamma. It accepts every input, so \textsf{Accept}(Y) = \Sigma^*\in\mathcal{L}.
N := M_{\textsf{Reject}}, with \delta(\textit{start}, a) = (\textit{reject}, a, +1) for every a\in\Gamma. It accepts nothing, so \textsf{Accept}(N) = \varnothing\notin\mathcal{L}.

By Rice’s theorem, \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) = \textsf{AtLeastTwo} is undecidable. \blacksquare


The property speaks about the strings M accepts, so the \textsf{AcceptIn} form of the theorem is the right one. For ”M rejects at least two strings” you would use the rejection version, \textsf{RejectIn}(\mathcal{L}), and describe the witnesses by their \textsf{Reject} languages: then M_{\textsf{Reject}} (\textsf{Reject} = \Sigma^*) is the Y and M_{\textsf{Accept}} (\textsf{Reject} = \varnothing) the N. Part (a) is the proof of Rice’s theorem specialized to this property, with Y = M_{\textsf{Accept}} — except that it reduces from \textsf{Accept}, where the book’s proof uses \textsf{Halt}.


                  
                  Rice traps 
                  
                


Vague witnesses. “A machine that accepts two strings” is not a witness; give the machine (its transitions, or an unmistakable description) and its language.
Swapped witnesses. Y’s language must have the property (\ge2 strings) and N‘s must not. Both are judged by \textsf{Accept}(\cdot) alone — not by how fast or whether the machines halt.
Applying Rice to behavior — the next part.



(c) A look-alike that is decidable


                  
                  Proof of (c) 
                  
                

A decider. Given \langle M\rangle, simulate M on the empty input for at most 374 steps, using the universal machine with a step counter. If M accepts or rejects within those steps, accept; if it is still running after 374 steps, reject. Only 374 steps of M are ever simulated, so this machine halts on every input, and it accepts exactly the encodings in \textsf{Quick374}. (A crash within the 374 steps is detected the same way; count it as halting or not, as your definition of “halts” says.)
Why Rice’s theorem does not apply. \textsf{Quick374} is not \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}) for any set of languages \mathcal{L}, because membership does not depend on the language alone. M_{\textsf{Accept}} halts on \varepsilon after one step, so \langle M_{\textsf{Accept}}\rangle\in\textsf{Quick374}. The machine M_{\textsf{slow}} that walks right for 400 steps and then accepts has the same language, \Sigma^*, but halts on \varepsilon only after 400 steps, so \langle M_{\textsf{slow}}\rangle\notin\textsf{Quick374}. Two machines with the same language, one in and one out: this is a property of machines, not of languages.


Rice’s theorem is silent about such behavioral properties: some are decidable, like this one and the book’s \textsf{ThisIsSparta}, and some are not (§7.13). What makes this one decidable is the step bound: the question is about a finite piece of one computation.
An even closer look-alike. ”M accepts at least two different strings, each within 374 steps” is decidable too. In 374 steps the head reads only cells 0,\dots,373, so whether M accepts x within 374 steps depends only on the first 374 symbols of x. Simulate M for 374 steps on every string of length at most 374. If some string of length exactly 374 is accepted within those steps, so are all of its infinitely many extensions: answer yes. Otherwise no longer string is accepted within 374 steps either, and you just count. That is 2^{375}-1 simulations — absurd, but finite, and decidability asks for nothing more. The step bound, not the “two strings”, is what changes the answer.
(d) Acceptable, but its complement is not


                  
                  Answer (d) 
                  
                

\textsf{AtLeastTwo} is acceptable: dovetail — for t = 1, 2, 3, \dots, run M for t steps on each of the first t strings in shortlex order, and accept as soon as two different strings have been accepted. Its complement is not acceptable: \textsf{AtLeastTwo} is acceptable but undecidable, so by Lemma 5 its complement cannot be acceptable as well.


Why dovetail? Running M on \varepsilon, 0, 1, 00, … one after the other fails when M runs forever on one of them: a machine that diverges on \varepsilon but accepts every other string is in \textsf{AtLeastTwo}, yet the one-at-a-time search never gets past \varepsilon. Dovetailing gives every string an ever-growing time budget, so if M accepts x\ne y, some round runs both long enough. (The same idea simulates nondeterminism in §9.4.) If M accepts at most one string, the acceptor runs forever — allowed for an acceptor.
The same answer from §7.12. “At least two strings” is monotone (a superset still has two strings), compact (any two of the strings form a finite subset with the property) and finitely acceptable (count the strings in a finite list), as the Rice–McNaughton–Myhill–Shapiro theorem requires of an acceptable \textsf{AcceptIn}(\mathcal{L}). The complementary property “at most one string” is not monotone — \varnothing has it, \Sigma^*\supseteq\varnothing does not — so Lemma 17 gives unacceptability again. (The complement also contains every string that encodes no machine; those form a decidable set and change nothing.)


                  
                  How these proofs are graded 
                  
                

Chapter 7 is tested on the final exam only. A reduction is graded out of 10: 4 for the reduction itself — a correct description of the new decider and of M', in the right direction — 3 for the yes-direction and 3 for the no-direction, which must cover both rejecting and diverging. A proof by Rice’s theorem: 4 for a machine whose language has the property, 4 for one whose language does not, and 2 for the details, including stating the property as a set of languages and using the right variant of the theorem.
